# Technical Specification

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 Executive Summary

### 1.1.1 Project Overview

`July2026_hello_world_repo` is a **minimal, single-file Node.js HTTP server** — a canonical "Hello World" reference implementation. The repository contains exactly **three tracked files**, totalling 382 bytes, and no source subdirectories:

| File | Size | Role |
|------|------|------|
| `server.js` | 342 bytes / 14 lines | The entire application: an HTTP listener built on the Node.js core `http` module |
| `README.md` | 27 bytes / 1 line | A name-only marker containing solely the heading `# July2026_hello_world_repo` |
| `test.js` | 13 bytes / 2 lines | **Not part of the application.** A placeholder containing the two bare words `asdsa` and `asdasd`; mode `100644`, no test, no assertion, no framework |

The complete system behavior is defined by `server.js`: it requires Node's built-in `http` module (line 1), declares the constants `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` (line 3) and `port = 3000` (line 4), creates a server whose inline handler unconditionally sets HTTP status `200` and `Content-Type: text/plain` before ending the response with the fixed body `Hello, World!\n` (lines 6–10), then binds the listener and logs a readiness message to stdout (lines 12–14).

```javascript
// server.js lines 7-9 — the entire request-handling logic
res.statusCode = 200;
res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
```

`server.js` is the **whole of the running system**, re-verified by execution: the process answers every request with `200` / `Content-Type: text/plain` / `Content-Length: 14` and the body `Hello, World!\n`. There is no routing layer, no configuration layer, no persistence, no authentication, no build step, and no third-party dependency of any kind.

`test.js` is tracked but inert and contributes nothing to that behavior. It is two bare identifier expression statements, so it is syntactically valid (`node --check test.js` exits 0) yet fails the moment it is evaluated: `node test.js` throws `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and exits 1. It exports nothing, no file requires it, and no documented procedure executes it — only `node server.js` is ever run. Its one observable side effect on tooling is recorded in 3.6 and 6.6: because Node's built-in test runner discovers `**/test.?(c|m)js` by default, `node --test` at the repository root now loads this file and fails.

### 1.1.2 Core Problem Addressed

The repository contains **no problem statement, product brief, or business-requirement documentation**. `README.md` holds only the repository name, and no `docs/`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or issue-tracking artifacts exist in the tree. Consequently, this specification does **not** attribute a commercial or business problem to the project; doing so would be unsupported by evidence.

What the artifact demonstrably solves is a narrow **engineering** problem, inferred directly from its observed behavior:

| Problem Addressed | How `server.js` Addresses It |
|-------------------|------------------------------|
| Establishing the smallest runnable HTTP service on a host | A 14-line module that binds a listener and answers every request, executed with a single `node server.js` invocation |
| Removing dependency, build, and configuration friction | The only import is Node's core `http` module; there is no manifest, lockfile, transpiler, or environment file to resolve |
| Providing a deterministic, verifiable HTTP endpoint | Every request — regardless of method, path, query, or body — yields an identical `200` / `text/plain` / 14-byte response, making the endpoint a stable target for connectivity checks |
| Validating that a Node.js runtime is correctly installed and can bind a socket | Successful startup emits `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, an unambiguous readiness signal on stdout |

### 1.1.3 Key Stakeholders and Users

The repository defines **no stakeholder register, ownership file, or user documentation**: there is no `CODEOWNERS`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md`, or `LICENSE`. The only stakeholder evidence available is version-control provenance and the technical shape of the interface itself.

| Stakeholder / User | Evidence Basis | Relationship to the System |
|--------------------|----------------|----------------------------|
| Sole contributor of record — `lakshya-blitzy <lakshya@blitzy.com>` | All three commits in the repository history (`241598b` "Initial commit" adding `README.md` and `06492d7` "Add files via upload" adding `server.js`, both dated 2026-07-29; `43ed37c` "Create test.js" adding `test.js`, dated 2026-07-30) | Author and only committer; no other identity appears in the history |
| Developer / operator on the host machine | `server.js` is a side-effect-only module with no exports; it can only be used by executing it directly | Starts the process, observes the stdout readiness log, and terminates it |
| Local HTTP client (browser, `curl`, health-check probe) | The `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` bind restricts reachability to the loopback interface | The single consumer role — issues a request and receives the fixed plain-text response |

No end-user roles, permission tiers, tenant model, or administrative persona exist in the code, because no request attribute is ever inspected and no user concept is modeled.

### 1.1.4 Value Proposition

The value of this repository lies in what it deliberately omits. Each of the following properties was verified by inspecting the tree and by executing the server and probing it over the loopback interface:

| Property | Verified Basis |
|----------|----------------|
| Zero third-party dependencies | `require('http')` (line 1) is the only import in the tree; no `package.json`, lockfile, or `node_modules/` exists anywhere in the repository |
| Zero build and zero configuration | No `tsconfig.json`, bundler config, `Makefile`, `.env`, or `config/`; the source file is executed exactly as committed |
| Immediate, single-command startup | `server.listen(...)` executes at module load (line 12); no bootstrap sequence, dependency injection, or migration step precedes it |
| Fully deterministic, stateless output | Probes with `GET /`, `POST /any/deep/path?q=1` (with a request body), and `DELETE /x` each returned an identical `200` response with `Content-Type: text/plain` and a 14-byte body |
| Loopback-only exposure by default | A probe to the host's non-loopback address on port 3000 was refused, confirming the `127.0.0.1` bind does not expose the service on external interfaces |
| Trivially auditable surface area | The complete implementation is 14 lines in one file, reviewable in full in a single pass; the other two tracked files add 40 bytes of non-executable text |

Correspondingly, the repository provides **no** measurable business impact, revenue linkage, adoption target, cost-savings model, or service-level commitment — no such artifact exists in the tree, and none is asserted here. Its practical worth is as a **baseline**: a known-good, dependency-free HTTP endpoint suitable as a runtime smoke test, a starting scaffold for further development, or a reference for the minimum viable shape of a Node.js HTTP service.

### 1.1.5 Documentation Basis and Confidence

Every claim in this Introduction is derived from one of three verified evidence sources, and the reader should interpret the section accordingly:

- **Direct file inspection** — the full contents of `server.js`, `README.md`, and `test.js`, which together constitute 100% of the non-VCS files in the repository (382 bytes).
- **Structured absence audit** — more than sixty conventional project paths (manifests, lockfiles, CI/CD definitions, container and IaC descriptors, test and coverage configuration, linters, environment files, and governance documents) were individually tested for existence; **none** were present. Statements of the form "the repository defines no X" rest on this audit rather than on inference.
- **Runtime observation** — the server was executed and probed across multiple HTTP methods and paths, including a reachability test from a non-loopback address, to confirm that observed behavior matches the source; `test.js` was likewise executed and observed to fail (`ReferenceError`, exit 1).

Because the repository is this small, coverage is complete: there are no unexplored modules, no conditional code paths, and no hidden configuration that could alter the described behavior. The three-file inventory and the three-commit history (HEAD `43ed37c`) are recorded in 1.4.

## 1.2 System Overview

### 1.2.1 Project Context

#### 1.2.1.1 Business Context and Positioning

The repository carries **no business, market, or product documentation**. `README.md` contains a single line — the heading `# July2026_hello_world_repo` — and there is no `docs/` directory, `CHANGELOG.md`, roadmap, license, or governance file anywhere in the tree. No commercial positioning can therefore be asserted from the repository itself.

The positioning that *can* be established rests on three verifiable signals:

| Signal | Observed Evidence | Interpretation |
|--------|-------------------|----------------|
| Repository naming | The directory name and the sole README line both read `July2026_hello_world_repo` | Self-identifies as a "Hello World" artifact rather than a named product or service |
| Implementation shape | 14 lines in one file, zero third-party dependencies, a single fixed response | An educational, reference, or baseline artifact — not a feature-bearing application |
| Alignment with canonical Node.js guidance | The implementation is functionally equivalent to the "Create an HTTP Server" example published on nodejs.org (create server, respond `200` with `text/plain` and a Hello World body, listen on port `3000` at `127.0.0.1`), differing chiefly in module system — this repository uses CommonJS `require('http')` where the published sample uses ESM `import` | Represents the community-standard minimum viable Node.js HTTP service |

Version-control provenance is consistent with this reading. The history contains exactly **three commits**, all by the same single author of record (`lakshya-blitzy <lakshya@blitzy.com>`), spanning two consecutive days: `241598b` "Initial commit" introducing `README.md` and `06492d7` "Add files via upload" introducing `server.js`, made eleven seconds apart on 2026-07-29, followed on 2026-07-30 by `43ed37c` "Create test.js", which adds a 13-byte placeholder file that is not part of the application and changes no capability (1.1.1). All three commits record `GitHub <noreply@github.com>` as committer and carry a `gpgsig` header applied server-side by the GitHub web flow, and there are **zero tags**. The working tree is clean, and the remote `origin` points at a GitHub repository (`lakshya-blitzy/July2026_hello_world_repo`) whose refs have since diverged: `main` remains at `06492d7` (two files) while `2907_01`, the branch under documentation, is one commit ahead at `43ed37c` (three files). There is still no branching strategy, release tag, or iterative feature-development history to document.

#### 1.2.1.2 Current Implementation Limitations

This project does not replace or upgrade a predecessor system — no migration script, legacy adapter, compatibility shim, or deprecation note exists in the tree. The limitations below are therefore properties of the **current implementation itself**, each confirmed by direct inspection of `server.js` and by the repository-wide absence audit. They are stated as factual constraints, not as defects, since the artifact's evident purpose is minimalism.

| Limitation | Verified Basis |
|------------|----------------|
| Network binding is hard-coded and not configurable | `hostname` (line 3) and `port` (line 4) are literal constants; there is no `process.env` access, no CLI argument parsing, no `.env` file, and no `config/` directory |
| Reachable only from the same host | The `127.0.0.1` bind was confirmed by probe: a request to the host's non-loopback address on port `3000` was refused |
| No routing or request differentiation | No `req.*` property is read anywhere in the file, and the handler contains no conditional logic; `GET /`, `POST /any/deep/path?q=1`, and `DELETE /x` all returned identical responses |
| Single immutable response payload | `res.end('Hello, World!\n')` (line 9) emits the same 14 bytes for every request; no templating, negotiation, or dynamic content exists |
| Plain HTTP only — no transport security | Only the `http` module is required; there is no `https`/`tls` usage, certificate material, or reverse-proxy configuration |
| No error handling or fault tolerance | No `try`/`catch`, no `throw`, and no `server.on('error', ...)` handler; a port conflict or socket error surfaces as an unhandled process-level failure |
| No graceful shutdown | No `process.on('SIGTERM'/'SIGINT')` listener and no `server.close()` call; the process can only be stopped abruptly |
| Not unit-testable in isolation | The module has no `module.exports`; importing it executes `server.listen(...)` as a load-time side effect, so behavior can only be exercised over the network |
| No automated verification | No `test/`, `tests/`, `__tests__/`, or `spec/` directory and no Jest, Vitest, or Mocha configuration exists; the root-level `test.js` contains no test and no assertion (1.1.1, 6.6.1) |
| No dependency, build, or packaging metadata | No `package.json`, lockfile, `node_modules/`, `tsconfig.json`, bundler config, or `Makefile`; the application is neither installable nor versioned |
| No deployment or runtime packaging | No `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.*`, Kubernetes/Helm manifests, Terraform, `Procfile`, or serverless descriptor |
| No CI/CD or quality gates | No `.github/` directory, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, or `.circleci/` configuration |
| No observability beyond one log line | The only instrumentation is the startup `console.log` (line 13); there are no per-request logs, metrics, traces, or health endpoints distinct from the single response |
| No security controls | No authentication, authorization, input validation (nothing is read to validate), rate limiting, CORS policy, or security response headers |
| No stated runtime version floor | Absence of `package.json` `engines` and of `.nvmrc`/`.node-version` means no supported-runtime range is declared |

#### 1.2.1.3 Enterprise Landscape Integration

The system integrates with **nothing beyond its host runtime**. This was verified by searching `server.js` for every common integration primitive and finding none:

| Integration Category | Status in Repository |
|----------------------|----------------------|
| Databases and caches (SQL, MongoDB, Redis) | Absent — no client library, connection string, or query code |
| Outbound HTTP / third-party APIs (`fetch`, `axios`, SDKs) | Absent — no outbound network call of any kind |
| Identity, auth, and secrets (JWT, OAuth, tokens, vaults) | Absent — no credential handling or authorization logic |
| Messaging, queues, and event streams | Absent — no broker client or event publication |
| Service discovery, configuration services, feature flags | Absent — no configuration source is consulted at any point |
| File system and object storage | Absent — no `fs` usage; the process performs no disk I/O after load |

The only genuine external couplings are structural rather than architectural:

- **The Node.js runtime**, whose built-in `http` module is the sole dependency (line 1). The repository declares no version constraint, so any Node.js release providing `http` will run the file; for reference, the Node.js project's Active LTS line at the time of writing is 24.x ("Krypton", maintained through April 2028), with 26.x as the Current line.
- **The host operating system's TCP/IP stack**, which supplies the loopback interface that `server.listen(3000, '127.0.0.1', ...)` binds (line 12).
- **The GitHub remote** recorded in `.git/config` as `origin`, which serves purely as source hosting and implies no runtime integration.

Because the listener is loopback-bound and no reverse proxy, ingress, or service-mesh configuration is present, the service is also **not reachable by any other system in an enterprise landscape** in its committed form.

### 1.2.2 High-Level Description

#### 1.2.2.1 Primary System Capabilities

The system exposes exactly one capability, decomposed here into the observable behaviors that constitute it. All rows were confirmed both by reading `server.js` and by executing and probing the running server.

| Capability | Implementation | Observed Behavior |
|------------|----------------|-------------------|
| Accept inbound HTTP connections | `http.createServer(...)` + `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` (lines 6, 12) | A listening socket is established on `127.0.0.1:3000` immediately at process start |
| Respond to every request uniformly | Inline handler setting `res.statusCode = 200` and ending the response (lines 7, 9) | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with body `Hello, World!` plus a trailing newline, for every method and path tested |
| Declare the response content type | `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')` (line 8) | `Content-Type: text/plain` present on every response |
| Signal process readiness | Template-literal `console.log` in the listen callback (line 13) | Exactly one stdout line: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` |

Framing headers observed on responses — `Content-Length: 14`, `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` — are generated by the Node.js `http` module's default behavior, **not** by application code, which sets only the status code and `Content-Type`.

#### 1.2.2.2 Major System Components

There is a single deployable unit, a single process, and a single module. "Components" below are the logical elements *within* that one file, plus the runtime it depends on.

| Component | Location | Responsibility |
|-----------|----------|----------------|
| Node.js runtime and core `http` module | External dependency, imported at `server.js` line 1 | Parses HTTP, manages sockets and keep-alive, serializes responses, and supplies default headers |
| Network binding constants | `server.js` lines 3–4 | Fix the bind address (`127.0.0.1`) and port (`3000`) at authoring time |
| Server instance | `server.js` line 6 | Holds the `http.Server` created from the request handler |
| Request handler (inline arrow function) | `server.js` lines 6–10 | The complete application logic: sets status `200`, sets `Content-Type`, ends the response with the fixed body |
| Listener activation and readiness log | `server.js` lines 12–14 | Binds the socket at module load and emits the single stdout readiness message |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client["Local HTTP Client<br/>browser / curl / probe"]

    subgraph HostBoundary["Host Machine - loopback only"]
        Socket["TCP listening socket<br/>127.0.0.1 port 3000"]

        subgraph NodeProcess["Node.js process - node server.js"]
            CoreHTTP["Node.js core http module<br/>required at line 1"]
            Handler["Inline request handler<br/>lines 6-10"]
            Listener["server.listen<br/>lines 12-14"]
            Stdout["stdout readiness log<br/>line 13"]
        end
    end

    Client -->|"any method, any path, any body"| Socket
    Socket --> CoreHTTP
    CoreHTTP -->|"req and res"| Handler
    Handler -->|"status 200, text/plain, fixed body"| CoreHTTP
    CoreHTTP --> Client
    Listener --> Socket
    Listener --> Stdout
```

#### 1.2.2.3 Core Technical Approach

The technical approach is defined as much by its deliberate omissions as by its constructs:

- **Single-file CommonJS entrypoint.** `require('http')` (line 1) establishes CommonJS as the module system; there is no `package.json` declaring `"type": "module"`, no ESM syntax, and no transpilation step. The file is executed exactly as committed.
- **Side-effect-driven startup.** The module exports nothing. Loading it *is* starting the server, because `server.listen(...)` executes at the top level (line 12). There is no bootstrap function, dependency-injection container, or lifecycle framework.
- **Node.js core primitives only, with no framework layer.** The `http` module is used directly — no Express, Koa, Fastify, or Nest abstraction, and consequently no middleware pipeline, router, or plugin system.
- **Stateless, synchronous request handling.** The handler performs three synchronous statements and returns; there is no `async`/`await`, Promise, callback chain, in-memory store, session, or cache. Because nothing is retained between requests, concurrent requests cannot interfere with one another.
- **Request-agnostic response generation.** The handler signature declares `req`, but no property of it is ever read. Method, URL, query string, headers, and body are all discarded, which is why the response is byte-identical across every probe performed.
- **Loopback-scoped exposure as an intentional default.** Passing `'127.0.0.1'` as the `listen` host (line 12) confines reachability to the local machine; this was confirmed empirically when a request via the host's routable address was refused.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Local HTTP Client
    participant N as Node.js http module
    participant H as Inline handler
    C->>N: HTTP request to 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    N->>H: invoke callback with req and res
    Note over H: req is never read - method, path, body ignored
    H->>H: set statusCode 200
    H->>H: set Content-Type text/plain
    H->>N: res.end with fixed 14-byte body
    N-->>C: 200 OK, Content-Length 14, text/plain
```

The repository **defines no success criteria of any kind**. This is an audited finding, not an inference: there are no automated tests, no coverage thresholds, no CI pipeline or merge gates, no benchmark or load-test harness, no performance budget, no service-level objective or agreement, no monitoring or alerting configuration, and no acceptance-criteria documentation. `README.md` states nothing beyond the repository name.

Accordingly, **no KPI, SLA, error budget, latency target, or throughput target is attributed to this system in this specification**, because none exists to report.

#### 1.2.3.2 Derived Objectives Verifiable Against the Implementation

In the absence of declared criteria, the following objectives are derived strictly from what `server.js` does, and each was verified during documentation. They should be read as *observed behavioral guarantees of the current code*, not as commitments made by the project.

| Derived Objective | Verification Method | Observed Result |
|-------------------|---------------------|-----------------|
| Process starts without external setup | Run `node server.js` from the repository root with no prior install step | Started successfully; no dependency resolution required |
| Readiness is signalled unambiguously | Capture process stdout | Exactly one line: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` |
| Endpoint answers with HTTP 200 | `GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` |
| Response content type is plain text | Inspect response headers | `Content-Type: text/plain` |
| Response payload is exact and fixed | Compare body bytes across requests | `Hello, World!` plus newline; `Content-Length: 14` every time |
| Behavior is uniform across methods and paths | Probe `GET /`, `POST /any/deep/path?q=1` with a body, and `DELETE /x` | All three returned identical `200` / `text/plain` / 14-byte responses |
| Exposure is confined to the local host | Request the same port via the host's non-loopback address | Connection refused — no external exposure |

#### 1.2.3.3 Critical Success Factors

The prerequisites for the system to function are minimal and follow directly from its construction:

| Factor | Why It Is Required |
|--------|--------------------|
| A Node.js runtime providing the core `http` module | `require('http')` at line 1 is the only dependency; the repository declares no version floor, so any Node.js release exposing `http` suffices |
| TCP port `3000` free on the host | The port is a hard-coded constant (line 4) with no fallback and no `server.on('error')` handler, so a conflict fails the process outright |
| An available loopback interface | The bind address `127.0.0.1` (line 3) is not configurable |
| Client access from the same host | Loopback binding excludes remote callers, as confirmed by probe |
| Direct file execution | With no `package.json` scripts, the only supported launch path is invoking the file directly with `node` |

#### 1.2.3.4 Key Performance Indicators

The repository specifies **no KPIs and captures no metrics**: there is no instrumentation library, metrics endpoint, structured logger, or telemetry export in `server.js`, and no monitoring configuration in the tree. The only machine-observable signals the system emits are enumerated below; they are indicators of *liveness and correctness*, not performance measurements, and any quantitative performance figure would be a property of the host and Node.js runtime rather than of this code.

| Observable Signal | Source | What It Indicates |
|-------------------|--------|-------------------|
| Startup log line on stdout | `console.log` at line 13 | The listener bound successfully and the service is ready |
| HTTP status code returned | `res.statusCode = 200` at line 7 | Correct operation; the code contains no path that yields any other status |
| Response body length of 14 bytes | `res.end('Hello, World!\n')` at line 9 | Payload integrity — the response is complete and unmodified |
| Process exit or absent listener | Operating-system process state | The only available failure indicator, since no error handler or health endpoint exists |

## 1.3 Scope

Scope below is stated descriptively: it delimits what the committed code **does** and what it demonstrably **does not** do. The repository contains no requirements document, backlog, or roadmap, so scope is reconstructed from the implementation in `server.js`, the contents of `README.md`, and the repository-wide artifact audit.

### 1.3.1 In-Scope

#### 1.3.1.1 Core Features and Functionalities

Four behaviors constitute the entire delivered functionality. All are implemented within the 14 lines of `server.js` and were confirmed by executing the server.

| Must-Have Capability | Implementation Point | Scope Note |
|----------------------|----------------------|------------|
| Create an HTTP server instance | `http.createServer(handler)` — line 6 | Uses the Node.js core `http` module directly; no framework wrapper is in scope |
| Bind and listen on a fixed local endpoint | `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` — line 12, with constants at lines 3–4 | `127.0.0.1:3000` only; alternate hosts, ports, or protocols are not in scope |
| Return a fixed successful response to every request | `res.statusCode = 200`, `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')`, `res.end('Hello, World!\n')` — lines 7–9 | One status code, one content type, one 14-byte payload |
| Emit a startup readiness signal | `console.log` with a template literal — line 13 | A single stdout line; no per-request or structured logging is in scope |

#### 1.3.1.2 Primary User Workflow

The system supports exactly **one** end-to-end workflow. Because `server.js` exports nothing and no `package.json` scripts exist, direct invocation is the only supported entry path.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Developer opens the repository checkout"] --> B["Run: node server.js"]
    B --> C["Listener binds 127.0.0.1 on port 3000"]
    C --> D["stdout readiness line is emitted"]
    D --> E["Local client sends any HTTP request"]
    E --> F["Server returns 200, text/plain, 14-byte body"]
    F --> G{"Another request?"}
    G -->|"yes"| E
    G -->|"no"| H["Process terminated externally - no shutdown hook exists"]
```

Two operator-facing observations are in scope for this workflow: the readiness line on stdout confirms successful binding, and any HTTP response received confirms correct operation. Nothing else is surfaced.

#### 1.3.1.3 Essential Integrations

The integration surface in scope is a single runtime dependency.

| In-Scope Integration | Nature of the Coupling |
|----------------------|------------------------|
| Node.js core `http` module | Required at line 1; supplies HTTP parsing, socket management, keep-alive handling, and default response headers (`Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`) |
| Host operating system TCP/IP loopback interface | Provides the `127.0.0.1` address that `server.listen` binds |
| Host stdout stream | Destination for the single readiness log line |

No other integration is in scope: the repository contains no third-party package, no database or cache client, no outbound HTTP client, no identity provider, no message broker, and no configuration or secret-management service.

#### 1.3.1.4 Key Technical Requirements

| Requirement | Basis in the Repository |
|-------------|-------------------------|
| A Node.js runtime exposing the core `http` module | The sole `require` in `server.js`; no version floor is declared anywhere (no `engines` field, no `.nvmrc`) |
| CommonJS module resolution | `require('http')` with no `"type": "module"` declaration and no ESM syntax present |
| TCP port `3000` available on the host | Hard-coded constant with no fallback logic and no `error` event handler |
| Loopback interface available | Hard-coded bind address `127.0.0.1` |
| Direct execution of the source file | No build, transpile, or install step exists; the file runs as committed via `node server.js` |
| Client access originating on the same host | Confirmed by probe — the port is not reachable via the host's routable address |

#### 1.3.1.5 Implementation Boundaries

**System boundary.** The system is one operating-system process running one CommonJS module. The boundary is the listening TCP socket at `127.0.0.1:3000`. Everything inside the boundary is the code in `server.js` plus the Node.js `http` machinery it invokes; everything outside — clients, proxies, orchestrators, other services — is external and unmanaged by this repository.

| Boundary Dimension | In-Scope Extent |
|--------------------|-----------------|
| Process and deployment unit | A single foreground `node` process; no clustering, worker threads, child processes, or multi-instance topology exists in the code |
| Network reach | The loopback interface of one host, port `3000`, plain HTTP only |
| Protocol surface | HTTP request/response with a single uniform reply; no WebSocket upgrade, HTTP/2, gRPC, or streaming behavior is implemented |
| Interface contract | One implicit endpoint matching every method and path, always answering `200` with `text/plain` |

**User groups covered.** The code models **no users, roles, or permissions** — no request attribute is inspected, so no caller can be identified or differentiated. Every caller is anonymous and receives identical treatment. In practical terms the covered population is "any process able to open a socket on the host's loopback interface," and the operational audience is the developer or operator who starts and stops the process.

**Geographic and market coverage.** There is no geographic dimension in scope. The repository contains no internationalization or localization resources, no locale or timezone handling, no `Accept-Language` processing (no request header is read at all), and no region, CDN, or multi-zone configuration. The response is a fixed ASCII English string, and coverage is limited to the single host on which the process runs.

**Data domains included.** No persistent data domain is in scope. The complete data inventory of the running system is:

| Data Element | Lifetime and Handling |
|--------------|----------------------|
| Inbound HTTP request (method, URL, headers, body) | Received by the `http` module, never read by application code, and discarded |
| Outbound response body — `Hello, World!\n` | A literal constant in source; identical for every request |
| Startup log line | Written once to stdout at listener binding |

There is no schema, model, migration, storage engine, or serialization format in the repository, and no personal, financial, or otherwise sensitive data is accepted, processed, or retained.

### 1.3.2 Out-of-Scope

#### 1.3.2.1 Explicitly Excluded Features and Capabilities

Each exclusion below was confirmed by direct search of `server.js` or by testing for the existence of the corresponding project artifact; none were present.

#### 1.3.2.2 Future Phase Considerations

The repository declares **no future phases**. There is no roadmap, milestone list, `TODO`/`FIXME` comment, `CHANGELOG.md`, backlog file, or design note anywhere in the tree, and the history consists of only three commits — two made eleven seconds apart on 2026-07-29 and one on 2026-07-30. That third commit (`43ed37c` "Create test.js") adds no roadmap, requirement, or capability: it introduces a 13-byte placeholder file that is not part of the application and that fails if executed. Any subsequent capability would therefore be entirely net-new work rather than a planned continuation.

For clarity, the structural gaps that a follow-on effort would most likely need to address — externalizing the host and port, exporting the server for testability, adding error handling and shutdown hooks, and introducing dependency and packaging metadata — are documented in this specification as **present-state absences (see 1.2.1.2), not as commitments, plans, or approved future scope**.

#### 1.3.2.3 Integration Points Not Covered

No integration point is covered beyond the Node.js runtime, the host loopback interface, and stdout. Specifically excluded, with absence verified in `server.js`: relational and NoSQL databases, caches and key–value stores, message brokers and event streams, outbound REST/GraphQL/gRPC calls to third-party or internal services, identity providers and secret managers, feature-flag and remote-configuration services, email/SMS/notification providers, payment or billing systems, object storage and file systems, service discovery and service meshes, API gateways and reverse proxies, and monitoring or log-aggregation backends. The GitHub remote recorded in `.git/config` is source hosting only and carries no runtime integration.

#### 1.3.2.4 Unsupported Use Cases

| Unsupported Use Case | Reason Grounded in the Implementation |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Serving traffic from other hosts or from the public internet | The `127.0.0.1` bind was empirically confirmed to refuse connections via the host's routable address |
| Production or internet-facing deployment | No TLS, authentication, error handling, rate limiting, health endpoint, packaging, or deployment descriptor exists |
| Building an application with more than one endpoint or response | The handler has no branching and reads no request attribute |
| Environment-specific operation (dev/staging/prod) | Host and port are compile-time constants with no configuration source |
| Multi-tenant or per-user behavior | No user, tenant, or session concept exists in the code |
| Unit or integration testing within a test harness | The module has no exports and binds a socket as a load-time side effect; the tracked `test.js` is not a harness and exercises nothing |
| Automated release, rollback, or zero-downtime restart | No versioning, packaging, or shutdown handling; the process can only be stopped abruptly |
| Handling port contention or transient socket failures | No `error` event handler and no port fallback; such conditions fail the process |
| Reuse as a library or dependency of another project | No `package.json` and no exported API; the file can only be executed |
| Redistribution under defined legal terms | No `LICENSE` file grants any rights |

# 2. Product Requirements

## 2.1 Feature Catalog

This catalog decomposes `July2026_hello_world_repo` into the discrete, individually testable features that the committed code actually delivers. The repository contains exactly three tracked files totalling 382 bytes — `server.js` (342 bytes, 14 lines), `README.md` (27 bytes, 1 line), and `test.js` (13 bytes, 2 lines) — of which only `server.js` executes any behavior, so the whole feature set resides in a single module.

`test.js` is deliberately **outside this catalog**. It contributes no observable behavior: it is two undefined bare words, it exports nothing, no file requires it, no documented procedure executes it, and running it fails immediately (`ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined`, exit 1). It therefore satisfies no capability, bears no requirement, and appears in Section 2 only where its existence must be acknowledged (2.5.5, 2.6).

### 2.1.1 Catalog Derivation Basis and Conventions

#### 2.1.1.1 Derivation Basis

The repository contains **no product-requirements source of any kind**. The following requirement-bearing artifacts were each individually tested for existence and none are present: `requirements.md`, `PRD.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `TODO.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/`, `openapi.yaml`, `openapi.json`, `swagger.json`, any issue-tracker export, and any test directory or test-runner configuration. A recursive search for `TODO`, `FIXME`, `XXX`, and `HACK` markers across all `.js` and `.md` files returned no matches, `README.md` contains only the heading `# July2026_hello_world_repo`, and `test.js` contains only the two bare words `asdsa` and `asdasd`.

Consequently every feature and requirement below is **reverse-derived** from two evidence sources only:

| Evidence Source | What It Establishes |
|-----------------|---------------------|
| Line-level reading and grep audit of `server.js` | Which behaviors exist in code, and — equally important — which do not |
| Execution of the committed source and HTTP probing of the running process | The observable contract used to write measurable acceptance criteria |

Features are aligned one-to-one with the capability inventory already established in **1.2.2.1 Primary System Capabilities** and **1.3.1.1 Core Features and Functionalities**, so that Section 1 scope and Section 2 requirements describe the same four delivered behaviors plus the runtime/execution model that carries them.

### 2.1.3 F-001: HTTP Server Instantiation and Request-Handler Registration

#### 2.1.3.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| Unique ID | F-001 | Assigned by this specification |
| Feature Name | HTTP Server Instantiation and Request-Handler Registration | — |
| Feature Category | Core Request Processing | Derived from the code's role |
| Priority Level | Critical | Without the server object and its handler, no request can be accepted or answered |
| Status | Completed | `server.js` lines 6–10; verified by probing the running process |

#### 2.1.3.2 Description

**Overview.** The feature creates the single `http.Server` instance that accepts every inbound connection and registers exactly one inline arrow-function handler to service them. A grep of `server.js` confirms a single `createServer` call and a single handler; there is no router, middleware chain, plugin registry, or secondary handler anywhere in the repository.

```javascript
// server.js line 6 - the only handler registration in the repository
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
```

**Business Value (derived engineering value — no business documentation exists in the repository).** The feature supplies the minimum viable request-acceptance layer for a Node.js service: the complete request path is four lines long and reviewable in a single pass, which makes the artifact usable as a known-good baseline or teaching reference without any framework knowledge.

**User Benefits.** For the local HTTP client, every request is accepted and answered with no negotiation, credential, or configuration prerequisite. For the developer or operator, the absence of dispatch logic means there is no route-matching failure mode to diagnose — a connected request is always a serviced request.

**Technical Context.** The handler is invoked by the Node core `http` module with the standard `(req, res)` pair. The `req` parameter is declared but **never dereferenced** — a grep for `req.<property>` returns no match — so method, URL, query string, headers, and body are structurally unreachable by application logic. The handler body is three synchronous statements with no branching, no `async`/`await`, no Promise, and no timer; probing confirmed 50 sequential requests produced exactly one unique response and 100 requests issued at concurrency 20 all returned `200`.

#### 2.1.3.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Detail | Evidence |
|-----------------|--------|----------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-005 — the `http` module binding must be established before `createServer` can be called | `server.js` line 1 precedes line 6 |
| System Dependencies | Node.js runtime supplying the core `http` module and its single-threaded event loop, which parses requests and invokes the handler | `require('http')` at line 1; handler invocation is entirely runtime-driven |
| External Dependencies | None — zero third-party packages | Only one `require` exists in the repository; no `package.json`, lockfile, or `node_modules/` |
| Integration Requirements | Consumes the `req`/`res` objects created by the Node HTTP parser and returns control to the module for serialization; F-002 must bind a socket before the handler is ever invoked | `server.listen(...)` at line 12 activates the instance created at line 6 |

### 2.1.4 F-002: Fixed Loopback Endpoint Binding and Listener Lifecycle

#### 2.1.4.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| Unique ID | F-002 | Assigned by this specification |
| Feature Name | Fixed Loopback Endpoint Binding and Listener Lifecycle | — |
| Feature Category | Network Interface and Service Lifecycle | Derived from the code's role |
| Priority Level | Critical | Without the `listen` call no socket exists and the service is unreachable |
| Status | Completed | `server.js` lines 3–4 and 12–14; verified by binding, probing, and termination tests |

#### 2.1.4.2 Description

**Overview.** The feature activates the server instance on a fixed local endpoint — `127.0.0.1` port `3000` — at module load. Both values are module-scoped literal constants (lines 3–4); the `listen` call at line 12 is a top-level statement, so **loading the module is starting the service**. The same two constants also feed the readiness message of F-004, so the advertised endpoint cannot drift from the bound endpoint.

**Business Value (derived engineering value — no business documentation exists in the repository).** Binding to the loopback interface by default confines the service to the host that starts it, which was empirically confirmed: a request to the host's non-loopback address on port `3000` failed to connect. This makes the artifact safe to run on a workstation without exposing an unauthenticated endpoint to a network.

**User Benefits.** A single command yields a reachable endpoint at a predictable, documented address with no configuration file, environment variable, or flag to supply. The operator can rely on the address being identical on every host and every run.

**Technical Context.** The feature also determines the system's complete lifecycle behavior, all of it inherited from Node defaults because the code registers no lifecycle handlers. There is no `server.on('error', ...)`, no `process.on('SIGTERM'/'SIGINT')`, and no `server.close()` anywhere in the file. Two measurements characterize the resulting behavior: starting a second instance while port `3000` was already bound terminated the new process with an unhandled `error` event (`Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`, `code: 'EADDRINUSE'`) and **exit code 1**; and `SIGTERM` terminated the running process immediately, after which the port stopped accepting connections with no draining of in-flight work.

#### 2.1.4.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Detail | Evidence |
|-----------------|--------|----------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 — `listen` is called on the instance returned by `createServer`; F-005 — module execution is what triggers the bind | Lines 6 and 12; top-level statement order |
| System Dependencies | Host TCP/IP stack with an available loopback interface, and TCP port `3000` free at start time | Bind address literal at line 3; EADDRINUSE crash observed when the port was occupied |
| External Dependencies | None — no reverse proxy, ingress controller, service registry, or orchestrator is referenced anywhere in the repository | No deployment, container, or IaC descriptor exists |
| Integration Requirements | The listening socket at `127.0.0.1:3000` is the system's only inbound interface; F-004 is triggered by this feature's `listen` callback | Line 12 callback contains line 13 |

### 2.1.5 F-003: Uniform Fixed-Payload HTTP Response

#### 2.1.5.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| Unique ID | F-003 | Assigned by this specification |
| Feature Name | Uniform Fixed-Payload HTTP Response | — |
| Feature Category | Response Contract and Content Delivery | Derived from the code's role |
| Priority Level | Critical | This is the system's sole delivered output; without it the service returns nothing |
| Status | Completed | `server.js` lines 7–9; verified across five HTTP methods and multiple paths |

#### 2.1.5.2 Description

**Overview.** Every request receives an identical response: HTTP status `200`, header `Content-Type: text/plain`, and the exact 14-byte body `Hello, World!` followed by a newline. A grep for every response-mutating API (`statusCode`, `setHeader`, `writeHead`, `res.end`) returns only lines 7, 8, and 9, which proves the response contract is fully described by three statements.

```javascript
// server.js lines 7-9 - the complete response contract
res.statusCode = 200;
res.end('Hello, World!\n');
```

**Business Value (derived engineering value — no business documentation exists in the repository).** Determinism is the value: because the payload is a source-code literal and no request attribute influences it, the endpoint is a stable, byte-exact target for connectivity checks, runtime validation, and reachability smoke tests. Body uniqueness was confirmed across 50 sequential requests.

**User Benefits.** The client needs no schema, content negotiation, parser, or error branch — a successful connection always yields the same parsable plain-text result. The response is also self-describing in that its content type is declared explicitly rather than left to client sniffing.

**Technical Context.** Application code sets only the status code and one header; the framing headers observed on the wire — `Content-Length: 14`, `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` — are generated by the Node `http` module's defaults, not by `server.js`. Node's own protocol handling also produces one measured edge behavior the application does not author: a `HEAD` request returns status `200` with `Content-Type: text/plain` and a zero-byte body.

#### 2.1.5.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Detail | Evidence |
|-----------------|--------|----------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 — the `res` object is supplied only by the registered handler's invocation | Handler parameters at line 6 |
| System Dependencies | Node core `http` module for header serialization, `Content-Length` computation, and keep-alive management | Observed headers absent from source but present on the wire |
| External Dependencies | None — no template engine, serializer, i18n catalog, or content source; the payload is a string literal | Line 9; no other executable file exists in the repository |
| Integration Requirements | Delivers bytes back through the same socket F-002 bound; requires no downstream call, cache, or datastore | No outbound client, `fs`, or database code exists in `server.js` |

### 2.1.6 F-004: Startup Readiness Logging

#### 2.1.6.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| Unique ID | F-004 | Assigned by this specification |
| Feature Name | Startup Readiness Logging | — |
| Feature Category | Observability | Derived from the code's role |
| Priority Level | Medium | Removing it would leave the HTTP contract and launch path intact, but eliminate the only operator-facing signal |
| Status | Completed | `server.js` line 13; verified byte-exactly on a clean start |

#### 2.1.6.2 Description

**Overview.** When the listener binds successfully, the `listen` callback writes exactly one line to stdout: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`. A fresh run produced stdout of exactly **41 bytes** — the message plus its newline — and an empty stderr. This single line is the entirety of the system's instrumentation.

**Business Value (derived engineering value — no business documentation exists in the repository).** The line provides an unambiguous, machine-greppable readiness signal, which is what allows the artifact to serve as a runtime installation check: seeing the line proves that the Node runtime loaded, the module executed, and the socket bound.

**User Benefits.** The operator learns both *that* the service is ready and *where* to reach it from one line of output, with no log configuration, verbosity flag, or health endpoint to consult.

**Technical Context.** The message is built with a template literal that interpolates the same `hostname` and `port` constants used by the `listen` call, so the advertised URL is structurally guaranteed to match the bound endpoint. Logging is confined to this event: after more than 150 probe requests, stdout remained 41 bytes, confirming there is no per-request logging, no error logging, no structured/JSON logger, and no metrics or tracing export.

#### 2.1.6.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Detail | Evidence |
|-----------------|--------|----------|
| Prerequisite Features | F-002 — the message is emitted from the `listen` callback and therefore only after a successful bind | Line 12 callback wraps line 13 |
| System Dependencies | An attached and writable `process.stdout` stream; the global `console` | `console.log` at line 13 |
| External Dependencies | None — no logging library, log shipper, or aggregation backend appears anywhere in the repository | Single `require` in the repository is `http` |
| Integration Requirements | Consumers must read process stdout; no log file, syslog target, HTTP log sink, or structured format is offered | Clean run wrote nothing to stderr and created no files |

### 2.1.7 F-005: Zero-Dependency Direct Execution Model

#### 2.1.7.1 Feature Metadata

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| Unique ID | F-005 | Assigned by this specification |
| Feature Name | Zero-Dependency Direct Execution Model | — |
| Feature Category | Runtime, Dependency and Packaging Model | Derived from the repository's composition |
| Priority Level | High | The response contract would still work if launched another way, but this is the only launch path the repository supports as committed |
| Status | Completed | `server.js` line 1 plus the verified absence of all manifests and build tooling |

#### 2.1.7.2 Description

**Overview.** The system runs exactly as committed. `grep -c "require("` over `server.js` returns **1**, and that single import is the Node built-in `http` module; across the whole tracked inventory there is no ESM `import`, no third-party package, no `package.json`, no lockfile, and no `node_modules/`. There is likewise no `tsconfig.json`, bundler configuration, Babel configuration, or `Makefile`, so no install, build, or transpile step precedes execution.

**Business Value (derived engineering value — no business documentation exists in the repository).** Zero dependencies means zero supply-chain surface and zero version-resolution work: the artifact cannot break because of a transitive update, and it can be executed on any host with a Node runtime with no network access to a package registry.

**User Benefits.** A developer can clone and run the service with one command and no prerequisites beyond Node itself; a reviewer can audit 100 % of the executed code in one file.

**Technical Context.** Because `server.listen(...)` is a top-level statement, starting the listener is a **module-load side effect**. This was verified directly: requiring `server.js` from another script returned an object with zero own keys (`Object.keys(...)` was empty) and simultaneously attempted the port bind. The model therefore has two structural consequences documented as constraints in 2.4 — there is no exported API to import, inject, or unit-test, and there is no packaging metadata by which the artifact could be versioned, published, or consumed as a library. Operation is a single foreground process: the file contains no `cluster` or `worker_threads` usage, and one process served 100 concurrently issued requests during verification.

#### 2.1.7.3 Dependencies

| Dependency Type | Detail | Evidence |
|-----------------|--------|----------|
| Prerequisite Features | None — F-005 is the root of the feature dependency graph | Line 1 is the first executed statement |
| System Dependencies | A Node.js runtime that exposes the core `http` module and CommonJS resolution; no version floor is declared anywhere (no `engines`, no `.nvmrc`, no `.node-version`) | Verified on Node v22.23.1 as an environment fact only |
| External Dependencies | None whatsoever — no registry, no package, no build service, no container image | Repository-wide absence audit of 76 conventional paths returned zero matches |
| Integration Requirements | Launch by direct invocation of the file with the `node` binary; there is no `npm start` script, entry-point declaration, or process manager configuration | No `package.json` and no `Procfile` exist |

### 2.1.8 Candidate Features Evaluated and Excluded

The following capability areas were explicitly searched for and are **not** present in the repository, so no feature, requirement, or acceptance criterion is defined for them anywhere in Section 2. This list is the feature-level counterpart of the exclusions recorded in **1.3.2.1 Explicitly Excluded Features and Capabilities**.

| Excluded Candidate Area | Basis for Exclusion |
|-------------------------|---------------------|
| Routing, multiple endpoints, method dispatch | No branching and no `req.url`/`req.method` access in `server.js` |
| Request parsing — query strings, headers, bodies, cookies, uploads | No `req.<property>` access at all; a `POST` body and custom header were ignored during probing |
| Dynamic, templated, or content-negotiated responses | Response body is a source literal; no template engine or negotiation logic |
| Externalized configuration and environment profiles | No `process.env`, `.env`, `config/`, or CLI argument parsing |
| Transport security (HTTPS/TLS), certificates, security headers | Only the `http` module is required; no `https`/`tls` usage or certificate material |
| Authentication, authorization, session management | No credential, token, cookie, or session code |
| Input validation, rate limiting, CORS policy | Nothing is read that could be validated; no such middleware exists |
| Persistence, caching, and state management | No database or cache client, no `fs` usage, no in-memory store |
| Error handling, retries, circuit breaking, graceful shutdown | No `try`/`catch`, no `server.on('error')`, no signal handlers, no `server.close()` |
| Dedicated health, readiness, or metrics endpoints | The handler is uniform; no path is treated as a probe target |
| Structured logging, metrics, and tracing | Instrumentation is one `console.log` at startup |
| Automated testing and coverage enforcement | No test directory or runner configuration and nothing to import (the module exports nothing); the tracked `test.js` holds no test, no assertion, and no framework reference, and fails on execution |
| Linting, formatting, and type checking | No ESLint, Prettier, `.editorconfig`, or `tsconfig.json` |
| Dependency, packaging, and release management | No `package.json`, lockfile, version field, or git tag |
| Build, bundling, and transpilation | No bundler, Babel, or `Makefile` configuration |
| CI/CD pipelines and quality gates | No `.github/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, or `.circleci/` |
| Containerization, orchestration, and infrastructure as code | No `Dockerfile`, compose file, Kubernetes/Helm manifest, Terraform, or serverless descriptor |
| Static asset serving, WebSocket, HTTP/2, streaming | Handler ends the response immediately with a fixed buffer |
| API documentation, OpenAPI schema, client SDKs | No specification file; `README.md` contains only the repository name |
| Internationalization and localization | No locale resources and no `Accept-Language` handling |
| Clustering, horizontal scaling, load balancing | No `cluster`/`worker_threads` usage and no proxy or multi-instance configuration |
| Licensing and project governance | No `LICENSE`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CODEOWNERS`, or `SECURITY.md` |

## 2.2 Functional Requirements Table

Twenty requirements are defined across the five catalogued features. Each one describes a behavior that is present in the committed source and that was confirmed by executing and probing the running process, so each is stated with an acceptance criterion that an independent reviewer can re-run.

### 2.2.1 Requirement Identification and Rating Conventions

| Convention | Definition Applied in This Section |
|------------|-----------------------------------|
| Requirement ID | `F-XXX-RQ-YYY`, where `F-XXX` is the parent feature and `YYY` is sequential within that feature |
| Priority — Must-Have | The behavior occurs unconditionally on every execution of the committed code and is required for the system's observable contract |
| Priority — Should-Have | The behavior is conditional (a failure or protocol edge path) or is inherited from Node `http`/runtime defaults rather than authored in `server.js` |
| Priority — Could-Have | Not assigned — the repository contains no optional, deferred, or feature-flagged behavior |
| Complexity — Low / Medium / High | Rated on authored implementation surface (statements plus branching). **All twenty requirements are Low**: none is implemented in more than three statements, none contains a conditional, and none involves a third-party library. No requirement in this repository qualifies as Medium or High |

Two conventions apply to every table below and are stated once here rather than repeated:

- **Verification posture.** The repository contains **no automated tests** — no `test/`, `tests/`, `__tests__/`, or `spec/` directory and no Jest, Vitest, or Mocha configuration exists. Every acceptance criterion is therefore an externally executable check (source inspection, process execution, or HTTP probe), not an assertion in a committed test suite.
- **Performance criteria.** The repository declares **no performance target for any requirement** — there is no benchmark, load-test harness, performance budget, SLO, latency ceiling, or timeout setting anywhere in the tree. Where a measurement is quoted, it is an observed characteristic of the verification environment (loopback interface, Node v22.23.1), explicitly **not** a requirement of the system.

### 2.2.2 F-001 Requirements — Core Request Processing

#### 2.2.2.1 Requirement Details

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | Instantiate exactly one HTTP server via the Node core `http` module, registering exactly one request handler | Must-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-002 | Service every inbound request with that single handler, without inspecting or dispatching on method, path, query string, headers, or body | Must-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-003 | Process each request synchronously and statelessly, retaining no data between requests | Must-Have | Low |

#### 2.2.2.2 Acceptance Criteria

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Verification Method |
|----------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | `server.js` contains exactly one `http.createServer(` call and one handler function; with the process running, an HTTP request to the bound endpoint returns a well-formed response | Source grep plus `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/` — returned `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` |
| F-001-RQ-002 | `GET /`, `POST /any/deep/path?q=1` (body `payload=ignored`, header `X-Custom: abc`), `DELETE /x`, and `PUT /a/b` each return `200` with `Content-Type: text/plain` and a 14-byte body; source contains zero `req.<property>` references | Four probes across four methods and three paths — all identical; grep for `req.[a-zA-Z]` returned no match |
| F-001-RQ-003 | 50 sequential requests yield exactly one unique response body; 100 requests issued at concurrency 20 all return `200`; source contains no `async`/`await`/`Promise`/timer and no cross-request variable | `sort -u` over 50 bodies produced one 14-byte result; `xargs -P 20` over 100 requests produced 100 × `200` |

#### 2.2.2.3 Technical Specifications

| Requirement ID | Input Parameters | Output / Response | Data Requirements |
|----------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | A single handler function literal passed to `createServer`; no options object | An `http.Server` instance held in the module-scoped `server` constant | None — no state is initialised at construction |
| F-001-RQ-002 | The parsed request object `req`, which is declared in the handler signature and never dereferenced | Handler execution proceeds directly to the F-003 response statements | None — the request is discarded unread when the handler returns |
| F-001-RQ-003 | One `(req, res)` pair per invocation | One completed response per invocation, independent of all others | No session, cache, counter, queue, or accumulator exists |

**Performance criteria for F-001.** None declared. Observed during verification: 10 loopback `GET /` samples had a median total time of 0.000161 s (min 0.000136 s, max 0.000943 s), and no request failed under 20-way concurrency. These figures characterise the host, not a requirement.

#### 2.2.2.4 Validation Rules

| Requirement ID | Business Rule as Implemented | Data Validation | Security and Compliance |
|----------------|------------------------------|-----------------|-------------------------|
| F-001-RQ-001 | One server, one handler — there is no second handler, listener, or fallback path | Not applicable; no external input is consumed at construction | No authentication or authorization gate precedes handler invocation; any client able to reach the loopback socket is served |
| F-001-RQ-002 | Every request is treated as valid; no rejection, `404`, or `405` path exists in the code | None — nothing is read, therefore nothing can be validated; this is a direct consequence of the request-agnostic design | No injection surface exists because no request data is parsed, interpolated, or executed; no compliance regime is declared in the repository |
| F-001-RQ-003 | Requests cannot influence one another; determinism is absolute | Not applicable — no data is retained to validate | No personal or sensitive data is stored, since request content is never read and never persisted |

### 2.2.3 F-002 Requirements — Network Interface and Service Lifecycle

#### 2.2.3.1 Requirement Details

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | Bind a listening TCP socket to `127.0.0.1` port `3000` at module load, requiring no further operator action | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-002 | Restrict reachability to the host's loopback interface | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-003 | Derive the bind address and port from single module-scoped constants that are also used to compose the readiness message, with no runtime override path | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-004 | On bind failure, terminate with a non-zero exit status and a diagnostic on stderr (inherited runtime disposition; no application-level handling) | Should-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-005 | On a termination signal, exit immediately without draining in-flight connections | Should-Have | Low |

#### 2.2.3.2 Acceptance Criteria

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Verification Method |
|----------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | After `node server.js`, a request to `http://127.0.0.1:3000/` succeeds with no intermediate step; `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` appears as a top-level statement | Fresh launch followed by `curl` — `200`, 14 bytes; listener accepted connections within the 1.2 s settle window used during verification |
| F-002-RQ-002 | A request to the host's non-loopback address on port `3000` fails to connect while the loopback request succeeds in the same window | `curl http://10.76.0.92:3000/` → connection failure (`curl` exit 7, `%{http_code}` = `000`) |
| F-002-RQ-003 | `hostname` and `port` are each declared once and referenced by both the `listen` call and the readiness log; no `process.env`, CLI argument, or config file is consulted; the logged URL equals the endpoint that answers | Source inspection; grep for `process.env|dotenv|argv|config` returned no match; logged URL matched the responding endpoint |
| F-002-RQ-004 | With port `3000` already bound, a second launch exits with code `1` and stderr containing `EADDRINUSE` and an unhandled `error` event report | Second instance launched deliberately — exit code `1`, `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`, `code: 'EADDRINUSE'` |
| F-002-RQ-005 | `SIGTERM` terminates the process promptly and the port stops accepting connections; source contains no signal handler and no `server.close()` | `kill -TERM <pid>` → process absent within one second, subsequent probe returned `000`; grep for `process.on|SIGTERM|SIGINT|.close(` returned no match |

#### 2.2.3.3 Technical Specifications

| Requirement ID | Input Parameters | Output / Response | Data Requirements |
|----------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | `port` = `3000` (number literal), `hostname` = `'127.0.0.1'` (string literal), plus a listen callback | A bound listening socket and one invocation of the callback | None persisted; two module-scoped constants only |
| F-002-RQ-002 | The bind-address constant, passed as the `host` argument to `listen` | Connections via loopback are accepted; connections via other interfaces are never established | None |
| F-002-RQ-003 | No external input — both values are source literals | Bind endpoint and advertised endpoint are guaranteed identical | Two constants; no configuration source is read at any point |
| F-002-RQ-004 | The operating system's bind result surfaced as a server `error` event | Process exit code `1` with a stack trace on stderr; no readiness line is produced | None |
| F-002-RQ-005 | `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` delivered by the operating system | Immediate process exit and release of the listening socket | Any in-flight request data is lost without acknowledgement |

**Performance criteria for F-002.** None declared. No backlog size, `keepAliveTimeout`, `headersTimeout`, connection limit, or restart policy is configured in `server.js`; keep-alive behavior observed on the wire (`Keep-Alive: timeout=5`) is a Node default rather than an authored setting.

#### 2.2.3.4 Validation Rules

| Requirement ID | Business Rule as Implemented | Data Validation | Security and Compliance |
|----------------|------------------------------|-----------------|-------------------------|
| F-002-RQ-001 | Exactly one endpoint is exposed; startup is unconditional and immediate | Bind arguments are literals and are not validated by application code | The endpoint is unauthenticated — anything that can reach the socket is served |
| F-002-RQ-002 | Loopback-only reachability is the system's sole access-control mechanism | Not applicable | This network-topological boundary is the **only** security control in the repository; there is no TLS, credential check, or allow-list to complement it |
| F-002-RQ-003 | The endpoint is fixed at authoring time; environment-specific operation is impossible by construction | No configuration parsing exists, so no configuration validation exists | Hard-coding removes configuration-injection risk but also prevents binding to a restricted or ephemeral port at deploy time |
| F-002-RQ-004 | Failure is fatal rather than degraded — there is no port fallback and no retry | The failure is detected by the OS/runtime, not by application validation | The stderr stack trace discloses the bind address, port, `errno`, and Node version; no secret material is exposed |
| F-002-RQ-005 | Shutdown is abrupt by design absence; no lifecycle contract is offered | Not applicable | Abrupt termination cannot leak persisted state because no state is persisted; no audit or retention obligation is declared in the repository |

### 2.2.4 F-003 Requirements — Response Contract and Content Delivery

#### 2.2.4.1 Requirement Details

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
|----------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| F-003-RQ-001 | Respond with HTTP status `200` to every request | Must-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-002 | Set the response header `Content-Type: text/plain` on every response | Must-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-003 | End every response with exactly the 14-byte payload `Hello, World!` followed by a newline | Must-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-004 | Delegate response framing headers (`Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`) to the Node `http` module rather than authoring them | Should-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-005 | For `HEAD` requests, return status and headers with a zero-byte body, as produced by Node's protocol handling | Should-Have | Low |

#### 2.2.4.2 Acceptance Criteria

| Requirement ID | Acceptance Criteria | Verification Method |
|----------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| F-003-RQ-001 | Every probe returns `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`; the source assigns `res.statusCode = 200` unconditionally and contains no other status assignment | Probes across `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `HEAD` — all `200`; grep confirms a single `statusCode` assignment |
| F-003-RQ-002 | `Content-Type: text/plain` is present on every response; the source contains exactly one `setHeader` call | Header inspection on all probes; grep for `setHeader|writeHead` returned only line 8 |
| F-003-RQ-003 | Response body is byte-exactly `Hello, World!\n` (14 bytes) and `Content-Length: 14` is reported; 50 sequential requests yield one unique body | `od -c` dump of the response body showed `H e l l o ,   W o r l d ! \n`; `sort -u` over 50 bodies yielded one result |
| F-003-RQ-004 | `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` appear on the wire but nowhere in `server.js` | `curl -i` header capture (`Content-Length: 14`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`) compared against a source grep that found no such header assignments |
| F-003-RQ-005 | A `HEAD` request returns `200` with `Content-Type: text/plain` and a downloaded size of `0` bytes, with no code change involved | `curl -I http://127.0.0.1:3000/` → `status=200 type=text/plain len=0` |

#### 2.2.4.3 Technical Specifications

| Requirement ID | Input Parameters | Output / Response | Data Requirements |
|----------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| F-003-RQ-001 | None — the status is a literal in the handler | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` status line on every response | None; no status is computed or looked up |
| F-003-RQ-002 | None — header name and value are literals | One application-set response header | None; no negotiation table or MIME map is consulted |
| F-003-RQ-003 | None — the payload is a source-code string literal | A 14-byte plain-text body terminating the response | The complete outbound data inventory of the system is this single literal |
| F-003-RQ-004 | The response object state as handed to `res.end` | Framing headers computed by the runtime, including a `Content-Length` of `14` | None |
| F-003-RQ-005 | The request method as interpreted by the runtime (not by application code) | Status and headers with an empty body | None |

**Performance criteria for F-003.** None declared. The payload is a fixed 14 bytes, so response size is constant by construction; no compression, caching, chunking, or streaming is configured, and no latency or throughput target exists in the repository.

#### 2.2.4.4 Validation Rules

| Requirement ID | Business Rule as Implemented | Data Validation | Security and Compliance |
|----------------|------------------------------|-----------------|-------------------------|
| F-003-RQ-001 | Success is the only outcome; no error, redirect, or empty-response path is reachable in the code | Not applicable — the status is a literal | Because no failure status can be produced, response codes convey no information about invalid input; no compliance regime is declared |
| F-003-RQ-002 | Content type is declared explicitly rather than left to client sniffing | Not applicable — the value is a literal | No security response headers (for example HSTS, CSP, or `X-Content-Type-Options`) are set, and no `Server` header is authored by application code |
| F-003-RQ-003 | The payload is immutable across requests, hosts, clients, and time | Output correctness is verifiable byte-wise rather than schema-wise | The body contains no personal, credential, environment, or diagnostic data — it is a fixed English greeting |
| F-003-RQ-004 | Protocol correctness is the runtime's responsibility, not the application's | Not applicable | Framing is handled by the runtime's HTTP implementation; the application adds no header that could leak internal detail |
| F-003-RQ-005 | Method-specific protocol semantics are honoured only to the extent the runtime provides them | Not applicable | No method restriction or allow-list exists; unsafe verbs are answered identically to safe ones |

| F-004-RQ-002 | The log statement interpolates the `hostname` and `port` constants, and the logged URL matches the endpoint that actually answers requests | Source inspection of the template literal plus a successful probe of the logged URL |
| F-004-RQ-003 | After more than 150 probe requests, stdout remains 41 bytes; the source contains exactly one `console.log` and no logging library, metrics client, or tracer | Byte comparison of the log file after probing; grep of the single `require` in the repository |

| Requirement ID | Input Parameters | Output / Response | Data Requirements |

| F-004-RQ-002 | The `hostname` and `port` constants | A URL string embedded in the readiness line | The same two constants that F-002 binds |
| F-004-RQ-003 | None | No further output for the process lifetime | No log file, rotation policy, or retention store exists |

**Performance criteria for F-004.** None declared. Because output is a single synchronous `console.log` at startup, logging adds no per-request work; there is no sampling rate, buffer size, flush interval, or log level to configure.

#### 2.2.5.4 Validation Rules

| Requirement ID | Business Rule as Implemented | Data Validation | Security and Compliance |
|----------------|------------------------------|-----------------|-------------------------|
| F-004-RQ-001 | Readiness is announced once per process lifetime and only on success — a failed bind yields a stderr stack trace instead (see F-002-RQ-004) | Not applicable — the message is composed from constants | The line discloses only the bind endpoint; no credential, token, or request data is logged |
| F-004-RQ-002 | The advertised endpoint is structurally identical to the bound endpoint | Not applicable | Prevents an operator from being directed to an endpoint the process is not actually serving |
| F-004-RQ-003 | Observability is intentionally bounded to liveness; correctness must be inferred from HTTP responses | Not applicable | No request attribute is logged, so no personal data can enter logs; no redaction, retention, or audit-trail obligation is declared in the repository |
