## 2.3 Feature Relationships

All five features live in one file, one module, and one process, so their relationships are statement-level rather than service-level. Every relationship documented below is visible in `server.js` as a direct data or control dependency; no inferred, planned, or conventional relationship is included.

### 2.3.1 Feature Dependency Map

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F005["F-005 Zero-Dependency<br/>Direct Execution Model<br/>server.js line 1"]
    F001["F-001 HTTP Server Instantiation<br/>server.js lines 6-10"]
    F002["F-002 Loopback Endpoint Binding<br/>and Listener Lifecycle<br/>server.js lines 3-4, 12-14"]
    F003["F-003 Uniform Fixed-Payload Response<br/>server.js lines 7-9"]
    F004["F-004 Startup Readiness Logging<br/>server.js line 13"]

    subgraph RuntimeLayer["Node.js runtime and host - external to the repository"]
        CoreHTTP["Core http module"]
        TCPStack["Host TCP-IP loopback stack"]
        StdOut["Process stdout stream"]
    end

    CoreHTTP -->|"module resolution"| F005
    CoreHTTP -->|"createServer factory"| F001
    CoreHTTP -->|"res API and header framing"| F003
    TCPStack -->|"loopback interface"| F002
    F005 -->|"prerequisite: http namespace bound"| F001
    F001 -->|"prerequisite: server instance"| F002
    F001 -->|"prerequisite: handler supplies res"| F003
    F002 -->|"prerequisite: socket bound before handler runs"| F003
    F002 -->|"trigger: listen callback"| F004
    F004 -->|"writes one line"| StdOut
```

| Feature | Depends On | Depended On By |
|---------|-----------|----------------|
| F-005 Zero-Dependency Direct Execution Model | Nothing in the repository — it is the dependency-graph root (line 1 is the first executed statement) | F-001 |
| F-001 HTTP Server Instantiation | F-005 (the `http` namespace must be bound before `createServer` is called) | F-002, F-003 |
| F-002 Endpoint Binding and Lifecycle | F-001 (`listen` is invoked on the instance created at line 6) | F-003, F-004 |
| F-003 Uniform Fixed-Payload Response | F-001 (the `res` object exists only inside the registered handler) and F-002 (no handler runs until the socket is bound) | Nothing — it is a leaf; its output leaves the system |
| F-004 Startup Readiness Logging | F-002 (the message is emitted from the `listen` callback, so only a successful bind produces it) | Nothing — it is a leaf; its output leaves the system |

The graph is a strict tree with two leaves and no cycles: there is no feedback path, no retry loop, and no feature that can re-enter another. This is why a bind failure (F-002-RQ-004) suppresses F-004 entirely and prevents F-003 from ever executing.

### 2.3.2 Requirement-Level Lifecycle Flow

The flow below annotates the single execution path of the process with the requirement IDs defined in 2.2, giving a direct visual traceability aid between behavior and requirement.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Launch["Operator runs: node server.js"] --> R502["F-005-RQ-002<br/>runs as committed, no install or build"]
    R502 --> R501["F-005-RQ-001<br/>single require of core http module"]
    R501 --> R101["F-001-RQ-001<br/>createServer registers one handler"]
    R101 --> R201["F-002-RQ-001<br/>listen binds 127.0.0.1 port 3000"]
    R201 --> PortFree{"Port 3000 available?"}
    PortFree -->|"no"| R204["F-002-RQ-004<br/>unhandled EADDRINUSE, exit code 1"]
    PortFree -->|"yes"| R401["F-004-RQ-001<br/>one readiness line on stdout"]
    R401 --> Idle["Listener idle, loopback only per F-002-RQ-002"]
    Idle --> Request["Any HTTP request: any method, path, query, body"]
    Request --> R102["F-001-RQ-002<br/>same handler, no routing or request inspection"]
    R102 --> R301["F-003-RQ-001<br/>status 200"]
    R301 --> R302["F-003-RQ-002<br/>Content-Type text/plain"]
    R302 --> R303["F-003-RQ-003<br/>14-byte body Hello, World!"]
    R303 --> R304["F-003-RQ-004<br/>runtime adds framing headers"]
    R304 --> Idle
    Idle --> Signal["SIGTERM or SIGINT delivered"]
    Signal --> R205["F-002-RQ-005<br/>immediate exit, no draining"]
```

### 2.3.3 Integration Points

| Integration Point | Direction | Features Involved | Observed Contract |
|-------------------|-----------|-------------------|-------------------|
| TCP listening socket at `127.0.0.1:3000` | Inbound | F-002 establishes it; F-001 and F-003 serve over it | HTTP/1.1 request/response with runtime-default keep-alive (`Keep-Alive: timeout=5` observed) |
| Node core `http` API (in-process) | Internal | F-005 binds the namespace; F-001 calls `createServer`; F-003 uses `res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader`, `res.end` | Direct library calls with no wrapper, adapter, or middleware layer |
| `process.stdout` | Outbound | F-004 | One newline-terminated plain-text line, written once per successful start |
| Operating-system process control | Bidirectional | F-002 | Exit code `1` with a stderr stack trace on bind failure; immediate exit on `SIGTERM` |

No other integration point exists. Searches of `server.js` for database clients, cache clients, message brokers, outbound HTTP clients, identity providers, secret managers, feature-flag services, file-system access, and log-aggregation clients all returned no matches, which is consistent with the integration inventory in **1.2.1.3 Enterprise Landscape Integration**. The GitHub remote recorded in `.git/config` is source hosting only and carries no runtime integration.

### 2.3.4 Shared Components

The "shared components" of this system are the module-scoped bindings that more than one feature reads. Each row was confirmed by locating every reference to the identifier in `server.js`.

| Shared Component | Defined At | Consumed By |
|------------------|-----------|-------------|
| `http` module namespace | Line 1 | F-001 only — the binding is referenced exactly once, at the `createServer` call on line 6 |
| `hostname` constant (`'127.0.0.1'`) | Line 3 | F-002 (bind argument, line 12) and F-004 (message interpolation, line 13) |
| `port` constant (`3000`) | Line 4 | F-002 (bind argument, line 12) and F-004 (message interpolation, line 13) |
| `server` instance | Line 6 | F-002 — the `listen` call on line 12 is its only consumer |
| `res` response object (handler parameter) | Line 6 | F-003 — lines 7, 8, and 9 are its only consumers |
| `req` request object (handler parameter) | Line 6 | No consumer — declared but never dereferenced anywhere in the file |
| `console` global | Line 13 | F-004 only |

Two consequences follow directly from this table. First, the `hostname` and `port` constants are the single point of coupling between the network layer and the observability layer, which is what makes the readiness message structurally consistent with the bound endpoint (F-004-RQ-002). Second, `req` is shared with nothing, which is the mechanical reason the response is request-agnostic (F-001-RQ-002).

### 2.3.5 Common Services

All common services consumed by the features are supplied by the runtime and host; **the repository contains no application-level shared service** — there is no logger module, configuration service, error-handling middleware, validation utility, authentication service, or dependency-injection container, because the entire application is one file with no abstractions.

| Common Service | Provided By | Serving Features |
|----------------|-------------|------------------|
| HTTP parsing, socket management, keep-alive handling, default framing headers, and `HEAD` body suppression | Node core `http` module | F-001, F-003 |
| Loopback network interface and TCP port allocation | Host operating system TCP/IP stack | F-002 |
| Standard output stream and the `console` global | Node.js process environment | F-004 |
| Event loop, module resolution, default signal disposition, and exit-code propagation | Node.js runtime | F-001 through F-005 |

Because every shared service is external to the repository, the features have no internal service contract to version, and there is no seam at which a service could be substituted — a constraint carried forward in 2.4.

## 2.4 Implementation Considerations

The considerations below are properties of the committed implementation, not recommendations or planned work. Where the repository declares nothing — as is the case for every performance target and every scaling policy — that silence is stated explicitly rather than filled in.

### 2.4.1 Technical Constraints

| Feature | Technical Constraint | Basis and Consequence |
|---------|---------------------|-----------------------|
| F-001 | Exactly one request handler exists and it cannot branch | Lines 6–10 contain no conditional; adding differentiated behavior requires editing the handler, since there is no router, middleware chain, or plugin seam |
| F-001 | Request data is structurally unreachable to application logic | `req` is declared but never dereferenced; any feature needing method, path, headers, or body must first introduce request inspection that does not exist today |
| F-002 | Bind address and port are compile-time literals | Lines 3–4 are constants and no `process.env`, CLI parsing, or config file is read; per-environment operation is impossible without a code change |
| F-002 | Port contention is fatal | No `server.on('error', ...)` handler exists; a second instance terminated with `EADDRINUSE` and exit code `1`, so port `3000` must be free before launch |
| F-002 | No lifecycle hooks exist | No `process.on('SIGTERM'/'SIGINT')` and no `server.close()`; `SIGTERM` terminated the process immediately with no draining, so restarts cannot be graceful |
| F-003 | The response is a single immutable literal | Line 9 emits a fixed 14-byte payload; there is no template engine, serializer, content negotiation, or data source to vary it |
| F-003 | Only the status code and one header are under application control | Lines 7–8 are the sole response-mutating statements; `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` are produced by the runtime and cannot be tuned from `server.js` |
| F-004 | Observability is a single stdout line | Line 13 is the only instrumentation; stdout remained 41 bytes after more than 150 requests, so there is no request-level signal to correlate with client behavior |
| F-005 | Startup is a module-load side effect with no exported API | `require` of the module returned an object with zero own keys while attempting the bind; there is no seam for injection, isolation, or in-process reuse |
| F-005 | No runtime version floor is declared | No `package.json` `engines`, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` exists; compatibility is asserted only by the fact that verification succeeded on Node v22.23.1 |
| F-005 | The artifact is unversioned and unpackaged | No manifest, lockfile, or git tag exists, so the only identifier for a given requirement baseline is a commit SHA (see 2.5.3) |

### 2.4.2 Performance Requirements and Observed Characteristics

The repository declares **no performance requirement for any feature**. There is no benchmark or load-test harness, no performance budget, no SLO or SLA document, and no tunable in `server.js` — no `keepAliveTimeout`, `headersTimeout`, `maxConnections`, backlog size, or compression setting is configured. The table therefore separates the declared column (uniformly empty) from measurements taken during verification, which characterise the verification host rather than any commitment of the system.

| Feature | Declared Performance Target | Observed Characteristic (verification host, loopback, Node v22.23.1) |
|---------|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| F-001 | None | 100 requests issued at concurrency 20 all returned `200` with no failures; handler work is three synchronous statements with no I/O |
| F-002 | None | The listener accepted connections within the 1.2 s settle window used after launch; no dependency graph or migration precedes the bind |
| F-003 | None | Response size is constant at 14 bytes; 10 loopback `GET /` samples had a median total time of 0.000161 s (min 0.000136 s, max 0.000943 s) |
| F-004 | None | One synchronous write at startup only; logging contributes no per-request cost |
| F-005 | None | Startup performs one module resolution and one bind; there is no install, build, or warm-up step |

Any figure above is reproducible only on comparable hardware and must not be read as a service level. Section **1.2.3.4 Key Performance Indicators** records the same finding: the system emits liveness and correctness signals, not performance metrics.

### 2.4.3 Scalability Considerations

| Feature | Scalability Consideration | Basis |
|---------|--------------------------|-------|
| F-001 | Concurrency is bounded by a single event loop; requests are serviced by one handler in one thread | No `cluster`, `worker_threads`, or child-process usage anywhere in `server.js`; verified as a single `node server.js` process while serving concurrent traffic |
| F-001 | Statelessness means the handler itself imposes no scaling ceiling — nothing is shared, locked, or accumulated across requests | 50 sequential requests produced one unique response; no cross-request variable exists |
| F-002 | Horizontal scaling on a single host is blocked by the fixed port | Two instances cannot coexist: the second exits with `EADDRINUSE`; running more requires editing the port constant |
| F-002 | The loopback bind precludes load balancing, reverse proxying, or service-mesh placement | A non-loopback probe was refused; no proxy, ingress, or discovery configuration exists in the repository |
| F-003 | Payload size is constant, so egress volume scales linearly with request count and nothing else | Body is a 14-byte literal; no pagination, streaming, or compression path exists |
| F-004 | Log volume is constant per process regardless of traffic | Exactly one line per successful start; stdout size was unchanged after sustained probing |
| F-005 | The process is the unit of failure and of capacity, with no supervisor or restart policy | No process manager, container, orchestrator, or systemd unit is present; a terminated process leaves no instance serving |

### 2.4.4 Security Implications

| Feature | Security Implication | Basis |
|---------|---------------------|-------|
| F-001 | No authentication or authorization gate precedes the handler; every caller that can open the socket is served identically | No credential, token, session, or access-control code exists in `server.js` |
| F-001 | The injection and deserialization attack surface is empty because no request data is read, parsed, or interpolated | Grep for `req.<property>` returned no match; a `POST` body and a custom header were ignored during probing |
| F-002 | The loopback bind is the **only** security control in the repository, and it is topological rather than credential-based | A request to the host's non-loopback address on port `3000` failed to connect; changing one constant would remove this control entirely |
| F-002 | Traffic is plain HTTP with no transport security | Only the `http` module is required; no `https`/`tls` usage, certificate material, or HSTS behavior exists |
| F-002 | A bind failure writes a stack trace to stderr that discloses the bind address, port, `errno`, and Node version | Captured verbatim during the port-contention test; no secret material appears in the trace |
| F-003 | Responses carry no security headers and no rate limiting or CORS policy | Exactly one `setHeader` call exists, and it sets `Content-Type`; no middleware of any kind is present |
| F-003 | The payload itself carries no sensitive data — it is a fixed English greeting with no environment or diagnostic detail | Line 9 is a string literal |
| F-004 | The single log line cannot leak request or credential data because no request attribute is ever logged | Line 13 interpolates only the two binding constants |
| F-005 | Zero third-party code means no transitive supply-chain exposure and nothing for a dependency audit to scan; conversely there is no SBOM, signature, or provenance attestation | One `require`, resolving to a Node built-in; no manifest, lockfile, or `node_modules/` |
| F-005 | No `LICENSE` accompanies the artifact, so no redistribution or usage rights are granted | Existence test for `LICENSE`, `LICENSE.md`, and `SECURITY.md` all failed |

### 2.4.5 Maintenance Requirements

| Feature | Maintenance Requirement | Basis |
|---------|------------------------|-------|
| F-001 | Any behavioral change must be made by editing the handler in place; regression risk is unmitigated because no test asserts current behavior | No test directory or runner configuration exists in the repository, and the tracked `test.js` contains no assertion |
| F-002 | Changing the endpoint requires a source edit and a commit, with no configuration path and no rollout mechanism | Constants at lines 3–4; no `.env`, `config/`, or deployment descriptor |
| F-002 | Operators must verify port availability before launch and must accept abrupt restarts | `EADDRINUSE` exit code `1` and immediate `SIGTERM` termination were both measured |
| F-003 | The response contract is verifiable only over the network, byte-for-byte; there is no schema or contract test to maintain | Verification required executing the process and probing it; the module exports nothing to assert against |
| F-004 | Operational monitoring depends on capturing process stdout; no log file, rotation, or shipping configuration is provided | `console.log` writes to stdout only; no logging dependency exists |
| F-005 | Runtime upgrades are unconstrained and unverified — nothing pins or checks the Node version | No `engines`, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version`; no CI job exercises the code on any version |
| F-005 | Code quality is unenforced: no linter, formatter, type checker, or CI quality gate exists | Existence tests for ESLint, Prettier, `.editorconfig`, `tsconfig.json`, and all CI configurations failed |
| F-005 | Change history is the only maintenance record — there is no changelog, release note, or version field | Three commits, zero tags; `README.md` contains only the repository name |

Because the repository has neither tests nor pipelines, every maintenance activity above is manual. The acceptance criteria in 2.2 are, in practice, the only executable regression suite available for this system, which is why each one is expressed as a reproducible command-level check.

### 2.5.5 Requirement Versioning and Change Control

The repository provides no requirement-versioning mechanism: there is no `package.json` version field, no git tag (`git tag -l` returns nothing), no `CHANGELOG.md`, and no release notes. Requirement versions are therefore pinned to commit identity, which is the only durable identifier available.

| Governance Attribute | Observed State |
|----------------------|----------------|
| Requirement-set version | Designated **1.0 (as-built baseline)**, pinned to HEAD commit `43ed37c` on branch `2907_01`. The baseline is unchanged in substance from `06492d7`: `server.js` is the same blob (`320a75a`) at both commits |
| Origin of the requirement set | Commit `06492d7` ("Add files via upload") introduced `server.js` and therefore introduced all twenty requirements simultaneously; it is now the parent of HEAD |
| Prior commit | `241598b` ("Initial commit") added `README.md` only and introduces no requirement |
| Most recent commit | `43ed37c` ("Create test.js", 2026-07-30) added the 13-byte `test.js`, which implements, changes, and retires no requirement; the requirement set is identical before and after it |
| Branch state | The branches have diverged: `main` (= `origin/main`) is at `06492d7` with two tracked files, while `2907_01` (= `origin/2907_01`) is one commit ahead at `43ed37c` with three. The working tree is clean, so no in-flight requirement change exists on either branch |
| Release identifiers | None — zero tags, no version field, no published package |
| Change-control artifacts in the repository | None — no `CODEOWNERS`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, pull-request or issue template, or CI gate that could enforce review of a requirement change |
| Practical change procedure | Any requirement change is a direct edit to `server.js` followed by a commit; this specification's requirement IDs must be re-verified against the new head, since no test suite will detect drift. Commit `43ed37c` is a worked example of that gap: a file was added, unreviewed and ungated, that fails on execution without affecting any requirement |

### 2.5.6 Assumptions and Constraints Register

#### 2.5.6.1 Assumptions

| ID | Assumption | Basis |
|----|-----------|-------|
| A-01 | A Node.js runtime exposing the core `http` module with CommonJS resolution is present on the host | `require('http')` is the only import; no version floor is declared anywhere, and verification succeeded on Node v22.23.1 |
| A-02 | TCP port `3000` is free on the host at launch | The port is a literal with no fallback; contention was measured to be fatal |
| A-03 | The loopback interface is available and clients originate on the same host | Bind address literal `127.0.0.1`; a non-loopback probe was refused |
| A-04 | The operator launches the service by invoking the file directly with `node` | No `package.json` script, `Procfile`, or process-manager configuration exists |
| A-05 | The operator captures process stdout in order to observe readiness | The readiness line is the only success signal and it is written to stdout |
| A-06 | This catalog is descriptive of as-built behavior at HEAD `43ed37c` — behaviourally identical to `06492d7`, whose `server.js` blob is unchanged — not an authored product backlog | The repository contains no requirements artifact of any kind (2.1.1.1) |
| A-07 | Quoted measurements characterise the verification environment, not a portable commitment | No performance target exists in the repository (2.4.2) |

#### 2.5.6.2 Constraints

| ID | Constraint | Basis |
|----|-----------|-------|
| C-01 | The endpoint is fixed at `127.0.0.1:3000` and cannot be reconfigured without a code change | Literal constants at lines 3–4; no configuration source is read |
| C-02 | Exactly one response exists — one status, one content type, one 14-byte payload | Lines 7–9; no branching and no data source |
| C-03 | There is no error handling, retry, or fallback; bind failure terminates the process | No `server.on('error')`; measured exit code `1` on `EADDRINUSE` |
| C-04 | Shutdown is abrupt, with no draining of in-flight requests | No signal handler and no `server.close()`; measured immediate exit on `SIGTERM` |
| C-05 | The module exports nothing and starts the listener on load, so it cannot be unit-tested or embedded | `require` returned zero own keys while attempting the bind |
| C-06 | There is no automated verification, linting, type checking, or CI gate | Existence tests for all test, lint, type, and CI configurations failed; the tracked `test.js` contains no test or assertion |
| C-07 | Transport is plain HTTP and the endpoint is unauthenticated; loopback binding is the only control | Only the `http` module is required; no credential or TLS code exists |
| C-08 | The artifact is unversioned, unpackaged, and unlicensed | No manifest, tag, changelog, or `LICENSE` file |
| C-09 | Capacity and fault domain are a single foreground process on one event loop | No `cluster`/`worker_threads`; no supervisor or orchestrator configuration |
| C-10 | Product documentation is limited to the repository name | `README.md` contains only the heading `# July2026_hello_world_repo` |

# 3. Technology Stack

## 3.1 Programming Languages

The language inventory for this system is exhaustive rather than representative. The repository tracks exactly three files — `server.js`, `README.md`, and `test.js`, 382 bytes in total — and contains no subdirectories, so every line of source that exists is accounted for below. `server.js` is the complete runnable application; `README.md` carries a single heading and no instructions; `test.js` is an inert placeholder that is never loaded by the application and is not part of it.

### 3.1.1 Language Inventory by Component

| Component / Artifact | Language | Edition or Dialect | Role in the System |
|---|---|---|---|
| `server.js` (14 lines, 342 bytes, mode `100644`) | JavaScript | ES2015 (ES6) syntax, CommonJS module format | The entire application: server creation, response generation, loopback binding, readiness log |
| `README.md` (1 line, 27 bytes, mode `100644`) | Markdown | Single ATX H1 heading (`# July2026_hello_world_repo`) | Repository identification only — no prerequisites, install steps, or run instructions |
| `test.js` (2 lines, 13 bytes, mode `100644`) | JavaScript | Two bare identifier expression statements (`asdsa`, `asdasd`); no module syntax at all | **Not part of the application.** Syntactically valid — `node --check test.js` exits 0 — but it exports nothing, is imported by nothing, and throws `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` (exit code 1) when executed |
| Host runtime (not authored in this repository) | Node.js JavaScript runtime | Version **not declared** by the repository | Supplies the JavaScript engine and the built-in `http` module that `server.js` requires on line 1 |

There is no second implementation language at any tier — no separate frontend, mobile, native, or scripting component. A file-type census across the tracked inventory yields exactly two `.js` files and one `.md` file and nothing else; only one of those `.js` files, `server.js`, is application source. A repository-wide search for `*.sql`, `*.yaml`, `*.yml`, `*.json`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `*.cfg`, `*.xml`, and `.env*` files returned no results, so the repository holds no configuration or serialization artifacts in any language either.

The absence of other language ecosystems was confirmed by existence-testing their conventional project descriptors rather than inferred. None of the following is present: `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `Pipfile`, `setup.py`, `.python-version` (Python); `tsconfig.json`, `jsconfig.json` or any `.ts`/`.tsx` file (TypeScript); `go.mod` (Go); `Cargo.toml` (Rust); `pom.xml`, `build.gradle` (JVM); `Gemfile` (Ruby); `composer.json` (PHP); `Package.swift`, `*.xcodeproj`, `Podfile` (Swift/Objective-C); `*.gradle`, `*.kt` sources (Kotlin); `*.csproj`, `*.sln` (.NET); `pubspec.yaml` (Dart); `mix.exs` (Elixir); `CMakeLists.txt` (C/C++). JavaScript is therefore the sole programming language of the system, and it is used **untyped** — there are no TypeScript annotations and no JSDoc type tags anywhere in the source.

### 3.1.2 Language Edition and Module System

The newest syntax the application source uses is ES2015. That is not an estimate; each construct was counted directly in `server.js`.

| Syntax Construct Observed | Occurrences | Location in `server.js` | Introduced By |
|---|---|---|---|
| `const` binding | 4 | Lines 1, 3, 4, 6 | ES2015 |
| Arrow function | 2 | Line 6 (request handler), line 12 (listen callback) | ES2015 |
| Template literal | 1 | Line 13 (readiness message) | ES2015 |
| `require()` module import | 1 | Line 1 (`require('http')`) | CommonJS (pre-ES2015 module system) |

Equally significant is what is absent: no `var` or `let`, no `function` keyword, no `class`, no `async`/`await` or `Promise`, no optional chaining (`?.`), nullish coalescing (`??`), or spread (`...`), no `'use strict'` directive, and no shebang line. ES2015 is consequently both the floor and the ceiling of the language edition in use — the file is syntactically valid on any ES2015-capable JavaScript engine, and no ES2016-or-later feature creates a modern-runtime requirement.

`test.js` does not shift that floor or ceiling. It contains no declaration, no operator, and no module syntax whatsoever — its two lines are bare identifier expression statements, which have been valid JavaScript since ES1 — so the language-edition analysis above remains a complete description of the repository's syntax surface.

The module system is CommonJS, used in its most minimal form. The application source contains exactly one `require(` occurrence, whose target is the bare specifier `'http'` (not the `node:http` prefixed form), and the tracked inventory contains zero ESM `import`/`export` statements, zero dynamic `import()`, and zero `module.exports` or `exports.` assignments — including in `test.js`, which neither imports nor exports anything. `server.js` therefore imports one thing and exports nothing: it is an entrypoint, not a reusable module.

```javascript
const http = require('http');                    // line 1 — CommonJS import of a built-in
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => { // line 6 — ES2015 arrow function
```

### 3.1.3 Selection Criteria and Justification

The language choice is inseparable from the system's defining property: it must run exactly as committed, with nothing installed and nothing built. JavaScript on Node.js is the only mainstream combination that satisfies every one of the following observed criteria simultaneously.

- **Standard-library HTTP capability.** The runtime's built-in `http` module provides a production-grade HTTP/1.1 server without any package installation, which is what allows the dependency count to be zero (feature F-005, Zero-Dependency Direct Execution Model). A language whose HTTP support lives in a third-party package would have forced a manifest, a lockfile, and an install step into the repository.
- **Zero-toolchain executability.** A JavaScript source file is interpreted directly by `node`; there is no compile, link, or transpile phase to configure. This is corroborated by the complete absence of build tooling (no `Makefile`, `webpack`, `rollup`, `vite`, `esbuild`, `babel`, or `swc` configuration) documented in section 3.6.
- **Maximum runtime portability within the language.** By confining itself to ES2015 syntax and to long-stable core APIs, the source imposes no lower bound tied to a recent runtime release, which matters precisely because the repository declares no runtime version.
- **Canonical-example fidelity.** As established in section 1.2.1.1, the implementation is functionally equivalent to the "Create an HTTP Server" example published in the Node.js documentation, differing chiefly in module system — this repository uses CommonJS `require('http')` where the current documentation sample uses ESM `import`. Choosing the language and idiom of the canonical example makes the artifact immediately legible to any reader familiar with Node.js.
- **Implicit CommonJS default.** Because no `package.json` exists, Node.js interprets a `.js` file as CommonJS by default, so the chosen module idiom needs no declaration to work (see 3.1.4).

For completeness against the default technology stack referenced in this document's authoring guidance: no Python, TypeScript, Swift, Kotlin, or Objective-C source exists in this repository, and no toolchain descriptor for any of them is present. Documenting those languages as part of this system would be inaccurate, so they are recorded here only as verified non-participants.

### 3.1.4 Language-Level Constraints and Dependencies

| Constraint | Evidence | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| The source **must** be evaluated as CommonJS | Executing the identical source in ESM scope fails at runtime with `ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope`, while `node --check` on an `.mjs` copy of the same bytes exits 0 | The incompatibility is semantic, not syntactic. It is satisfied *implicitly* today because no `package.json` exists, so `.js` defaults to CommonJS. Introducing `"type": "module"` or renaming the file to `.mjs` would break startup. |
| No language or runtime version floor is declared | No `package.json` `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, or `.tool-versions` exists | Runtime selection is entirely an operator decision. Compatibility is asserted only by verification succeeding on Node.js v22.23.1 (consistent with 2.4.1 and assumption A-01). |
| No tracked file is a directly executable script | All three files are Git mode `100644` with no `#!` interpreter line | `server.js` must be launched through the interpreter as `node server.js`; it cannot be invoked as `./server.js`. |
| Syntactic validity is not evidence of executability | `node --check` exits 0 for both `.js` files, yet `node test.js` exits 1 with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` | The only pre-flight check available in the repository (3.6.4) proves parseability, not correctness; a `.js` file can be tracked, parse cleanly, and still fail immediately on evaluation. |
| No static typing and no compile-time verification | No `.ts` source, no `tsconfig.json`, no JSDoc type annotations | All errors — including a failed port bind — surface only at runtime; there is no compile-time or lint-time guarantee (no linter or formatter configuration exists either). |
| No language-level dependency graph | The sole `require` target resolves to a runtime built-in: `require('module').isBuiltin('http')` returns `true` and `require.resolve('http')` returns `http` with no filesystem path | There is no module resolution against `node_modules`, nothing to download, and no version to pin at the language level (see 3.3). |

The practical dependency chain of the language layer is therefore exactly two links long: the JavaScript source depends on a Node.js runtime, and the runtime depends on the host operating system. Nothing else intervenes.

## 3.2 Frameworks &amp; Libraries

This system uses no application framework and exactly one library — the Node.js core `http` module, which ships inside the runtime rather than being installed. Everything the application does at the protocol level is delegated to that module; everything the application contributes is thirteen lines of glue around it.

### 3.2.1 Framework Inventory

No web, application, or utility framework is present. This was established by case-insensitive pattern matching for more than eighty widely used package names across all three tracked files — `server.js`, `README.md`, and `test.js` — which produced zero matches, and corroborated by the absence of any dependency manifest that could declare one. The scan surface grew from two files to three when `test.js` was added, and the result did not change: that file contains no package name, no import, and no framework token of any kind.

| Framework / Library Category | Representative Packages Checked | Status in This Repository |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP / web framework | `express`, `koa`, `fastify`, `nest`, `hapi`, `restify` | Absent — no match in source, no manifest to declare one |
| Real-time / alternative protocol | `socket.io`, `ws`, `graphql`, `apollo` | Absent |
| HTTP client | `axios`, `node-fetch`, `got`, `superagent`, `undici` | Absent — the application makes no outbound HTTP calls |
| Logging / observability | `winston`, `pino`, `bunyan`, `morgan`, `debug`, `prom-client`, `opentelemetry`, `sentry`, `datadog`, `newrelic`, `elastic` | Absent — `console.log` is used directly (line 13) |
| Configuration / CLI | `dotenv`, `config`, `yargs`, `commander` | Absent — the two runtime parameters are inline literals (lines 3–4) |
| Validation / utility | `zod`, `joi`, `ajv`, `lodash`, `moment`, `dayjs`, `uuid` | Absent |
| Security middleware | `helmet`, `cors`, `cookie-parser`, `session`, `passport`, `jsonwebtoken`, `bcrypt`, `argon2` | Absent |
| Test frameworks and runners | `jest`, `mocha`, `chai`, `vitest`, `ava`, `tap`, `jasmine`, `supertest`, `sinon` | Absent — no framework is referenced anywhere, including in `test.js` (6.6.1) |
| AI / LLM frameworks | `langchain`, `openai`, `anthropic` | Absent |

The consequence, already stated architecturally in section 1.2.2.3 and at the integration level in 2.3.3, is that there is no middleware pipeline, no router, and no plugin system — the request handler registered on line 6 *is* the entire request-processing layer, invoked directly by the runtime with no wrapper or adapter in between.

### 3.2.2 The Sole Library: Node.js Core `http`

That `http` is a runtime built-in rather than an installed package was verified programmatically, not assumed: `require('module').isBuiltin('http')` returns `true`, `require('module').builtinModules.includes('http')` returns `true`, and `require.resolve('http')` returns the bare string `http` with no filesystem path. There is no `node_modules` directory to search and no package resolution step at startup.

The API surface the application actually consumes is small enough to enumerate completely. Each of the following symbols appears exactly once.

| API Symbol | Line | Responsibility Delegated to the Runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `http.createServer(handler)` | 6 | Instantiates the HTTP/1.1 server and registers the single inline request handler |
| `res.statusCode = 200` | 7 | Sets the response status on the runtime-provided response object |
| `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')` | 8 | Sets the only application-controlled response header |
| `res.end('Hello, World!\n')` | 9 | Writes the 14-byte body and terminates the response |
| `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` | 12 | Binds TCP port 3000 on `127.0.0.1` and registers the readiness callback |
| `console.log(...)` | 13 | Emits the single readiness line to standard output |

Two negative findings sharpen this picture: the source performs **zero** `req.*` accesses (the request object is accepted as a parameter and never inspected) and **zero** `process.*` accesses (no environment variables, no `process.exit`, no signal handlers). The application is therefore write-only with respect to the HTTP transaction and inert with respect to the process environment.

Everything else observable on the wire is supplied by the runtime, not by application code. During a verified run, the response carried `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, and `Content-Length: 14` headers that appear nowhere in the source — these are Node.js `http` defaults, consistent with the runtime-supplied services catalogued in 2.3.5.

The runtime's own embedded components are the de facto lower layers of this stack. The versions below were read from `process.versions` on the runtime used for verification and are **environment observations, not repository-declared versions** — the repository pins nothing.

| Embedded Component | Version Observed (Node.js v22.23.1) | Relevance to This System |
|---|---|---|
| V8 JavaScript engine | 12.4.254.21-node.56 | Executes the ES2015 source |
| llhttp | 9.4.2 | The HTTP/1.1 request parser inside the `http` module — all protocol parsing happens here |
| libuv | 1.51.0 | Event loop, TCP socket handling, and the single-threaded concurrency model |
| OpenSSL | 3.5.7 | Present in the runtime but **unused** — the source never requires `https` or `tls`, so traffic is plaintext |
| Module ABI | 127 | Irrelevant in practice: no native addons are loaded because there are no dependencies |

### 3.2.3 Compatibility Requirements

The compatibility contract for this system reduces to three conditions, all of which are met by every currently supported Node.js release line:

1. **A Node.js runtime that exposes the core `http` module** — the sole import on line 1.
2. **CommonJS evaluation of the `.js` file** — a hard requirement demonstrated in 3.1.4; satisfied implicitly because no `package.json` exists.
3. **An ES2015-capable engine** — trivially satisfied, since the source uses no syntax newer than ES2015.

Empirically, all six consumed symbols are long-stable APIs: during the verified run the process wrote exactly 41 bytes to standard output and **0 bytes to standard error**, so the runtime emitted no deprecation or experimental-feature warnings for any of them. The negotiated protocol was HTTP/1.1 (`curl` reported `http_version=1.1`, status `200`, body size `14`); no HTTP/2 or TLS/ALPN path exists.

Because the repository declares no engine range, runtime-line selection is an operator decision. The following release-line facts are **external context** gathered from published Node.js release information as of this writing, aligned with the figures already recorded in section 1.2.1.3 — they are not commitments made by this repository.

| Node.js Line | Phase (as of July 2026) | Supported Through | Bearing on This System |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24.x | Active LTS | 2028-04-30 | The recommended target for any long-lived deployment |
| 22.x | Maintenance LTS | 2027-04-30 | The line used for all verification in this specification (v22.23.1); still receives security fixes |
| 26.x | Current (latest 26.5.0, released May 2026; LTS promotion expected October 2026) | 2029-04-30 | Usable, but a Current line is conventionally reserved for development and testing |
| 25.x / 20.x | End of Life (2026-06-01 / 2026-04-30 respectively) | — | Not suitable: no further security patches for the runtime that performs all HTTP parsing here |

Forward compatibility risk is low but non-zero and, notably, unguarded. Node.js 26 removed long-deprecated internals such as the `_stream_*` modules and enabled the Temporal API by default; the source references neither, so those specific changes have no effect. However, since there is no test suite, no CI pipeline, and no declared engine range (see 3.6), any future runtime regression would be discovered only by manually launching the server — a gap consistent with the maintenance posture described in 2.4.5.

### 3.2.4 Justification, Trade-offs, and Security Implications

**Why no framework.** The functional requirement set is a single fixed response on a single loopback port. A framework's value — routing, middleware composition, negotiation, validation, plugin lifecycles — has no requirement to serve here, while its cost would be immediate and structural: a `package.json`, a lockfile, a `node_modules` tree, an install step before first run, and an ongoing dependency-update obligation. Using core `http` alone preserves the property that makes this artifact what it is: the file executes exactly as committed. This is the technology-layer expression of feature F-005 (Zero-Dependency Direct Execution Model).

**What that costs.** The trade-offs are real and should be understood before this code is extended: there is no routing (every method and path receives the identical response), no request parsing or validation, no error-handling middleware, no structured logging, no graceful-shutdown handling, and no configuration layer. Any of these would have to be written by hand against core `http` or introduced together with the first third-party dependency — which would simultaneously introduce the install workflow the project currently does not have.

**Security implications.**

- **No third-party attack surface, and nothing to audit.** With zero installed packages there is no transitive supply-chain exposure; correspondingly, `npm audit` cannot run at all (it fails with `ENOLOCK` — no lockfile), and as noted in 2.4.4 there is no SBOM, signature, or provenance attestation either. The absence of risk here comes from the absence of dependencies, not from any control.
- **All protocol-level vulnerability exposure sits in the runtime.** Because parsing and framing are handled entirely by the runtime's `http`/llhttp implementation, any HTTP-parser, V8, or crypto CVE affecting this deployment is remediated by upgrading Node.js and by no other means. With no declared engine floor and no automated update path, keeping the runtime on a supported line is a purely manual operator responsibility.
- **No application-level input handling to exploit.** The handler never reads the request method, URL, headers, or body (zero `req.*` accesses), so there is no injection, deserialization, or parsing logic in application code. The one deliberate control is topological: `server.listen` binds `127.0.0.1`, restricting reachability to same-host clients (2.4.4).
- **No transport security.** Although the runtime embeds OpenSSL 3.5.7, the application requires neither `https` nor `tls`; all traffic is plaintext HTTP/1.1. There is likewise no `helmet`-style header hardening, CORS policy, or rate limiting — the only response headers are the one the application sets and the runtime's defaults.

## 3.3 Open Source Dependencies

The system declares no open-source dependencies. It consumes exactly one open-source component — the Node.js runtime itself — and consumes it as an installed platform rather than as a versioned, resolvable package. This sub-section records the audit that establishes that claim, the resulting registry posture, and the licensing and supply-chain consequences.

### 3.3.1 Dependency Manifest and Lockfile Audit

Every conventional JavaScript dependency descriptor was existence-tested in the repository root, which is also the only directory the repository has. All are absent.

| Artifact Class | Paths Tested | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Package manifest | `package.json` | Absent |
| Lockfiles | `package-lock.json`, `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, `yarn.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `bun.lockb` | All absent |
| Workspace / monorepo | `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `lerna.json`, `turbo.json`, `nx.json` | All absent |
| Installed dependency tree | `node_modules/` | Absent |
| Registry & client config | `.npmrc`, `.yarnrc`, `.yarnrc.yml` | All absent |
| Runtime version pins | `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.tool-versions` | All absent |
| Alternative runtime manifests | `deno.json`, `deno.lock`, `import_map.json`, `jsr.json` | All absent |

Because there is no manifest, every dependency class is empty by construction rather than by policy:

| Dependency Class | Count | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Direct runtime dependencies | 0 | The sole `require` target resolves to a runtime built-in, not a package |
| Development dependencies | 0 | No manifest; no test, lint, format, or build tooling configuration exists |
| Peer / optional dependencies | 0 | No manifest in which to declare them |
| Transitive dependencies | 0 | Verified empirically: `npm ls --all` in the repository root prints an empty tree |
| Bundled / vendored code | 0 | The repository tracks three files totalling 382 bytes — `server.js` (342 B), `README.md` (27 B), and `test.js` (13 B) — and no vendor directory exists. `test.js` requires nothing, so it adds no dependency of any kind |

This is the technology-layer evidence behind requirement F-005-RQ-001 (exactly one import, and that import is a Node.js core module).

### 3.3.2 Package Registry Posture

No package registry participates in this project's lifecycle. The public npm registry — the default source for Node.js packages — is never contacted, and no alternate or private registry is configured, since `.npmrc` does not exist. Three measured probes confirm that there is no install workflow to speak of:

```text
npm ls --all   ->  (empty)
npm audit      ->  npm error code ENOLOCK / This command requires an existing lockfile.
npm install    ->  npm error code ENOENT / Could not read package.json
```

The `npm` client is present in the verification environment (version 11.18.0) but has nothing to act upon. Practically, this means the first-run path requires no network access at all: obtaining the source and starting the server involve no dependency download, no integrity verification, and no post-install script execution. The only network operation anywhere in the lifecycle is retrieving the source itself from its GitHub origin, which is source hosting with no runtime role (see 1.2.1.3 and 3.4.4).

### 3.3.3 The Single Upstream Open-Source Component

The one open-source project this system depends on is Node.js. It is supplied by the host, and its identity is therefore an environment observation rather than a repository declaration. On the runtime used for all verification in this specification, that identity resolves as follows.

| Attribute | Observed Value | How Obtained |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime | Node.js v22.23.1, LTS line codename `Jod` | `process.release.name`, `process.release.lts` |
| Upstream source archive | `nodejs.org/download/release/v22.23.1/node-v22.23.1.tar.gz` | `process.release.sourceUrl` — confirms an official upstream release, not a fork |
| Installed distribution build | OS package `nodejs` version `22.23.1-1nodesource1` | Host package database |
| Bundled OSS components | V8 12.4.254.21-node.56, llhttp 9.4.2, libuv 1.51.0, OpenSSL 3.5.7 | `process.versions` |

An important distinction: those bundled components are transitively *present* in the execution environment, but they are not dependencies of this project in any actionable sense. The repository cannot pin, upgrade, or substitute them — they arrive and depart with whichever Node.js build the operator installs. The application's only interface to any of them is indirect: the core `http` module it requires is implemented on top of llhttp and libuv (see 3.2.2).

### 3.3.4 Licensing and Supply-Chain Implications

**Licensing.** The repository itself publishes no license terms: `LICENSE`, `LICENSE.md`, `LICENSE.txt`, `COPYING`, and `NOTICE` are all absent. As noted in 2.4.4, this leaves downstream reuse and redistribution rights undefined for the project's own 342 bytes of source. On the inbound side there is no compliance burden at all — the Node.js distribution ships a permissive MIT-style license (the license text bundled with the installed distribution grants unrestricted use, copying, modification, publication, distribution, sublicensing, and sale), and because the repository vendors no third-party code, there is nothing that would require an attribution or NOTICE file.

**Supply-chain security.** The posture is unusual and worth stating precisely in both directions:

- **Nothing to compromise upstream.** With zero installable packages there is no exposure to typosquatting, dependency confusion, malicious `postinstall` scripts, compromised maintainer accounts, or lockfile drift. There is no transitive graph to review and no install-time code execution.
- **Nothing to attest, either.** As recorded in 2.4.4, there is no SBOM, no signature, and no provenance attestation, and `npm audit` cannot even run (`ENOLOCK`). The absence of findings reflects the absence of a scannable artifact, not a clean scan.
- **Patch responsibility is displaced onto the runtime.** Since all HTTP parsing and socket handling live in Node.js, every security patch relevant to this service arrives through a runtime upgrade — an operator action that is neither declared (no engine floor) nor automated (no CI, see 3.6).
- **The first dependency is a threshold decision.** Adding any package would simultaneously introduce a manifest, a lockfile, a `node_modules` tree, a pre-run install step, and the entire supply-chain surface this project currently does not have. That trade-off should be made deliberately rather than incidentally.

## 3.4 Third-Party Services

The system integrates with no third-party service of any kind. It calls no external API, delegates no authentication, reports to no monitoring backend, and consumes no managed cloud resource. This is verifiable from two independent angles: the source imports exactly one module (a runtime built-in) and therefore instantiates no client of any kind, and the repository contains no credential, endpoint, or service-configuration artifact that such an integration would require.

### 3.4.1 External APIs and Outbound Integrations

No outbound integration exists. Pattern matching across all three tracked files — `server.js`, `README.md`, and `test.js` — found no reference to any HTTP client (`axios`, `node-fetch`, `got`, `superagent`, `undici`), messaging or queueing client (`amqplib`, `kafkajs`, `bull`, `agenda`), email or communications provider (`nodemailer`, `twilio`), or payment provider (`stripe`). The third file adds nothing to the scan surface: `test.js` contains no identifier beyond the two undefined bare words `asdsa` and `asdasd`. Structurally, the single import on line 1 of `server.js` is used only to *create a server* (`http.createServer`, `server.listen`); it is never used to issue a request. The application makes no DNS lookup and opens no outbound socket, so it requires no egress allowance in any network policy.

### 3.4.2 Authentication and Identity Services

No authentication service, identity provider, or credential-handling library is present. Verified absent from the source: `auth0`, `passport`, `jsonwebtoken`, `oauth`, `openid`, `saml`, `session`, `cookie-parser`, `bcrypt`, and `argon2`. Verified absent from the repository: `.env`, `.env.example`, `.env.local`, `.env.production`, `credentials/`, `secrets/`, `.secrets/`, and `serviceAccount.json`. Reinforcing this, the source performs zero `process.*` accesses, so it reads no environment variables — even if a secret were injected into the process environment, no code path exists that could consume it.

Access control is consequently not identity-based at all. As established in 2.4.4, the single control is topological: `server.listen` binds `127.0.0.1`, so only same-host clients can reach the endpoint (a probe from a non-loopback host address was refused during verification, per requirement F-002-RQ-002). Every request that does reach the listener receives an identical `200` response with no challenge of any kind.

### 3.4.3 Monitoring, Logging, and Observability Services

No observability service or agent is integrated. Verified absent: `sentry`, `datadog`, `newrelic`, `elastic`, `prom-client`, `opentelemetry`, and every structured-logging library (`winston`, `pino`, `bunyan`, `morgan`, `debug`).

Observability is limited to what the standard library provides directly:

| Signal | Mechanism | Scope Observed |
|---|---|---|
| Readiness | `console.log` on line 13 → standard output | Exactly one 41-byte line at startup (feature F-004) |
| Per-request telemetry | None | Standard output remained at 41 bytes after sustained request traffic during verification (F-004-RQ-003) |
| Errors | Runtime default | A failed bind produces an unhandled `error` event, a stack trace on standard error, and exit code 1 (F-002-RQ-004) |
| Metrics, traces, health endpoint | None | No metrics endpoint, no tracing instrumentation, and no dedicated health route exist |

Whatever aggregation exists is therefore supplied by whatever captures the process's standard streams — a shell, a supervisor, or a container log driver — none of which the repository configures.

### 3.4.4 Cloud Services and Managed Infrastructure

No cloud provider SDK, managed service, or platform binding is present. Verified absent from the source: `aws-sdk`, `@aws-sdk`, `googleapis`, `@google-cloud`, `azure`, `@azure`, `firebase`, and `supabase`. Verified absent from the repository: `aws-exports.js`, `firebase.json`, `amplify/`, and every platform deployment descriptor (`vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `app.yaml`, `app.json`, `fly.toml`, `railway.json`, `render.yaml`, `heroku.yml`, `Procfile`) — see 3.6.3 and 3.6.4 for the full deployment-tooling audit.

For completeness against the default technology stack referenced in this document's authoring guidance: there is no AWS, Auth0, or any other managed-service integration in this repository, and no artifact from which one could be inferred. These are recorded as verified non-participants only.

The one external system that genuinely exists in this project's lifecycle is its source host. The Git remote points at a GitHub repository, and its role is confined to source distribution — it has no runtime coupling whatsoever, as already stated in 1.2.1.3. One operational caution belongs here: the remote URL configured in this checkout is a token-bearing HTTPS URL, so the local Git configuration is credential-sensitive and must not be shared, published, or copied into images or documentation. The token grants repository access only and has no relationship to the running service, which requires no credential to operate.

### 3.4.5 The Actual Integration Surface

With third-party services excluded, the complete integration surface of the running system is four interfaces, all of them local to the host. This restates, at the technology layer, the integration points catalogued in 2.3.3.

| Interface | Direction | Technology | Provided By |
|---|---|---|---|
| `127.0.0.1:3000` TCP listener | Inbound | HTTP/1.1, plaintext, keep-alive with a 5-second idle timeout | Node.js core `http` + host TCP/IP stack |
| Core `http` request/response API | Internal | Direct calls — no wrapper, adapter, or middleware layer | Node.js runtime |
| Standard output | Outbound | One newline-terminated readiness line | Node.js process environment |
| Process lifecycle | Bidirectional | Exit code 1 with a stack trace on bind failure; immediate termination on `SIGTERM` | Host operating system |

Every one of these is satisfied by the runtime and the host. No service contract, API key, rate limit, quota, or third-party availability dependency applies to this system.

## 3.5 Databases & Storage

The system has no data tier. There is no primary database, no secondary or replica store, no cache, no object storage, and no filesystem interaction at runtime. The only "data" the service holds is a 14-byte string literal compiled into the request handler. This sub-section documents the audit behind that statement and the architectural consequences of a fully stateless design.

### 3.5.1 Databases

No database engine, driver, ORM, query builder, or migration tool is present. Both dimensions of the audit — source references and repository artifacts — came back empty.

| Category | Evidence Checked | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Relational drivers | `pg`, `mysql`, `sqlite3` referenced in source | Absent |
| Document / NoSQL drivers | `mongodb`, `mongoose` referenced in source | Absent |
| ORMs and query builders | `sequelize`, `prisma`, `knex`, `typeorm` referenced in source | Absent |
| Schema and migration assets | `migrations/`, `migrate/`, `db/`, `database/`, `prisma/`, `schema.prisma`, `schema.sql`, `init.sql`, `seed.sql`, `alembic.ini` | All absent |
| ORM / client configuration | `ormconfig.json`, `knexfile.js`, `sequelize.config.js`, `drizzle.config.ts` | All absent |
| Engine configuration files | `mongod.conf`, `my.cnf`, `postgresql.conf` | All absent |
| Embedded database files | Repository-wide search for `*.db`, `*.sqlite*`, `*.sql` | No matches anywhere |
| Data / model directories | `data/`, `models/` | Absent |
| Connection strings | `.env`, `.env.example`, `.env.local`, `.env.production`, `config/`, `configs/`, `settings.json` | All absent; the source reads no environment variables |

The absence is structural rather than configurational: a database client cannot be reached from this code, because the only module the process ever imports is the core `http` module.

### 3.5.2 Data Persistence Strategy

The persistence strategy is *no persistence*. The response payload is a literal argument to `res.end` on line 9 — a 14-byte constant that lives in the source file, not in any store — and the two operational parameters (`hostname`, `port`) are literals on lines 3 and 4. Nothing is read, written, computed, or accumulated.

This is enforced by three verified properties of the implementation:

- **No retained state between requests.** The handler is synchronous and assigns to the response object only; there is no module-level mutable variable, counter, collection, or cache (requirement F-001-RQ-003).
- **No request data is captured.** The source performs zero `req.*` accesses, so no inbound method, path, header, or body is ever read — there is nothing to store even in memory (F-001-RQ-002).
- **No session or client-side state.** The application sets exactly one response header, `Content-Type`, so it never emits `Set-Cookie`, and no session library or session store is present.

Because process memory holds nothing but the string constant, a restart loses nothing and recovers nothing. Consequently no backup, restore, retention, replication, or disaster-recovery procedure applies, and none is defined in the repository. Likewise there is no data migration or schema-evolution concern, and no data-at-rest encryption question, because there is no data at rest.

### 3.5.3 Caching

No caching layer exists at any tier.

- **No cache service or client.** `redis`, `ioredis`, and `memcached` are absent from the source, and `redis.conf` is absent from the repository.
- **No in-process cache.** Since the response is a constant and no state is retained, there is nothing to memoize; the "cache hit rate" for a fixed 14-byte literal is not a meaningful quantity.
- **No HTTP cache directives.** The only header the application sets is `Content-Type`. It emits no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, or `Vary`, so caching behavior in any intermediary or client is left entirely to defaults rather than being specified. The remaining headers observed on the wire (`Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Content-Length`) are runtime-supplied framing headers, not cache controls (F-003-RQ-004).

The only reuse mechanism actually in effect is transport-level: the runtime's default HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with a 5-second idle timeout, which allows a client to reuse the TCP connection across requests. That is provided by Node.js `http`, not configured by the application.

### 3.5.4 Storage Services and Filesystem Interaction

No storage service and no filesystem access exist.

- **No object or blob storage.** No S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob client is referenced (`aws-sdk`, `@aws-sdk`, `@google-cloud`, `azure`, `@azure` all absent — see 3.4.4).
- **No local filesystem I/O.** The core `fs` module is never required. The process therefore reads and writes no file at runtime; it needs no writable directory, no temporary space, and no volume.
- **No static assets.** There is no `public/`, `static/`, or `assets/` directory, and no static-file handling code — every response body is generated from the source literal.
- **No volume or mount declarations.** These would live in container or orchestration manifests, and as documented in 3.6.3 none exists.

The only durable artifacts associated with this project are the version-controlled source objects in the Git object store — `server.js` (blob `320a75a`) and `README.md` (blob `5fb5231`). That is source retention, not application storage.

### 3.5.5 Consequences of the Stateless Design

The technology-stack implications of having no data tier are worth making explicit, because several are positive and one is a real limitation:

- **Operational simplicity.** Startup requires no connection pool, no migration run, and no readiness gate on a dependency; the listener is available as soon as the bind succeeds. There is no failure mode in which the service is up but its data store is not, because there is no data store.
- **No data-security surface.** No credentials, connection strings, or datasets exist to protect, rotate, or classify; correspondingly there is no PII, no retention obligation, and no encryption-at-rest requirement.
- **Statelessness does not confer scalability here.** In principle a stateless service replicates freely, but this implementation cannot: the port and interface are hard-coded literals with no override path (F-002-RQ-003), so a second instance on the same host fails to bind with `EADDRINUSE` and exits with code 1 (F-002-RQ-004). Horizontal scaling would require introducing configurability first — the constraint is in the binding model, not in the data model.

## 3.6 Development & Deployment

The development and deployment toolchain is as minimal as the runtime stack. Two tools are actually involved — Git for version control and the `node` interpreter for execution — and every intermediate stage that a conventional Node.js project would have (install, build, lint, test, package, pipeline) has no artifact in this repository. The evidence for that is definitive rather than sampled: `git ls-files` returns exactly three tracked files (`README.md`, `server.js`, `test.js`), so any configuration file for any of those stages would necessarily appear in that list, and none does.

```mermaid
    COMMIT --> PUSH["Push to GitHub origin<br/>source hosting only, no runtime role"]
    PUSH --> CLONE["git clone or pull on target host<br/>3 files, 382 bytes"]
    CLONE --> RUN["node server.js<br/>file interpreted exactly as committed"]
    RUN --> LIVE["Listening on 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>41-byte readiness line on stdout"]
    subgraph Skipped["Conventional stages with no artifact in this repository - verified absent"]
        S1["Dependency install<br/>no package.json, no lockfile"]

    end
```

### 3.6.1 Development Tooling and Environment

| Tool | Version Observed | Status | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Git | 2.43.0 | Present and in use — the repository's `.git/` directory is the only tooling artifact that exists | Version control, source distribution |
| `node` interpreter | v22.23.1 (verification host) | Present in the environment; required to run the code, but not declared by the repository | Executes and verifies the application |
| `npm` | 11.18.0 (verification host) | Present but idle — there is no manifest for it to operate on (see 3.3.2) | None in this project |
| `node --test` (built-in runner) | Bundled with v22.23.1 | Present in the runtime and **no longer inert**: with `test.js` tracked at the repository root, the runner's default discovery pattern `**/test.?(c|m)js` matches it, so `node --test` loads a file that is not a test and exits 1 (6.6.1) | None in this project; it is an accidental interaction, not a configured stage |

Nothing else is configured. The following developer-experience and code-quality tooling was existence-tested and is absent in every case: editor conventions (`.editorconfig`); linting (`.eslintrc`, `.eslintrc.js`, `.eslintrc.json`, `.eslintrc.yml`, `eslint.config.js`, `eslint.config.mjs`, `.jshintrc`, `biome.json`); formatting (`.prettierrc`, `.prettierrc.json`, `.prettierrc.js`, `prettier.config.js`, `.clang-format`); style linting (`.stylelintrc`); type checking (`tsconfig.json`, `jsconfig.json`); commit-time hooks (`.husky/`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`); development server / reload tooling (`nodemon.json`); and static-analysis integrations (`sonar-project.properties`, `codecov.yml`).

Two consequences deserve emphasis:

- **Onboarding information is absent from the repository.** `README.md` contains a single H1 heading and no prose — no prerequisite runtime, no install step, no run command. There is no `docs/` directory, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or `SECURITY.md`. A newcomer discovers the technology requirement only by reading line 1 of the source, and nothing in the tree indicates that `test.js` must not be run.
- **The code offers no testable surface even if tooling were added.** Requiring `server.js` from another script yields an empty exports object (`Object.keys(exports)` is `[]`) and starts the listener as a module-load side effect — the require attempt itself contends for port 3000 (F-005-RQ-003). Any future unit test would therefore need the code refactored to separate construction from binding.

### 3.6.2 Build System

There is no build system, and no build step is required — the committed file is the deployed artifact.

This zero-build property is what makes the system's defining claim literally true: as stated in 1.2.2.3, the file is executed exactly as committed.

No containerization, orchestration, infrastructure-as-code, or process-management definition exists.

Deployment is therefore manual host-level execution (3.6.5). Two implications follow directly from the observed code rather than from convention:

- **Containerizing this service would be trivial but is not defined.** A single-file, dependency-free application needs only a Node.js base image and a copy step; no such definition is committed, so no image build, tag, or registry is part of this project.
- **The hard-coded loopback bind is a containerization hazard.** Because `server.listen` binds `127.0.0.1` with no override path (F-002-RQ-003), a containerized instance would listen only inside its own network namespace and would remain unreachable through a published port. Making this deployable in a container would require changing the bind address in source — the constraint is in the code, not in the missing Dockerfile.

| Static analysis / quality | `sonar-project.properties`, lint and type-check configuration | All absent |
| Commit-time enforcement | `.husky/`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml` | All absent |

All three commits in the repository's history therefore landed without any automated verification, and no branch-protection, review, or ownership metadata exists in-tree (a `CODEOWNERS` file or pull-request template would appear in `git ls-files`, which lists only `README.md`, `server.js`, and `test.js`). The most recent commit, `43ed37c` "Create test.js", is direct evidence of that gap: it added a file that fails the moment it is executed, and nothing in the repository or the hosting configuration could have caught it. Change verification is entirely manual: launch the server and probe it. This is the mechanism behind the specification's treatment of acceptance criteria as externally verifiable rather than automated, and behind the maintenance limitations recorded in 2.4.5.

### 3.6.5 Execution and Deployment Procedure

The deployment procedure is a single command, and it was executed and measured as part of preparing this specification.

```bash
node server.js
```

Observed stdout: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`

| Step | Action | Verified Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Obtain the source (`git clone` / `git pull`) | Three files, 382 bytes total; nothing to install. Only `server.js` (342 bytes) is executed — `README.md` and `test.js` ship with the checkout but no step of this procedure runs them |
| 2 | Ensure TCP port 3000 on `127.0.0.1` is free | If occupied, startup fails — see failure row below |
| 3 | Run `node server.js` in the foreground | Single process (`pgrep -fc "node server.js"` returns 1); 41 bytes on stdout, 0 bytes on stderr |
| 4 | Verify | `GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/` returns `HTTP/1.1 200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14` |
| 5 | Stop | `SIGTERM` terminates the process immediately; no connection draining occurs |
| Failure mode | Port already bound | Unhandled `error` event, `EADDRINUSE` stack trace on stderr, process exit code 1 (F-002-RQ-004) |

Operationally this is a foreground, non-daemonized, single-process service: there is no PID file, no log file, no daemonization flag, no health endpoint, and no restart policy — the process's standard streams are whatever the launching shell or supervisor provides. Critically, **the launch command is not encoded anywhere in the repository**: there is no `npm start` script (no manifest), no `Procfile`, and no service unit, so `node server.js` is an operator convention documented here and in assumption A-04 rather than a repository artifact. One command that must *not* be part of the procedure is `node --test`: run at the repository root it discovers `test.js` and exits 1 without ever starting the service.

### 3.6.6 Version Control, Versioning and Provenance

| Aspect | Observed Value |
|---|---|
| Version control system | Git (client 2.43.0 in the verification environment) |
| Branch under documentation | `2907_01`; `main` also exists in the checkout |
| HEAD commit | `43ed37c` "Create test.js" — working tree clean, no uncommitted or untracked files |
| History | Three commits: `241598b` "Initial commit" (adds `README.md`), `06492d7` "Add files via upload" (adds `server.js`, 14 insertions), and `43ed37c` "Create test.js" (adds `test.js`, 2 insertions) |
| Branch state | Diverged: `main` (= `origin/main`) is at `06492d7` with two tracked files; `2907_01` (= `origin/2907_01`) is one commit ahead at `43ed37c` with three |
| Tags | None — `git tag -l` returns nothing |
| File modes | All three files `100644`; no executable bit anywhere in the tree |
| Release metadata | None — no `CHANGELOG.md`, no `package.json` `version` field, no tags |

Because no tag, changelog, or version field exists, the commit SHA is the only version identity this artifact has, exactly as recorded in 2.5.5: the as-built baseline is commit `43ed37c` on branch `2907_01`, and the application it deploys is byte-identical to the one introduced by its parent `06492d7` (`server.js` blob `320a75a` in both). There is no release process, no artifact registry, and no published package — distribution is by Git clone alone.

One security note closes the deployment picture: the Git remote in this checkout is configured with a token-bearing HTTPS URL. That credential governs source access only — it has no relationship to the running service, which requires no credential — but the local Git configuration must not be copied into images, logs, or documentation.
