# 4. Process Flowchart

## 4.1 System Workflows

This section documents the workflows that the committed code in `server.js` actually executes. The repository contains three tracked files — `server.js` (14 lines, 342 bytes), `README.md` (1 line, 27 bytes), and `test.js` (2 lines, 13 bytes), 382 bytes in total across zero subdirectories — and no workflow definition, orchestration descriptor, scheduler, queue, or business-process artifact of any kind. Every flow below was derived by line-level reading of `server.js` and then confirmed by executing the unmodified file and observing the running process.

`test.js` participates in no workflow. Nothing requires or imports it, no documented procedure invokes it (the only supported entry path remains `node server.js`, per 3.6.5), and executing it directly fails at once: its two bare identifier statements raise `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and the process exits 1. It therefore contributes no trigger, no step, no decision point, and no terminating condition, and the workflow inventory below is exactly what it was before that file was committed.

Three points frame everything that follows and are stated once here rather than repeated in every diagram:

- **There are no business processes in the domain sense.** The system models no user, account, order, transaction, or record. `server.js` contains zero conditional statements, and the request object `req` is declared at line 6 but never dereferenced, so no request attribute can influence any outcome. The "core processes" documented below are therefore the *operational* processes of the service: bringing the listener up, answering requests, and stopping.
- **Every decision point belongs to the runtime, not to the repository.** Each decision diamond in the diagrams below is evaluated by the Node.js core `http` module or the host TCP stack. This is verifiable in two directions: a grep of `server.js` finds no `if`, `switch`, or ternary, and probing the running process produced runtime-generated outcomes (`400`, `431`, `100 Continue`, `HEAD` body suppression) that no line of `server.js` authors.
- **All timing figures are measured properties, not commitments.** As established in 2.2, no requirement in this repository carries a declared performance target, and no benchmark, SLO, or timeout setting exists in the tree. Where a duration appears in a diagram it is either a Node.js default read from the live server object or a wall-clock observation from this documentation environment (Node v22.23.1, loopback interface).

### 4.1.1 Core Business Processes

#### 4.1.1.1 Workflow Inventory

Three operational workflows exist. Workflow identifiers `WF-01` through `WF-03` are assigned by this specification for cross-referencing; they do not appear in the repository.

| Workflow | Trigger | Terminating Condition |
|----------|---------|-----------------------|
| WF-01 Process startup and listener activation | Shell invocation `node server.js` (the only supported entry path — the module has no exports and no `package.json` scripts exist) | Readiness line written to stdout, or process exit code 1 on bind failure |
| WF-02 Request reception and response emission | Any inbound HTTP request on the loopback listener | `res.end` completes at line 9 and the response is flushed; the socket is then kept alive or closed by the runtime |
| WF-03 Process termination | `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` delivered by the operating system, or an unhandled `error` event | Immediate process exit; the listening socket and all open connections are released without draining |

WF-01 and WF-03 each run at most once per process lifetime. WF-02 runs once per request and is fully re-entrant because it retains nothing: 20 sequential requests produced exactly one unique 14-byte body, and 60 requests issued at concurrency 15 all returned `200`.

#### 4.1.1.2 High-Level System Workflow

The diagram below places the complete system in swim lanes for the four participants that exist: the operator, the host boundary, the Node.js process, and the local HTTP client. It is the end-to-end view; the two detailed flows appear in 4.2.1 and 4.2.2.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph OperatorLane["Actor - Developer or Operator"]
        OpStart(["Start - operator opens the repository checkout"])
        OpLaunch["Run node server.js from the repository root"]
        OpObserve["Read the single readiness line on stdout"]
        OpStop["Send SIGINT or SIGTERM to the process"]
        OpEnd(["End - process exited and port released"])
    end
    subgraph HostLane["System Boundary - host loopback interface only"]
        Socket["TCP listening socket 127.0.0.1 port 3000"]
    end
    subgraph RuntimeLane["Node.js Process - single foreground process"]
        Load["Execute server.js, line 1 requires core http"]
        Create["createServer registers exactly one handler, line 6"]
        Listen["server.listen port 3000 host 127.0.0.1, line 12"]
        BindOK{"Bind succeeded?"}
        Ready["console.log readiness line, line 13"]
        Idle["Event loop idle, listener accepting connections"]
        Handle["Handler sets 200, text-plain, 14-byte body, lines 7-9"]
        Crash["Unhandled error event, stderr trace, exit code 1"]
        Exit["Immediate exit, no drain, no shutdown hook"]
    end
    subgraph ClientLane["Actor - Local HTTP Client"]
        Req["Send any method, any path, any body"]
        Resp["Receive 200, Content-Type text-plain, 14 bytes"]
    end
    OpStart --> OpLaunch
    OpLaunch --> Load
    Load --> Create
    Create --> Listen
    Listen --> BindOK
    BindOK -->|"no - EADDRINUSE"| Crash
    Crash --> OpEnd
    BindOK -->|"yes"| Socket
    Socket --> Ready
    Ready --> OpObserve
    Ready --> Idle
    Req --> Socket
    Socket --> Idle
    Idle --> Handle
    Handle --> Resp
    Resp -->|"another request"| Req
    OpObserve --> OpStop
    OpStop --> Exit
    Exit --> OpEnd
```

The single system boundary is the listening socket at `127.0.0.1:3000`. Nothing crosses that boundary except HTTP bytes on the loopback interface; the two other channels leaving the process — stdout and stderr — are host-local streams, not network interfaces.

#### 4.1.1.3 End-to-End User Journey

The journey below is the same path annotated with the requirement identifiers defined in 2.2 and with every abort path that was reproduced during verification. Three of the five decision diamonds can terminate the journey before a response is ever produced.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A(["Journey start - host with a Node.js runtime"])
    B["Operator runs node server.js"]
    C{"Core http module resolvable, F-005-RQ-001?"}
    C1["Load fails at line 1, no socket, no readiness line"]
    D["createServer registers the single handler, F-001-RQ-001"]
    E{"TCP port 3000 free on 127.0.0.1, F-002-RQ-001?"}
    E1["Unhandled EADDRINUSE error, exit code 1, F-002-RQ-004"]
    F["Listener bound, 41-byte readiness line on stdout, F-004-RQ-001"]
    G{"Client originates on the same host, F-002-RQ-002?"}
    G1["Connection refused, curl exit 7, observed status 000"]
    H["Client sends any HTTP request"]
    I{"Byte stream is a well-formed HTTP request?"}
    I1["Runtime answers 400 or 431 and closes, handler never runs"]
    K["Handler sets 200, text-plain, 14-byte literal, F-003-RQ-001 to RQ-003"]
    J{"Another request on this process?"}
    L["Operator sends SIGINT or SIGTERM"]
    M["Exit 130 or 143, sockets closed without drain, F-002-RQ-005"]
    Z(["Journey end - aborted, manual remediation required"])
    Z2(["Journey end - completed"])
    A --> B
    B --> C
    C -->|"no"| C1
    C1 --> Z
    C -->|"yes"| D
    D --> E
    E -->|"no"| E1
    E1 --> Z
    E -->|"yes"| F
    F --> G
    G -->|"no"| G1
    G1 --> Z
    G -->|"yes"| H
    H --> I
    I -->|"no"| I1
    I1 --> J
    I -->|"yes"| K
    K --> J
    J -->|"yes"| H
    J -->|"no"| L
    L --> M
    M --> Z2
```

**Decision points.** Every branch in the system, with the component that evaluates it and the observed outcomes:

| Decision Point | Evaluated By | Observed Outcomes |
|----------------|--------------|-------------------|
| Is the core `http` module resolvable? | CommonJS resolution in the Node.js runtime | Success on Node v22.23.1; failure would abort at line 1 before any socket exists |
| Is the loopback bind granted for port 3000? | Host TCP stack, surfaced through `server.listen` | Granted, or `EADDRINUSE` raised as an `error` event with zero listeners registered |
| Is the caller on the loopback interface? | Host TCP stack, because `'127.0.0.1'` is passed as the `listen` host | Loopback request answered; request to the host's routable address `10.76.0.92:3000` failed to connect (`curl` exit 7, status `000`) |
| Does the byte stream parse as HTTP? | Node core `http` parser; `clientError` listener count on the live server is `0`, so the runtime default applies | Valid request dispatched to the handler; `THIS IS NOT HTTP` answered `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close` |
| Is the request head within `maxHeaderSize`? | Node core parser, `http.maxHeaderSize` = 16384 bytes | A 20 000-byte header field was answered `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` with `Connection: close` |
| Is an `Expect: 100-continue` header present? | Node core; `checkContinue` listener count is `0` | Runtime auto-emitted `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` and then the handler's normal `200` |
| Is the method `HEAD`? | Node core response serializer | `200` with `Content-Type: text/plain` and a zero-byte body (F-003-RQ-005) |
| Is keep-alive negotiated, and has the socket gone idle? | Node core, `keepAliveTimeout` = 5000 ms | HTTP/1.1 client received `Connection: keep-alive` and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`; an idle socket was closed by the server after approximately 5.8 s; an HTTP/1.0 request received `Connection: close` |
| **Any application-level decision** | **None exists** | `server.js` contains no `if`, `switch`, or ternary; all six methods probed (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, `PATCH`) on a deep path with a query string, a body, and a custom header returned byte-identical `200` responses |

**User touchpoints.** The complete set of surfaces through which a human interacts with the system:

| Touchpoint | Direction | Content Observed |
|------------|-----------|------------------|
| Shell invocation `node server.js` | Operator into system | The only supported entry path; no install, build, or transpile step precedes it (F-005-RQ-002) |
| Process stdout | System to operator | Exactly one 41-byte line, `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, emitted once on successful bind; still 41 bytes after roughly 80 requests |
| HTTP request and response on `127.0.0.1:3000` | Client into system and back | Any method and path in, `200` / `text/plain` / 14 bytes out |
| Process stderr | System to operator | Empty on success; carries the unhandled-`error` stack trace on bind failure only |
| Signal delivery and exit code | Operator into system, status back | `SIGINT` observed exit `130`, `SIGTERM` observed exit `143`, bind failure exit `1` |

**Error handling paths.** All four reachable failure paths, each reproduced during verification. None is handled by repository code, because `server.js` contains no `try`/`catch`, no `throw`, and no `error` listener.

| Failure Path | Where It Surfaces | Client-Visible and Operator-Visible Result |
|--------------|-------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Port already bound | `server.listen`, line 12 | No listener, no readiness line, stderr stack trace, exit code 1 |
| Malformed request | Node core parser, before dispatch | `400 Bad Request` plus `Connection: close`; handler never invoked; nothing logged |
| Request head over 16 KiB | Node core parser, before dispatch | `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` plus `Connection: close`; handler never invoked; nothing logged |
| Termination signal during traffic | Default signal disposition, no handler registered | Process exits immediately; an already-open keep-alive socket observed a peer close with no response; subsequent probes return status `000` |

### 4.1.2 Integration Workflows

#### 4.1.2.1 Integration Surface

The integration inventory is closed and consists of four couplings, consistent with 2.3.3. No database, cache, broker, outbound HTTP client, identity provider, secret manager, feature-flag service, file-system access, or log-aggregation client appears anywhere in `server.js`.

| Integration | Direction | Contract as Observed |
|-------------|-----------|----------------------|
| TCP listening socket `127.0.0.1:3000` | Inbound | HTTP/1.1 request and response, runtime-default keep-alive (`Keep-Alive: timeout=5` on the wire) |
| Node core `http` API, in-process | Internal | Direct calls to `createServer`, `listen`, `res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader`, `res.end` with no wrapper, adapter, or middleware |
| `process.stdout` | Outbound | One newline-terminated line, once per successful start |
| Operating-system process control | Bidirectional | Signals in; exit codes 1, 130, 143 out; stderr trace on bind failure |

#### 4.1.2.2 Startup Integration Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant OP as Operator shell
    participant NR as Node.js runtime and core http
    participant AH as Application code in server.js
    participant OS as Host OS TCP stack
    participant SO as Process stdout
    OP->>NR: exec node server.js
    NR->>AH: execute module body
    AH->>NR: require http, line 1
    AH->>NR: createServer with one handler, line 6
    AH->>NR: listen 3000 and 127.0.0.1, line 12
    NR->>OS: bind and listen on loopback
    OS-->>NR: bind acknowledged
    NR->>AH: invoke listen callback
    AH->>SO: write 41-byte readiness line, line 13
    SO-->>OP: Server running at http 127.0.0.1 3000
    Note over NR,OS: listener idle, no further output for the process lifetime
```

Because `server.listen(...)` is a top-level statement, this sequence is a module-load side effect: loading the file *is* starting the service, and requiring it from another script produces an exports object with zero own keys while still attempting the bind (F-005-RQ-003). A poll loop started immediately after launch observed the socket accepting connections 13 ms into polling — an environment measurement, not a target.

#### 4.1.2.3 Request and Response Integration Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CL as Local HTTP client
    participant OS as Host OS TCP stack
    participant NR as Node core http parser
    participant AH as Inline handler lines 6 to 10
    CL->>OS: TCP connect 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    OS->>NR: accept, runtime attaches its connection listener
    CL->>NR: request line, headers, optional body
    NR->>NR: parse under headersTimeout 60000 ms and requestTimeout 300000 ms
    NR->>AH: invoke handler with req and res
    Note over AH: req is never dereferenced, method, path, query, headers and body discarded
    AH->>NR: statusCode 200, then Content-Type text-plain, then end with 14-byte literal
    NR->>NR: append Date, Content-Length 14, Connection and Keep-Alive headers
    NR-->>CL: HTTP 200 response, 14-byte body
    Note over NR,CL: socket retained, runtime closes it after keepAliveTimeout 5000 ms
```

The division of labour visible in this sequence is the system's defining integration characteristic: application code contributes three statements (status, one header, body), while the runtime contributes parsing, dispatch, `Content-Length` computation, `Date`, connection management, and keep-alive negotiation (F-003-RQ-004).

#### 4.1.2.4 Bind-Failure Integration Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant OP as Operator shell
    participant NR as Node.js runtime
    participant OS as Host OS TCP stack
    participant SE as Process stderr
    OP->>NR: exec node server.js while port 3000 is already bound
    NR->>OS: bind 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    OS-->>NR: EADDRINUSE
    NR->>NR: emit error on the server object, zero error listeners registered
    NR->>SE: unhandled error event and stack trace
    NR-->>OP: exit code 1, empty stdout, no readiness line
    Note over OP,SE: no retry and no port fallback, recovery is a manual relaunch
```

Reproduced verbatim during verification: a second launch while the port was held exited with code `1`, wrote 0 bytes to stdout, and wrote a stderr trace beginning `throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event` followed by `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`.

#### 4.1.2.5 Data Flow Across the System Boundary

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Outside["Outside the system boundary"]
        C1["Inbound request bytes - method, path, query, headers, body"]
        C2["Outbound response bytes"]
        C3["Operator terminal attached to stdout"]
        C4["Operator terminal attached to stderr"]
    end
    subgraph Inside["Inside the boundary - loopback socket 127.0.0.1 port 3000"]
        P1["Runtime parses the request into a req object"]
        P2["req discarded unread - never stored, transformed or forwarded"]
        P3["Response literal Hello World newline, server.js line 9"]
        P4["Readiness string composed from lines 3, 4 and 13"]
        P5["Bind failure trace, produced only by the runtime"]
    end
    C1 --> P1
    P1 --> P2
    P3 --> C2
    P4 --> C3
    P5 --> C4
```

The critical structural property is that **inbound and outbound data are not connected by any transformation**. The response literal at line 9 is the sole outbound payload source, so there is no data flow *through* the system — only data flow *in* (discarded) and data flow *out* (constant). Consequently there is no serialization format, schema, mapping layer, or data-quality step to document, and no persistence point anywhere in the flow.

| Data Element | Lifetime | Handling |
|--------------|----------|----------|
| Inbound request (method, URL, headers, body) | Duration of the handler invocation | Parsed by the runtime, never read by application code, released with the request object |
| Outbound response body | Source-code literal, line 9 | Identical 14 bytes for every request; `Content-Length: 14` computed by the runtime |
| Readiness line | Written once at bind | 41 bytes to stdout; no file, rotation, or retention target exists |
| Bind-failure trace | Written once on failure | stderr only; discloses bind address, port, and `errno`, no secret material |

#### 4.1.2.6 Event Processing and Batch Processing

Neither exists in this repository, and each absence was verified rather than assumed.

| Prompted Capability | Verified Status |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| Event processing flows | No broker or stream client, no publish or subscribe call, no `EventEmitter` usage authored in `server.js`. The only events in play are internal Node.js lifecycle events (`request`, `connection`, `error`) whose listener counts on the live server object are 1, 1, and **0** respectively — the first two registered by the runtime and by `createServer`, none by application code |
| Batch processing sequences | No cron entry, scheduler, timer, or job runner. `grep` for `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `cron` in `server.js` returns zero matches; the process performs no work between requests |
| Asynchronous or deferred work | None. The handler is three synchronous statements with no `async`, `await`, `Promise`, or callback chain (F-001-RQ-003) |
| Message durability, retries, dead-letter handling | Not applicable — no message-oriented middleware exists to configure |

The single "event-driven" behavior that does exist is the Node.js event loop itself accepting connections and dispatching the one registered `request` listener, which is already captured in 4.1.2.3.

## 4.2 Flowchart Requirements

This section presents the detailed process flow for each core feature, followed by the validation rules and timing characteristics that apply to those flows. The two detailed flows correspond to the two code paths that exist in `server.js`: the startup path (lines 1–4, 6, 12–14) and the request path (lines 6–10).

The prompted flowchart elements are represented as follows, so each diagram can be read consistently:

| Required Element | How It Is Represented in 4.2 |
|------------------|------------------------------|
| Start and end points | Stadium-shaped terminator nodes; every flow has exactly one start and at least one success and one failure terminator |
| Process steps | Rectangular nodes, each annotated with the `server.js` line number that implements it |
| Decision diamonds | Diamond nodes, each labelled with the component that evaluates it, since none is evaluated by repository code |
| System boundaries | Subgraph zones separating the client, the Node.js runtime, and the repository code |
| User touchpoints | Nodes in the client and operator zones; enumerated in 4.1.1.3 |
| Error states and recovery paths | Distinct failure terminators plus the recovery flow in 4.3.2 |
| Timing and SLA considerations | Consolidated in 4.2.4; no SLA is declared anywhere in the repository |

### 4.2.1 Process Flow — Startup and Listener Binding

This flow implements F-002 (endpoint binding and listener lifecycle), F-004 (readiness logging), and F-005 (direct execution model). It begins with a shell invocation and ends either with an idle, accepting listener or with an aborted process.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S(["Start - shell invokes node server.js"])
    A1["Runtime resolves and executes the CommonJS module, F-005-RQ-002"]
    A2{"require http succeeds?"}
    A3["Module load throws, exit non-zero, nothing bound"]
    A4["Bind constants read from lines 3 and 4, no env or CLI override, F-002-RQ-003"]
    A5["createServer builds the server object with one request listener, F-001-RQ-001"]
    A6["listen requested on 127.0.0.1 port 3000, F-002-RQ-001"]
    A7{"OS grants the loopback bind?"}
    A8["Server emits error, zero error listeners, trace on stderr, exit code 1"]
    A9["Listening socket established, system boundary now open"]
    A10["listen callback runs, 41-byte readiness line on stdout, F-004-RQ-001"]
    A11(["End of startup - event loop idle, listener accepting"])
    E(["End - startup aborted, operator must remediate"])
    S --> A1
    A1 --> A2
    A2 -->|"no"| A3
    A3 --> E
    A2 -->|"yes"| A4
    A4 --> A5
    A5 --> A6
    A6 --> A7
    A7 -->|"no - EADDRINUSE or permission denied"| A8
    A8 --> E
    A7 -->|"yes"| A9
    A9 --> A10
    A10 --> A11
```

| Step | Implementation | Verified Behavior |
|------|----------------|-------------------|
| Module execution | Direct invocation of `server.js`; the file has no exports, so loading it is starting it | A bare checkout runs with no install or build step; requiring the module yields zero own keys while still binding |
| Constant resolution | `hostname` at line 3, `port` at line 4 | Literals only; a `grep` for `process.env`, `argv`, `dotenv`, and `config` in `server.js` returns no match, so there is no override path |
| Handler registration | `http.createServer` at line 6 | Live server object reports exactly one `request` listener |
| Bind request | `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` at line 12 | Live server object reports `listening: true` and address `{127.0.0.1, IPv4, 3000}` |
| Readiness signal | `console.log` template literal at line 13 | stdout exactly 41 bytes, stderr 0 bytes; the advertised URL is composed from the same constants that were bound |
| Bind failure | No handling in repository code — the live server object reports **0** `error` listeners | Second launch exited with code 1 and a stderr stack trace; no readiness line and no partial listener |

There is no readiness gate beyond the log line: the socket begins accepting connections when `listen` succeeds, and no health or readiness endpoint distinct from the single response exists.

### 4.2.2 Process Flow — Request Reception and Response Emission

This flow implements F-001 (handler dispatch) and F-003 (response contract). The three zones make explicit which steps are performed by the client, which by the Node.js runtime, and which by the fourteen lines in the repository — a distinction that matters because the runtime owns every decision.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ClientZone["Actor - Local HTTP Client, outside the system boundary"]
        CStart(["Start - client issues a request"])
        CConn["Open or reuse a TCP connection to 127.0.0.1 port 3000"]
        CRecv["Receive response bytes"]
        CEnd(["End - response consumed"])
    end
    subgraph RuntimeZone["Node.js core http - inside the process, not repository code"]
        RAccept["Accept connection on the loopback listener"]
        RParse{"Request parses as valid HTTP?"}
        RErr400["Emit 400 Bad Request with Connection close"]
        RHdr{"Header block within maxHeaderSize 16384 bytes?"}
        RErr431["Emit 431 Request Header Fields Too Large with Connection close"]
        RExpect{"Expect 100-continue present?"}
        RCont["Auto-emit 100 Continue, no checkContinue listener registered"]
        RDispatch["Invoke the single registered request listener with req and res"]
        RFrame["Compute Date, Content-Length 14, Connection and Keep-Alive headers"]
        RHead{"Method is HEAD?"}
        RSuppress["Suppress body, send headers only, F-003-RQ-005"]
        RSend["Serialise status line, headers and 14-byte body onto the socket"]
        RKeep{"Keep-alive negotiated?"}
        RClose["Close the socket"]
        RIdleWait["Hold socket idle up to keepAliveTimeout 5000 ms"]
    end
    subgraph AppZone["Repository code - server.js lines 6 to 10"]
        HEnter["Handler entry, req present but never dereferenced, F-001-RQ-002"]
        HStatus["res.statusCode 200, line 7, F-003-RQ-001"]
        HType["res.setHeader Content-Type text-plain, line 8, F-003-RQ-002"]
        HEnd["res.end with the 14-byte literal, line 9, F-003-RQ-003"]
        HReturn["Handler returns, no state retained, F-001-RQ-003"]
    end
    CStart --> CConn
    CConn --> RAccept
    RAccept --> RParse
    RParse -->|"no"| RErr400
    RErr400 --> CRecv
    RParse -->|"yes"| RHdr
    RHdr -->|"no"| RErr431
    RErr431 --> CRecv
    RHdr -->|"yes"| RExpect
    RExpect -->|"yes"| RCont
    RCont --> RDispatch
    RExpect -->|"no"| RDispatch
    RDispatch --> HEnter
    HEnter --> HStatus
    HStatus --> HType
    HType --> HEnd
    HEnd --> HReturn
    HReturn --> RFrame
    RFrame --> RHead
    RHead -->|"yes"| RSuppress
    RSuppress --> RSend
    RHead -->|"no"| RSend
    RSend --> CRecv
    RSend --> RKeep
    RKeep -->|"yes"| RIdleWait
    RIdleWait -->|"new request on same socket"| RParse
    RIdleWait -->|"idle timer expires"| RClose
    RKeep -->|"no - HTTP 1.0 or Connection close"| RClose
    CRecv --> CEnd
```

The application zone is three statements long, and the response contract they establish was confirmed byte-wise:

```javascript
res.statusCode = 200;                              // line 7
res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');       // line 8
```

| Aspect | Observed Result |
|--------|-----------------|
| Method independence | `GET`, `POST`, `DELETE`, `PUT`, `OPTIONS`, and `PATCH` against `/any/deep/path?q=1` with body `payload=ignored` and header `X-Custom: abc` all returned `status=200 size=14 type=text/plain` |
| `HEAD` handling | `status=200 size=0 type=text/plain` — body suppression performed by the runtime, not by application code |
| Header set on the wire | `Content-Type` (application-set) plus `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, `Content-Length: 14` (runtime-set) |
| Body bytes | `od -c` shows `H e l l o , space W o r l d ! \n` — 14 bytes |
| Recovery paths inside this flow | None are needed and none exist: the handler has no branch that can fail, and protocol failures are terminated by the runtime with `400` or `431` before dispatch |

### 4.2.3 Validation Rules

The repository implements **no validation layer**. This is a structural consequence of F-001-RQ-002 rather than an omission at a particular step: because no property of `req` is ever read, there is no value in the system that could be validated, rejected, or sanitized. The flow below traces a request through the five checkpoint classes a conventional service would apply and records, at each, what the code actually does.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    In(["Inbound request reaches the handler"])
    V1{"Authentication checkpoint?"}
    V2{"Authorization checkpoint?"}
    V3{"Schema or payload validation?"}
    V4{"Rate limit or quota check?"}
    V5{"Regulatory or audit check?"}
    Out(["Fixed 200 response emitted"])
    N1["Not implemented - no credential is read"]
    N2["Not implemented - no role, tenant or scope exists"]
    N3["Not implemented - no request attribute is read"]
    N4["Not implemented - no counter or limiter exists"]
    N5["Not implemented - no regime declared in the repository"]
    In --> V1
    V1 -->|"absent"| N1
    N1 --> V2
    V2 -->|"absent"| N2
    N2 --> V3
    V3 -->|"absent"| N3
    N3 --> V4
    V4 -->|"absent"| N4
    N4 --> V5
    V5 -->|"absent"| N5
    N5 --> Out
```

#### 4.2.3.1 Business Rules Enforced at Each Step

The rules that *are* enforced are invariants guaranteed by construction rather than by validation code. Each is enforced because the alternative is unrepresentable in the source.

| Step | Invariant Enforced | Enforcement Mechanism |
|------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| Startup, line 12 | Exactly one endpoint is exposed, at exactly one address | A single `listen` call with literal arguments; no loop, list, or configuration source |
| Startup, lines 3–4, 13 | The advertised endpoint always equals the bound endpoint | Both the `listen` call and the readiness message interpolate the same two constants (F-004-RQ-002) |
| Dispatch, line 6 | Every accepted request is serviced; no request is rejected by the application | One registered handler and no dispatch logic, so there is no `404` or `405` path to reach |
| Handler, lines 7–9 | Success is the only representable outcome | `200` is assigned unconditionally, and no other status assignment exists in the file |
| Handler, line 9 | The payload is immutable across requests, clients, and time | The body is a source-code string literal; 20 sequential requests produced one unique body |
| Handler exit, line 10 | No request can influence any other | No module-scoped mutable state; nothing is written to memory, disk, or a cache |

#### 4.2.3.2 Data Validation Requirements

None apply, and the reason is mechanical: the request never reaches application code as data. The runtime performs *protocol* validation only, and its two rejection outcomes were reproduced directly — `400 Bad Request` for a malformed request line and `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` for a head exceeding `http.maxHeaderSize` (16384 bytes). Both are emitted before the handler is invoked, so the application cannot observe or influence them. There is no schema, type check, length limit, encoding check, or sanitizer in the repository, and no library that could provide one, since the only import is the core `http` module.

#### 4.2.3.3 Authorization Checkpoints

There is exactly one access-control mechanism in the entire system, and it is topological rather than logical: the `'127.0.0.1'` argument at line 12 confines reachability to the host's loopback interface. This was confirmed by probing the host's routable address `10.76.0.92:3000`, which failed to connect (`curl` exit 7, status `000`). Beyond that boundary, every caller is anonymous and identically privileged — the code contains no credential handling, token verification, session, role, scope, tenant, or allow-list, and it reads no request header that could carry an identity.

#### 4.2.3.4 Regulatory Compliance Checks

No compliance regime is declared or implemented anywhere in the repository, and no compliance-relevant processing occurs. Two verified facts bound the exposure: request content is never read, so no personal or sensitive data can be inspected, logged, or retained; and the process writes nothing to disk, which was confirmed by an unchanged working tree (`git status --porcelain` reported 0 changed files) and the absence of any `fs` usage. There is no audit trail, retention policy, consent mechanism, data-subject-access path, or encryption of data in transit — the service speaks plain HTTP only.

### 4.2.4 Timing and SLA Considerations

**No SLA, SLO, error budget, latency target, or throughput target exists in this repository.** As recorded in 2.2, zero of the twenty requirements carry a declared performance target, and there is no benchmark, load-test harness, or performance budget in the tree. The timing values below are of two distinct kinds, and the distinction is material: the first group are Node.js defaults that govern the flow (read from the live server object created by `server.js`, none of which the application overrides), and the second group are wall-clock observations from this documentation environment.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CL as Local HTTP client
    participant NR as Node core http
    participant AH as Handler lines 7 to 9
    CL->>NR: TCP connect and first byte of the request
    Note over NR: headersTimeout budget 60000 ms for the complete head
    Note over NR: requestTimeout budget 300000 ms for the complete request
    CL->>NR: complete request head received
    NR->>AH: dispatch req and res
    AH-->>NR: res.end after three synchronous statements, no await and no I O
    NR-->>CL: 200 response with 14-byte body
    Note over NR,CL: keepAliveTimeout idle budget 5000 ms, close observed at about 5.8 s
    NR-->>CL: FIN, socket closed by the server
    Note over NR: server.timeout is 0 so no per-socket inactivity timer, maxRequestsPerSocket is 0 so unlimited
```

#### 4.2.4.1 Runtime Timing Constraints Governing the Flows

All values were read from the live `http.Server` instance that `server.js` creates. Because `server.js` assigns none of these properties, every value is a Node.js v22.23.1 default.

| Constraint | Value on the Live Server | Effect on the Flow |
|------------|--------------------------|--------------------|
| `keepAliveTimeout` | 5000 ms | Idle keep-alive sockets are closed by the server; also advertised to clients as `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`. An idle socket was observed closing at approximately 5.8 s, reflecting the timer plus Node's periodic connection-check granularity |
| `headersTimeout` | 60000 ms | Upper bound for receiving a complete request head before the runtime aborts the request |
| `requestTimeout` | 300000 ms | Upper bound for receiving a complete request, including body |
| `server.timeout` | 0 | No per-socket inactivity timeout is active |
| `maxRequestsPerSocket` | 0 | Unlimited requests per keep-alive connection |
| `http.maxHeaderSize` | 16384 bytes | Head larger than this is rejected with `431` before dispatch |
| `maxHeadersCount` | null | No explicit cap on header count |
| Server `timeout` listeners | 0 | No application-level timeout handling exists |

#### 4.2.4.2 Observed Latency Characteristics

These figures characterize the verification host and the loopback path, **not** the system's obligations. They are included because the prompt asks for timing considerations and because no declared target exists to report instead.

| Measurement | Observation |
|-------------|-------------|
| Startup to accepting connections | The listening socket accepted a connection 13 ms into a poll loop begun immediately after launch |
| Response time, first request on a new connection | 0.0038 s total, including TCP setup |
| Response time, subsequent requests | 0.00031 s to 0.00055 s across `POST`, `DELETE`, `PUT`, `OPTIONS`, and `PATCH` probes |
| Concurrency behavior | 60 requests issued at concurrency 15 returned `200` in every case, served by a single process and a single event loop |
| Shutdown latency | `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` both removed the listener within the sub-second window measured; a follow-up probe returned status `000` |

#### 4.2.4.3 Timing-Related Risks Visible in the Flow

Three timing properties follow directly from the code's construction and are stated as observations, not defects: capacity is bounded by one event loop in one process because there is no `cluster` or `worker_threads` usage; a slow or stalled client occupies a connection for up to the runtime's `requestTimeout` of 300000 ms with no application-level guard, since the server's `timeout` listener count is 0; and no request-level latency is measurable from the system itself, because the only instrumentation is the startup log line, which remained 41 bytes after roughly 80 requests.

## 4.3 Technical Implementation

This section documents how the flows in 4.1 and 4.2 are realized in terms of state and error handling. Both topics are unusual in this repository because `server.js` implements neither: it holds no mutable state and contains no error-handling construct. What follows therefore documents the state and error behavior that the system genuinely exhibits — most of it owned by the Node.js runtime and the operating system — and records precisely which mechanisms are absent, each verified rather than assumed.

### 4.3.1 State Management

#### 4.3.1.1 State Inventory

The complete state inventory of the running system is four items long. Nothing in it is mutable by a request, and nothing survives the process.

| State Item | Where It Lives | Mutability and Lifetime |
|------------|----------------|-------------------------|
| `hostname` and `port` constants | Module scope, `server.js` lines 3–4 | Immutable literals, fixed at authoring time; read by `listen` (line 12) and by the readiness log (line 13) |
| `http.Server` instance | Module scope, `server.js` line 6 | Created once; its only application-level consumer is the `listen` call at line 12 |
| Per-request `req` and `res` pair | Runtime-managed, handler parameters at line 6 | Created per request by the runtime and released when the response completes; `req` is never dereferenced by application code |
| Connection and keep-alive bookkeeping | Runtime-internal, inside the Node.js `http` and `net` layers | Managed entirely by the runtime; the application registers no `connection`, `timeout`, or `clientError` listener |

There is **no application-level state at all**: no module-scoped `let` or `var`, no counter, no session store, no in-memory map, and no closure variable shared across invocations. This is what makes F-001-RQ-003 (stateless processing) structural rather than aspirational, and it was confirmed behaviourally — 20 sequential requests produced exactly one unique response body and 60 requests at concurrency 15 all returned `200`.

#### 4.3.1.2 Process Lifecycle State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "No process, port 3000 free" as S0
    state "Module executing, lines 1 to 10" as S1
    state "Listen requested, line 12" as S2
    state "Listening and idle, readiness line written" as S3
    state "Handling one request, lines 7 to 9" as S4
    state "Bind failed, unhandled error event" as S5
    state "Terminated by signal" as S6
    [*] --> S0
    S0 --> S1: operator runs node server.js
    S1 --> S2: createServer then listen
    S2 --> S3: bind granted, callback fires
    S2 --> S5: EADDRINUSE, exit code 1
    S3 --> S4: runtime dispatches req and res
    S4 --> S3: res.end completes, nothing retained
    S3 --> S6: SIGINT exit 130 or SIGTERM exit 143
    S4 --> S6: signal during handling, response lost
    S5 --> [*]: process exits, no readiness line
    S6 --> [*]: port released immediately
```

Two properties of this machine are worth stating explicitly. First, there is **no draining state** between "listening" and "terminated": with zero `SIGTERM` and zero `SIGINT` listeners registered on the process, the default disposition applies, and a keep-alive socket that was open when `SIGTERM` arrived observed an immediate peer close with no further response. Second, the transition into `S5` is terminal and unrecoverable in-process — there is no port fallback, no retry timer, and no supervisor, so `S5` always leads to process exit.

#### 4.3.1.3 Connection and Keep-Alive State Transitions

Connection state is the only state in the system with non-trivial transitions, and all of it belongs to the runtime. Every transition below was reproduced during verification.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Socket accepted by the runtime" as C0
    state "Receiving request head" as C1
    state "Handler executing" as C2
    state "Response framed and flushed" as C3
    state "Keep-alive idle" as C4
    state "Protocol error answered by the runtime" as C5
    state "Closed" as C6
    [*] --> C0
    C0 --> C1: first bytes arrive
    C1 --> C2: head parsed within the headersTimeout 60000 ms budget
    C1 --> C5: malformed request 400 or oversized head 431
    C2 --> C3: three handler statements complete
    C3 --> C4: HTTP 1.1 keep-alive negotiated
    C3 --> C6: HTTP 1.0 client or Connection close
    C4 --> C1: next request on the same socket
    C4 --> C6: idle beyond keepAliveTimeout 5000 ms
    C5 --> C6: idle beyond keepAliveTimeout 5000 ms
    C6 --> [*]: descriptor released
```

The `C1 → C5` transition is the only path in the system that produces a non-`200` status, and it never involves repository code: the live server object reports **0** `clientError` listeners, so the runtime's default response applies (`400 Bad Request` or `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`, each followed by `Connection: close`).

#### 4.3.1.4 Response Object State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "res created by the runtime" as R0
    state "Status assigned, line 7" as R1
    state "Content-Type staged, line 8" as R2
    state "Head and body flushed by res.end, line 9" as R3
    state "Response complete, res unreachable" as R4
    [*] --> R0
    R0 --> R1: handler entry
    R1 --> R2: setHeader call
    R2 --> R3: end with the 14-byte literal
    R3 --> R4: runtime appends Date, Content-Length, Connection, Keep-Alive
    R4 --> [*]: object eligible for garbage collection
```

The ordering matters and is enforced by the runtime rather than by the code: `setHeader` at line 8 must precede `res.end` at line 9, because headers are flushed with the first body write. Since the handler contains no branch, the sequence `R0 → R1 → R2 → R3 → R4` is the only reachable path, which is why every probe returned an identical header set.

#### 4.3.1.5 Data Persistence Points

There are none. The system has **zero persistence points**, verified from three angles: `server.js` contains no `fs` usage, no database or cache client, and no `require` other than `http`; the repository working tree was unchanged after all verification runs (`git status --porcelain` reported 0 changed files, and no new files appeared in the checkout); and the only output channels are the network socket and the two standard streams. Consequently there is no write-ahead point, no checkpoint, no durable queue, and no recovery-from-storage procedure to document. The startup readiness line is written to stdout only — it is not persisted to a log file, and no rotation or retention target exists.

#### 4.3.1.6 Caching

No caching layer exists at any tier: no in-process cache or memoization, no cache client, and no HTTP cache-control directives. This last point is worth stating precisely because it is observable on the wire — the application sets exactly one response header (`Content-Type`), so no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Expires`, or `Vary` header is emitted, and clients therefore receive no caching guidance for a payload that is in fact permanently constant. The nearest thing to a cache in the system is the runtime's keep-alive connection reuse (`keepAliveTimeout` 5000 ms), which caches the *connection*, not the response.

#### 4.3.1.7 Transaction Boundaries

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A(["Request arrives at the listener"])
    B["Unit of work begins - runtime invokes the handler"]
    C["Three synchronous statements, no await, no external call, no shared variable"]
    D["Unit of work ends - res.end returns and the handler exits"]
    E{"Any durable state written during the unit of work?"}
    F["No - no database, cache, file, queue or in-memory accumulator exists"]
    G(["No commit, rollback, idempotency key or compensation applies"])
    A --> B
    B --> C
    C --> D
    D --> E
    E -->|"no"| F
    F --> G
```

The unit of work is one handler invocation, and it is atomic by construction: it is fully synchronous, so the single-threaded event loop cannot interleave another request inside it, and it touches nothing outside the `res` object handed to it. There is no transaction manager, no two-phase commit, no saga or compensation, and no idempotency mechanism — and none is needed, because every invocation is a pure write of a constant to one socket. The only partial-failure mode is a process termination mid-invocation, in which case the client's connection is closed without a response and there is nothing to roll back.

### 4.3.2 Error Handling

#### 4.3.2.1 Error Handling Inventory

The starting point for this sub-section is an audited absence. `server.js` contains no `try`, no `catch`, no `throw`, no `.catch()`, no `server.on('error', ...)`, no `clientError` handler, and no `process.on('uncaughtException'/'unhandledRejection')`. This was confirmed twice: by a grep of the source, and by reading listener counts from the live server and process objects, where `error`, `clientError`, `timeout`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `uncaughtException`, and `unhandledRejection` all report **0** listeners. Every error behavior the system exhibits is therefore a default of the Node.js runtime or the operating system.

#### 4.3.2.2 Error Classification and Disposition

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F(["Fault occurs"])
    Q1{"Fault surfaces during bind or during a request?"}
    B1["Server error event raised by the runtime"]
    B2{"Any error listener registered?"}
    B3["Zero listeners - Node rethrows as an uncaught exception"]
    B4["stderr stack trace, process exit code 1, no readiness line"]
    R1{"Fault is a protocol fault or an application fault?"}
    R2["Runtime answers 400 or 431 and closes the socket, handler never invoked"]
    R3["No application fault path exists - handler has no branch, no throw, no try or catch"]
    R4["Client observes a response, process stays alive, nothing logged"]
    T1["Signal delivered - no SIGTERM or SIGINT listener registered"]
    T2["Default disposition, immediate exit 130 or 143, in-flight sockets closed"]
    Rec(["Recovery - operator relaunches node server.js manually"])
    End(["End - client-visible outcome only, no notification channel exists"])
    F --> Q1
    Q1 -->|"bind, startup"| B1
    B1 --> B2
    B2 -->|"no"| B3
    B3 --> B4
    B4 --> Rec
    Q1 -->|"request, steady state"| R1
    R1 -->|"protocol"| R2
    R2 --> R4
    R1 -->|"application"| R3
    R3 --> R4
    R4 --> End
    Q1 -->|"termination signal"| T1
    T1 --> T2
    T2 --> Rec
```

| Fault Class | Disposition | Verified Evidence |
|-------------|-------------|-------------------|
| Bind failure (`EADDRINUSE`) | Fatal — unhandled `error` event becomes an uncaught exception | Exit code `1`, 0 bytes on stdout, stderr beginning `throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event` then `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` |
| Malformed request | Handled by the runtime before dispatch | `HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; the application never sees it and logs nothing |
| Oversized request head | Handled by the runtime before dispatch | `HTTP/1.1 431 Request Header Fields Too Large` with `Connection: close` |
| Application exception | Not reachable | The handler is three unconditional statements with no operation that can throw on valid inputs; there is no code path that produces a `5xx` |
| Client disconnect mid-response | Runtime default (socket error on write) | No application handling exists; the process continues serving other connections |
| Termination signal | Default disposition, immediate exit | `SIGINT` exit `130`, `SIGTERM` exit `143`, stderr empty, listener removed and subsequent probes returning status `000` |

#### 4.3.2.3 Retry Mechanisms and Fallback Processes

Neither exists, at any layer. There is no retry loop, no backoff, no jitter, no circuit breaker, no bulkhead, no timeout-and-retry wrapper, and no fallback response, degraded mode, or secondary endpoint. The two places where a retry would conventionally appear were both examined directly: the bind path has no `error` listener and therefore cannot re-attempt or fall back to another port, and the request path has no downstream dependency to retry against, because the system makes no outbound call of any kind. The only retry in the whole picture is external and client-side — a client that receives a refused connection or a closed socket may reconnect, and the runtime will accept it if the process is still listening.

#### 4.3.2.4 Error Notification Flows

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Signals["Available failure signals - complete inventory"]
        Sig1["Absent readiness line on stdout"]
        Sig2["stderr stack trace, bind failures only"]
        Sig3["Process exit code 1, 130 or 143"]
        Sig4["Connection refused, observed status 000"]
    end
    subgraph Detection["Detection - external and manual"]
        Watch["Operator inspects the foreground process or probes the endpoint"]
        NoAgent["No health endpoint, metric, alert rule or supervisor exists"]
    end
    subgraph Recovery["Recovery - manual only"]
        Free["Free port 3000 or stop the conflicting process"]
        Relaunch["Run node server.js again"]
        Verify["Confirm the 41-byte readiness line and probe for 200"]
    end
    Sig1 --> Watch
    Sig2 --> Watch
    Sig3 --> Watch
    Sig4 --> Watch
    Watch --> NoAgent
    NoAgent --> Free
    Free --> Relaunch
    Relaunch --> Verify
```

Notification is entirely passive: there is no alerting integration, no email, SMS, webhook, or chat sink, no error-tracking client, and no structured error log. The four signals above are the complete set available to an operator, and three of them are only observable by someone already watching the process or actively probing the endpoint. Two verified corollaries deserve emphasis — protocol errors (`400`, `431`) generate **no server-side record at all**, since stdout remained 41 bytes across all probing, and a successful termination writes nothing to stderr, so a stopped process is indistinguishable from a never-started one except by the absence of a listener.

#### 4.3.2.5 Recovery Procedures

Recovery is manual restart, and it was verified end to end: after termination, re-running `node server.js` restored `200` responses and re-emitted the 41-byte readiness line. Because the system holds no state, restart is inherently complete — there is nothing to replay, reconcile, or repair.

| Failure | Recovery Procedure | Recovery Characteristics |
|---------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| Port already bound | Stop the process holding port 3000, then relaunch | No in-process alternative exists; the port is a literal with no fallback |
| Process crashed or terminated | Relaunch `node server.js` and confirm the readiness line | Verified to restore service; no supervisor, `systemd` unit, container restart policy, or process manager is configured in the repository |
| In-flight requests lost at termination | None — the client must retry | No draining, no graceful shutdown, and no acknowledgement to the client |
| Client cannot connect from another host | Not a failure to recover from — it is the designed loopback boundary | Would require a code change, since the bind address is a literal at line 3 |

No automated recovery exists at any level: no restart policy, no health-check-driven replacement, no rollback, and no zero-downtime restart path. Any restart is a full outage for the duration of the relaunch.
