# 5. System Architecture

## 5.1 High-Level Architecture

The architecture described in this section is derived exclusively from the three tracked files in the repository — `server.js` (342 bytes, 14 lines, nine statements of which five are at module top level), `README.md` (27 bytes, a single H1 heading), and `test.js` (13 bytes, two bare identifier statements) — together with the runtime and operating-system behaviour observed when `server.js` is executed unmodified. There are no subdirectories, no dependency manifest, no configuration files, and no deployment descriptors of any kind. Consequently this is an architecture of *minimum viable surface area*: almost every architectural concern that a conventional service specification would allocate to a dedicated component is instead either delegated to the Node.js runtime, delegated to the host operating system, or genuinely absent. Each of those three dispositions is stated explicitly rather than glossed over, because the allocation of responsibility — not the volume of code — is what defines this system's architecture.

Of those three files, only `server.js` is an architectural element. `README.md` is documentation and `test.js` is an inert artifact: it defines no component, exposes no interface, participates in no data flow, is imported by nothing, and is never loaded into the process — executing it directly aborts with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` (exit 1). Its presence in the tree therefore adds no node, edge, layer, or boundary to any diagram in this section; every component, interface, and flow documented below is entirely a property of `server.js` and its delegated substrate.

### 5.1.1 System Overview

#### 5.1.1.1 Architectural Style and Rationale

The system is a **single-process, single-module, event-driven network service** — architecturally the degenerate case of a monolith, in which the entire application tier consists of one module evaluated once at process start. It is most precisely classified as a **"script-as-service"**: the artifact is a plain script whose evaluation has the side effect of establishing a long-lived server, rather than a library or framework-hosted application that is composed, configured, and then started by separate machinery.

Four style attributes were verified directly in the source:

- **Event-driven / reactor concurrency.** `server.js` never creates a thread, a worker, or a child process (`grep` for `cluster`, `worker_threads`, and `child_process` returns zero matches). All concurrency is achieved by the Node.js event loop demultiplexing readiness events for one listening socket and its accepted connections. Under a load probe of 60 simultaneously held keep-alive connections, the process thread count remained constant at 7 while its open descriptor count rose from 22 to 82 — exactly one descriptor per connection and zero additional threads. Concurrency is therefore purely I/O-multiplexed, not thread- or process-parallel.
- **Inversion of control as the sole extension seam.** Application logic does not drive the HTTP protocol; it is registered *into* the runtime as a callback at line 6 and invoked by the runtime once per parsed request. The server object carries exactly one `'request'` listener and zero `'error'`, `'clientError'`, or `'upgrade'` listeners. There is no middleware pipeline, router, filter chain, or plugin registry, so the single callback registration is the only place where behaviour can be attached.
- **Shared-nothing, stateless request handling.** The handler at lines 6–10 declares no variables, closes over no mutable state, and reads no external state. Every invocation performs the same three writes — `res.statusCode = 200`, `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')`, `res.end('Hello, World!\n')` — and returns. There is no `Map`, `Set`, module-level counter, or `global` assignment anywhere in the file, so no two requests can influence one another.
- **Configuration by literal, not by injection.** The endpoint identity is fixed at authoring time in two `const` declarations (line 3 `'127.0.0.1'`, line 4 `3000`). The file contains no reference to `process.env`, no argument parsing, and no configuration file read (`grep -c 'process\.'` returns 0), so there is no runtime override channel of any kind.

The **rationale** for this style is inferable from the artifact itself rather than from any design document — `README.md` contains only the repository title and states nothing about intent. What the artifact optimises for is unambiguous: it eliminates every step between obtaining the source and observing a working HTTP endpoint. Because line 1 resolves a *built-in* specifier, there is nothing to install (`require.resolve('http')` returns the bare string `http` with no filesystem path, and `npm ls --all` reports an empty tree). Because startup is a module-evaluation side effect, there is nothing to wire up. Because the response is a literal, there is nothing to seed. The cost of that optimisation is that the same properties preclude configurability, testability in isolation, multi-host deployment, and observability — trade-offs formalised as decision records in section 5.3.

#### 5.1.1.2 Architectural Principles and Patterns

The following patterns are *observed in the code*, distinguished from patterns that are conventional for HTTP services but demonstrably not present here.

| Pattern | Where It Appears | Architectural Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reactor / event demultiplexing | Runtime-provided event loop serving the socket created at line 12 | One thread serves all connections; a blocking handler would stall every peer |
| Inversion of control (callback registration) | Handler passed to `http.createServer` at line 6 | Runtime owns the protocol lifecycle; application owns only response content |
| Delegation over implementation | Only seven distinct runtime calls are made in total | Parsing, framing, keep-alive, and error responses are inherited, not written |
| Stateless service | Handler body, lines 7–9 | Any invocation is interchangeable; no affinity, no session, no recovery state |
| Immutable configuration by literal | Lines 3–4, reused at lines 12 and 13 | Single source of truth for the endpoint, but zero deployment flexibility |
| Fail-fast startup | `server.listen` with no `'error'` listener, lines 12–14 | A bind conflict terminates the process rather than degrading it |
| Side-effect module | Whole file; `module.exports` left untouched | Importing the module *is* starting the server; the two cannot be separated |

Patterns explicitly **not** present, each verified by exhaustive path and content scans across all three tracked files: layered or hexagonal separation (there is one module, so no layer boundary exists inside the application); repository or data-access abstraction; middleware or interceptor chain; API gateway or reverse-proxy fronting; circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, or timeout-with-fallback; publish/subscribe or message-broker mediation; CQRS or event sourcing; sidecar or service-mesh participation. No file matching any of roughly 120 conventional artifact names for these patterns exists in the repository, and a case-insensitive content scan of all three files across fifty concern keyword families (database, cache, queue, broker, token, session, metric, trace, health, retry, circuit, replica, cluster, proxy, ingress, and others) produced zero matches. Extending the scan surface from two files to three changed no result: the 13 bytes of `test.js` contain no keyword from any family.

Two architectural assumptions are therefore load-bearing and should be recorded as such:

1. **The runtime is assumed correct and present.** Because the application implements no protocol logic and no error handling, the correctness, performance, and security posture of the HTTP surface are entirely properties of the Node.js build that executes the file. On the verification host that build was Node.js v22.23.1 embedding the `llhttp` 9.4.2 parser. The repository declares no engine floor, no `.nvmrc`, and no `package.json`, so this coupling is implicit and unpinned.
2. **The execution context is assumed to be a single host with a free TCP port 3000 and an available loopback interface.** No fallback exists for any of these preconditions.

#### 5.1.1.3 System Boundaries and Major Interfaces

The system boundary is the boundary of a single operating-system process. Everything inside that boundary is one module plus the runtime that hosts it; everything outside is either an actor or a delegated platform facility.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Operator(["Operator / Developer<br/>same host"])
    Client(["HTTP Client<br/>curl, browser, script<br/>loopback-reachable only"])

    subgraph SystemBoundary["System Boundary — one OS process"]
        direction TB
        AppModule["Application Module<br/>server.js<br/>9 statements, 0 dependencies"]
        RuntimeLayer["Node.js Runtime Layer<br/>core http module + event loop"]
        AppModule -->|"registers handler,<br/>requests bind"| RuntimeLayer
    end

    subgraph HostPlatform["Host Platform — delegated, not owned"]
        direction TB
        TCPStack["OS TCP/IP stack<br/>loopback interface, port 3000,<br/>accept queue"]
        StdOut["Process stdout<br/>inherited descriptor"]
    end

    ExcludedSystems["No external systems in scope:<br/>no database, cache, broker,<br/>identity provider, or API peer"]

    Operator -->|"node server.js<br/>foreground launch"| AppModule
    Operator -->|"reads readiness line"| StdOut
    Client -->|"HTTP/1.1 request<br/>127.0.0.1:3000"| TCPStack
    TCPStack --> RuntimeLayer
    RuntimeLayer -->|"200 text/plain<br/>14-byte body"| TCPStack
    RuntimeLayer -.->|"one 41-byte line"| StdOut
```

The boundary is crossed by exactly **three interfaces**, and no others exist:

- **Inbound network interface (the only service interface).** A single TCP listening endpoint at `127.0.0.1:3000`, IPv4 only, serving plaintext HTTP/1.1. `/proc/net/tcp` shows one entry — `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A` (LISTEN) — while `/proc/net/tcp6` contains no entry for that port, confirming there is no dual-stack listener. There is no TLS listener (an HTTPS probe fails with a transport-level SSL error) and no HTTP/2 or WebSocket upgrade path (the server has zero `'upgrade'` listeners). The interface is uniform across the entire URI space: no path, method, header, or query participates in dispatch.
- **Process control interface.** Invocation is `node server.js` in the foreground; termination is by signal. Because the process registers no `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, or `uncaughtException` handlers, signal handling is entirely the runtime and OS default. This is the only administrative surface — there is no admin port, no configuration reload, and no control endpoint.
- **Outbound diagnostic interface.** A single 41-byte line written once to the inherited stdout descriptor at line 13. Nothing further is ever written: after roughly 360 requests plus deliberate protocol-error probes, stdout remained at exactly 41 bytes and stderr at 0 bytes. stderr is written only by the runtime's own crash reporting.

Three boundary characteristics deserve emphasis because they determine the system's deployability. First, the bind address is a *loopback* address, so the boundary is not merely a process boundary but a host boundary: a request to the host's routable address on port 3000 is refused at the transport layer. Second, there is no egress interface at all — the module opens no outbound socket, reads no file, and spawns no process, so the system cannot initiate communication with anything. Third, the boundary has no authentication or authorisation layer, meaning the loopback bind is simultaneously the deployment topology *and* the entire access-control mechanism.

The allocation of responsibility across the three layers inside and beneath the boundary is the most consequential fact about this architecture and is shown below. Only the left-hand layer is defined by repository content; the other two are inherited.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph LayerApp["Layer 1 — Application, owned by server.js"]
        direction LR
        APP1["Endpoint constants<br/>L3-L4"]
        APP2["Response composition<br/>L7-L9"]
        APP3["Readiness message<br/>L13"]
    end
    subgraph LayerRuntime["Layer 2 — Node.js runtime, delegated"]
        direction LR
        RT1["HTTP/1.1 parsing and framing<br/>llhttp"]
        RT2["Event loop and connection<br/>multiplexing"]
        RT3["Protocol error responses<br/>400 and 431"]
        RT4["Keep-alive and timeout<br/>enforcement"]
    end
    subgraph LayerOS["Layer 3 — Operating system, delegated"]
        direction LR
        OS1["Loopback interface and<br/>port reservation"]
        OS2["Accept queue<br/>somaxconn"]
        OS3["Signal delivery and<br/>process teardown"]
        OS4["stdout file descriptor"]
    end
    APP2 -->|"mutates response object"| RT1
    APP1 -->|"bind parameters"| OS1
    APP3 -->|"synchronous write"| OS4
    RT2 --> OS2
    RT4 --> RT2
    RT3 --> RT1
```

### 5.1.2 Core Components

The application decomposes into five logical components. Because the module contains no classes, no named functions, and no exports, these components are not separate code units — they are cohesive statement groups distinguished by responsibility, and they correspond one-to-one with the components identified in the high-level description in section 1.2.2.2. A sixth element, the delegated platform substrate, is included because it owns capabilities the application relies on but does not implement; it is detailed in section 5.2.6. No component corresponds to `test.js`: it is not part of the composition graph below.

| Component | Primary Responsibility | Key Dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C1 — Runtime Dependency Binding** (line 1) | Acquire the only dependency in the system by binding the built-in `http` module into module scope | Node.js CommonJS loader; the built-in `http` specifier (no filesystem or registry resolution occurs) |
| **C2 — Endpoint Configuration Constants** (lines 3–4) | Define the network identity of the service as two immutable literals: host `127.0.0.1` and port `3000` | None — pure literals with no upstream input |
| **C3 — HTTP Server Instance** (line 6) | Construct the runtime server object and register the application's single `'request'` listener, establishing the inversion-of-control seam | C1 (the `http` factory); C4 (the callback being registered) |
| **C4 — Request Handler** (lines 6–10) | Produce the invariant response: status 200, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and a 14-byte body | The `ServerResponse` object injected by the runtime on each invocation |
| **C5 — Listener Activation and Readiness Reporter** (lines 12–14) | Open the listening socket at the configured endpoint and emit the single readiness signal once binding succeeds | C2 (host and port); C3 (the server handle); `console` for the stdout write |
| **Delegated Platform Substrate** | Parse and frame HTTP, multiplex connections, enforce timeouts, answer protocol errors, reserve the port, deliver signals | Not repository content — supplied by the Node.js build and the host OS |

| Component | Integration Points | Critical Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C1** | Sole consumer is C3, at line 6; the textual `http` on line 13 is the URL scheme inside the readiness message, not a use of this binding | Uses the bare `'http'` specifier rather than `node:http`; the file must be evaluated as CommonJS — executing the same source in an ES-module scope fails with `require is not defined in ES module scope` |
| **C2** | Consumed twice — by C5 for binding (line 12) and by C5 for the readiness message (line 13) | Single source of truth guarantees the logged endpoint always matches the bound endpoint, but there is no override channel, so relocating the service requires editing source |
| **C3** | Bridges C1 and C4; hands the resulting server handle to C5 | Exactly one `'request'` listener and zero `'error'`, `'clientError'`, or `'upgrade'` listeners, so every non-request event falls through to runtime defaults |
| **C4** | Invoked only by the runtime, once per successfully parsed request; writes only to the injected response object | The request object it receives is never read — zero references to `req` exist — so inbound data is structurally discarded; the handler is synchronous with no branch, `throw`, or `try`/`catch` |
| **C5** | Calls into the runtime's `listen`, which in turn calls the OS; writes one line to stdout | No `backlog` argument is supplied and no `'error'` listener is attached, so accept-queue depth and bind-failure disposition are both runtime defaults; a bind conflict terminates the process with exit code 1 |
| **Delegated Platform Substrate** | Interfaces upward to C3/C4 by invoking the handler and downward to the kernel socket | Every timing limit, connection limit, and protocol error response is a runtime default that the repository neither sets nor pins |

The coupling between these components is a five-node directed acyclic graph with a single fan-in point — the runtime's invocation of C4 — and no shared mutable state. It was derived by mapping every identifier to the lines that reference it.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Composition["Application composition — server.js module scope"]
        direction TB
        CC1["C1 Runtime Dependency Binding<br/>L1 require of core http"]
        CC2["C2 Endpoint Configuration<br/>L3-L4 hostname, port"]
        CC3["C3 HTTP Server Instance<br/>L6 http.createServer"]
        CC4["C4 Request Handler closure<br/>L6-L10"]
        CC5["C5 Listener Activation and<br/>Readiness Reporter L12-L14"]
        CC1 -->|"http factory"| CC3
        CC4 -->|"single 'request' listener"| CC3
        CC3 -->|"server handle"| CC5
        CC2 -->|"port, hostname"| CC5
    end
    subgraph Runtime["Runtime-owned objects"]
        direction TB
        RT["http.Server instance<br/>request listeners = 1"]
        EL["Event loop"]
        SOCK["Listening socket<br/>127.0.0.1:3000 IPv4"]
    end
    OUT["stdout"]
    CC3 -->|"constructs"| RT
    CC5 -->|"listen port, hostname"| SOCK
    RT -->|"invokes handler per request"| CC4
    EL -->|"dispatches ready events"| RT
    SOCK -->|"accepted connections"| EL
    CC5 -->|"41-byte readiness line"| OUT
    CC2 -.->|"interpolated into message"| OUT
```

Two structural properties follow from this graph. Components C1, C2, C3, and C5 execute exactly once, during module evaluation, and are then inert — they constitute a *composition phase*. Only C4 executes repeatedly, and it is the only component that ever runs after startup, which is why the system's steady-state behaviour is fully described by three statements. Because C4 is reached solely through the runtime's fan-in edge, the application has no call graph of its own at steady state.

### 5.1.3 Data Flow Description

The system has two data paths that are, unusually, **not connected by data**. The inbound path terminates unread, and the outbound path is generated from constants. The runtime invokes the handler as a *control* signal derived from the inbound path, but no byte of inbound content reaches the outbound path.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inbound["Inbound path — terminates unread"]
        direction TB
        I1["TCP byte stream on<br/>127.0.0.1:3000"]
        I2["llhttp parse to<br/>IncomingMessage"]
        I3{{"Does application code<br/>read the request?"}}
        I4["Discarded: zero references<br/>to the request object"]
        I1 --> I2
        I2 --> I3
        I3 -->|"No"| I4
    end
    subgraph Outbound["Outbound path — the only data production"]
        direction TB
        O1["Handler mutates<br/>ServerResponse"]
        O2["statusCode = 200"]
        O3["Content-Type: text/plain"]
        O4["14-byte literal body"]
        O5["Runtime appends Date,<br/>Content-Length, Connection,<br/>Keep-Alive"]
        O6["Serialized HTTP/1.1<br/>response bytes"]
        O1 --> O2
        O2 --> O3
        O3 --> O4
        O4 --> O5
        O5 --> O6
    end
    I2 -.->|"triggers invocation only,<br/>supplies no data"| O1
    O6 --> RCL["Client socket"]
    NoStore["No data store, cache, queue,<br/>or log sink on either path"]
```

**Primary data flows.** There are three, and only three. The first is the *request flow*: a client's bytes arrive on the loopback socket, the kernel places the connection on the accept queue, the runtime parses the byte stream into an `IncomingMessage`, and the runtime invokes C4. The flow ends there — C4 holds a reference to the parsed request but never dereferences it, so the request's method, URI, headers, and body are all discarded without inspection. The second is the *response flow*: C4 mutates the `ServerResponse` object with a status code, one header, and a body literal; the runtime serialises that object into a wire-format HTTP/1.1 response and writes it back over the same socket. The third is the *readiness flow*: the two configuration constants are interpolated into a template literal by C5 and written once to stdout. No other data moves anywhere at any time.

**Integration patterns and protocols.** The single integration pattern is **synchronous request/response over HTTP/1.1**, in a strictly one-request-in / one-response-out shape with no batching, streaming, chunking, long-polling, or callback pattern. Connection reuse is enabled by the runtime's default and confirmed on the wire: responses carry `Connection: keep-alive` and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`. No asynchronous integration pattern exists — the module contains no `Promise`, `async`, `await`, `setTimeout`, or `setInterval`, and there is no queue, topic, webhook, scheduler, or file-drop mechanism anywhere in the repository.

**Data transformation points.** There are exactly two transformations, both performed by the runtime rather than the application. The first is *parse*: an inbound octet stream becomes an `IncomingMessage` object — a transformation whose output is then dropped. The second is *serialise*: the mutated `ServerResponse` becomes an outbound octet stream, during which the runtime supplies framing metadata the application never sets. Observed response headers appear in the order `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, `Content-Length: 14`; of these, only the status line and `Content-Type` originate in application code. The application itself performs **no** transformation: it does not decode, validate, map, enrich, aggregate, filter, or format anything, because the only data it produces is a compile-time literal.

**Key data stores and caches.** There are none, at any tier. No database, ORM, schema, migration set, or embedded store is present; the module performs no filesystem access (no `fs` or `path` usage); no in-process collection is created to hold state; and no external cache is configured or contacted. Because the response is a literal rather than a computed value, there is nothing that *could* be cached, and the responses carry no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, or `Last-Modified` header, so no client- or intermediary-side caching is directed either. The architectural consequence is that the system holds **no state whose loss matters**: the sole persistent artifact in the entire architecture is the source file itself.

### 5.1.4 External Integration Points

The system integrates with **no external system**. This is not an omission in the documentation but a verified property of the repository: there is no API contract artifact (no OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Protobuf, or GraphQL schema), no client SDK or integration module, no broker or cloud-provider configuration, and no outbound network call in the source. The module never constructs an HTTP client, never resolves a hostname, and never opens a socket other than the one it listens on. Section 1.2.1.3 records the same conclusion from the business-context perspective: in its committed form the system is not reachable by, and does not reach, any other system.

What follows, therefore, is not a list of third-party integrations but the complete set of *boundary interactions* — the counterparties the process actually exchanges data with.

| Counterparty | Integration Type | Data Exchange Pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same-host HTTP client (`curl`, browser, script) | Inbound network service call | Synchronous request/response, one response per request, connection reusable within the keep-alive window |
| Host OS TCP/IP stack (loopback interface) | Platform facility, bidirectional | Socket bind and listen at startup, then accept plus read/write per connection |
| Host process environment (stdout, signals) | Platform facility | One-way write of a single readiness line at startup; one-way inbound signal delivery for termination |
| Node.js runtime and core `http` module | In-process delegated dependency | In-process function calls outward and callback invocation inward — not a network integration |
| GitHub repository (`origin` remote) | Source-code hosting only | Developer-time `git` operations; the running process never contacts it |

| Counterparty | Protocol / Format | SLA Requirements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same-host HTTP client | HTTP/1.1 over plaintext TCP; response body `text/plain`, 14 bytes; IPv4 only, no TLS, no HTTP/2 | None declared in the repository |
| Host OS TCP/IP stack | Berkeley sockets via the runtime; IPv4 loopback, port 3000 | None declared; accept-queue depth is the OS default, not a stated capacity |
| Host process environment | UTF-8 text on stdout (41 bytes); POSIX signals inbound | None declared; no readiness, liveness, or startup-time budget is specified |
| Node.js runtime and core `http` module | CommonJS module interface; `http.Server` and `ServerResponse` object contracts | None declared; the repository pins no engine version and no `.nvmrc`, so no compatibility floor is stated |
| GitHub repository | HTTPS `git` transport | Not applicable — no runtime dependency |

**On SLA requirements.** Every cell above reads "none declared" because the repository declares no service-level objective, error budget, latency target, throughput target, availability target, or capacity assumption. There is no SLA, SLO, benchmark, load-test, or performance-budget artifact, and none of the three tracked files mentions any such concept. Section 1.2.3.1 records the same finding: the repository defines no success criteria of any kind. Timing values that appear elsewhere in this section — such as the 5-second keep-alive window or the 60-second header timeout — are **Node.js runtime defaults inherited by the application**, and measured figures reported in section 5.4.5 are **characteristics of the host on which they were observed**. Neither category may be read as a commitment made by this system.

## 5.2 Component Details

This section specifies each component identified in section 5.1.2 across five facets: purpose and responsibilities, technologies and frameworks, key interfaces and APIs, data persistence requirements, and scaling considerations. Two facets have the same answer for every application component and are stated once here rather than repeated as filler: **no application component has any data persistence requirement** — the module performs no filesystem, database, or cache access of any kind — and **no application component can be scaled independently**, because all five are statements inside one module inside one process. Where a component's scaling behaviour is nonetheless architecturally meaningful, it is described in terms of what the component *imposes* on the single process it lives in.

A vocabulary note that governs the whole section: components C1, C2, C3, and C5 belong to a **composition phase** that executes exactly once during module evaluation, whereas C4 is the only component that executes during the **serving phase**. This split, rather than any module or package boundary, is the system's real internal structure.

### 5.2.1 C1 — Runtime Dependency Binding

**Purpose and responsibilities.** C1 is the system's entire dependency-acquisition mechanism. Its single statement at line 1 binds the Node.js core `http` module into module scope, and that binding is the only capability the application imports from anywhere. Architecturally, C1 is the point at which the decision to build on runtime primitives rather than a framework becomes concrete: because it resolves a built-in specifier, the dependency graph has depth one and breadth one.

**Technologies and frameworks.** The CommonJS module system as implemented by the Node.js loader, and the Node.js core `http` module. No framework is involved. The specifier used is the bare form `'http'` rather than the prefixed `'node:http'` form; both resolve to the same built-in, and `require.resolve('http')` returns the bare string with no filesystem path, confirming that no package resolution, download, or link step occurs. `npm ls --all` reports an empty tree.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Exactly one call, `require('http')`, whose return value is used exactly once — by C3 at line 6. The `http` text appearing at line 13 is the URL scheme inside a template literal and is not a reference to this binding, a distinction confirmed by mapping every occurrence of the identifier to its line.

**Data persistence requirements.** None. The binding lives in module scope for the process lifetime and is never written to disk or shared.

**Scaling considerations.** C1 imposes no scaling limit of its own, but it establishes the system's most important scaling *constraint indirectly*: by importing only `http`, the application inherits the runtime's single-event-loop concurrency model without importing `cluster` or `worker_threads`, so there is no in-process path to multi-core utilisation. C1 also carries a hard compatibility constraint that any packaging change must respect — the file must be evaluated as CommonJS. Executing the same source in an ES-module scope fails with `require is not defined in ES module scope`, so introducing a `package.json` containing `"type": "module"`, or renaming the file to `.mjs`, would break startup.

### 5.2.2 C2 — Endpoint Configuration Constants

**Purpose and responsibilities.** C2 defines the network identity of the service as two immutable literals — `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` at line 3 and `port = 3000` at line 4 — and is responsible for keeping the bound endpoint and the advertised endpoint identical. It is the system's complete configuration layer.

**Technologies and frameworks.** Plain JavaScript `const` declarations. There is no configuration framework, schema, defaulting layer, or validation. The file contains no reference to `process.env`, no command-line argument parsing, and no configuration-file read, and the repository contains no `.env`, `.env.example`, or `config/` directory.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** C2 exposes no callable interface; it is consumed by identifier reference at two sites, both inside C5 — as positional arguments to `server.listen` at line 12, and interpolated into the readiness template literal at line 13. This dual consumption is a deliberate single-source-of-truth property: the logged endpoint cannot drift from the bound endpoint.

**Data persistence requirements.** None. The values are compile-time literals; there is no persisted or externally supplied configuration state, and therefore nothing to reload, version, or reconcile.

**Scaling considerations.** C2 is the binding constraint on horizontal scaling and the reason the system cannot be replicated on one host. Because the port is a literal with no override channel and no `'error'`-driven fallback, two instances cannot coexist: launching a second process while the first holds the port terminates the second with `EADDRINUSE` and exit code 1. Because the address is a loopback address, no instance is reachable from another host, so a load balancer could not distribute traffic to it even if replicas existed. Any scale-out strategy therefore begins with a source change to C2 — externalising both values — which is why section 5.3 records this as a distinct architecture decision rather than a coding detail.

### 5.2.3 C3 — HTTP Server Instance

**Purpose and responsibilities.** C3 constructs the runtime's `http.Server` object and, in the same expression, registers the application's request handler as the server's sole `'request'` listener. It is the inversion-of-control seam: after line 6 executes, the runtime owns the protocol lifecycle and the application owns only response content.

**Technologies and frameworks.** The `http.createServer` factory from the Node.js core `http` module. The resulting object is a runtime-managed `EventEmitter` subclass, but the application never treats it as one — no `.on(...)` call appears anywhere in the file.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** One outbound call, `http.createServer(handler)`. Runtime introspection of the resulting object confirms its listener topology: `request` = 1, and `error`, `clientError`, and `upgrade` all = 0. The `connection` listener count of 1 is registered internally by the runtime, not by application code. The consequence is that every server-level event other than `'request'` falls through to runtime defaults — this single fact explains most of the error-handling architecture described in section 5.4.3.

**Data persistence requirements.** None. The server object is in-memory and process-scoped.

**Scaling considerations.** C3 sets no capacity properties on the object it creates. `server.maxConnections` is left unset, so the application imposes no ceiling on concurrent connections, and `server.maxRequestsPerSocket` remains 0, so no socket is ever retired after a request quota. Practical capacity is therefore bounded only by the platform limits catalogued in section 5.2.6. Because exactly one server object is created and it is never closed or re-listened, the object's lifecycle is strictly linear.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Unconstructed
    Unconstructed --> Constructed : L6 createServer with handler<br/>request listeners = 1
    Constructed --> Binding : L12 listen with port and hostname
    Binding --> Listening : bind succeeds<br/>address resolves to 127.0.0.1:3000
    Binding --> BindFailed : EADDRINUSE<br/>no error listener registered
    Listening --> Listening : connection accepted<br/>handler invoked, response written
    BindFailed --> [*] : unhandled error event throws<br/>process exit code 1
    Listening --> Terminated : SIGTERM or SIGINT<br/>no close call, no draining
    Terminated --> [*]
    note right of Constructed
        address() is null and no
        socket exists yet
    end note
    note right of Listening
        Absent transitions: no close(),
        no closed state, no re-listen
    end note
```

The diagram makes two absences explicit. There is no transition out of `Listening` other than process death: because `server.close()` is never called, the object has no reachable *closed* state, and because `listen` is called once, there is no re-listen path. And `BindFailed` is terminal rather than recoverable, since no `'error'` listener exists to intercept it.

### 5.2.4 C4 — Request Handler

**Purpose and responsibilities.** C4 is the entire application logic of the system. Its responsibility is to produce one invariant response — HTTP status 200, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and a 14-byte body — for every request the runtime hands it, without reference to what was requested.

**Technologies and frameworks.** A plain JavaScript arrow-function closure written inline as the argument to `http.createServer`. No framework, no middleware, no decorator, no validation library. The function is synchronous: the file contains no `async`, `await`, `Promise`, `setTimeout`, or `setInterval`, so the handler runs to completion within a single event-loop turn.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** C4's interface is the `(req, res)` pair injected by the runtime. It uses three response APIs — `res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader`, and `res.end` — and **zero** request APIs. A scan for references to the request parameter returns none, which is the single most architecturally significant fact about this component: the inbound half of its interface is declared but never read, so requests are structurally indistinguishable from one another. Behavioural probes confirm the design intent, with `GET /`, `POST /any/deep/path?q=1` carrying a body, and `DELETE /x` all producing byte-identical 200 / `text/plain` / 14-byte responses.

**Data persistence requirements.** None, and structurally none possible. C4 declares no variables, closes over no mutable state, allocates no collection, and touches no `global`. It therefore has no read set and no write set beyond the response object handed to it, which makes every invocation fully independent.

**Scaling considerations.** C4 is where the single-threaded model's risk concentrates. Because all requests are dispatched to this one function on the one event-loop thread, its execution time is the system's serialisation point; the current body — three property and method calls with no I/O — is effectively free, but any blocking work added here would stall every concurrent peer. Correspondingly, C4 has no per-request resource footprint to scale: it allocates no buffers beyond the literal and holds nothing across invocations, which is consistent with the observed steady memory profile in section 5.4.5.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CL as Loopback client
    participant OS as OS accept queue
    participant RT as Node runtime, llhttp and event loop
    participant H as C4 request handler
    participant OUT as stdout
    CL->>OS: TCP connect to 127.0.0.1:3000
    OS->>RT: accepted connection, one descriptor each
    CL->>RT: request line and headers
    alt Parse succeeds
        RT->>H: invoke with request and response objects
        H->>H: set statusCode to 200
        H->>H: set Content-Type to text/plain
        H->>RT: end with the 14-byte literal
        RT->>CL: 200 plus Date, Content-Length, Connection
    else Malformed request or oversize headers
        RT->>CL: 400 or 431 with Connection close
        Note over H: handler is never invoked
    end
    RT->>RT: hold socket open for keepAliveTimeout of 5000 ms
    Note over H,OUT: no application logging on any path —<br/>stdout remains at 41 bytes for the process lifetime
```

The `else` branch is not hypothetical. A request whose start line is not valid HTTP receives `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`, and a request carrying a header field larger than the runtime's 16 KiB limit receives `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`, in both cases produced by the runtime with C4 never entered and nothing written to stdout or stderr by the application.

### 5.2.5 C5 — Listener Activation and Readiness Reporter

**Purpose and responsibilities.** C5 performs the two remaining startup responsibilities: it asks the runtime to bind and listen at the endpoint C2 defines, and it emits the system's only readiness signal once the runtime reports success. It therefore owns both the transition into serving state and the sole observable evidence that the transition occurred.

**Technologies and frameworks.** `server.listen` from the core `http` module (delegating to `net`), plus `console.log` for the stdout write. No logging framework, log level, structured format, or transport is involved — the repository contains no logging configuration of any kind.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** `server.listen(port, hostname, callback)` at line 12, with the callback at lines 12–14 registered as a one-shot `'listening'` handler, and `console.log` with a template literal at line 13. Two arguments that are *not* supplied are architecturally significant: no `backlog` value, so accept-queue depth is a runtime default, and no `'error'` listener, so bind failure has no application-level disposition.

**Data persistence requirements.** None. The readiness line is written to a stream, not stored; there is no log file, rotation policy, or sink.

**Scaling considerations.** C5 fixes the ingress to a single listening socket on a single address family. `/proc/net/tcp` shows exactly one LISTEN entry for the port and `/proc/net/tcp6` shows none, so there is no dual-stack or multi-interface ingress to distribute load across. Because `listen` is invoked without `exclusive` or cluster participation and the module never imports `cluster`, socket sharing across worker processes is not available. C5 is also the component that makes startup fail-fast rather than resilient, which has a direct availability consequence documented in section 5.4.6.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant OP as Operator
    participant CJS as CommonJS loader
    participant APP as server.js module scope
    participant HTTP as Node core http
    participant OS as OS TCP/IP stack
    participant OUT as stdout
    OP->>CJS: node server.js
    CJS->>APP: evaluate module, side-effect startup
    APP->>HTTP: C1 require built-in http specifier
    HTTP-->>APP: module namespace, no filesystem resolution
    APP->>APP: C2 bind hostname and port literals
    APP->>HTTP: C3 createServer with C4 handler
    HTTP-->>APP: http.Server, address is null
    APP->>HTTP: C5 listen with port and hostname
    HTTP->>OS: bind and listen, default backlog 511
    OS-->>HTTP: socket enters LISTEN state
    HTTP->>APP: listening callback
    APP->>OUT: C5 writes 41-byte readiness line
    Note over APP,OUT: exports remain empty — the process stays alive<br/>only because the listening socket is a referenced handle
```

The final note captures a subtle architectural property: the process has no main loop, no `await`, and no blocking call. It remains alive purely because the listening socket is a referenced libuv handle, which means process liveness and service availability are the same condition — there is no state in which the process runs but does not serve.

### 5.2.6 Delegated Platform Substrate

**Purpose and responsibilities.** This element is not repository content, but it must be specified as a component because it owns the majority of the system's behaviour. The Node.js runtime is responsible for parsing HTTP/1.1, framing responses, multiplexing connections on the event loop, enforcing every timeout, answering malformed and oversize requests, and surfacing socket errors as events. The host operating system is responsible for reserving the port, maintaining the accept queue, delivering signals, and providing the stdout descriptor. Every architectural quality attribute the application does not implement resides here.

**Technologies and frameworks.** A Node.js build providing the core `http` module. On the verification host this was Node.js v22.23.1, embedding V8 12.4.254.21-node.56, libuv 1.51.0, OpenSSL 3.5.7, and the `llhttp` 9.4.2 HTTP/1.1 parser; the platform package was `nodejs 22.23.1-1nodesource1`, and Node.js is MIT-licensed. **These are properties of the observed environment, not requirements of the repository** — no `package.json` `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, or `.node-version` file exists, so the artifact states no compatibility floor. The practical implication is that the system's HTTP-parsing and TLS-library exposure is a function of whichever Node.js build an operator happens to use.

**Key interfaces and APIs.** Upward toward the application, the substrate offers the `http.createServer` and `server.listen` entry points and invokes the registered handler with `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse` objects. Downward toward the kernel, it performs the socket `bind`, `listen`, and `accept` sequence. All seven application-to-runtime calls in the entire system cross this interface.

**Data persistence requirements.** None introduced by the substrate for this workload: no temporary files, spool, or state directory is created, because the application requests no file, cache, or database operation.

**Scaling considerations.** Because the application sets none of the following, every one of them is an inherited default that constitutes the system's real capacity and timing envelope.

| Inherited Setting | Value Observed | Architectural Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `keepAliveTimeout` | 5000 ms | Idle connections are reclaimed after five seconds, bounding descriptor accumulation without any application logic |
| `headersTimeout` | 60000 ms | A client may take up to a minute to finish sending headers before the runtime intervenes |
| `requestTimeout` | 300000 ms | A single request may occupy a connection for five minutes, which is the practical slow-client exposure window |
| `server.timeout` | 0 — disabled | There is no general per-socket inactivity timeout beyond the keep-alive and request timers |
| `maxRequestsPerSocket` | 0 — unlimited | A single connection may serve unbounded requests, so no socket recycling occurs |
| `maxHeadersCount` | `null` — unlimited | Header *count* is unbounded, although total header size is not |
| `server.maxConnections` | unset — no cap | The application imposes no concurrency ceiling of its own |
| `http.maxHeaderSize` | 16384 bytes | Requests exceeding this receive a runtime-generated `431` and never reach C4 |
| `listen` backlog | runtime default 511, capped by the OS | Node documents 511 as the default, with the effective queue determined by `somaxconn` and `tcp_max_syn_backlog`; the observed host reported 1024 and 4096 respectively |
| libuv thread pool | 4 threads, unused by this workload | Present but idle, since the workload performs no filesystem, DNS, or crypto work |

Measured process topology on the verification host reinforces how narrow the scaling envelope is: one process, seven threads, and 22 open descriptors at idle, with a resident set of roughly 47 MiB. Under a burst of 300 requests at concurrency 30 the process remained a single process with seven threads and its descriptor count returned to 22, while resident memory rose to roughly 58 MiB. Holding 60 simultaneous keep-alive connections open raised descriptors from 22 to 82 — precisely one per connection — with the thread count unchanged. The descriptor ceiling on that host was 1,048,576, so concurrency is limited in practice by event-loop throughput and memory rather than by descriptors. All of these figures are host observations and are not capacity commitments.

The deployment view below completes the component picture by showing what the substrate provides and, equally important, which conventional platform tiers have no representation in the repository at all.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    ClientNode["Same-host client<br/>loopback only"]
    subgraph HostBox["Single host — no orchestrator, no supervisor"]
        direction TB
        Proc["OS process: node server.js<br/>1 process, 7 threads observed"]
        Loop["1 event-loop thread<br/>all request handling"]
        Pool["libuv thread pool, default 4<br/>unused by this workload"]
        Sock["1 listening socket<br/>127.0.0.1:3000 IPv4"]
        Conn["1 file descriptor per<br/>concurrent connection"]
        Proc --> Loop
        Proc --> Pool
        Loop --> Sock
        Sock --> Conn
    end
    subgraph AbsentTier["Absent scale-out tier — no artifact in the repository"]
        direction TB
        LB["Load balancer or reverse proxy"]
        Rep["Replica processes, cluster workers"]
        Orc["Container image, orchestration manifest"]
        Sup["Process manager, restart policy"]
    end
    ClientNode -->|"TCP connect"| Sock
```

The lower subgraph is a documentation of absence, verified rather than assumed: the repository contains no `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose` file, Kubernetes or Helm manifest, Terraform or other infrastructure-as-code definition, `Procfile`, process-manager configuration, reverse-proxy configuration, or CI/CD pipeline definition. Deployment consists of an operator running `node server.js` in the foreground on one host. There is consequently no supervisor to restart the process — after termination by signal, the process count stayed at zero and the endpoint remained unreachable until a manual relaunch.

## 5.3 Technical Decisions

A necessary caveat frames this entire section. **The repository contains no design documentation, no architecture decision records, no comments, and no rationale of any kind** — `README.md` holds only the repository title, and `server.js` contains zero comment lines. Every decision documented below is therefore *reconstructed from the artifact*: the decision itself is inferred from what the code demonstrably does and does not do, while the alternatives and trade-offs are the standard options that the observed choice excludes. Nothing here should be read as a statement of the original author's intent, and no decision date, author, or approval status is claimed, because none is recorded anywhere in the repository.

### 5.3.1 Architecture Style Decisions and Trade-offs

**The decision.** Build the service as a single-file CommonJS script that uses the Node.js core `http` module directly, with the listener started as a side effect of module evaluation. This is evidenced by the file's complete construct inventory: one `require`, no classes, no named functions, no `module.exports` assignment, no framework import, and no separation between a composition unit and a bootstrap unit.

The decision path below shows the gates that the observed implementation clears, and the alternative that each gate excludes. Each gate is a question answerable from the code rather than from speculation.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Q1{{"Must the endpoint serve more than<br/>one route or representation?"}}
    Q1 -->|"No — one fixed payload"| Q2
    Q1 -->|"Yes"| ALT1["Rejected alternative:<br/>router or web framework<br/>Express, Fastify, Koa"]
    Q2{{"Does application code read any<br/>request attribute?"}}
    Q2 -->|"No — request object unreferenced"| Q3
    Q2 -->|"Yes"| ALT2["Rejected alternative:<br/>body parsing and<br/>validation middleware"]
    Q3{{"Is third-party code acceptable<br/>as a runtime dependency?"}}
    Q3 -->|"No — zero install, zero<br/>supply-chain surface"| Q4
    Q3 -->|"Yes"| ALT3["Rejected alternative:<br/>npm dependency graph,<br/>lockfile and audit pipeline"]
    Q4{{"Must the module be importable<br/>and unit-testable in isolation?"}}
    Q4 -->|"No — direct execution only"| DEC["Selected architecture:<br/>single-file CommonJS script on<br/>core http with side-effect startup"]
    Q4 -->|"Yes"| ALT4["Rejected alternative:<br/>factory export plus a<br/>separate bootstrap entrypoint"]
```

**Trade-offs.** The style is strongly optimised for one quality attribute — immediacy of execution — at the direct cost of most others.

| Quality Attribute | Effect of the Chosen Style | What the Rejected Alternative Would Have Provided |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time to first working request | Optimal: no install, no build, no configuration; `node server.js` is the entire procedure | A dependency install and, for typed or bundled stacks, a build step |
| Dependency and supply-chain risk | Optimal: exactly one dependency, and it is built into the runtime, so there is no lockfile, registry fetch, or audit surface | A transitive dependency graph requiring lockfile pinning and vulnerability scanning |
| Extensibility | Poor: the single `'request'` listener is the only extension seam, so adding a route or filter means editing the handler | Declarative route registration and a composable middleware pipeline |
| Testability | Poor: because startup is a module side effect and `module.exports` is untouched, the server cannot be imported without binding port 3000, and no unit boundary exists | An exported factory that can be instantiated on an ephemeral port inside a test |
| Configurability | Absent: endpoint values are literals with no override channel | Environment-variable or configuration-file resolution with defaults |
| Operational fitness | Poor: no configuration, no observability, no graceful shutdown, no error handling | Framework-provided logging hooks, error middleware, and shutdown coordination |

**Assessment.** The style is well matched to the artifact's evident purpose as a minimal, self-contained demonstration of an HTTP listener, and it would be a poor fit for any workload requiring configuration, multi-tenancy, or operational instrumentation. The most consequential structural trade-off is the side-effect startup: it is the single property that simultaneously blocks unit testing, blocks reuse as a library, and makes the module unable to participate in a process that hosts anything else.

### 5.3.2 Communication Pattern Choices

**The decision.** Expose exactly one synchronous request/response interface over plaintext HTTP/1.1 on a loopback TCP socket, accept the runtime's default connection-reuse behaviour, and provide no asynchronous or outbound communication path.

| Pattern Dimension | Choice Made | Evidence and Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interaction style | Synchronous request/response | The handler writes the complete response and returns within one event-loop turn; no callback, polling, or deferred-completion pattern exists |
| Protocol and version | Plaintext HTTP/1.1 only | Wire probes report HTTP/1.1; the server has zero `'upgrade'` listeners, so WebSocket and HTTP/2 upgrade are unavailable, and an HTTPS attempt fails at the transport layer |
| Transport scope | IPv4 loopback only | One LISTEN entry in `/proc/net/tcp` and none in `/proc/net/tcp6`; a probe of the host's routable address is refused |
| Connection management | Runtime-default keep-alive | Responses carry `Connection: keep-alive` and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`; an idle connection was observed closing shortly after the 5-second window, and an HTTP/1.0 request was answered with `Connection: close` by runtime negotiation |
| Content negotiation | None | `Content-Type: text/plain` is set unconditionally; the `Accept` header is never read, and no alternative representation exists |
| Outbound communication | None | No client construction, hostname resolution, or outbound socket appears in the module |
| Asynchronous messaging | None | No queue, topic, broker, webhook, or scheduler artifact exists in the repository, and the module contains no `Promise`, `async`, or timer construct |

**Rationale and trade-offs.** Synchronous request/response is the only pattern the workload requires: the response is a constant, so there is no long-running computation to defer, no result to deliver out of band, and no back-pressure problem to mediate with a queue. Choosing HTTP/1.1 over a raw TCP protocol buys interoperability with every ordinary client for free, and choosing the core `http` module means the entire protocol implementation — parsing, framing, keep-alive negotiation, and 100-continue handling — is inherited rather than written. The cost is that all protocol-level policy is inherited too: the application cannot alter status codes for malformed input, cannot add security headers on the error paths, and cannot cap requests per connection, because it registers no listener for any of those events. A second cost is that plaintext-over-loopback is not a pattern that survives a change of deployment context; the moment the bind address becomes routable, the absence of TLS becomes a confidentiality defect rather than an acceptable local simplification.

### 5.3.3 Data Storage and Caching Decisions

**The decision.** Introduce no storage tier and no caching tier at any level — no database, no embedded store, no filesystem persistence, no in-process cache, no external cache, and no HTTP cache directives.

This decision is not an omission but a direct consequence of the response being a compile-time literal. The gates below trace the reasoning, and each is answerable from the code.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    S1{{"Does any request mutate or<br/>read state beyond the response?"}}
    S1 -->|"No — handler writes three<br/>properties and returns"| S2
    S1 -->|"Yes"| SA1["Would require a data store,<br/>schema and migration path"]
    S2{{"Is any value reused across<br/>requests or restarts?"}}
    S2 -->|"No — the payload is a<br/>compile-time literal"| S3
    S2 -->|"Yes"| SA2["Would require a cache with an<br/>invalidation and coherency policy"]
    S3{{"Is the response sensitive or<br/>caller-specific?"}}
    S3 -->|"No — identical for every caller"| S4
    S3 -->|"Yes"| SA3["Would require authentication,<br/>authorization and TLS"]
    S4{{"Must non-local callers reach<br/>the endpoint?"}}
    S4 -->|"No — same-host use only"| DEC2["Selected posture: no storage tier,<br/>no cache tier, and network topology<br/>as the sole access control"]
    S4 -->|"Yes"| SA4["Would require a routable bind<br/>address plus transport security<br/>and an identity boundary"]
```

**Storage rationale.** A storage solution exists to make state durable across requests or restarts. This system has no such state: the handler declares no variables, allocates no collection, and never touches `global`; the module never imports `fs` or `path`; and the repository contains no schema, migration, seed, ORM configuration, or database server configuration among roughly 120 conventional artifact paths that were checked. Adding any store would introduce a connection lifecycle, a failure mode, a credential, and a backup obligation in exchange for holding data the system does not have. The architectural benefit of the decision is that it eliminates an entire category of concern: there is no data model to version, no consistency model to reason about, and — as section 5.4.6 develops — nothing whose loss requires recovery.

**Caching rationale.** Caching trades memory or an extra network hop for the cost of recomputation. Here recomputation costs nothing measurable: the response body is a 14-byte string literal already resident in the module. A cache would therefore add invalidation logic and a coherency question with no possible hit-rate benefit. Consistent with this, the responses carry no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, or `Vary` header, so no client-side or intermediary caching is directed either — a defensible position for a constant payload, but one that would need revisiting if the body ever became computed or client-specific. It is worth noting the one *implicit* optimisation the system does accept: runtime-default keep-alive reuses the TCP connection across requests, which is connection reuse rather than content caching, and it is inherited rather than chosen in code.

### 5.3.4 Security Mechanism Selection

**The decision.** Rely on **network topology as the sole access-control mechanism**, and implement no application-level security control whatsoever.

The mechanism is the bind address at line 3. Because the listener is bound to `127.0.0.1` rather than `0.0.0.0`, the kernel accepts connections only from the local host; a probe of the host's routable address on port 3000 was refused at the transport layer. This is a *deployment-level* control expressed in application source, which is an important distinction: it is enforced by the operating system's routing, not by any check the application performs.

| Security Concern | Mechanism Selected | Residual Exposure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Network reachability | Loopback bind at line 3 | Any local process or local user, regardless of identity, can reach the endpoint; there is no host-level allow-list |
| Caller identity | None — no authentication of any kind | Every request is anonymous and indistinguishable; no credential, token, session, or cookie mechanism exists |
| Authorisation | None — no roles, scopes, or permission checks | The handler contains no conditional logic at all, so no request can be refused by the application |
| Transport confidentiality | None — no TLS | Traffic is plaintext; an HTTPS attempt fails at the transport layer, and no certificate or key material exists in the repository |
| Input validation | None — the request object is never read | No injection surface exists precisely *because* input is discarded, but equally no request can be rejected |
| Response hardening | None | No `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Content-Security-Policy`, or CORS header is set |
| Secret management | Not applicable — no secrets exist | Nothing sensitive is stored, logged, or transmitted by the application |
| Dependency vulnerability exposure | Structurally minimised: zero third-party packages | Exposure is concentrated entirely in the chosen Node.js build, whose HTTP parser and TLS library the repository does not pin |

**Rationale and trade-offs.** For a same-host demonstration artifact the selection is internally coherent: with no sensitive data, no caller-specific behaviour, and no non-local reachability, authentication and TLS would protect nothing that is exposed. Two properties even make the posture unusually robust for its size — discarding the request eliminates the entire injection and deserialisation attack class, and having zero third-party dependencies eliminates the supply-chain attack class outright.

The trade-off is that the security model is **entirely load-bearing on a single line of source**. Changing `'127.0.0.1'` to `'0.0.0.0'` — a one-token edit — silently converts the system from unreachable-off-host to fully exposed with no authentication, no authorisation, no TLS, and no rate limiting, because none of those mechanisms exist to fall back on. There is also no defence-in-depth: the repository contains no `SECURITY.md`, no certificate material, and no reverse-proxy or firewall configuration that might supply a second control. Section 5.4.4 treats the operational consequences of this posture.

The six records below consolidate the decisions above into a consistent format. Each is reconstructed from artifact evidence; the "Evidence" column identifies what in the repository substantiates the decision, in place of an approval record that does not exist.

| Record | Decision | Evidence in the Artifact |

| **ADR-001** | Use the Node.js core `http` module directly instead of a web framework | One `require` of a built-in specifier at line 1; no dependency manifest, lockfile, or `node_modules` |
| **ADR-002** | Structure the service as a single-file CommonJS module whose evaluation starts the listener | 14 lines in one file; no `module.exports` assignment; requiring the module binds the port and yields zero exported keys |

| **ADR-004** | Serve a single stateless, request-agnostic response | Handler at lines 7–9 with zero references to the request object; identical responses observed across six HTTP methods and arbitrary paths, queries, and bodies |
| **ADR-005** | Use network topology as the sole access control, in place of authentication and TLS | Loopback bind; no auth, session, token, TLS, or CORS construct in either tracked file; non-loopback probe refused |
| **ADR-006** | Ship no dependency manifest, build pipeline, packaging, or CI/CD | Verified absence of `package.json`, lockfiles, build and lint configuration, test suites, container and orchestration descriptors, and pipeline definitions |
