## 6.2 Database Design

### 6.2.1 Applicability Assessment

**Database Design is not applicable to this system.**

The repository contains exactly three tracked files — `server.js` (342 bytes, 14 lines), `README.md` (27 bytes), and `test.js` (13 bytes) — 382 bytes in total, and no subdirectories whatsoever. `server.js` imports one module (`require('http')` on line 1), registers one request handler that never dereferences the request object, and writes a fixed 14-byte string literal as every response. `test.js` is not a data artifact: its 13 bytes are two bare identifier statements, so it contains no schema, no DDL, no fixture, no seed, no serialized record, and no connection string, and it is never loaded by any process. There is no database engine, driver, ORM, query builder, migration tool, cache client, object-storage client, or filesystem call anywhere in the repository, and there is no dependency manifest through which any of those could be introduced. The system therefore has **no schema to design, no entity to relate, no index to define, no partition or replica to configure, and no dataset to back up, migrate, retain, or archive**.

The absence is *structural* rather than configurational. A database client cannot be reached from this code because the only module the process ever loads is Node's core `http`; and no connection string could enter the process even if a client existed, because `server.js` reads no environment variable, no command-line argument, and no configuration file (requirement F-002-RQ-003). Section 3.5 reaches the same conclusion from the technology-stack perspective ("the system has no data tier"), and section 1.3.1.5 records the corresponding scope position ("no persistent data domain is in scope").

This sub-section states the determination and the evidence behind it. Sub-sections 6.2.2 through 6.2.5 then walk every topic the section mandates — schema design, data management, compliance, and performance optimization — because a documented gap is more useful to a reader than a silent one: for each concern the reader is told what does not exist, which mechanism (if any) occupies its place, which layer owns that mechanism, and what would have to change in the source before the concern could become meaningful. Sub-section 6.2.6 consolidates the result into a single traceability matrix.

#### 6.2.1.1 Determination Criteria

Applicability was assessed against the structural preconditions that any database design presupposes. **Every precondition fails.**

| Precondition for a Data Tier | Observed in This Repository | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A storage engine, driver, or embedded database is reachable from the code | The only module loaded is core `http`; `grep -c "require("` over the whole repository returns `1` (requirement F-005-RQ-001) | No connection can be opened, so no read or write path exists |
| A schema, model, or serialization contract is declared | No DDL, ORM model, schema file, or serialization format exists; 21 data and schema file-extension globs return zero matches repository-wide | There is no entity, attribute, key, or type to document |
| Data crosses the process boundary inbound | `req` appears exactly once in `server.js` — as the handler parameter on line 6 — and is never dereferenced (F-001-RQ-002) | Nothing arrives that could be stored, indexed, or queried |
| State survives a request or a restart | Zero `let`/`var` declarations, zero `Map`/`Set`/array/object literals, zero globals; the handler retains nothing (F-001-RQ-003) | A restart loses nothing and recovers nothing |
| A configuration channel could supply a connection endpoint | No `process.env`, no `process.argv`, no `.env*`, no `config/`, no manifest (F-002-RQ-003) | A data tier could not be attached without editing tracked source |
| A durability, retention, or recovery obligation is declared | No SLA, RPO, RTO, retention schedule, backup script, or compliance artifact exists anywhere in the tree | No policy target exists against which a storage design could be evaluated |

#### 6.2.1.2 Persistence-Artifact Audit

A persistence-specific existence and content audit was executed over the complete three-file tracked inventory and the entire repository tree. **125 probes returned zero positive results**, with the single exception of line 1's core-module import, which is itself the proof that no storage client is loaded.

| Audit Dimension | Probes Executed | Positive Results |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Database clients and drivers in source — relational, document, key-value, wide-column, graph, search | 12 | 0 |
| ORMs, query builders, and migration tooling, plus raw DDL and DML keywords | 8 | 0 |
| Filesystem and persistence-adjacent core modules, plus the whole import surface | 6 | 0 — the only `require(` is core `http` |
| Object-storage SDKs, session stores, and cookie emission | 4 | 0 |
| Configuration inputs able to carry a connection string, and HTTP cache directives | 2 | 0 |
| Well-known data-tier port literals — 5432, 3306, 27017, 6379, 1433, 9042, 11211, 9200, 1521 | 1 | 0 — the only literals present are the loopback address and 3000 |
| Repository-wide data and schema file extensions — `*.sql`, `*.db`, `*.sqlite*`, `*.csv`, `*.json`, `*.yaml`, `*.prisma`, `*.dump`, and 13 more | 21 | 0 |
| Data, schema, and storage directory names — `migrations/`, `db/`, `models/`, `data/`, `seeds/`, `storage/`, `cache/`, and 19 more | 26 | 0 |
| Engine, ORM, and client configuration files — `schema.prisma`, `knexfile.js`, `ormconfig.json`, `alembic.ini`, `postgresql.conf`, `my.cnf`, `redis.conf`, `init.sql`, and 6 more | 14 | 0 |
| Dependency manifests, lockfiles, env files, and container descriptors able to introduce or configure a data tier | 31 | 0 |
| **Total** | **125** | **0** |

Two further checks corroborate the path and content audit:

- **Git history.** `git rev-list --all --objects` yields a path set of exactly `{README.md, server.js, test.js}` across all three commits (`241598b` "Initial commit", `06492d7` "Add files via upload", `43ed37c` "Create test.js"). No schema, seed, dump, fixture, or migration artifact was **ever** tracked, so the absence is not the result of a recent deletion; the one file added since the application was committed is 13 bytes of placeholder text with no data content.
- **Structural scan of `server.js`.** Four `const` declarations and no `let` or `var`; no collection constructor, array literal, object literal, `global`, or `globalThis` reference. With no mutable binding in the module, no in-process store can exist even transiently across requests.

#### 6.2.1.3 Runtime Corroboration

Static absence was confirmed behaviourally by executing the unmodified `server.js` on Node.js v22.23.1 and observing the process while it served traffic. Every observation below is a **host observation** in the sense of section 6.1.1.3 — a measurement, never a declared target.

| Behavioural Probe | Observed Result | What It Establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open file descriptors while serving | `/dev/null`, the inherited stdio descriptors, event-loop internals, and **exactly one socket** (the listener); one additional socket per live client connection | No data-file descriptor and no outbound client socket ever exists, so neither local nor remote storage is contacted |
| `POST /users/42?token=xyz` with a JSON body | Identical `200`, `text/plain`, 14-byte `Hello, World!` response; submitted data neither echoed, stored, nor logged | Inbound data has no persistence path — it is discarded unread |
| Five sequential `GET /` requests | One unique response-body checksum across all five | No counter, accumulator, or cache mutates behaviour between requests |
| stdout after startup plus three requests | Still exactly the one 41-byte readiness line; stderr empty | No request-level write reaches any sink, including the log (F-004-RQ-003) |
| Working directory after traffic | No file created by the process | No embedded database, journal, spool, or temp artifact is materialised at runtime |
| Fresh restart of the process | Byte-identical response, no warm-up, no rebuild step | Nothing was persisted to reload and nothing was lost |
| libuv thread-pool activity under load | Pool of four threads remains idle; one event-loop thread does all work (recorded in 6.1.3.3) | The workload performs no filesystem, DNS, or crypto work — the signature of zero storage I/O |

#### 6.2.1.4 The Complete Data Inventory and Conceptual Model

The system's entire data inventory is four elements, none of which is persisted. Two are compile-time constants in tracked source, one is a runtime-parsed structure that application code never reads, and one is a single write-once line on stdout.

| Data Element | Origin and Location | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inbound request — method, URL, headers, body | Materialised by the Node `http` parser; never read by application code | Duration of one handler invocation, then unreachable |
| Response constant — status `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, 14-byte body | String and number literals at `server.js` lines 7–9 | Process lifetime; identical for every request (F-003-RQ-003) |
| Endpoint constants — `hostname`, `port` | String and number literals at `server.js` lines 3–4 | Process lifetime; no override path (F-002-RQ-003) |
| Readiness line — 41 bytes on stdout | Template literal at `server.js` line 13 | Written once at bind success; never re-read by the process |

The entity-relationship view of that inventory is shown below. It is presented as a formal ERD to satisfy the documentation standard for this section, but its principal content is the explicit record that **no persisted entity exists**: zero tables, zero collections, zero indexes, and zero constraints.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    TRANSIENT_INBOUND_REQUEST {
        string method "parsed by the runtime, never read by application code"
        string url "parsed by the runtime, never read by application code"

        string body "not consumed, discarded when the handler returns"
    }

        int statusCode "literal 200 at server.js line 7"
        string contentType "literal text-plain at server.js line 8"
        string payload "fixed 14 byte greeting literal at server.js line 9"
    }
    COMPILED_IN_ENDPOINT_CONSTANTS {
        string hostname "literal loopback address at server.js line 3"
        int port "literal 3000 at server.js line 4"
    }
    WRITE_ONCE_READINESS_LINE {
        string text "41 byte startup line, stdout only, never re-read"
    }
    NO_PERSISTED_ENTITY {

        string collections "zero, no schema artifact exists"
        string indexes "zero, no index definition exists"
        string constraints "zero, no key or check constraint exists"
    }
    TRANSIENT_INBOUND_REQUEST ||--|| COMPILED_IN_RESPONSE_CONSTANT : "answered by, with no lookup, join, or key"
    COMPILED_IN_ENDPOINT_CONSTANTS ||--|| WRITE_ONCE_READINESS_LINE : "interpolated into, once per process"
    NO_PERSISTED_ENTITY }o--o{ TRANSIENT_INBOUND_REQUEST : "no relationship, nothing is stored or retrieved"
    NO_PERSISTED_ENTITY }o--o{ COMPILED_IN_RESPONSE_CONSTANT : "no relationship, the payload is source, not data"
```

**Diagram 6.2-A — Conceptual data model (ERD): four non-persisted data elements and an empty persistent-entity set.** The four populated blocks are the complete data inventory of the running system; the `NO_PERSISTED_ENTITY` block records the audited emptiness of the persistence layer. Every relationship shown is an in-process association resolved by source literals — there is no key, no join, and no lookup anywhere in the system.

#### 6.2.1.5 Evidence Conventions for the Remainder of This Section

Because the repository declares no durability, retention, or performance target of any kind, every claim in sub-sections 6.2.2 through 6.2.6 carries one of the following provenance labels, and none may be read as a commitment. The convention is inherited verbatim from section 6.1.1.3 so that the two sections remain directly comparable.

| Label | Meaning | Example in This Section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Source fact** | A property verifiable by reading a tracked file at a cited line | The response payload is a literal at `server.js` line 9 |
| **Audit result** | The outcome of an existence or content probe over the repository tree | Zero matches for 21 data and schema file-extension globs |
| **Runtime default** | Behaviour supplied by Node.js because `server.js` configures nothing | `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` on every response |
| **Host observation** | A figure measured by executing the unmodified source on one verification host | One socket descriptor at idle; no file created during traffic |

Two status words are used consistently for each mandated topic. **Not applicable** means the topic presupposes a structure this system does not have (for example, an index presupposes a table). **Absent** means the topic would be meaningful for a stateless HTTP service but nothing in the repository implements it (for example, HTTP cache directives). Where a mechanism exists but is owned by the runtime or the host rather than by repository code, it is labelled **delegated**.

### 6.2.2 Schema Design

No schema exists at any level of formality — no DDL, no ORM model, no document schema, no serialization contract, and no validation schema. This sub-section documents each mandated schema-design topic as a verified absence, records the empty index and constraint inventories explicitly, and shows the replication position that follows from having no data.

#### 6.2.2.1 Entity Relationships and Data Models

**Status: not applicable.** The system defines no entity, because it never accepts, derives, or retains a record of any kind. The closest analogue to a "data model" in the repository is three source literals, and they are code rather than data — they are compiled into the request handler and the bind call, not stored in or loaded from anything.

```javascript
const hostname = '127.0.0.1';   // line 3 — endpoint constant
const port = 3000;              // line 4 — endpoint constant
res.end('Hello, World!\n');     // line 9 — the entire outbound data inventory
```

| Modelling Concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entity set | Empty — zero entities | No table, collection, class, struct, interface, or type definition exists in any of the three tracked files |
| Attributes and value types | None modelled | The only typed values are two literals plus one string literal; no field is named, declared, or validated (source fact) |
| Relationships and cardinality | None — no foreign key, embedded reference, or join path | No second entity exists with which to form a relationship; the only association in the system is source-literal interpolation into the readiness line |
| Identity and keys | None — no primary key, surrogate key, natural key, or UUID | No identifier is generated or consumed; the handler produces no per-request identity, so responses are indistinguishable from one another |
| Normalisation or denormalisation posture | Not applicable | Normalisation is a property of a relational schema; there is no schema to normalise |
| Schema-on-read alternatives | Not applicable | No document, event, or column-family store exists in which schema-on-read could apply |
| Model layer in code | Absent | `models/`, `schemas/`, `entities/`, and `domain/` directories are all absent; the repository has **no subdirectories at all** (audit result) |

An architectural point worth stating plainly: the request is not merely unmodelled, it is **unread**. `req` occurs exactly once in `server.js`, as the handler parameter on line 6, and is never dereferenced (requirement F-001-RQ-002). Any data model would therefore have no input to populate it.

#### 6.2.2.2 Index Inventory and Indexing Strategy

**Status: not applicable.** An index presupposes a stored collection and a query workload; the system has neither. The inventory is recorded explicitly below rather than omitted, so that a reader auditing this specification for index coverage finds a definitive answer rather than a gap.

| Index Class | Instances Present | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary key or clustered index | 0 | No `CREATE TABLE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, or equivalent appears in any tracked file |
| Secondary, composite, or covering index | 0 | No `CREATE INDEX` statement and no ORM index annotation exists |
| Unique index or unique constraint | 0 | No uniqueness declaration exists anywhere in the repository |
| Full-text, spatial, or vector index | 0 | No search or geospatial engine is referenced; the search-client probe group returned zero matches |
| In-memory lookup structure serving as an index | 0 | No `Map`, `Set`, array, or object literal is constructed in `server.js` (source fact) |
| **Total index definitions in the repository** | **0** | 125-probe persistence audit, zero positive results (6.2.1.2) |

There is consequently **no indexing strategy to state** — no selectivity analysis, no covering-index policy, no index-maintenance window, and no index-bloat concern. The one lookup the system performs on the request path is the runtime's internal dispatch to the single registered `request` listener, which is a function call rather than a data lookup and costs the same for every request.

#### 6.2.2.3 Constraint Inventory

**Status: not applicable.** No constraint of any kind is declared, because there is no schema to constrain and no input to validate. Section 2.2 records the same finding per requirement: for F-001-RQ-002 the data-validation position is "nothing is read, therefore nothing can be validated".

| Constraint Class | Instances Present | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NOT NULL`, default, and domain constraints | 0 | No column or field is declared |
| Primary and foreign key constraints | 0 | No key and no referential relationship exists |
| `CHECK`, exclusion, and trigger-enforced rules | 0 | No database object and no application-level validation branch exists — `server.js` contains zero conditionals |
| Application-level input validation | 0 | No request attribute is read, so there is nothing to validate (F-001-RQ-002) |
| Application-level output invariants | 1, enforced by construction rather than by a rule | The response is a literal, so the 14-byte body and `text/plain` type cannot vary (F-003-RQ-003) |

#### 6.2.2.4 Partitioning Approach

**Status: not applicable.** Partitioning distributes stored rows or documents across physical or logical units; with zero stored records there is nothing to distribute. No partition key, shard key, tenant discriminator, time-bucket, or hash-slot concept exists anywhere in the repository, and no request attribute is read from which such a key could ever be derived.

| Partitioning Dimension | Position | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal partitioning — sharding by key, range, or hash | Not applicable — no dataset, no key | No routing layer, no shard map, and no rebalancing procedure exists |
| Vertical partitioning — splitting attributes across stores | Not applicable — no attributes | No hot or cold column separation is possible |
| Time-based or list-based table partitioning | Not applicable — no table and no timestamped record | No partition-pruning benefit and no partition-maintenance job exists |
| Tenant isolation by partition or schema | Not applicable — the code models no user, tenant, or session (section 1.3.1.5) | Every caller receives identical treatment; there is no tenant identifier to isolate on |
| Workload partitioning inside the process | Absent, and the process is single-threaded by construction | All work executes on one event-loop thread; `cluster` and `worker_threads` are never imported (recorded in 6.1.3.1) |

#### 6.2.2.5 Replication Configuration

**Status: not applicable for data; the only replication in the architecture is of source objects.** There is no primary, no replica, no standby, no write-ahead log or change stream, and no declared replication mode, quorum, or lag budget. The one durability mechanism that genuinely exists is Git object replication between the local checkout and the remote that hosts it — and that is source-code retention, explicitly not application storage (section 3.5.4).

| Replication Element | Position | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary data node | None | Zero database engines present; 125-probe audit returned zero positive results |
| Replica, standby, or read pool | None | No replica configuration artifact exists; the resilience and disaster-recovery path group in section 6.1.1.2 returned zero matches across 28 paths |
| Change-propagation channel — WAL, binlog, change stream, CDC | None | No engine to emit changes and no consumer to receive them; the process opens no outbound socket |
| Synchronous or asynchronous mode, quorum, lag budget | None declared | The repository declares no durability or consistency target of any kind |
| Application-instance replication | Blocked by two source literals | A second same-host instance exits with code `1` and `EADDRINUSE` (F-002-RQ-004); the loopback bind makes an off-host instance unreachable (F-002-RQ-002) |
| Source-artifact replication | Present, operator-initiated | Git object store holds `server.js` (blob `320a75a`), `README.md` (blob `5fb5231`), and `test.js` (blob `2c87c79`); the remote is source hosting only and carries no runtime coupling (section 1.3.2.3) |

The middle lane enumerates the data-replication elements and records each as absent. The lower lane shows why instance replication — the closest available substitute for data redundancy in a stateless service — is closed by the two endpoint literals rather than by missing configuration.

#### 6.2.2.6 Backup Architecture

**Status: not applicable for data; source-only retention is what exists.** No backup exists because there is no dataset, journal, or state file to capture: the process creates no file at runtime, holds no data-file descriptor, and reconstructs nothing on restart (host observations, 6.2.1.3).

| Backup Concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full, incremental, or snapshot backup of application data | Not applicable — no data exists to capture | No `fs` usage, no embedded database file, no volume or mount declaration (section 3.5.4) |
| Backup schedule, tooling, and destination | Absent | No backup script, cron entry, or storage target exists; the 28-path resilience and disaster-recovery probe group returned zero matches |
| Restore and point-in-time-recovery procedure | Not applicable | Restore has no target; a "recovery" is simply relaunching the process, measured at roughly 32 ms in 6.1.4.2 |
| Recovery point objective | Not applicable rather than unmet | Nothing is retained between requests, so no data can be lost by definition (F-001-RQ-003) |
| Backup verification and integrity checking | Not applicable | With no backup artifact, there is nothing to verify or checksum |
| Source-artifact retention | Present, via version control only | Three commits and zero tags; a commit SHA is the only baseline identifier for the artifact (recorded in 6.1.4.3). `server.js` is byte-identical at `06492d7` and at HEAD `43ed37c`, so two distinct SHAs identify the same application bytes |

The architectural consequence is that the durability posture is inverted relative to a conventional system: **the only asset that requires protection is the source file itself**, and the only mechanism protecting it is the Git repository. A host loss destroys no data and forfeits no recovery point; it forfeits only the running process, which is reconstituted from source by a single command.

### 6.2.3 Data Management

With no store to manage, the conventional data-management disciplines have no object. This sub-section records the position for each mandated topic and then documents the one mechanism that does exist in place of storage and retrieval: a constant returned from process memory.

#### 6.2.3.1 Migration Procedures

**Status: not applicable.** No migration tool, migration script, or versioned change set exists, and no migration step occurs at any point in the lifecycle.

| Migration Concern | Position | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Migration framework | None | `alembic`, `flyway`, `liquibase`, `knex`, `prisma`, `sequelize`, and `typeorm` are all absent from source; `migrations/`, `migrate/`, and `alembic/` directories are all absent (audit result) |
| Change-script inventory | Empty | Zero `*.sql`, `*.ddl`, and `*.prisma` files exist repository-wide |
| Startup migration or schema check | None | Launch emits exactly one 41-byte readiness line and nothing else; there is no connection handshake, migration run, or readiness gate on a dependency (host observation; section 3.5.5) |
| Forward and rollback procedure | Not applicable | There is no schema state to advance or revert |
| Data backfill or transformation jobs | None | No batch script, job runner, or scheduled task exists in the repository |
| Zero-downtime migration technique | Not applicable | No schema, and no multi-instance topology in which a rolling change could be staged (6.2.2.5) |

Because deployment is literally `node server.js` on the committed file, the ordinary coupling between a release and a schema change does not exist here: a change to the response payload is a source edit and a process restart, with no data-tier coordination of any kind.

#### 6.2.3.2 Versioning Strategy

**Status: absent for the artifact; not applicable for data.** There is no schema version, no record version, no migration version, and no application version. The only identity the artifact has is its Git commit SHA.

| Versioning Dimension | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schema or model version | Not applicable — no schema exists | No DDL, ORM model, or schema registry entry exists (6.2.2.1) |
| Row, document, or event version — optimistic concurrency | Not applicable — no records | No `version`, `revision`, `updated_at`, or `etag` field is declared anywhere |
| Payload or API contract version | Absent | The response is an unversioned 14-byte literal; no `Accept` header is read and no `/v1` path prefix exists, since no request attribute is inspected (F-001-RQ-002) |
| Application or release version | Absent | No `package.json` and therefore no `version` field; section 1.3.2.1 records the artifact as unversioned |
| Source revision identity | Present, via Git only | Three commits (`241598b`, `06492d7`, `43ed37c`) and **zero tags**; blob identities `320a75a` for `server.js`, `5fb5231` for `README.md`, and `2c87c79` for `test.js`. `server.js` is byte-identical at `06492d7` and at HEAD, so the application's identity is unchanged by the most recent commit |
| Configuration version | Not applicable | Configuration is two source literals inside the versioned file, so it cannot drift from the code (F-002-RQ-003) |

One useful consequence of collapsing configuration into source: the bound endpoint and the advertised endpoint are versioned together and cannot disagree, which is exactly the property requirement F-004-RQ-002 records. The cost is that changing an endpoint is a code change with a new commit, not a configuration change.

#### 6.2.3.3 Archival Policies

**Status: not applicable.** Archival presupposes accumulated records that age out of a hot store; nothing accumulates anywhere in this system.

| Archival Concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cold-storage tiering or aged-record movement | Not applicable | No record is created, so no record ages; no object-storage or archive client exists (audit result) |
| Purge, truncate, or time-to-live policy | Not applicable | Nothing is retained beyond a single handler invocation (F-001-RQ-003) |
| Log archival and rotation | Not applicable — no log file exists | Output is a single 41-byte line on an inherited stdout descriptor; no log file, rotation policy, or retention store exists (F-004-RQ-003) |
| Export or extract for downstream analytics | Absent | No serialization format, extract job, or outbound connection exists; the process is a communication leaf (6.1.2.2) |
| Archive of source history | Present, incidental | The Git object store retains all three commits and their three blobs; this is source retention, not data archival (section 3.5.4) |

#### 6.2.3.4 Data Storage and Retrieval Mechanisms

**Storage: none. Retrieval: a constant read from process memory.** No storage mechanism of any tier is used — not a database, not a key-value store, not the filesystem, not object storage, and not an in-process collection. The complete "retrieval" operation the system performs is passing a string literal to `res.end`, which the runtime frames with a computed `Content-Length: 14` (F-003-RQ-004).

| Mechanism | Present? | Detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Database read or write path | No | Zero drivers and zero client sockets; only one socket descriptor — the listener — exists at idle (host observation) |
| Filesystem read or write path | No | `fs` is never required; no file is created in the working directory during traffic; the libuv thread pool stays idle under load (host observations) |
| In-process data structure | No | No `let`/`var`, no `Map`/`Set`, no array or object literal in `server.js` (source fact) |
| Constant read from module memory | **Yes — the only mechanism** | The 14-byte literal at line 9 is written directly to the response; cost is identical for every request |
| Inbound data capture | No | The request object is materialised by the parser and discarded unread when the handler returns (F-001-RQ-002) |
| Outbound data emission other than the response | No | Exactly one 41-byte stdout write for the process lifetime, produced at bind success rather than per request |

The full data flow, including every persistence target the system could have contacted and did not, is shown below.

**Diagram 6.2-C — Data flow: ingress, handling, and disposal, with every candidate persistence target unreached.** Stages 1 and 3 are owned by the Node.js runtime and the garbage collector; stage 2 is the three application statements at lines 7 to 9. The dotted edges into the lower subgraph are the writes a conventional service would perform at this point in the flow; each is annotated with the audit evidence establishing that it does not occur. The single stdout write is drawn off the process-start node rather than the request path, because it happens once per process rather than once per request.

#### 6.2.3.5 Caching Policies

**Status: absent at every tier.** No cache exists in the application, in front of it, or behind it, and no caching policy is expressed to clients or intermediaries.

| Cache Tier | Position | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remote cache service — Redis, Memcached | Absent | `redis`, `ioredis`, and `memcached` are absent from source; `redis.conf` is absent from the repository (audit result) |
| In-process or application-level cache | Absent, and pointless by construction | No mutable binding exists to memoise into; the response is already a constant, so there is nothing to compute and cache (source fact) |
| HTTP response cache directives | Absent | The single `setHeader` call sets `Content-Type` only; no `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Expires`, or `Vary` is emitted (F-003-RQ-004) |
| Client or intermediary caching behaviour | Unspecified — left to defaults | Because no freshness or validator header is sent, any cache in the path applies its own default heuristics rather than a policy chosen by this system |
| Connection-level reuse | Present as a **runtime default** | Responses carry `Connection: keep-alive` and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`; idle sockets are reclaimed after 5,000 ms by Node.js, not by application code |

Two observations complete the picture. First, the absence of validators is materially harmless *for this payload specifically*: the body is an immutable 14-byte literal, so a client or proxy serving a stale copy would serve a byte-identical response. That reasoning holds only while the payload remains a constant — it is a property of the current content, not a designed caching strategy. Second, the only reuse mechanism actually in force is transport-level rather than data-level, which is consistent with the finding in 6.1.3.4 that connection reuse here is inherited behaviour rather than an authored optimisation.

### 6.2.4 Compliance Considerations

The repository names **no regulatory regime and declares no data-governance policy**. A keyword scan of all three tracked files for `gdpr`, `hipaa`, `pci`, `sox`, `ccpa`, `pii`, `personal data`, `retention`, `encrypt`, `audit`, `consent`, `redact`, and `anonym` returned zero matches, and no `LICENSE`, `SECURITY.md`, `PRIVACY.md`, `CODEOWNERS`, or threat-model document exists. Consequently every compliance topic below is documented as an observed property of the implementation rather than as conformance to a stated obligation — this specification records what the code does with data, not what any framework requires of it.

The determining fact for this entire sub-section is that **no data ever enters the system's custody**. The request object is parsed by the runtime and discarded unread (requirement F-001-RQ-002), and nothing is retained across requests (F-001-RQ-003). A system that reads nothing and stores nothing cannot mishandle, over-retain, or leak what it never held.

#### 6.2.4.1 Data Retention Rules

**Status: not applicable — retention period is effectively zero, by construction rather than by policy.**

| Retention Concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declared retention schedule or policy document | None exists | No policy artifact anywhere in the tree; no retention term appears in any of the three tracked files (audit result) |
| Actual retention of request data | Zero — discarded when the handler returns | Request attributes are never read; the object becomes unreachable at handler exit (source fact, 6.2.3.4) |
| Actual retention of derived or aggregated data | Zero — nothing is derived | No counter, accumulator, or aggregate exists (F-001-RQ-003) |
| Actual retention of logs | Zero beyond process lifetime | One 41-byte stdout line on an inherited descriptor; no log file is written (F-004-RQ-003) |
| Legal hold, deletion request, or right-to-erasure workflow | Not applicable | There is no record to hold, locate, export, or delete |
| Retention of source artifacts | Indefinite, via Git history | Three commits retained in the object store, holding three blobs; this is source retention, not data retention (section 3.5.4) |

#### 6.2.4.2 Backup and Fault-Tolerance Policies

**Status: not applicable for data; the fault-tolerance posture is documented in full in 6.1.4 and is summarised here only where it bears on data.**

| Policy Area | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backup policy for data | None, and none required | No dataset, journal, or state file exists to capture (6.2.2.6) |
| Recovery point objective | Not applicable rather than unmet | Nothing is retained, so no data can be lost in any failure mode |
| Recovery time behaviour | Manual relaunch; no data-restore phase in the path | Recovery action measured at roughly 32 ms launch-to-first-200, with no warm-up or state rebuild (host observation, 6.1.4.2) |
| Fault tolerance for a data tier — replica promotion, failover, quorum | Not applicable | No primary, no replica, no arbiter (6.2.2.5) |
| Data integrity under abrupt termination | No exposure | `SIGTERM` terminates without draining (F-002-RQ-005); as section 2.2.3.4 records, abrupt termination cannot leak persisted state because no state is persisted — there is no partial write, torn record, or uncommitted transaction to reconcile |
| Corruption detection or checksum verification | Not applicable | No stored bytes exist to checksum; response-body checksums were verified identical across restarts purely as evidence of statelessness |

#### 6.2.4.3 Privacy Controls

**Status: not applicable in the sense that no personal data can enter the system — which is a stronger position than any control.**

| Privacy Concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Collection of personal data | None possible | No `req.*` property is ever read — not the method, path, query string, headers, body, or client address (F-001-RQ-002); a POST carrying a JSON body was verified to be ignored entirely |
| Personal data in logs | None possible | No request attribute is logged; stdout remained at exactly 41 bytes after sustained traffic (host observation) |
| Cookies, identifiers, or client-side state | None | No `Set-Cookie` is emitted and no session library or session store exists (audit result) |
| Data-at-rest encryption | Not applicable | There is no data at rest; no file, database page, or object is ever written (section 3.5.2) |
| Data-in-transit encryption | Absent | The listener is plaintext HTTP/1.1; no `https` or `tls` module is used (section 1.3.2.1). Because the payload is a fixed public greeting and no request content is processed, no confidential data traverses the connection |
| Data-subject rights, consent, and purpose limitation | Not applicable | No caller is identified or differentiated; the code models no user, role, tenant, or session (section 1.3.1.5) |
| Cross-border transfer | Not applicable | No data leaves the process; the listener is loopback-bound and no outbound connection is ever opened |
| Secret and credential handling | None to handle | No connection string, token, or key material exists; the process reads no environment variable (F-002-RQ-003) |

#### 6.2.4.4 Audit Mechanisms

**Status: absent for runtime activity; present for source change only.** There is no audit trail of data access because there is no data access — but it is worth stating explicitly that there is also **no access log**, so requests leave no record of any kind.

| Audit Dimension | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data-access audit trail — who read or wrote which record | Not applicable | No store, no query, no record (6.2.2.1) |
| Change or history table — temporal tables, soft deletes, event sourcing | Not applicable | No table and no append-only log exists |
| Request or access log | **Absent** | Exactly one `console.log`, executed at bind success; stdout byte count is invariant under traffic and stderr stays empty (F-004-RQ-003, host observation) |
| Administrative-action log | Not applicable | The only administrative actions are starting and stopping the process; neither is recorded by the application, and no signal handler exists to note a shutdown (F-002-RQ-005) |
| Audit-log integrity, immutability, and retention | Not applicable | With no log content beyond the readiness line, there is nothing to protect, sign, or retain |
| Source-change audit | Present, via Git only | All three commits are attributable in history; the repository has no `CODEOWNERS`, review policy, or signed-commit requirement, and the most recent commit reached the branch head with no review or gate (6.4.3.5) |

The operational implication is that **the system is not auditable at runtime**: an operator cannot reconstruct what was requested, when, or by whom, because no request-scoped record is created anywhere. Section 5.4.1 documents the same gap from the monitoring perspective, and section 6.1.4.2 quantifies its consequence — detection latency for any incident is unbounded.

#### 6.2.4.5 Access Controls

**Status: no data-layer access control exists, because there is no data layer. One network-topological control exists and it is the system's only access control of any kind.**

| Access-Control Layer | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Database authentication, roles, grants, and row-level security | Not applicable | No engine, no user catalogue, no privilege model (6.2.1.2) |
| Application authentication and authorization | Absent | No credential handling, token verification, or access-control logic exists; no gate precedes handler invocation (section 2.2.2.4) |
| Network reachability control | **Present — the sole control** | The loopback bind at `server.js` line 3 restricts callers to the same host; a probe of the host's routable address on port 3000 failed to connect while loopback returned 200. Section 2.2.3.4 records this as "the **only** security control in the repository" (F-002-RQ-002) |
| Transport-layer protection | Absent | No TLS, certificate material, or HSTS; no security response headers are set |
| Secret storage and rotation | Not applicable | No secret exists to store or rotate |
| Filesystem permissions on the tracked artifacts | Host-managed, non-executable | All three tracked files are mode `100644` in the Git index and `-rw-r--r--` on the verification host; there is no key file, credential file, or data file to protect |

Because the single control is topological, its granularity is binary: any process able to open a socket on the host's loopback interface is served identically, and no finer-grained data permission can exist in a system with no data. Section 6.1.2.1 states the corollary at the service level — every caller is anonymous and receives identical treatment.

### 6.2.5 Performance Optimization

No database-layer performance work exists, because there is no database layer to optimise. What follows records each mandated optimisation topic, identifies where an equivalent mechanism exists at the transport layer instead, and states the one property that actually determines data-path performance here: the request path performs **zero I/O**. Service-level throughput and latency measurements are deliberately not restated — they belong to section 6.1.3 — and this sub-section confines itself to the data dimension.

#### 6.2.5.1 Query Optimization Patterns

**Status: not applicable.** There is no query language, no query, no plan, and no planner. The audit found zero `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, and DDL keywords across all three tracked files, and zero ORM or query-builder imports.

| Optimisation Pattern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Execution-plan inspection and hinting | Not applicable | No engine exists to produce or accept a plan |
| Index selection, covering indexes, selectivity tuning | Not applicable | The index inventory is empty (6.2.2.2) |
| N+1 query elimination, eager loading, projection narrowing | Not applicable | Zero queries are issued per request; the handler performs three unconditional response operations and returns |
| Prepared statements and statement caching | Not applicable | No statement is ever prepared or parsed |
| Materialised views, summary tables, or pre-aggregation | Not applicable | No source data exists to aggregate |
| Per-request work profile that replaces querying | **Constant** | Assign status, set one header, write a 14-byte literal — identical cost for every request regardless of method, path, or body (source fact, lines 7–9) |

The architecturally significant consequence is that the usual dominant term in request latency — waiting on a store — is exactly zero here. The verification host's idle libuv thread pool under sustained load (recorded in 6.1.3.3) is the direct empirical signature of that: a pool that would service filesystem, DNS, and crypto work never activates, because the workload issues none.

#### 6.2.5.2 Caching Strategy

**Status: absent at every tier.** The full inventory — remote cache service, in-process cache, HTTP cache directives, and the runtime's transport-level keep-alive — is documented in 6.2.3.5 and is not repeated here. Two data-layer-specific points complete it:

- There is **no cache-aside, read-through, write-through, or write-behind pattern**, because each of those patterns is defined relative to a backing store, and no backing store exists.
- There is **no cache invalidation concern**, because the only "cached" value conceivable in this system is the response literal, which is immutable for the lifetime of the source file and therefore can never become stale relative to a source of truth.

#### 6.2.5.3 Connection Pooling

**Status: not applicable for data connections; the inbound analogue is a runtime default.** A connection pool amortises the cost of establishing outbound connections to a dependency. This process has **zero outbound dependencies** — it opens no client socket, resolves no hostname, and imports nothing beyond core `http` — so there is nothing to pool. Section 6.1.3.4 records the same finding from the service perspective.

| Pooling Concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outbound database or cache connection pool | Not applicable — no outbound connection exists | Exactly one socket descriptor (the listener) at idle; the descriptor count rises only with live client connections (host observation) |
| Pool sizing, acquisition timeout, and leak detection | Not applicable | No pool object exists to size, time out, or instrument |
| Connection warm-up at startup | Not applicable — and its absence is a benefit | Startup performs one bind and emits one readiness line; there is no failure mode in which the service is up but its store is not (section 3.5.5) |
| Inbound connection reuse | Present as a **runtime default** | `Connection: keep-alive` with `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` on every response; idle sockets reclaimed after 5,000 ms by Node.js, not by application code |
| Inbound connection accounting | Delegated, uncapped | Cost is exactly one file descriptor per concurrent connection against a host ceiling of 1,048,576, with `maxConnections` unset (recorded in 6.1.3.3) |

#### 6.2.5.4 Read/Write Splitting

**Status: not applicable.** Read/write splitting routes reads to replicas and writes to a primary. This system performs **neither reads nor writes** against any store, and has neither a primary nor a replica.

| Prerequisite for Splitting | Observed | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A distinguishable read path and write path | Neither exists | Every request executes the identical three-statement path; there is no branch of any kind in `server.js` |
| A primary node accepting writes | None | Zero database engines present (6.2.2.5) |
| One or more read replicas | None | Zero replica configuration; instance replication itself is blocked by the endpoint literals |
| A router able to classify a request as read or write | None, and impossible without a source change | Classification would require inspecting the request method or path, and no `req` property is ever read (F-001-RQ-002) |
| Replication-lag tolerance or read-your-writes policy | Not applicable | With no writes and no replicas, consistency is trivially total — every response is byte-identical (verified by checksum across repeated requests and across restarts) |

#### 6.2.5.5 Batch Processing Approach

**Status: not applicable.** No batch, bulk, or asynchronous processing exists in any form, and the request path is strictly one-in, one-out.

| Batch Concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bulk insert, upsert, or `COPY`-style load | Not applicable | No store and no dataset to load (6.2.2.1) |
| Batched reads, cursors, pagination, or streaming result sets | Not applicable | No query is issued; the 14-byte response is written in a single `res.end` call rather than streamed |
| Scheduled or offline jobs — ETL, compaction, vacuum, reindex | None | No job runner, scheduler, cron entry, or maintenance script exists in the repository (audit result) |
| Queue- or broker-driven asynchronous work | None | Zero broker artifacts and zero outbound sockets; the service is a communication leaf (6.1.2.2) |
| Request coalescing or write batching in the application | None | The handler is synchronous with no timer, `Promise`, or buffer; requests cannot influence one another (F-001-RQ-003) |
| Transaction boundaries and commit batching | Not applicable | No transactional resource participates in a request |

#### 6.2.5.6 What Actually Determines Data-Path Performance

Because every mandated optimisation topic resolves to a non-applicability, it is worth stating positively what governs the data path in this system. Three properties do, and all three are consequences of doing nothing rather than of tuning anything:

| Property | Nature | Effect on the Data Path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero storage I/O per request | Source fact — no `fs`, no driver, no client | Removes the term that normally dominates latency; the libuv pool stays idle under load |
| Constant-size, constant-content response | Source fact — a 14-byte literal at line 9 | Response size is invariant, so there is nothing to compress, paginate, or project |
| No state to synchronise | Source fact — no mutable binding in the module | No lock, latch, transaction, or cache-coherence cost exists inside the process |

The single serialisation point in the system is therefore the event-loop thread rather than any store, connection pool, or lock — the constraint documented and measured in section 6.1.3. Any future introduction of a data tier would relocate that constraint, and at that point every topic in this sub-section would become live; none of it is live today.

#### 6.2.6.3 Source Facts That Foreclose a Data Tier

Every gap documented in this section traces to a small number of facts about the committed source. The mapping below is provided as a change-impact reference for anyone assessing what introducing persistence would entail. It records what each fact currently forecloses; consistent with section 1.3.2.2, these are **present-state absences, not commitments, plans, or approved future scope**.

| Source Fact | Location | Data-Tier Concerns It Forecloses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only the core `http` module is imported | `server.js` line 1 | Every driver, ORM, query builder, migration tool, cache client, and object-storage SDK |
| No dependency manifest, lockfile, or `node_modules/` exists | Repository root | Any dependency resolution path for a storage client, plus any SBOM or dependency audit of one |
| No `process.env`, `process.argv`, `.env`, or `config/` is read | Whole file | Any externally supplied connection string, credential, or endpoint; a data tier would currently require hard-coded credentials in tracked source |
| `req` is never dereferenced | `server.js` line 6 | Any inbound record to persist, any key or tenant discriminator, and any read/write request classification |
| No `let`, `var`, collection, or global binding exists | `server.js` lines 1–14 | Any in-process cache, accumulator, counter, or session store |
| The response is a fixed literal | `server.js` line 9 | Any response that varies with stored state; the payload cannot be sourced from a store |
| `fs` is never required | Whole file | Local file persistence, embedded database files, journals, spools, and log files |
| No conditional, `try`/`catch`, or error listener exists | `server.js` lines 6–14 | Transaction rollback, retry on transient store failure, connection-error handling, and degraded read paths — a data tier would introduce failure modes the current structure cannot express |
| The endpoint is two literals consumed by a positional `listen` | `server.js` lines 3, 4, 12 | Instance replication, and therefore the only redundancy substitute available to a stateless service (6.2.2.5) |
| The repository has three files and no subdirectories, only one of which is application code | Repository root | Any location for schema, model, migration, seed, or fixture assets without creating new structure; the one non-application file, `test.js`, holds 13 bytes of placeholder text and no data |

For reproducibility, the determination in this section rests on four independent classes of evidence, each of which independently supports the non-applicability finding:

| Evidence Class | Scope | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Content probes over tracked source | 33 probe expressions covering drivers, ORMs, DDL/DML keywords, core modules, storage SDKs, config inputs, cache directives, and data-tier port literals | Zero matches; the only `require(` is core `http` |
| Existence probes over the repository tree | 92 paths — 21 data and schema file extensions, 26 directory names, 14 engine and ORM config files, 31 manifests, env files, and container descriptors | Zero present |
| Git history inspection | All objects in all commits (`git rev-list --all --objects`) | Path set is exactly `{README.md, server.js, test.js}` across three commits; no data artifact was ever tracked |
| Runtime behavioural probes | Node.js v22.23.1 execution: descriptor inventory, POST-with-body handling, repeat-request checksums, stdout byte count, working-directory diff, restart comparison, second-instance bind | No data-file descriptor, no outbound socket, no file created, no state retained, no request data captured |

## 6.3 Integration Architecture

### 6.3.1 Integration Applicability Assessment

**Integration Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The repository contains exactly three tracked files — `server.js` (14 lines, 342 bytes), `README.md` (27 bytes), and `test.js` (13 bytes) — 382 bytes in total, and no subdirectories. `server.js` imports one Node.js built-in module, registers one request handler, and binds one listening socket to the loopback address. It opens no outbound socket, resolves no hostname, reads no environment variable, imports no client library, and declares no contract with any counterparty. `test.js` introduces no integration of any kind: it holds two bare identifiers, imports nothing, exposes no endpoint or handler, and is never loaded by any process. Section 3.4 records the same determination at the technology layer — the system "integrates with no third-party service of any kind" — and section 5.1.4 records that it integrates with no external system at all, with every counterparty service level stated as "none declared".

Two independent facts make the determination structural rather than incidental:

- **No egress exists.** The single import on line 1 is used only to *create* a server (`http.createServer`, `server.listen`); it is never used to *issue* a request. There is therefore no direction in which an integration could flow outward, and no network policy egress allowance is required.
- **No ingress from outside the host is possible.** `server.listen` receives the loopback literal defined on line 3, so the listener is reachable only from the same host. A probe of the verification host's routable address on port 3000 failed at the transport layer while the loopback probe returned `200` (host observation, requirement F-002-RQ-002). No external system can connect to the endpoint as committed.

What *does* exist is a single inbound protocol boundary — a plaintext HTTP/1.1 listener at `127.0.0.1:3000` — and it is an interface in the strict sense: a caller speaks a standardised wire protocol to it and receives a defined response. Sub-sections 6.3.2 through 6.3.5 therefore document that boundary in full and then walk every remaining topic the section prompt mandates, because in a specification of this kind a documented gap is more useful than a silent one. For each API, messaging, and external-system concern the reader is told what does not exist, which layer occupies its place if any, and which source fact would have to change for the concern to become meaningful.

#### 6.3.1.1 Determination Criteria

Applicability was assessed against the preconditions that an integration architecture presupposes. Every precondition fails.

| Precondition for Applicability | Observed in This Repository | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At least one external system, service, or peer to integrate with | Zero outbound sockets, zero clients, zero SDKs; no endpoint, credential, or service descriptor exists anywhere | No counterparty to contract with, authenticate to, or version against |
| A network path over which an external caller could reach the system | Loopback literal at line 3; routable-address probe failed at connect while loopback returned `200` | The interface is host-local; no external consumer can be onboarded without a source change |
| A protocol or schema contract shared with another party | 0 of 23 tested API-contract descriptor paths present (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, GraphQL SDL, Protobuf, RAML, API Blueprint, WSDL, Pact) | Nothing to publish, negotiate, validate, or deprecate |
| Asynchronous middleware — broker, queue, topic, stream, or scheduler | 0 of 22 broker/queue/stream paths and 0 of 21 batch/scheduler/worker paths present | No message-processing architecture to specify |
| A mediation tier — gateway, proxy, ingress, or service mesh | 0 of 22 tested gateway, proxy, ingress, and mesh configuration paths present | No policy enforcement point exists at which integration concerns could be centralised |
| A declared availability, quota, or throughput commitment on either side | No SLA, SLO, quota, rate-limit, or capacity artifact exists; section 2.4.2 records that no feature declares a performance requirement | No integration contract terms exist to document or honour |

An integration-specific existence test was run over 146 conventional artifact paths grouped by integration concern. **Every group returned zero matches.** This audit is narrower than the 171-path distributed-artifact audit reported in section 6.1.1.2 and is reported here because it is the primary evidence for the determination above.

| Authentication, identity, and secret material — `.env` family, `credentials/`, `secrets/`, service-account JSON, JWKS, `.htpasswd`, `keys/`, `certs/`, TLS key and certificate files, `.netrc` | 21 | 0 |
| Gateway, reverse proxy, ingress, and mesh configuration — nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy, Traefik, Kong, Tyk, Kubernetes Ingress, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, CloudFront, Istio, Linkerd, `.htaccess` | 22 | 0 |
| Broker, queue, stream, and event configuration — Kafka, RabbitMQ, AMQP, NATS, Redis, Pub/Sub, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Celery, Bull, ActiveMQ, Pulsar, Mosquitto, Kinesis, Flink, Spark, Debezium | 22 | 0 |
| Batch, scheduler, and worker artifacts — crontab, `cron/`, `scheduler/`, `jobs/`, `workers/`, `worker.js`, `batch/`, `etl/`, Airflow `dags/`, Jenkinsfile, `.github/workflows`, systemd units and timers, `queue/`, `consumer.js`, `producer.js` | 21 | 0 |
| Client SDK and dependency manifests — `package.json`, all lockfiles, `node_modules/`, and the equivalent manifests for six other ecosystems | 16 | 0 |

| **Total** | **146** | **0** |

Four independent checks corroborate the path audit:

- **Content scan.** A case-insensitive scan of all three tracked files for `fetch`, `axios`, `request(`, `kafka`, `rabbit`, `amqp`, `redis`, `sqs`, `sns`, `mqtt`, `grpc`, `graphql`, `websocket`, `oauth`, `jwt`, `api_key`, `api-key`, `swagger`, `openapi`, `cron`, `queue`, `webhook`, `database`, `mongo`, `postgres`, `mysql`, and `sqlite` produced **zero hits in any file** — including `test.js`, whose 13 bytes contain no identifier other than two undefined bare words.
- **Library-level exclusion.** Section 3.4 records the verified absence of every conventional integration client — HTTP clients (`axios`, `node-fetch`, `got`, `superagent`, `undici`), messaging clients (`amqplib`, `kafkajs`, `bull`, `agenda`), communications and payment providers (`nodemailer`, `twilio`, `stripe`), identity libraries (`auth0`, `passport`, `jsonwebtoken`, `oauth`, `openid`, `saml`), observability exporters (`sentry`, `datadog`, `newrelic`, `prom-client`, `opentelemetry`), and every major cloud SDK.
- **Configuration-consumption impossibility.** The source performs zero `process.*` accesses (section 3.4.2), so no endpoint, credential, broker URL, or feature flag could be injected at deployment time and consumed. An integration cannot be enabled by configuration because there is no configuration layer to enable it through.
- **Semantic index sweeps.** Searches for API gateway and ingress routing configuration, for broker publisher or consumer code, for clients calling an external web service, and for request-authentication middleware, plus a folder search for integration adapters, external service clients, or webhook handlers, all returned empty result sets — consistent with the three-file inventory, only one file of which contains executable application code.

#### 6.3.1.3 Status Vocabulary and Evidence Conventions

Every mandated topic in this section resolves to exactly one of three statuses, used consistently throughout:

| Status | Meaning | Example in This Section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Delegated** | A mechanism exists and is exercised, but it is owned by the Node.js runtime or the host operating system rather than by repository code | HTTP/1.1 parsing and framing; `400` and `431` protocol rejection; keep-alive connection reuse |
| **Absent** | The concern is meaningful for the interface that exists, but nothing implements it at any layer | Authentication, authorization, rate limiting, versioning, published documentation |
| **Not applicable** | The concern presupposes a structure the system does not have | Message queue architecture, stream processing, gateway policy, external service contracts |

This section adopts the two-label provenance convention established in section 6.1.1.3 without extension. **Runtime default** marks a Node.js `http` or `net` behaviour in force because `server.js` configures nothing; the authoritative catalogue of these values is section 5.2.6. **Host observation** marks a figure produced by executing the unmodified `server.js` on one verification host on one occasion. There is no third category: the repository contains no SLA, SLO, error budget, quota, latency target, or throughput target, so no value in this section may be read as a commitment.

All behavioural evidence cited here was produced against the unmodified working tree — verified clean before and after every probe, with HEAD at commit `43ed37c` on branch `2907_01` — using probe scripts written outside the repository checkout. `server.js` is byte-identical at HEAD and at its parent `06492d7`, so every observation applies to the application exactly as committed. No tracked file was modified. Standard output remained at exactly 41 bytes and standard error at zero bytes across every probe in this section, which independently confirms requirement F-004-RQ-003: the system emits no per-request and no per-error telemetry, so the wire observations below are the only evidence an integrator could ever obtain.

### 6.3.2 API Design

The system exposes one interface, and it was not designed as an API in the conventional sense: there is no contract artifact, no policy tier, and no negotiation channel. Everything a caller can rely on comes from exactly two sources — **three application literals** (status `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, and a 14-byte body, at `server.js` lines 7 through 9) and **the Node.js runtime's defaults** for everything else. The sub-sections below specify that contract precisely, then record the status of each mandated API-design concern.

#### 6.3.2.1 Protocol Specifications

The protocol stack is fixed at authoring time and has no configuration surface. The endpoint is two source literals (`'127.0.0.1'` on line 3 and `3000` on line 4) consumed directly by the positional `server.listen(port, hostname, callback)` call on line 12.

| Protocol Attribute | Specification | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transport | TCP, IPv4 only — one IPv4 `LISTEN` entry for `127.0.0.1:3000` and zero IPv6 entries | Application (line 12) |
| Endpoint | `127.0.0.1:3000`, loopback-only; unreachable from any other host | Application (lines 3–4) |
| Application protocol | Plaintext HTTP/1.1; the response status line is `HTTP/1.1` even when the request is `HTTP/1.0` | Delegated to runtime |
| Transport security | None — an HTTPS request to port 3000 fails during the TLS handshake with a version-mismatch error and `http_code 000` | Host observation |
| HTTP/2, h2c, and WebSocket | No upgrade path; a full WebSocket handshake with `Upgrade: websocket` and `Sec-WebSocket-Key` is answered with the ordinary 163-byte `200` response and no `101 Switching Protocols` | Host observation; server `upgrade` listener count is 0 |
| Interim responses | `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` is generated automatically when a request carries `Expect: 100-continue`, followed by the normal `200` | Delegated to runtime — no `checkContinue` listener exists |
| Connection management | Keep-alive by default with `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`; idle sockets reclaimed after 5000 ms; HTTP/1.0 requests receive `Connection: close` | Runtime default |
| Request pipelining | Honoured — two requests written in a single TCP segment produced two complete `200` responses (326 bytes total) in order | Host observation |
| Header size ceiling | 16,384 bytes; a 20,000-byte header field is rejected before dispatch | Runtime default (`maxHeaderSize`) |

Every property of the request is discarded rather than interpreted. This is the defining characteristic of the interface and the reason no routing, negotiation, or validation layer exists.

| Request Property | Treatment | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Method | Ignored for every standard method — `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, and `HEAD` all produce the same response. An unrecognised method token such as `FOOBAR` is rejected with `400` by the runtime's parser before dispatch | Host observation |
| URI path and query string | Ignored entirely — `/`, `/healthz`, `/metrics`, `/api/v1/hello`, `/v2/hello`, `/a/b/c/d/e`, a percent-encoded path, and a 300-character query string all returned `200` with byte-identical bodies (identical SHA-256) | Host observation, requirement F-001-RQ-002 |
| Request headers | Never inspected by the application — `Accept: application/json` still yields `Content-Type: text/plain`; `Authorization` and `Origin` have no effect. Only the runtime's own parsing limits apply | Host observation |
| Request body | Never read, parsed, buffered, or awaited — a `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` POST received the complete 163-byte response **before any body chunk was transmitted** | Host observation; `req` is declared but never dereferenced (section 2.3.4) |

The response contract is correspondingly invariant. Across 300 probe requests the response header *name set* never varied: `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, and `Content-Length`.

| Response Element | Value | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status | `200 OK` for every request that parses; `400` or `431` for requests that do not | Application (line 7) / runtime for rejections |
| `Content-Type` | `text/plain` — the only header the application sets | Application (line 8) |
| Body | `Hello, World!` plus a newline, 14 bytes, byte-identical across every probe and across process restarts | Application (line 9) |
| `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Content-Length` | Generated per response; `Content-Length: 14` is added because the entity length is known, and is omitted for `HEAD` and for HTTP/1.0 connection-close framing | Delegated to runtime, requirement F-003-RQ-004 |
| `Server`, `X-Powered-By`, `Access-Control-*`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `X-RateLimit-*`, `Retry-After`, `ETag`, `Cache-Control`, any version header | **Never emitted** — absent from every observed response | Not implemented at any layer |

The complete authored contract is three statements, which is why there is no schema, envelope, or error model to specify:

```javascript
res.statusCode = 200;                          // the only status the application can produce
res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');   // the only header the application sets
```

#### 6.3.2.2 Authentication Methods

**Status: absent at every layer.** No authentication mechanism is implemented, and no credential could be supplied to one if it were: the source performs zero `process.*` accesses (section 3.4.2) and the repository contains none of the 21 tested credential or key-material artifacts.

| Mechanism | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP Basic, Bearer token, or API key header | Absent | A request carrying `Authorization: Bearer junk` received the standard `200` response; the header is never read |
| Mutual TLS or client certificates | Not applicable | The listener is plaintext; no TLS context exists and no `certs/`, `tls/`, `*.pem`, or `*.key` artifact is present |
| OAuth 2.0, OIDC, SAML, or a delegated identity provider | Absent | Section 3.4.2 records `auth0`, `passport`, `jsonwebtoken`, `oauth`, `openid`, and `saml` all verified absent; no `.well-known` document is served |
| Session cookie or signed-token scheme | Absent | No `Set-Cookie` is ever emitted; `session` and `cookie-parser` verified absent; the process holds no state between requests |
| Request signing — HMAC, JWS, or timestamped digest | Absent | No cryptographic module is imported; `server.js` imports only `http` |
| Authentication challenge on failure | Structurally impossible | No `401` or `WWW-Authenticate` response can be produced — the application sets exactly one status code and the runtime's only rejection codes are `400` and `431` |

The one control actually in force is **topological, not identity-based**, as established in section 2.4.4: the loopback bind restricts callers to the same host. This is a network-reachability constraint enforced by the host TCP/IP stack, not an authentication decision — it distinguishes *where* a caller is, never *who* it is, and it grants every same-host process, regardless of user or privilege, identical unauthenticated access.

#### 6.3.2.3 Authorization Framework

**Status: not applicable — no authorization framework exists, and none of its structural elements is present.** Authorization requires a subject, a resource model, and a policy; the interface has none of the three.

| Framework Element | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject or principal | None — no identity is ever established | `req` is never dereferenced; no header, token, or peer attribute is read |
| Resource model | None — the URI space is undifferentiated | Eight structurally different URIs, including `/metrics` and `/healthz`, returned byte-identical `200` responses |
| Policy expression — roles, scopes, ACLs, or rules | None | `server.js` contains zero conditional constructs (no `if`, `switch`, or ternary), so no decision can be expressed |
| Policy decision and enforcement points | None | There is no middleware chain, filter, guard, or interceptor; the runtime dispatches directly to the single handler |
| Denial response path | None | No `403` can be produced; the application's only status is `200` |
| Effective policy in force | "Permit every request, from the loopback interface only" | Invariant `200` across every method, URI, and header combination probed |

#### 6.3.2.4 Rate Limiting Strategy

**Status: absent — no rate limiting, throttling, quota, or admission control exists at any layer.** The repository contains none of the nine tested rate-limit, WAF, and quota descriptors, and the runtime's own protective controls are all left unset.

| Control | Configured Value | Effect of the Setting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application-level limiter, token bucket, or quota counter | None — no such code exists | Offered load is never counted, so it can never be compared against a threshold |
| `server.maxConnections` | `undefined` (runtime default) | No ceiling on concurrent connections; each accepted connection consumes one descriptor |
| `server.maxRequestsPerSocket` | `0`, meaning unlimited (runtime default) | A single connection may issue an unbounded number of requests |
| `'dropRequest'` event hook | 0 listeners registered | Node's load-shedding signal is never observed, so overload cannot be detected or acted upon |
| `keepAliveTimeout` | 5000 ms (runtime default) | The only reclamation mechanism in force; it bounds *idle* socket accumulation, not request rate |

A burst probe of 300 requests issued at 50-way parallelism across distinct URIs returned **300 responses with status `200`**, every one carrying the standard 14-byte body, with zero `429` responses, zero connection rejections, and no `Retry-After` or `X-RateLimit-*` header on any response (host observation). Load is therefore absorbed rather than shed: excess demand converts into queueing latency on the single event-loop thread, which section 6.1.4.5 documents as the degradation behaviour and section 6.1.3.1 quantifies. Because no latency or request-count metric is emitted, a throttled-in-practice condition would be invisible to both the operator and the caller.

#### 6.3.2.5 Versioning Approach

**Status: absent — the interface is unversioned, and no versioning channel exists in either direction.**

| Versioning Mechanism | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| URI path versioning | Absent | `/api/v1/hello` and `/v2/hello` return byte-identical responses; version segments are ordinary path characters that are never parsed |
| Query-parameter or custom-header versioning | Absent | No request header or query parameter is read; a 300-character query string had no effect on the response |
| Media-type versioning and content negotiation | Absent | `Accept: application/json` yielded `Content-Type: text/plain`; the single `setHeader` call is unconditional |
| Deprecation and sunset signalling | Absent | No `Deprecation`, `Sunset`, `Warning`, or `Link` header is ever emitted; no version identifier appears in any response |
| Version identifier available to a consumer | None from the interface | The only version identifier for the system is a Git commit SHA; section 6.1 records three commits and zero tags, and the SHA is not exposed over the wire |

Two consequences follow. First, because the response body, status, and content type are the whole contract, **any change to them is a breaking change** with no negotiation channel through which a caller could pin the prior behaviour. Second, section 2.3.5 records that the system has no internal service contract to version either — there is no seam at which a versioned component could be substituted — so versioning would have to be introduced at the same time as the first consumer-facing change rather than retrofitted around an existing boundary.

#### 6.3.2.6 Documentation Standards

**Status: absent — the repository publishes no interface documentation, and the interface is not self-describing.**

| Documentation Artifact | Status | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Machine-readable specification — OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, GraphQL SDL, Protobuf, RAML, API Blueprint, WSDL | None | 0 of 23 tested contract-descriptor paths present |
| Human-readable API documentation | None | `README.md` contains exactly one non-blank line, the heading `# July2026_hello_world_repo`; it provides no setup, usage, dependency, API, or architecture detail |
| Source-level documentation | None | `server.js` contains no comments and no JSDoc across its 14 lines; it exports nothing, so no interface is described in code |
| Runtime discovery endpoint — `/openapi.json`, `/.well-known/*`, or a schema route | None | Every URI, including discovery-style paths, returns the same 14-byte plaintext body |
| Self-description in the response | Minimal | `Content-Type: text/plain` is the only metadata a caller receives; there is no envelope, schema reference, or version marker |
| Endpoint advertisement | One startup line | The 41-byte readiness message on standard output interpolates the same `hostname` and `port` constants used for the bind, so the advertised endpoint cannot drift from the bound endpoint (requirement F-004-RQ-002) |

In practice the endpoint's contract is documented in exactly two places outside the source: the readiness line, which names the endpoint but not its behaviour, and this specification. An integrator has no artifact to generate a client from, no schema to validate against, and no channel through which to discover the contract other than issuing a request and observing the reply.

#### 6.3.2.7 API Architecture Diagram

The diagram below traces a request through the tiers a conventional HTTP API would traverse, marking which tiers exist, which layer owns each, and which are absent. It is a *policy-ownership* view and deliberately does not restate the component decomposition of section 5.1.2 or the service-boundary view of diagram 6.1-A.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Client(["Same-host HTTP client<br/>the only reachable caller"])
    subgraph EdgeAbsent["Edge tiers a deployed API would have — none exist here"]
        direction TB
        E1["TLS termination<br/>HTTPS probe failed at the handshake, http_code 000"]
        E2["API gateway or reverse proxy<br/>0 of 22 gateway, proxy, ingress, mesh paths present"]
        E3["CORS policy evaluation<br/>0 Access-Control headers on a preflight-shaped OPTIONS"]
        E1 --> E2
        E2 --> E3
    end
    subgraph RuntimeTier["Node.js runtime tier — the only tier that enforces anything"]
        direction TB
        P1["Accept connection on the loopback socket<br/>default backlog 511, capped by host somaxconn 1024"]
        P2{{"Start line and headers<br/>parse within limits?"}}
        P3["Reject before dispatch<br/>400 Bad Request or 431 Too Large, Connection close"]
        P4["Emit 100 Continue if Expect was sent<br/>no checkContinue listener exists"]
        P5["Dispatch to the single request listener<br/>request listener count is 1"]
        P1 --> P2
        P2 -->|"no"| P3
        P2 -->|"yes"| P4
        P4 --> P5
    end
    subgraph PolicyAbsent["Policy tiers a conventional API places here — all absent"]
        direction TB
        A1["Authentication<br/>Authorization header ignored, 0 challenges possible"]
        A2["Authorization<br/>no subject, no resource model, no policy"]
        A3["Rate limiting<br/>300 of 300 burst requests returned 200"]
        A4["Version resolution<br/>/api/v1 and /v2 answer identically"]
        A5["Routing and dispatch<br/>8 of 8 probed URIs byte-identical"]
        A1 --> A2
        A2 --> A3
        A3 --> A4
        A4 --> A5
    end
    Handler["Application handler, server.js lines 7 to 9<br/>3 unconditional statements, no branch"]
    Framing["Runtime response framing<br/>Date, Connection keep-alive, Keep-Alive timeout 5, Content-Length 14"]
    Client -->|"plaintext HTTP/1.1, any method or URI"| P1
    Client -.->|"path a conventional deployment would take"| E1
```
