**Diagram 6.3-A — API architecture: request path by tier, with owning layer and verified absences.** Solid edges are the path a request actually takes; dotted edges mark tiers that a conventional API deployment would interpose and that this system does not have. The middle lane is the only lane with enforcement authority, and everything it enforces is a runtime default rather than an authored policy.

### 6.3.3 Message Processing

**Message processing in the enterprise sense — asynchronous exchange mediated by a broker, queue, topic, stream, or scheduler — is not applicable to this system.** No such middleware is configured, imported, or reachable: 0 of the 22 tested broker, queue, and stream configuration paths exist, 0 of the 21 tested batch, scheduler, and worker paths exist, and section 3.4.1 records `amqplib`, `kafkajs`, `bull`, and `agenda` as verified absent from the source.

Exactly one message-exchange pattern exists, and it is synchronous: one inbound HTTP request produces one outbound HTTP response on the same connection. The sub-sections below characterise that pattern precisely and record the status of each mandated messaging concern.

#### 6.3.3.1 Event Processing Patterns

An event-driven substrate genuinely exists, but it belongs entirely to the Node.js runtime. The application contributes a single event subscription — the request listener passed to `http.createServer` on line 6 — and subscribes to nothing else. Section 6.1.2.2 records the measured listener topology: `request` = 1, while `error`, `clientError`, `upgrade`, `timeout`, `checkContinue`, `dropRequest`, and `close` are all 0, and the single `connection` listener is registered internally by Node rather than by application code.

| Pattern | Status | Evidence and Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Event-loop-driven, non-blocking I/O dispatch | **Delegated — present** | The libuv event loop demultiplexes socket readiness and invokes the one registered listener; all requests are served on a single event-loop thread (section 6.1.3.1) |
| Callback-based event subscription | **Present — one subscription only** | `http.createServer(handler)` registers the sole application listener; the `listen` callback on line 12 fires exactly once at startup |
| Synchronous request/response exchange | **Present — the only exchange pattern** | One request in, one response out; no batching, aggregation, fan-out, or long-polling; no `res.write` streaming — the response is completed in a single `res.end` call on line 9 |
| Publish/subscribe or topic-based distribution | Not applicable | No broker or bus exists; the source contains no `publish`, `subscribe`, or `emit` reference |
| Event sourcing, CQRS, or an outbox pattern | Not applicable | No persistence of any kind exists; section 5.1.3 records no data store or cache at any tier |
| Saga or long-running process orchestration | Not applicable | The exchange completes within one handler invocation with no continuation, correlation identifier, or state |
| Webhook or callback egress | Absent | No outbound socket is ever opened; 0 of 12 tested webhook, callback, and push-protocol paths exist |
| Server-sent events or WebSocket push | Absent | No `upgrade` listener; a WebSocket handshake receives the ordinary `200` response, and no `text/event-stream` response is ever produced |

Two properties of the exchange are worth stating explicitly because they bound what any integrator can build on it. **The inbound message payload is never consumed:** a chunked POST received its complete response before any body chunk was transmitted, so the application cannot be described as processing messages at all — it emits a fixed reply upon connection-level request *arrival*. And **the exchange is stateless and uncorrelated:** no request identifier, trace context, or correlation token is read or generated, so consecutive messages from the same caller are indistinguishable from messages sent by different callers.

#### 6.3.3.2 Message Queue Architecture

**Not applicable — no message queue, broker, or queueing abstraction exists at any layer.** The concern presupposes middleware the system does not have, and no partial capability exists either.

| Queue Architecture Element | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broker or queue service | None | 0 of 22 tested broker and queue configuration paths (Kafka, RabbitMQ, AMQP, NATS, Redis, Pub/Sub, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Celery, Bull, ActiveMQ, Pulsar, Mosquitto) |
| Producer or consumer client | None | No client library is importable — the repository has no dependency manifest and `server.js` imports only `http` |
| Queue, topic, exchange, or subscription topology | None | Nothing to declare, bind, or route; no such identifier appears in any of the three tracked files |
| Durability, acknowledgement, and redelivery semantics | None | No persistence layer exists, so no message can survive the process; delivery is at-most-once over a TCP connection with no application-level acknowledgement |
| Dead-letter queue, retry queue, or poison-message handling | None | No retry construct exists anywhere — `server.js` contains zero conditionals and zero `try`/`catch` blocks |
| Ordering and partitioning guarantees | Delegated to TCP and the runtime | Responses to pipelined requests were returned in request order on a single connection; there is no ordering guarantee across connections and no partition key concept |

The only queue that exists anywhere in the request path is the operating system's TCP accept queue — a platform facility, not an architectural choice. Its depth is the runtime's default backlog of 511, capped in practice by the verification host's `somaxconn` of 1024, as catalogued in section 5.2.6 and analysed in section 6.1.2.4.

#### 6.3.3.3 Stream Processing Design

**Not applicable — no stream processing design exists.** No stream platform, processor, or windowing construct is present: the broker audit above covers Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, Flink, Spark, and Debezium, all absent.

| Stream Processing Element | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stream source or sink | None | No stream client, connector, or topic reference exists; the process opens no outbound socket |
| Stateful operators — windowing, joins, aggregation | None | The handler performs three unconditional operations and retains no state between invocations |
| Checkpointing, watermarks, or replay | None | No persistence and no offset concept exist; a restart returns the system to a byte-identical condition (section 6.1.4.3) |
| Backpressure propagation to an upstream producer | Not applicable | The response is a 14-byte literal written in one call; the runtime owns socket-level write buffering, and the application never reads the request stream so it can exert no backpressure |
| Node.js `stream` semantics on `req` and `res` | Delegated — transport plumbing only | `req` and `res` are streams provided by the runtime, but `req` is never dereferenced and `res` is written once via `res.end`; neither is piped, transformed, or consumed incrementally |

The distinction matters for anyone assessing this system against a streaming requirement: streams exist as a transport implementation detail inside the runtime, but no data-stream processing occurs, because no inbound data is read and no outbound data is derived from any input.

#### 6.3.3.4 Batch Processing Flows

**Not applicable — no batch processing flow exists.** There is no scheduled, triggered, or long-running batch path of any kind, and no mechanism through which one could be invoked.

| Batch Processing Element | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduler or trigger — cron, timer, or queue-driven worker | None | 0 of 21 tested batch, scheduler, and worker paths (crontab, `cron/`, `jobs/`, `workers/`, `batch/`, `etl/`, Airflow `dags/`, systemd timers, `.github/workflows`, Jenkinsfile) |
| In-process timer or interval | None | `server.js` contains no `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, or `setImmediate` call; the only scheduled callback is the one-shot `listen` callback on line 12 |
| Bulk input or output — file, object store, or database | None | The process performs no filesystem, DNS, or crypto work, which is why the libuv thread pool stays idle (section 6.1.3.3) |
| Job state, checkpointing, or restartability | Not applicable | No job exists; there is no state to checkpoint and nothing to resume after a restart |
| Batch-oriented API affordances — bulk endpoints, multipart upload, pagination | None | Every request receives the same 14-byte response regardless of method, URI, or body |

The system's entire execution model is request-triggered and synchronous. Four of its five components execute once during composition and only the request handler executes during serving (section 6.1.2.1), so there is no background execution context in which batch work could run.

#### 6.3.3.5 Error Handling Strategy

**Status: delegated in full — every error path in force belongs to the Node.js runtime or the host operating system.** The application registers no error listener, wraps nothing in `try`/`catch`, and emits no diagnostic output after the startup line. Section 5.4.3 documents the same finding as an ownership question; the table below states it in message-exchange terms.

| Error Class | Detected By | Wire and Process Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Malformed request line | Runtime HTTP parser | `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`, then socket closure; the handler is never entered and nothing is written to stdout or stderr |
| Unrecognised method token | Runtime HTTP parser | `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close`; observed for a `FOOBAR` request line carrying `Authorization` and `Origin` headers |
| Header field exceeding 16,384 bytes | Runtime (`maxHeaderSize`) | `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` with `Connection: close`; handler never entered |
| Socket-level fault — client abort, reset, or truncated request | Runtime default | No `clientError` or `error` listener is registered, so disposition is entirely the runtime's default behaviour (section 5.4.3); the application observes nothing |
| Idle connection exceeding the keep-alive window | Runtime (`keepAliveTimeout` 5000 ms) | Socket closed by the server; a caller wishing to continue must reconnect, which is client-side behaviour, not a server retry |
| Failure inside the handler | Not reachable | Three unconditional statements on the response object with no failure mode of its own; every probed URI returned an identical `200` (section 6.1.2.6) |
| Endpoint unavailable at startup — port already held | Runtime, unhandled | `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` raised as an unhandled `'error'` event; stack trace on stderr, no readiness line, exit code `1` (requirement F-002-RQ-004) |
| Shutdown during an in-flight exchange | Host signal delivery | Immediate termination with no draining; a client holding a keep-alive connection observes a peer close (requirement F-002-RQ-005) |

Four strategy-level consequences follow directly, and each is a design fact rather than an inference:

- **Fail-fast, never degrade.** Protocol errors terminate the connection immediately and the process exits on a bind conflict. Section 6.1.2.6 records that this posture is *inherited* from the absence of handlers rather than chosen as a policy.
- **Runtime-generated error responses are not fallbacks.** `400` and `431` are produced *instead of* invoking the application, not as a degraded substitute for its output, so a caller cannot distinguish an application error from a protocol error — the application has no error representation at all.
- **No retry, redelivery, or idempotency machinery exists.** There is no dead-letter path, no replay log, and no idempotency key; because the response is a constant, however, every request is trivially idempotent from the caller's perspective.
- **Errors are unobservable.** Standard output remained at exactly 41 bytes and standard error at zero bytes across every probe in this section, including all deliberate protocol-error probes (requirement F-004-RQ-003). An integrator debugging a rejected exchange has only the wire response to work from; the server retains no record of it.

#### 6.3.3.6 Message Flow Diagram

The diagram below shows the single message channel that exists alongside the asynchronous middleware classes that were verified empty. It complements diagram 6.3-A by taking the *message*, rather than the policy tier, as its subject.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Producer(["Message producer<br/>same-host HTTP client"])
    subgraph Channel["The only message channel — one TCP connection over loopback"]
        direction TB
        M1["Inbound message is one HTTP/1.1 request<br/>method, URI, headers, optional body"]
        M2["Framing and ordering owned by the runtime<br/>2 pipelined requests produced 2 ordered responses"]
        M3["Payload never consumed<br/>chunked POST answered before any chunk arrived"]
        M4["Outbound message is a fixed 14-byte reply<br/>identical for every inbound message"]
        M1 --> M2
        M2 --> M3
        M3 --> M4
    end
    subgraph Rejected["Runtime-terminated exchanges — handler never entered"]
        direction TB
        X1["Malformed start line or unknown method<br/>400 Bad Request, connection closed"]
        X2["Header field over 16384 bytes<br/>431 Too Large, connection closed"]
        X1 --> X2
    end
    subgraph NoMiddleware["Asynchronous middleware classes — every class verified empty"]
        direction TB
        B1["Queue or topic broker<br/>0 of 22 broker and queue paths present"]
        B2["Stream or log platform<br/>no Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, Flink, Spark, Debezium artifact"]
        B3["Scheduler or batch runner<br/>0 of 21 cron, job, worker paths present"]
        B4["Dead-letter, replay, or outbox store<br/>no persistence exists at any tier"]
        B5["Event bus or webhook egress<br/>0 outbound sockets ever opened"]
    end
    Sink["Reply consumed by the caller<br/>nothing retained, logged, or forwarded"]
    Producer -->|"synchronous, at-most-once, uncorrelated"| M1
    Producer -.->|"unparseable input"| X1
    X2 -.->|"no record kept, stdout stays 41 bytes"| Sink
    M4 -->|"200, text/plain, keep-alive socket reused"| Sink
    Sink -.->|"caller may reissue after the 5 s idle close"| Producer
```

**Diagram 6.3-B — Message flow: the single synchronous channel, the runtime-terminated exchanges, and the empty asynchronous middleware classes.** The upper-left lane is the whole message path that exists; the middle lane shows the two exchange outcomes the application never sees; the right-hand lane enumerates the middleware categories tested and found absent, each with the evidence establishing the absence.

### 6.3.4 External Systems

**No external system participates in the runtime behaviour of this system.** The running process communicates with exactly four counterparties, all of them host-local facilities rather than external systems: the inbound loopback TCP listener, the in-process Node core `http` API, standard output, and the operating-system process-control surface. Section 3.4.5 catalogues these four as the actual integration surface and records that "no service contract, API key, rate limit, quota, or third-party availability dependency applies to this system."

#### 6.3.4.1 Third-Party Integration Patterns

**Status: absent — no third-party integration pattern is implemented, and none could be enabled without editing the source.**

| Integration Pattern | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outbound synchronous call — REST, RPC, gRPC, GraphQL | Absent | Zero outbound sockets are ever opened; the single `require` on line 1 is used only to create a server, never to issue a request; no `.proto` or GraphQL SDL artifact exists |
| Vendor SDK or managed-service client | Absent | Section 3.4.4 records `aws-sdk`, `@aws-sdk`, `googleapis`, `@google-cloud`, `azure`, `@azure`, `firebase`, and `supabase` all verified absent; the repository has no dependency manifest through which any SDK could be installed |
| Inbound webhook receiver or outbound webhook publisher | Absent | 0 of 12 tested webhook, callback, SSE, and WebSocket paths exist; every URI receives the same 14-byte plaintext reply, so no callback route is distinguishable |
| File- or object-transfer integration — SFTP, S3, shared volume | Absent | The process performs no filesystem work at all, which is why the libuv thread pool remains idle under load (section 6.1.3.3) |
| Database or cache used as an integration channel | Not applicable | Section 5.1.3 records no data store or cache at any tier; no driver, connection string, or ORM exists |
| Identity federation or delegated authentication | Absent | Section 3.4.2 records the full set of absent identity libraries; no `.well-known` document is served and no redirect is ever issued |
| Telemetry export to an external collector | Absent | Section 3.4.3 records `sentry`, `datadog`, `newrelic`, `elastic`, `prom-client`, and `opentelemetry` all absent; the only output is one 41-byte startup line |

Two structural facts make this absence unconditional rather than a matter of current configuration. First, **there is no configuration channel:** the source performs zero `process.*` accesses, so no endpoint, credential, or broker URL could be injected at deployment time and consumed (section 3.4.2). Second, **there is no substitution seam:** section 2.3.5 records that the repository contains no application-level shared service — no client factory, adapter, or dependency-injection container — so an integration could only be introduced by adding new statements to `server.js` itself.

#### 6.3.4.2 Legacy System Interfaces

**Status: not applicable — the system has no legacy counterpart and exposes no legacy-oriented interface.**

| Legacy Interface Class | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mainframe, terminal, or screen-scraping adapter | None | No such client is importable; the source imports only the Node core `http` module |
| SOAP or XML-RPC endpoint | None | No WSDL or XSD artifact exists among the 23 tested contract descriptors; the only content type emitted is `text/plain` |
| Fixed-width or delimited file exchange, batch drop directories | None | 0 of 21 tested batch, ETL, and scheduler paths exist; the process reads and writes no files |
| Database link, stored-procedure call, or ODBC/JDBC bridge | None | No driver or connection artifact exists at any path |
| Message-oriented middleware bridge — MQ series, JMS, ESB | None | 0 of 22 tested broker paths exist |
| Migration, strangler-facade, or coexistence pattern | Not applicable | The repository's entire history is three commits — `241598b` adding `README.md`, `06492d7` adding `server.js`, and `43ed37c` adding the 13-byte `test.js` — with no predecessor implementation, compatibility shim, or deprecated path in any commit or branch |

#### 6.3.4.3 API Gateway Configuration

**Status: not applicable — no API gateway, reverse proxy, ingress controller, or service mesh is configured, and in the committed form none could be interposed.**

| Gateway Concern | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway, proxy, or ingress artifact | None | 0 of 22 tested paths, covering nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy, Traefik, Kong, Tyk, Kubernetes Ingress, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, CloudFront, Istio, Linkerd, and `.htaccess`; section 6.1.1.2 reports the same result for its own 17-path proxy and mesh group |
| Routing, path rewriting, or upstream pooling | None | There is no upstream to pool and no route table; the application answers every path identically |
| Edge policy — TLS termination, authentication, rate limiting, CORS, WAF | None | Each of these is documented as absent in 6.3.2; no tier exists at which such a policy could be attached |
| Request and response transformation | None | The response is a fixed literal; no transformation stage exists in or around the process |
| Reachability for a gateway that an operator might add | **Structurally blocked** | The loopback bind at line 3 means a gateway in another network namespace, container, or host cannot connect; a probe of the routable host address returned a connect failure while loopback returned `200` |

The last row is the architecturally decisive one. A gateway could only be placed in front of this service if it ran **on the same host and in the same network namespace**, or if `server.js` were edited to bind a routable address. Section 6.1.5.2 records the same source fact as the gate on off-host reachability, load balancing, and mesh placement.

#### 6.3.4.4 External Service Contracts

**Status: none exist, in either direction.** No contract, service-level commitment, quota, or availability dependency binds this system to any counterparty.

| Contract Dimension | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contracts this system consumes | None | The system depends on no external service, so it inherits no counterparty availability, latency, or quota terms; section 5.1.4 records every counterparty service level as "none declared" |
| Contracts this system offers | None published | No specification artifact, versioning channel, deprecation signal, or documented behaviour exists (6.3.2.5 and 6.3.2.6); the de facto contract is the observed wire response |
| Commercial or licensing terms attached to an integration | None | No third-party service is consumed, so no API key, subscription, quota, or usage-based cost applies (section 3.4) |
| Availability or performance commitments | None declared | The repository contains no SLA, SLO, error budget, or capacity artifact; section 2.4.2 records that no feature declares a performance requirement |
| Contract testing or verification | None | 0 of 23 tested contract descriptors, including Pact, exist; the repository contains no test suite — the root-level `test.js` added by `43ed37c` holds no assertion and no framework (section 6.6.1) |

One external system does exist in the project's **lifecycle**, and it is important to place it precisely so that it is not mistaken for a runtime integration. The repository has a single Git remote named `origin` hosted on `github.com`, with no submodules and no Git LFS configuration. Its role is confined to source distribution: it delivers `server.js` to a workstation *before* execution, and the running process never contacts it — there is no install, build, fetch, or update step at runtime, which is the substance of requirement F-005-RQ-002 (the system runs as committed). Section 1.2.1.3 and section 3.4.4 record the same scoping. Section 3.4.4 additionally flags an operational caution that applies to this checkout's local Git configuration: the configured remote URL embeds an access token, so the local Git configuration is credential-sensitive and must not be shared, published, or copied into images or documentation. That credential grants repository access only and has no relationship to the running service, which requires no credential to operate.

#### 6.3.4.5 Complete External Dependency Inventory

The prompt requires that all external dependencies be documented. The inventory is complete at five entries, only four of which exist at runtime, and none of which is a third-party service.

| Dependency | Direction and Role | Coupling Strength |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node.js runtime — core `http` module, libuv event loop, module resolution | Internal; provides HTTP parsing, framing, connection multiplexing, all timeouts, protocol error responses, and default signal disposition | **Hard and total** — the entire behaviour of the system beyond three literals is inherited from it; no version is pinned anywhere in the repository, since there is no `package.json` `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, or container image |
| Host TCP/IP stack — loopback interface, port reservation, accept queue | Inbound; carries every request and enforces the loopback restriction | Hard — it is the enforcement point for the system's only access control |
| Host standard output stream | Outbound; receives exactly one 41-byte readiness line per successful start | Soft — whatever captures the stream (shell, supervisor, or log driver) is unconfigured by the repository |
| Host process-control surface — signals and exit codes | Bidirectional; delivers `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT`, receives exit code `1` on bind failure | Hard for lifecycle, absent for behaviour — zero signal listeners are registered, so disposition is the runtime default |
| Git remote `origin` on `github.com` | Development-time only; source distribution | **None at runtime** — the process never contacts it; no submodules or LFS objects are involved |

Every runtime entry in this table is a facility of the platform the process happens to run on. There is no entry for which an outage, quota, credential rotation, or contract renegotiation could occur, which is the concrete meaning of the determination in 6.3.1: the system has no external integration to architect.

### 6.3.5 Integration Flows and Sequence Diagrams

This sub-section renders the integration behaviour documented above as flow and sequence views, then consolidates the section's findings into a coverage matrix and a change-impact reference. The diagrams are integration-specific: the per-request interaction in section 1.2.2.3, the component interaction in section 5.1.2, and the service-inventory view in diagram 6.1-A cover different subjects and are deliberately not restated.

#### 6.3.5.1 Integration Flow Diagram

The flow below places every actor and channel in the system relative to the three perimeters that matter for integration: what is outside the host and cannot reach the process, what is inside the host and constitutes the whole runtime perimeter, and what participates only at development time.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph OffHost["Off-host actors — cannot reach the system"]
        direction TB
        R1(["Remote HTTP client on another host"])
        R2["Probe of the routable address on port 3000<br/>returned a connect failure, http_code 000"]
        R1 --> R2
    end
    subgraph HostPerimeter["Verification host — the entire runtime perimeter"]
        direction TB
        L1(["Local client process — the only reachable caller"])
        K1["Host TCP/IP stack<br/>1 IPv4 LISTEN entry for 127.0.0.1:3000, 0 IPv6 entries"]
        N1["Node.js runtime<br/>parsing, framing, timeouts, protocol errors"]
        H1["server.js handler<br/>3 unconditional statements, no branch"]
        O1["Standard streams<br/>41 bytes on stdout, 0 on stderr, for the process lifetime"]
        S1["Process control<br/>signals in, exit codes out, 0 listeners registered"]
        L1 -->|"plaintext HTTP/1.1 over loopback"| K1
        K1 --> N1
        N1 -->|"in-process invocation"| H1
        H1 -->|"mutated response object"| N1
        N1 -->|"200, text/plain, 14 bytes"| L1
        N1 -.->|"one readiness line, at startup only"| O1
        S1 -.->|"SIGTERM or SIGINT, no draining"| N1
    end
    subgraph Lifecycle["Development-time integration — no runtime coupling"]
        direction TB
        G1["Git remote origin on github.com<br/>source distribution only"]
        G2["Delivers server.js to a workstation before execution<br/>no install, build, or fetch step at runtime"]
        G1 --> G2
    end
    R2 -.->|"blocked by the loopback literal on line 3"| K1
    G2 -.->|"file present on disk before node server.js runs"| H1
```

**Diagram 6.3-C — Integration flow across the three perimeters.** Solid edges inside the host perimeter are the only integration paths that carry traffic. The dotted edge from the off-host lane records a blocked path, not a supported one. The lifecycle lane exists to make explicit that the project's one genuinely external system touches the source file, never the running process.

#### 6.3.5.2 Sequence — Successful Synchronous Exchange

This is the only successful integration flow the system has. The two annotations mark the properties that most distinguish it from a conventional API exchange: no policy lookup occurs, and the reply does not wait for the request payload.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Local HTTP client
    participant K as Host TCP-IP stack, loopback
    participant N as Node.js runtime, core http
    participant H as Handler, server.js lines 7 to 9
    C->>K: TCP SYN to 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    K->>N: accepted connection, one descriptor consumed
    C->>N: POST /ingest, chunked body, Authorization and Origin headers present
    Note over N: No credential, quota, version, or route lookup occurs
    N->>H: invoke the single request listener
    H->>N: status 200, Content-Type text/plain, end with the 14-byte literal
    N-->>C: 200, Date, Connection keep-alive, Keep-Alive timeout 5, Content-Length 14
    Note over C,N: Reply observed before any body chunk was sent, so the payload is never read
    C->>N: second request on the same connection, different URI
    N-->>C: byte-identical 200 reply
    Note over N: Idle socket closed by the runtime after 5000 ms, a runtime default
```

**Diagram 6.3-D — Sequence: successful exchange, including connection reuse.** The handler is entered exactly once per parsed request and contributes three response mutations; every other step belongs to the runtime or the host.

#### 6.3.5.3 Sequence — Rejected and Blocked Exchanges

Three of the four branches below never reach the application. Together they are the complete set of negative outcomes an integrator can observe.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant X as Off-host client
    participant C as Local client
    participant K as Host TCP-IP stack
    participant N as Node.js runtime
    participant H as Handler, server.js lines 7 to 9
    X->>K: TCP SYN to the routable host address, port 3000
    K-->>X: connect failure, no listener on that interface
    Note over X,K: The loopback literal on line 3 excludes every off-host caller
    C->>K: TCP SYN to 127.0.0.1 port 3000
    K->>N: accepted connection
    alt malformed start line
        C->>N: NOT-A-VALID REQUEST LINE
        N-->>C: 400 Bad Request, Connection close
    else header field larger than 16384 bytes
        C->>N: GET with a 20000-byte header field
        N-->>C: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large, Connection close
    else unrecognised method token
        C->>N: FOOBAR /any/path HTTP/1.1
        N-->>C: 400 Bad Request, Connection close
    else well-formed request
        C->>N: any standard method, any URI, any headers
        N->>H: invoke the single listener
        H->>N: three response mutations
        N-->>C: 200, text/plain, 14 bytes
    end
    Note over N,H: In the three rejection branches the handler is never entered and nothing is logged
```

**Diagram 6.3-E — Sequence: connection refusal and protocol rejection paths.** Every rejection is generated by the runtime before dispatch, which is why an integrator cannot distinguish an application error from a protocol error — the application has no error representation at all.

#### 6.3.5.4 Sequence — Endpoint Publication and Bind Failure

The endpoint is "published" exactly once, to standard output, by interpolating the same two constants used for the bind. This is the only advertisement mechanism in the system, and the failure branch is the only integration-relevant startup outcome.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant OP as Operator shell
    participant P as node server.js process
    participant K as Host TCP-IP stack
    participant SS as Standard streams
    OP->>P: node server.js, no install or build step
    P->>P: require http, then createServer with one handler
    P->>K: listen with positional arguments 3000 and 127.0.0.1
    alt port 3000 free
        K-->>P: bind and listen succeed
        P->>SS: one 41-byte readiness line naming the bound endpoint
        Note over SS: The only endpoint advertisement the system ever produces
    else port 3000 already held
        K-->>P: EADDRINUSE
        P->>SS: stack trace on standard error, no readiness line
        Note over P: Unhandled error event, process exits with code 1
    end
```

**Diagram 6.3-F — Sequence: endpoint publication and the bind-conflict branch.** Because the readiness line interpolates the bind constants, the advertised endpoint cannot drift from the bound endpoint (requirement F-004-RQ-002); because no `'error'` listener is registered, the conflict branch is fatal rather than recoverable (requirement F-002-RQ-004).

#### 6.3.5.5 Integration Point Summary

The complete integration inventory is four runtime interfaces plus one development-time interface. This restates section 2.3.3 and section 3.4.5 in contract terms, adding the observed guarantee for each.

| Integration Point | Direction | Contract Actually In Force |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TCP listener at `127.0.0.1:3000` | Inbound | Plaintext HTTP/1.1; any standard method and any URI yields `200`, `text/plain`, 14 bytes; keep-alive with a 5-second idle close; `400` or `431` for unparseable input; no authentication, quota, version, or negotiation |
| Node core `http` request/response API | Internal, in-process | Direct library calls with no wrapper, adapter, or middleware; the runtime owns parsing, framing, interim responses, and all timeouts |
| Standard output | Outbound | Exactly one newline-terminated readiness line per successful start; 41 bytes for the process lifetime regardless of traffic |
| Operating-system process control | Bidirectional | Exit code `1` with a stack trace on bind failure; immediate termination on `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` with no draining |
| Git remote `origin` on `github.com` | Development-time only | Source distribution; the running process never contacts it, and no submodule or LFS object is involved |

#### 6.3.5.7 Source Facts That Gate Each Integration Concern

Every gap in this section traces to a small number of source facts. The mapping below is a change-impact reference recording what each fact currently forecloses; it is not a recommendation or a plan, and the architectural trade-offs behind these facts are recorded as decisions in section 5.3.

| Source Fact | Location | Integration Concerns It Forecloses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hostname` is the loopback literal | `server.js` line 3 | External consumer onboarding, gateway or proxy placement, off-host monitoring, mutual TLS termination at an edge, any inbound integration from another host |
| `port` is a fixed literal and `listen` is called positionally | `server.js` lines 4 and 12 | Multi-instance endpoints behind a shared listener, environment-specific endpoints, backlog tuning for admission control |
| Only the built-in `http` module is imported | `server.js` line 1 | Every outbound integration, every messaging client, every identity library, every telemetry exporter |
| `req` is never dereferenced | `server.js` line 6 | Authentication, authorization, routing, versioning, content negotiation, payload validation, correlation and tracing, idempotency keys |
| The response is three unconditional statements | `server.js` lines 7–9 | Error representations, status-code variety, structured payloads, schema evolution, deprecation signalling |
| No `.on(...)` registration exists | `server.js` lines 6–14 | Protocol-error interception, load shedding via `dropRequest`, graceful drain on shutdown, connection-level integration telemetry |
| Zero `process.*` accesses and no manifest, container, or environment file | `server.js`, repository root | Configuration-driven endpoints and credentials, dependency installation, gateway or broker wiring, contract publication in a build pipeline |

Also established, by direct scan, zero comment lines, zero `process.*` accesses, zero `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`setImmediate` calls, zero conditionals, and zero `try`/`catch` blocks.

- `test.js` - 13 bytes, two bare identifier statements. Established that it introduces no integration: it imports no client, opens no socket, exposes no endpoint or callback route, declares no contract, and is never loaded by the running process. Its addition is the reason the scan surface for this section is three files rather than two, and it changed no result.

#### 6.3.6.2 Behavioural Probes Used as Evidence

All probes executed the unmodified `server.js` on one verification host running Node.js v22.23.1, with probe scripts written outside the repository checkout and the working tree verified clean before and after. Each item lists the integration fact it established.

- Baseline request probes across `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, and `HEAD` - established the invariant response contract (`200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, 14-byte body) and the invariant response header name set (`Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Content-Length`), together with the absence of `Server`, `X-Powered-By`, `Access-Control-*`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `X-RateLimit-*`, `Retry-After`, `ETag`, `Cache-Control`, and any version header.
- URI-space uniformity probe over `/`, `/healthz`, `/metrics`, `/api/v1/hello`, `/v2/hello`, `/a/b/c/d/e`, a percent-encoded path, and a 300-character query string - established byte-identical `200` responses for all eight, which is the evidence for the absence of routing, versioning, and health-endpoint differentiation.
- Credential and origin probes (`Authorization: Bearer junk`, `Origin` with `Access-Control-Request-Method`, `Accept: application/json`) - established that no authentication, CORS, or content-negotiation evaluation occurs.
- Protocol-error probes (malformed start line, unrecognised `FOOBAR` method token, 20,000-byte header field) - established the runtime-generated `400 Bad Request` and `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` responses with `Connection: close`, produced before dispatch.
- Protocol-variant probes (HTTP/1.0 request, `Expect: 100-continue`, WebSocket upgrade handshake, HTTPS handshake, two pipelined requests in one TCP segment) - established connection-close framing for HTTP/1.0, runtime-generated `100 Continue`, the absence of any upgrade path with no `101` response, the absence of TLS support, and honoured request pipelining.
- Chunked-body probe (`Transfer-Encoding: chunked` POST) - established that the complete response is emitted before any body chunk is transmitted, which is the decisive evidence that no inbound payload is ever read, parsed, or awaited.
- Burst probe of 300 requests at 50-way parallelism across distinct URIs - established 300 responses with status `200`, uniform 14-byte bodies, and no throttling, rejection, or backoff signalling of any kind.
- Reachability probe of the verification host's routable address on port 3000 versus loopback - established that only same-host callers can connect, which is the basis for the applicability determination and for the gateway-placement finding.
- Second-instance probe - established the unhandled `EADDRINUSE` `'error'` event, the stack trace on standard error, the absence of a readiness line, and exit code `1`.
- Standard-stream measurement after every probe above - established that standard output remained at exactly 41 bytes and standard error at 0 bytes, confirming that no integration exchange, successful or rejected, produces any server-side record.

## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Security Architecture Applicability Assessment

#### 6.4.1.1 Determination

**Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The repository tracks exactly three files — `server.js` (14 lines, 342 bytes), `README.md` (27 bytes, a single heading line), and `test.js` (2 lines, 13 bytes), 382 bytes in total. `server.js` performs one `require` of the Node.js built-in `http` module, binds a listener to the hard-coded literals `127.0.0.1` and `3000`, and answers every accepted request with a fixed status code, a single `Content-Type` header, and a 14-byte constant body. There is no user, no credential, no session, no token, no key, no certificate, no stored data, no third-party package, and no configuration input of any kind.

`test.js` is not a security-relevant artifact and is not part of the running system. Its 13 bytes are two bare identifier expression statements (`asdsa` and `asdasd`); it contains no credential, token, secret, key, URL, or import, it is required by nothing, and it is never loaded into the server process. Executing it directly raises `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and exits 1 (**Host observation**). Its only security significance is evidentiary rather than architectural: the commit that added it (`43ed37c`) passed through no review and no gate, which is the change-management finding recorded in 6.4.3.5.

Each of the three security domains this section is required to cover presupposes a structure the system does not possess:

- An **authentication framework** presupposes a principal to identify. `server.js` never dereferences the request object (`req.` occurs zero times), so the application cannot observe a credential, a header, an address, or a method — let alone evaluate one.
- An **authorization system** presupposes at least two distinguishable outcomes. `server.js` contains zero conditional constructs (`if`, `switch`, and ternary occurrences all zero) and exactly one status-code assignment, so no request can be refused by application logic.
- **Data protection** presupposes data. The only payload is a constant English greeting; nothing is persisted, derived, cached, or logged per request.

What the repository *does* contain is a single, real security control: the loopback bind address at `server.js` line 3. That control is **topological rather than credential-based** — it distinguishes *where* a caller is, never *who* a caller is — a characterisation already established in section 2.4.4 and section 5.4.4 and independently re-verified for this section.

Accordingly, this section does not describe an authentication framework, an authorization model, or an encryption scheme, because none exists. Instead it discharges its obligation in four ways: it presents the evidence that establishes non-applicability (6.4.1); it walks **every** mandated topic explicitly, recording a status and its evidence rather than silently omitting it (6.4.2 – 6.4.4); it documents the one control that is in force, its trust boundary, and its verified reachability (6.4.5); and it states the standard security practices that apply instead, together with the compliance position and the change conditions that would void this determination (6.4.6).

#### 6.4.1.2 Determination Criteria

A detailed security architecture is warranted when at least one of the following preconditions holds. Each was tested against the committed source rather than assumed.

| Precondition for a detailed security architecture | Evidence examined | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An identifiable principal or subject exists | Case-insensitive scan of all three tracked files for `auth`, `login`, `credential`, `password`, `token`, `jwt`, `session`, `cookie` returned zero matches; `req.` occurrences in `server.js` = 0 | Not satisfied |
| Two or more resources are distinguishable from one another | `server.js` conditional constructs = 0; status-code literals = 1 (`statusCode = 200`); eight structurally distinct URIs return byte-identical bodies (recorded in 6.3.2.3) | Not satisfied |
| Data exists with a confidentiality or integrity requirement | Sole payload is the 14-byte constant at line 9; no persistence mechanism of any kind exists (established in 6.2) | Not satisfied |
| Secret, key, or certificate material must be managed | 46 secret-management and PKI paths tested across audit groups 3 and 4 below, 0 present; `crypto`, `'https'`, and `'tls'` occurrences in `server.js` all 0 | Not satisfied |
| A trust boundary is crossed by untrusted input | Bind literal at line 3 confines reachability to the loopback interface; a request to the host's own non-loopback address was refused at connect time (requirement F-002-RQ-002) | Partially satisfied — exactly one topological boundary |
| A regulatory, contractual, or policy obligation applies | 18 compliance terms (`gdpr`, `hipaa`, `pci`, `dss`, `sox`, `ccpa`, `pii`, `personal data`, `retention`, `consent`, `redact`, `anonym`, `threat`, `cve`, `owasp`, `license`, `privacy`, `codeowners`) each returned 0 matches; no `LICENSE`, `SECURITY.md`, `PRIVACY.md`, or `COMPLIANCE.md` artifact exists | Not satisfied |

Exactly one of six preconditions is even partially satisfied, and it is satisfied by a single string literal rather than by a security mechanism. That is the basis of the determination in 6.4.1.1.

#### 6.4.1.4 Security-Relevant Source Facts

Every security-relevant construct in the only executable file, keyed to its line. The complete authentication, authorization, and data-protection behaviour of the system is contained in these eight rows.

| `server.js` line | Construct | Security consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `require('http')` — the single import | Core `http` only; `https`, `tls`, and `crypto` are never loaded, so no in-process TLS termination and no cryptographic primitive is available |
| 3 | `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` | The system's only security control; confines reachability to the loopback interface (topological, not identity-based) |
| 4 | `port = 3000` | Unprivileged port (>1024); binding requires neither root nor `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` |
| 6 | `http.createServer((req, res) => {` | One inline handler; `req` is never dereferenced, so method, URI, headers, and body are all unread |
| 7 | `res.statusCode = 200` | Unconditional success; no `401`, `403`, `404`, `405`, or `429` code path exists anywhere in the repository |
| 8 | `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')` | The only header the application sets; no HSTS, CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `Set-Cookie`, or CORS header is ever emitted |
| 9 | `res.end('Hello, World!\n')` | A 14-byte constant; no user input, data source, template, or serialiser is involved, so the injection and disclosure sink set is empty |
| 12–14 | `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` and the readiness `console.log` | Startup diagnostics only; there is no per-request logging, therefore no access log, audit trail, correlation ID, or security event record |

The two constants that constitute the entire network posture of the system:

```javascript
const hostname = '127.0.0.1';
const port = 3000;
```

A content probe over `server.js` quantifies the absences that matter for this section.

| Construct probed in `server.js` | Occurrences | Security consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `require(` | 1 | Exactly one dependency edge, to a Node built-in; zero third-party or transitive packages |
| `process.` | 0 | No environment variable, argument, or ambient configuration is read, so no secret could be injected even if one were provided |
| `crypto`, `'https'`, `'tls'` | 0, 0, 0 | No hashing, signing, encryption, or transport-security capability is present |
| `if`, `switch`, ternary | 0 | Zero decision points, therefore no policy, no branch, and no denial path can exist |
| `setHeader` | 1 | Response header surface is a single `Content-Type`; every other header is runtime-generated |
| `req.` | 0 | Request data is structurally unreachable to application code |
| `Set-Cookie`, `WWW-Authenticate` | 0, 0 | No session establishment and no authentication challenge is possible |
| `eval(`, `child_process`, `fs.`, `JSON.parse` | 0, 0, 0, 0 | No code-execution, command-execution, filesystem, or deserialisation sink |
| `setuid`, `setgid` | 0, 0 | No privilege drop; the process inherits the invoking user's identity unchanged |

The same probe set was run over `test.js` for completeness and returned zero occurrences of every construct above: its two bare identifiers reference nothing and reach nothing (**Audit result**).

#### 6.4.1.5 Attack Surface Inventory

| Surface | Reachable by | Exposure assessment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inbound TCP listener `127.0.0.1:3000` | Any process on the same host, at any privilege level | The only intentional entry point; unauthenticated by design, plaintext, and unrate-limited |
| HTTP request line, headers, and body | Same-host clients | Parsed by the runtime, then discarded unread by the application; no application-visible input surface exists |
| Response payload | Same-host clients | A 14-byte constant with no environment, version, or diagnostic detail; no information-disclosure vector |
| Standard output stream | Whoever captures the process's stdout | One 41-byte readiness line composed solely from the two bind constants; cannot carry request or credential data |
| Process control surface | Any user able to signal the process | Termination is immediate and undrained; no signal handler is registered (measured in 5.4.3). A bind failure prints a stack trace disclosing address, port, `errno`, and Node version, but no secret material (2.4.4) |
| Filesystem | The invoking user | All three tracked files are mode `100644` (non-executable, no shebang); the running process opened no regular file for writing during probing |
| Third-party dependency chain | Not applicable | Empty: no manifest, lockfile, or `node_modules` exists, so there is no transitive CVE surface and nothing for a software-composition scan to analyse |
| Git remote credential | Whoever can read the local `.git/config` | Development-time only: the configured `origin` URL embeds an access token (verified present; value deliberately never printed). It grants repository access, has no relationship to the running service, and must never be published or copied into an image or document (3.4.4, 6.3.4.4) |

Nine attack-shaped requests were issued against the unmodified source to confirm that the application-visible sink set really is empty. Every one produced the same 14-byte body, whose SHA-256 prefix `c98c24b677ef` matches both the baseline `GET /` and the value independently recorded in 6.3.2.3.

| Probe class | Payload shape | Observed result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | `GET /` | `200`, 14 bytes, `c98c24b677ef` |
| Path traversal (raw and encoded) | `/../../etc/passwd` sent with `--path-as-is`; `/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd` | `200`, byte-identical — no filesystem sink |
| Command injection | Query string carrying `; cat /etc/passwd || id` | `200`, byte-identical — no shell sink |
| Cross-site scripting | Path carrying `<script>alert(1)</script>` | `200`, byte-identical — no template or reflection sink |
| SQL injection | Query string carrying `1' OR '1'='1` | `200`, byte-identical — no query sink |
| Prototype pollution / deserialisation | `POST /login` with `{"__proto__":{"admin":true},"role":"root"}` | `200`, byte-identical — body never read or parsed |
| Identity spoofing | `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Original-URL: /admin`, `Cookie: session=forged` | `200`, byte-identical — headers never read |
| Credential presentation | HTTP Basic `admin:admin` to `/admin` | `200`, byte-identical; response header names unchanged (`Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Content-Length`) with no `WWW-Authenticate` |
| Reflection canary | `?secret=CANARY123` | Zero occurrences of the canary or of `admin`/`session` in the response body |

Two secondary findings from the same run are load-bearing for later sub-sections. First, after all nine probes the process's stdout remained at exactly 41 bytes and stderr at 0 bytes: **attack-shaped traffic generates no security event record at all**. Second, the repository tree was unchanged (`git status --porcelain` reported zero tracked-file lines before and after every probe; the directory still contained only `.git`, `README.md`, `server.js`, and `test.js`), confirming that all evidence was gathered against the committed artifact without modifying it.

#### 6.4.1.6 Evidence Conventions

This section reuses the vocabulary established in 6.3.1.3 and 6.2.1.5 so that a status word means the same thing across chapter 6.

| Status | Meaning in this section |
| --- | --- |
| **Delegated** | A mechanism exists and is exercised, but it is owned by the Node.js runtime or the host operating system rather than by repository code |
| **Absent** | The concern is meaningful for the interface that exists, but nothing implements it at any layer |
| **Not applicable** | The concern presupposes a structure the system does not have |

Every factual claim carries one of the four provenance labels defined in 6.1.1.3.

| Provenance label | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Source fact** | A property verifiable by reading a tracked file at a cited line |
| **Audit result** | The outcome of an existence or content probe over the repository tree |
| **Runtime default** | Behaviour supplied by Node.js because `server.js` configures nothing |
| **Host observation** | A value measured by executing the unmodified source on one verification host |

No number or behaviour in this section may be read as a commitment. The repository declares no security policy, no service level, no threat model, and no compliance obligation, so nothing here constitutes a control guarantee. All runtime evidence was produced on a single verification host running **Node.js v22.23.1** — the same runtime version used elsewhere in this specification — against **HEAD `43ed37c`** on branch `2907_01` with a clean working tree. `server.js` is byte-identical at HEAD and at its introducing commit `06492d7` (blob `320a75a`), so every source fact recorded here applies unchanged to both revisions.

#### 6.4.1.7 Standard Security Practices Applied Instead

Because no security architecture exists to document, the operative question becomes which standard practices are already satisfied, which are inherited from the platform, and which must be supplied by whoever runs or extends the system. The four groups below are summarised here and specified with full control matrices in 6.4.6.

| Practice group | Position in this system |
| --- | --- |
| Properties the committed code already satisfies | Zero third-party dependencies (no supply-chain or transitive-CVE surface); no secret, key, or certificate committed to version control; a loopback-only default bind; a constant response with no data or version disclosure; no write, exec, or deserialisation sink |
| Protections delegated to the platform | HTTP/1.1 parser strictness, malformed-request rejection (`400`), header-size capping at 16,384 bytes with `431` rejection, and a 5-second keep-alive reclamation window — all Node.js defaults, none configured by the repository |
| Practices the operating environment must supply | A patched, supported runtime (no version is pinned anywhere); a least-privilege, non-root service account; host-level network filtering; process supervision and restart; capture and retention of the single stdout line |
| Practices mandatory before any exposure change | Section 5.4.4 records that exposure here is a step function of one source token: changing the line 3 literal to a wildcard would remove the only control that exists. An authentication boundary and TLS must therefore be introduced in the *same* change that makes the service network-reachable, never afterwards |

### 6.4.2 Authentication Framework

There is no authentication framework in this system, at any layer. That is a verified absence rather than an inference: no authentication artifact exists in the repository (audit groups 1 and 2 of 6.4.1.3, 33 paths tested, zero present), the application never reads the request object, and a request that presented HTTP Basic credentials and a Bearer token received exactly the same response as an anonymous one.

The five topics this sub-section is required to cover are each addressed explicitly below, with a status word from 6.4.1.6 and the evidence that establishes it. The single control actually in force — the loopback bind — is an authentication *substitute* only in the weakest sense: it constrains *where* a caller may be, never *who* the caller is, and it grants every same-host process identical unauthenticated access regardless of operating-system user or privilege level (a characterisation established in 6.3.2.2 and re-verified here).

The complete request path, showing that no credential is ever observed:

```javascript
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.statusCode = 200;
```

#### 6.4.2.1 Identity Management

**Status: Absent** for inbound principals; **Not applicable** for outbound service identity.

There is no identity store, no directory integration, no identity provider configuration, and no user record of any kind. The audit in 6.4.1.3 tested 22 identity-artifact paths — including `.htpasswd`, `users.json`, `saml`, `oauth.json`, `oidc.json`, `jwks.json`, `keycloak.json`, `realm.json`, `passport`, and `.well-known` — and found none present (**Audit result**). No `.well-known` document is served, so the system publishes no identity metadata either (**Audit result**, corroborating 6.3.2.2).

The mechanical reason no identity can exist is in the source: `req.` occurs zero times in `server.js`, so the handler cannot inspect an `Authorization` header, a cookie, a client certificate, a peer address, or even the HTTP method (**Source fact**, lines 6–10; requirement F-001-RQ-002). The operating system's TCP stack does not convey a peer user identity to a TCP listener, and the application makes no attempt to obtain one — no peer-credential mechanism, no reverse lookup, no allow-list. The effective inbound identity model is therefore a **single implicit anonymous principal whose population is every process on the host**.

Outbound identity is not applicable for a different reason: the system makes no outbound call at all, so it holds no service account, API key, client credential, or workload identity toward any counterparty (established in 6.3.1 and 3.4). The one credential present anywhere in the checkout is the access token embedded in the Git remote URL, which is a development-time repository credential outside the runtime trust boundary; it is never read by the running service, and its value is deliberately not reproduced in this specification (3.4.4, 6.3.4.4).

The service's own process identity is also unmanaged by the repository: `setuid` and `setgid` occurrences in `server.js` are zero, so the process inherits the invoking user's identity and capability set verbatim (**Source fact**). On the verification host the launched process was measured at `Uid 0`, `Gid 0`, full effective capabilities, `NoNewPrivs 0`, and `Seccomp 0` (**Host observation**). Port `3000` is unprivileged, so elevated identity is not required to bind; the elevated posture observed is a property of the verification environment, and no repository artifact — `Dockerfile` `USER`, systemd `User=`, or Kubernetes `securityContext`, all audited absent — constrains it.

#### 6.4.2.2 Multi-Factor Authentication

**Status: Not applicable.**

Multi-factor authentication is a second factor conditioned on the successful evaluation of a first. No first factor exists, so there is nothing to which a second could be added. Three independent facts foreclose it:

- No MFA artifact or dependency exists — no TOTP, HOTP, WebAuthn, FIDO, SMS, or push-approval configuration appears among the 224 audited paths, and there is no dependency manifest through which such a library could be introduced (**Audit result**).
- One-time-password and WebAuthn schemes require HMAC or signature verification. `server.js` never imports `crypto`, so the primitives are not even loaded into the process (**Source fact**, line 1).
- Step-up authentication requires a conditional branch. `server.js` contains zero `if`, `switch`, and ternary constructs, so no request can be routed down a challenge path (**Source fact**).

#### 6.4.2.3 Session Management

**Status: Absent** at the application layer; a transport-level connection-reuse window is **Delegated** to the runtime.

No session exists and none can be created. `Set-Cookie` occurrences in `server.js` are zero, and across every probe in this section and in 6.3.2.1 the response header name set never varied from `Content-Type`, `Date`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, and `Content-Length` — no cookie was ever emitted (**Source fact** plus **Host observation**). No session store artifact exists among the 11 paths of audit group 2, and the application holds no in-memory session map: it retains no data across requests at all (requirement F-001-RQ-003).

A distinction matters here and is easy to get wrong. The `Connection: keep-alive` and `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` headers observed on every response are a **transport-level connection-reuse window supplied by the Node.js runtime** with a 5,000 ms idle default that `server.js` does not configure (**Runtime default**, catalogued authoritatively in 5.2.6). That window carries no identifier, no principal, and no state; it reclaims an idle TCP connection and nothing more. It is not a session and confers no continuity of identity.

Consequently every session-security concern is vacuous rather than unaddressed: there is no session identifier to fix or hijack, no idle or absolute timeout policy to set, no concurrent-session limit, no logout or invalidation path, and no CSRF exposure, because no cookie is set and no state-changing operation exists.

#### 6.4.2.4 Token Handling

**Status: Absent.**

Tokens presented by a caller are neither parsed nor rejected — they are simply never read. A request carrying `Authorization: Bearer totally-invalid` to `/admin`, and a separate request carrying HTTP Basic `admin:admin`, both received the ordinary `200` response with a byte-identical 14-byte body (**Host observation**; the same result is recorded independently in 6.3.2.2). A reflection canary confirmed that no supplied value re-appears in the response: the body contained zero occurrences of the canary string or of `admin` and `session` (**Host observation**).

Nothing exists on the issuing side either. There is no JWT, PASETO, opaque-token, or API-key implementation; no JWKS endpoint or key file; no signing or verification key; and no `crypto` import through which a signature could be produced or checked (**Source fact** plus **Audit result**, groups 2 and 4). Because no token is minted or consumed, the entire token lifecycle is vacuous: no expiry, no refresh, no rotation, no revocation list, no audience or issuer validation, and no replay protection.

The absence of a challenge is structural rather than incidental. `WWW-Authenticate` occurrences are zero, `server.js` assigns exactly one status code, and the only rejection codes the system can produce — `400` and `431` — are generated by the runtime's parser before the handler is entered (6.3.2.2, 5.4.3). **A `401 Unauthorized` response is therefore impossible to produce with the code as committed.**

#### 6.4.2.5 Password Policies

**Status: Not applicable.**

There is no credential store, no registration or login flow, and no password field anywhere in the repository — the keyword scan for `password`, `credential`, and `login` over all three tracked files returned zero matches (**Audit result**). There is likewise no password hashing capability: `bcrypt`, `argon2`, and `scrypt` cannot be present because no dependency manifest exists, and the built-in `crypto` module — which would supply PBKDF2 or `scrypt` — is never imported (**Source fact**).

A password policy is a set of rules attached to a credential lifecycle. With no credential, every element of such a policy is vacuous: complexity and length rules, history and reuse restrictions, rotation intervals, breach-list screening, and reset flows all have no subject. Account lockout deserves a specific note because it is often treated as a compensating control: it is not merely unimplemented but unachievable here, since there is no failed-authentication event to count, no rate limiting of any kind, and no denial path — a 300-request burst at 50-way parallelism returned 300 `200` responses with zero `429`s (6.3.2.4).

#### 6.4.2.6 Authentication Flow

Diagram 6.4-A traces what actually happens to a request, including the runtime-owned rejection paths that do exist and the authentication stages that do not. Every solid edge is a verified path; the dashed edge marks the transition that no code performs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Caller["Same-host client process<br/>any OS user, any privilege level"] --> Attempt{"TCP connect attempt<br/>to 127.0.0.1:3000"}
    Attempt -->|"source outside loopback interface"| Refused["Connection refused by host TCP/IP stack<br/>Host observation: connect to the host's<br/>own non-loopback address failed"]
    Attempt -->|"source on loopback interface"| Parser["Node.js HTTP/1.1 parser<br/>Runtime default - no application code"]
    Parser -->|"malformed request line or headers"| Reject400["400 Bad Request<br/>Connection: close<br/>handler never entered"]
    Parser -->|"header block over 16384 bytes"| Reject431["431 Request Header Fields Too Large<br/>Connection: close<br/>handler never entered"]
    Parser -->|"well-formed request"| Handler["Application handler<br/>server.js lines 6-10"]
    Handler --> Ignore["req is never dereferenced<br/>Authorization, Cookie, method, URI all unread"]
    Ignore --> Reply["statusCode = 200<br/>Content-Type: text/plain<br/>14-byte constant body"]
    Reply --> Delivered["Identical response delivered<br/>to every caller, credentialled or not"]
    Delivered --> NoRecord["No security event recorded<br/>stdout invariant at 41 bytes"]

    subgraph Missing["Authentication stages with no artifact in the repository"]
        direction TB
        Extract["Credential extraction from request"] --> Lookup["Identity store or IdP lookup"]
        Lookup --> Verify["First-factor verification"]
        Verify --> Factor2["Second-factor or step-up challenge"]
        Factor2 --> Issue["Session or token issuance"]
        Issue --> Deny["401 Unauthorized with WWW-Authenticate"]
    end

    Handler -.->|"no code path reaches any of these stages"| Extract
```

**Diagram 6.4-A — Authentication flow as implemented. The only gate is topological and is enforced by the host network stack before the runtime is involved; the only rejections are protocol-level and runtime-owned; the application itself has no authentication stage at all.**

| Multi-factor authentication | Not applicable | Source fact | No first factor exists; `crypto` never imported; 0 conditionals for a step-up branch |
| Session establishment and lifecycle | Absent | Source fact | `Set-Cookie` = 0; no session store artifact; no state retained across requests |
| Connection reuse window | Delegated | Runtime default | `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` on every response; 5,000 ms idle default not set by the repository |
| Bearer, Basic, and API-key handling | Absent | Host observation | `Authorization: Bearer …` and Basic `admin:admin` both answered with the identical 14-byte `200` |
| Token issuance, expiry, rotation, revocation | Absent | Source fact | No token implementation, no signing key, no `crypto` import |
| Mutual TLS and client certificates | Not applicable | Audit result | Plaintext listener only; 22 PKI paths tested, 0 present; `tls` never imported |
| Federated SSO — OAuth 2.0, OIDC, SAML | Absent | Audit result | No IdP configuration, client secret, or metadata document in 224 audited paths |

| Authentication challenge — `401` plus `WWW-Authenticate` | Not applicable | Source fact | One status-code literal (`200`); `WWW-Authenticate` = 0; only `400` and `431` exist, both runtime-generated |
