#### 6.4.2.8 Standard Practices If Authentication Is Introduced

Section 5.4.4 records the governing risk for this system: exposure is a **step function of one source token**. As committed, the service is unreachable from off-host; substituting a wildcard for the line 3 literal would make it fully reachable with no authentication, no authorization, no transport security, and no rate limiting to fall back on. The practices below are therefore stated as change conditions, not as descriptions of existing behaviour.

| Practice | Rationale grounded in this system |
| --- | --- |
| Introduce an authentication boundary in the *same* change that widens the bind address | The loopback literal is the only control; removing it without a replacement leaves the service with none at all (5.4.4, ADR-003 and 5.3.4) |
| Introduce TLS in that same change | The process imports neither `https` nor `tls`; an HTTPS request to port 3000 fails during the TLS handshake, so any credential sent today would traverse the network in plaintext (6.4.4) |
| Add a denial path before adding a credential check | With zero conditionals and a single `200` literal, the codebase currently has no mechanism to refuse a request; a check without a refusal path is not a control |
| Add per-request security logging alongside the first credential check | The single `console.log` fires once at bind time, so authentication successes and failures would otherwise be unobservable (5.4.2, 6.2.4.4) |
| Add rate limiting together with any credential check | No limiter exists at any layer, so an added credential check would be brute-forceable without restraint (6.3.2.4) |
| Keep credentials and keys out of the source tree | No secret is committed today, and the source reads no environment variable (`process.` = 0), so a secret-consumption path would have to be designed deliberately rather than retrofitted casually |

### 6.4.3 Authorization System

There is no authorization system in this system, and unlike authentication — which is *absent* from an interface where it would be meaningful — most authorization concerns here are **not applicable**, because they presuppose structures the system does not have: a subject to authorize, a resource to protect, and a policy to evaluate. `server.js` contains **zero conditional constructs** and exactly one status-code literal, so the codebase is mechanically incapable of reaching two different outcomes for two different callers (**Source fact**; the same finding is recorded in 6.3.2.3).

One enforcement point nevertheless exists, and it is worth naming precisely because it is the entire access-control story of the system: the **host TCP/IP stack**, acting on the loopback bind address at `server.js` line 3. It decides admission, it does so before any application code runs, and its granularity is binary — any process able to open a socket on the host's loopback interface is served identically (6.2.4.5).

#### 6.4.3.1 Role-Based Access Control

**Status: Not applicable.**

No role exists, no role is assigned, and no artifact defines one. Audit group 5 of 6.4.1.3 tested 20 authorization and policy-as-code paths — `rbac.yaml`, `roles.yaml`, `roles.json`, `permissions.json`, `acl.json`, `casbin_model.conf`, `casbin_policy.csv`, `policy.rego`, `authz.rego`, `opa/`, `cedar.json`, `oso.polar`, `policy/`, `authz/`, `guards/`, `middleware/`, and others — and found none present (**Audit result**). The keyword scan over all three tracked files for `role`, `permission`, `acl`, and `auth` returned zero matches (**Audit result**).

RBAC requires a subject before it requires a role, and 6.4.2.1 establishes that no subject can be observed: the request object is never dereferenced. There is also no administrative or privileged surface to which an elevated role could apply — a property already recorded in 5.4.4 — because every URI resolves to the same handler and the same response.

#### 6.4.3.2 Permission Management

**Status: Not applicable.**

There is no permission catalogue, no scope or claim vocabulary, no grant or revoke operation, no ownership or delegation model, and no administrative endpoint through which any of these could be manipulated. Two structural facts make this permanent rather than incidental for the code as committed:

- **No state.** A permission assignment must be stored somewhere. The system has no persistence of any kind — no database, file store, cache, or in-memory registry — as established comprehensively in 6.2, so there is nowhere for a grant to live (**Audit result**).
- **No mutation surface.** Every request, regardless of method, produces the same read-only constant response; `DELETE` and `TRACE` requests both returned `200` with the standard body (**Host observation**). There is no write path through which a permission change could be requested.

Because no permission exists, the operations that surround permission management are equally vacuous: there is no least-privilege review, no separation-of-duties constraint, no access recertification, and no privileged-access workflow.

#### 6.4.3.3 Resource Authorization

**Status: Not applicable.**

The system exposes no resource model. Eight structurally distinct URIs — including `/`, `/healthz`, `/metrics`, `/api/v1/hello`, a deep path, a percent-encoded path, and a long query string — returned byte-identical bodies with the same SHA-256 (recorded in 6.3.2.3), and the nine attack-shaped probes in 6.4.1.5, including raw and percent-encoded path traversal, produced exactly the same 14-byte body (**Host observation**). Paths that conventionally carry privileged semantics, such as `/metrics` and `/admin`, receive no special treatment whatsoever.

Method-level authorization is likewise absent: `GET`, `POST`, `DELETE`, and `TRACE` all returned `200`, so there is no allow-list and no `405 Method Not Allowed` path anywhere in the system (**Host observation**). Object-level, row-level, field-level, and tenant-level authorization are all not applicable for the same underlying reason — there is no object, row, field, or tenant. The response is a constant, not a projection of any resource.

#### 6.4.3.4 Policy Enforcement Points

**Status: Delegated** — exactly one enforcement point exists, and it lives outside the application.

Mapping the system onto the conventional policy architecture makes the shape of the gap explicit.

| Policy component | Where it exists in this system | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Policy enforcement point | The host TCP/IP stack, refusing connections whose source is not on the loopback interface, before any application code executes | Source fact plus Host observation |
| Policy decision point | None — `server.js` has zero conditionals, so no decision is ever computed | Source fact |
| Policy administration point | None — no policy artifact exists among the 224 audited paths, and the source reads no configuration (`process.` = 0) | Audit result |
| Policy information point | None — no attribute about subject, resource, or environment is ever retrieved; `req.` = 0 | Source fact |

Within the application there is no middleware chain, no guard, no filter, no interceptor, and no decorator: the system uses no web framework, and `http.createServer` receives exactly one inline handler that runs unconditionally (**Source fact**, lines 6–10; corroborated by 6.3.2.3). It is worth distinguishing the runtime's protocol-level rejections — `400 Bad Request` for a malformed request and `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` for a header block exceeding the 16,384-byte default — from authorization. Those are parser outcomes produced before the handler is entered (5.4.3); they evaluate syntax, not entitlement, and they cannot be configured or extended by the repository.

The effective policy in force, stated exactly, is: **"Permit every request, from the loopback interface only."** It is enforced topologically, at connection-admission time, by a component the repository does not own.

#### 6.4.3.5 Audit Logging

**Status: Absent** for runtime security auditing; **present but unenforced** for source-change auditing.

The complete logging implementation is a single `console.log` at line 13, which fires once when the listener binds and interpolates only the two bind constants (**Source fact**; requirement F-004-RQ-002). There is no per-request logging (requirement F-004-RQ-003), therefore no access log, no authentication or authorization event record, no correlation identifier, and no security alerting.

This was verified adversarially rather than assumed. After the nine attack-shaped probes of 6.4.1.5 — traversal, injection, spoofed identity headers, and presented credentials among them — the process's **stdout remained at exactly 41 bytes and its stderr at 0 bytes**, and the process's open file descriptors comprised only event-loop anonymous inodes, pipes, and `/dev/null`, with no regular file opened for writing (**Host observation**). Attack traffic therefore leaves no trace of any kind. Audit group 11 of 6.4.1.3 confirms there is no log-shipping or audit infrastructure to compensate: 13 paths tested — `auditd.rules`, `audit.log`, `rsyslog.conf`, `fluentd.conf`, `fluent-bit.conf`, `filebeat.yml`, `vector.toml`, `promtail.yaml`, `logs/` and others — none present (**Audit result**). The conclusion recorded in 6.2.4.4 holds without qualification: **the system is not auditable at runtime.**

Source-change auditing is a different matter and does exist, in the minimal form Git provides. The history contains three commits by a single author of record — `241598b` (2026-07-29), `06492d7` (2026-07-29), and `43ed37c` (2026-07-30) — each carrying a `gpgsig` header, with the committer identity recorded on all three as GitHub's no-reply address, the signature shape produced by a server-side web flow. `git verify-commit HEAD` reports a signature made with RSA key `B5690EEEBB952194` and cannot check it because the public key is absent from this checkout's keyring (**Audit result**). Nothing in the repository requires or enforces that property: there is no `CODEOWNERS` file, no review policy artifact, no branch-protection descriptor, no tag, and `.git/hooks` contains only `*.sample` templates. Release provenance is entirely absent — no SBOM, signature bundle, or attestation exists among the 15 supply-chain paths audited — a point also recorded in 2.4.4 for feature F-005.

The gap between *recorded* and *enforced* is no longer hypothetical, and the most recent commit demonstrates it concretely. Commit `43ed37c` added a new root-level file, `test.js`, whose 13 bytes are two undefined bare identifiers: `node --check test.js` reports valid syntax and exits 0, but executing the file raises `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and exits 1 (**Host observation**). No review approval, status check, test run, lint pass, or hook stood between that change and the branch head — because none exists to stand there. The change is fully attributed and signed, and it was nevertheless **admitted without any verification of correctness**. That is the exact meaning of *present but unenforced*: Git records who changed what and when, and nothing whatsoever constrains what may be recorded. The commit is harmless to the running service only because `server.js` does not require `test.js` and the documented start procedure invokes `node server.js` alone (3.6.5); a change of the same governance quality to `server.js` would have reached the branch head just as freely.

| Audit requirement | Status | Provenance | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Authentication event log | Not applicable | Source fact | No authentication occurs, so no event exists to record |
| Authorization decision log | Not applicable | Source fact | No decision is computed; zero conditionals |
| Request or access log | Absent | Host observation | stdout invariant at 41 bytes and stderr at 0 across all probe traffic |
| Administrative action log | Not applicable | Source fact | No administrative surface exists |
| Data access and change history | Not applicable | Audit result | No data store of any kind exists (6.2) |
| Security alerting and detection | Absent | Audit result | No monitoring, SIEM, or alerting artifact in 224 audited paths |
| Log integrity and tamper protection | Not applicable | Source fact | The only log line is emitted to stdout and never persisted by the application |
| Log retention policy | Not applicable | Audit result | Retention is effectively zero by construction (6.2.4.1); no policy artifact exists |
| Source-change audit trail | Present, unenforced | Audit result | Three-commit Git history, each commit signed server-side and attributed to one author; no `CODEOWNERS`, review policy, branch-protection descriptor, or enforcing hook |
| Change verification and segregation of duties | Absent | Audit result and Host observation | `43ed37c` added `test.js` — a file that exits 1 with `ReferenceError` when executed — with no review, status check, or gate of any kind between commit and branch head |
| Release provenance and SBOM | Absent | Audit result | 15 supply-chain and provenance paths tested, 0 present |

#### 6.4.3.6 Authorization Decision Flow

Diagram 6.4-B traces the authorization path. Every solid edge is a verified path; the single dashed edge marks the policy consultation that no code performs. Note that the only decision in the entire diagram is made before the process is reached.

```mermaid
flowchart LR

    PEP -->|"source not on loopback interface"| Blocked["Connection never established<br/>Host observation: connect refused<br/>process never involved"]
    PEP -->|"source on loopback interface"| Handler["Application handler<br/>server.js lines 6-10"]
    Handler --> NoEval["No subject resolution<br/>No resource identification<br/>No policy evaluation<br/>Zero conditionals in source"]
    NoEval --> Grant["Unconditional grant<br/>statusCode = 200"]
    Grant --> Uniform["Byte-identical 14-byte response<br/>for every URI, method and caller"]
    Uniform --> NoTrace["No decision record produced<br/>stdout invariant at 41 bytes"]

    subgraph MissingAuthz["Authorization components with no artifact in the repository"]
        direction TB
        PDP["Policy decision point"] --> Store["Role and policy definition store"]
        Store --> Catalogue["Permission and scope catalogue"]
        Catalogue --> PerResource["Per-URI, per-method and per-object checks"]
        PerResource --> DenyPath["403 Forbidden denial path"]
        DenyPath --> AuditRec["Authorization decision audit record"]
    end

    Handler -.->|"no code path consults a policy"| PDP
```

**Diagram 6.4-B — Authorization flow as implemented. Admission is decided topologically by the host network stack; inside the process the grant is unconditional, uniform, and unrecorded. Every component in the lower group is absent from the repository.**

#### 6.4.3.8 Effective Policy and Change Conditions

| Item | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| Effective policy in force | Permit every request, from the loopback interface only |
| Policy granularity | Binary and topological — any process able to open a loopback socket is served identically, regardless of operating-system user or privilege (6.2.4.5) |
| Policy owner | The host operating system's network stack; the repository owns only the address literal at `server.js` line 3 |
| Policy expression | One string constant; no policy language, file, or decision logic exists |
| Condition that voids this assessment | Any change that widens the bind address, introduces a second response path, or adds a data source creates a subject or resource distinction and therefore requires a genuine authorization model, a denial path, and decision auditing to be introduced in the same change |
| Change-admission posture | Unenforced: nothing gates a commit to the branch head, as demonstrated by `43ed37c` (6.4.3.5). Any control introduced above must be paired with an enforcement mechanism in version control, or it can be removed as freely as it was added |

### 6.4.4 Data Protection

Data protection divides cleanly in this system. Everything concerning data *at rest* and data *classification* is **not applicable**, because the system holds no data: it reads nothing from the request, persists nothing, caches nothing, and returns a constant. Everything concerning data *in transit* is **Absent** and is a genuine gap: the listener speaks plaintext HTTP/1.1, and neither the `https` nor the `tls` module is ever loaded. The gap is currently contained — not mitigated — by the loopback bind, which keeps the plaintext channel inside a single host.

#### 6.4.4.1 Data Classification and Inventory

The complete data inventory of the system is seven rows long, and only one row involves a secret — a development-time repository credential that the running service never touches.

| Data element | Origin | Classification | Protection status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Response body, 14 bytes | Source literal at `server.js` line 9 | Public, non-sensitive | None required; the value is published in this specification |
| Readiness log line, 41 bytes | `console.log` at line 13 | Internal diagnostic | Plaintext on stdout; interpolates only the two bind constants |
| Bind constants `127.0.0.1` and `3000` | Source literals at lines 3–4 | Public configuration | Committed in version control by design; no secret character |
| Inbound request — method, URI, headers, body | Client | Unclassified; never enters the application | Discarded by the runtime after parsing; `req.` = 0, so it cannot be stored, logged, or echoed |
| Bind-failure stack trace | Node.js runtime on `EADDRINUSE` | Internal diagnostic | Plaintext on stderr; discloses address, port, `errno`, and Node version, but no secret material (2.4.4) |
| Git remote access token | Local `.git/config` in a developer environment | Secret — repository credential | Outside the runtime trust boundary; never read by the service; must never be published or copied into an image or document. Its value is deliberately not reproduced anywhere in this specification |
| Persisted application data | Does not exist | Not applicable | Nothing is written at runtime; the only durable artifacts are the three tracked files, none of which holds data — `server.js` is the application, `README.md` a single heading line, and `test.js` 13 bytes of placeholder text with no schema, fixture, or seed content |

Two consequences follow and are worth stating plainly. First, **no personal, confidential, or regulated data can enter the system**, because the sole ingress path discards the request unread — a `POST` carrying a JSON body was verified to be ignored entirely, and the complete response was observed to be emitted before any chunked body was even transmitted (6.3.2.1, 6.2.4.3). Second, **no data can leave it**, because the response is a compile-time constant and the reflection canary probe found zero occurrences of any supplied value in the body (**Host observation**, 6.4.1.5).

#### 6.4.4.2 Encryption Standards

| Data state | Mechanism in force | Status | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| In transit, client to service | None — plaintext HTTP/1.1 over TCP | Absent | Source fact and Host observation |
| In transit, service to any counterparty | None needed — the system makes no outbound call | Not applicable | Audit result |
| At rest, application data | None needed — no data is written at runtime | Not applicable | Audit result |
| At rest, source artifacts | Git object store, unencrypted; all three tracked files mode `100644`; no secret content in any of them | Not applicable | Audit result |
| In use, process memory | No encryption, enclave, or memory-protection mechanism | Not applicable | Source fact |
| Hashing, signing, MAC | None — `crypto` is never imported | Not applicable | Source fact |

The absence of transport encryption is established three ways rather than assumed. The single import at line 1 is core `http`; occurrences of `'https'` and `'tls'` in `server.js` are both zero (**Source fact**). An HTTPS request to `https://127.0.0.1:3000/` fails during the TLS handshake with an OpenSSL version-mismatch error and an HTTP status of `000` — the listener is not speaking TLS at all (**Host observation**, independently recorded in 6.3.2.1). And no certificate or key material exists to terminate TLS with: audit group 4 tested 22 PKI paths and found none (**Audit result**).

Because no TLS exists, the attributes that would normally be specified here have no subject: there is no protocol version floor, no cipher suite list, no curve or key-size selection, no certificate authority or validity window, no OCSP or stapling configuration, and no HSTS policy. The one cryptographic operation associated with the project is Git commit signing (6.4.3.5), which is a version-control lifecycle property and not a runtime control.

#### 6.4.4.3 Key Management

**Status: Not applicable — there is no key, and no path by which one could be supplied.**

Audit groups 3 and 4 together tested 46 secret-management and PKI paths — the entire `.env` family, `secrets/`, `credentials/`, `vault.hcl`, `.vault-token`, `.sops.yaml`, `.age-key`, `sealed-secrets.yaml`, `.gitleaks.toml`, `.secrets.baseline`, `.netrc`, `.pgpass`, `serviceAccount.json`, `certs/`, `keys/`, `*.pem`, `keystore.jks`, `identity.p12`, `id_rsa`, `cosign.key` and more — and found **zero present** (**Audit result**). No key management service, HSM, or secrets manager is referenced anywhere.

A stronger fact reinforces this: `process.` occurrences in `server.js` are zero, so the application reads no environment variable, command-line argument, or configuration file. **Even a correctly injected secret could not be consumed by this code** (**Source fact**; the same observation appears in 3.4). Consequently every key-management activity is vacuous — generation, distribution, storage, access control, rotation, escrow, revocation, and destruction all lack a subject. Requirement F-002-RQ-003 records the same structural point from the configuration side: there is no runtime override path of any kind.

The single credential associated with the project is the access token embedded in the local Git remote URL. Its presence was verified for this section without ever printing it; it grants repository access only, has no relationship to the running service, which requires no credential to operate, and it must be excluded from images, logs, and documentation (3.4.4, 6.3.4.4).

#### 6.4.4.4 Data Masking Rules

**Status: Not applicable — there is nothing to mask.**

Masking, redaction, tokenisation, pseudonymisation, and field-level encryption all presuppose a sensitive value flowing through a channel. Every candidate channel here is provably constant:

- **Response body.** A 14-byte literal, identical for every caller and every payload shape across all probes (**Host observation**).
- **Application log.** The only log statement interpolates the two bind constants and nothing else, and it executes once at bind time (requirements F-004-RQ-002 and F-004-RQ-003). Stdout remained at exactly 41 bytes after nine attack-shaped requests, including ones carrying credentials and a canary string (**Host observation**).
- **Reflection.** The response body contained zero occurrences of the canary value, of `admin`, or of `session` (**Host observation**), so no supplied value can be echoed back.

Two disclosure surfaces do exist and are documented rather than masked. The bind-failure stack trace on stderr reveals the bind address, port, `errno`, and Node.js version — infrastructure detail, no secret material (2.4.4, 5.4.3). And on the success path the response deliberately omits both `Server` and `X-Powered-By`, so the runtime version is *not* disclosed to callers; that suppression is a Node.js default rather than a repository choice (**Runtime default**, corroborated by the invariant header-name set in 6.3.2.1).

#### 6.4.4.5 Secure Communication

| Communication control | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TLS termination in process | Absent | `https` and `tls` never imported; HTTPS request fails at handshake with status `000` |
| HSTS policy | Absent | Only one header is set by the application; HSTS would also be moot without TLS |
| Security response headers — CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy` | Absent | `setHeader` occurrences = 1, setting `Content-Type` only |
| Version-disclosure headers — `Server`, `X-Powered-By` | Delegated, favourable | Never emitted; the header-name set was invariant across 300 probe requests (6.3.2.1) |
| CORS policy | Absent | A preflight-shaped `OPTIONS` with `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method` produced zero `Access-Control-*` headers |
| Protocol upgrade — HTTP/2, h2c, WebSocket | Not applicable | A complete WebSocket handshake is answered with the ordinary 163-byte `200`; no `101` is ever emitted |
| Interim responses — `Expect: 100-continue` | Delegated | The runtime auto-generates `100 Continue`; no `checkContinue` listener is registered |
| Connection and header limits | Delegated | `requestTimeout` 300,000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60,000 ms, `keepAliveTimeout` 5,000 ms, `maxHeaderSize` 16,384 bytes, `maxRequestsPerSocket` 0 — all Node.js defaults, none set by the repository (5.2.6) |
| Address-family exposure | Delegated, favourable | One IPv4 loopback listener; `/proc/net/tcp6` contained zero entries for port 3000 (**Host observation**) |
| Network confinement | Delegated | Host TCP/IP stack enforcing the line 3 literal; a connect attempt to the host's non-loopback address was refused |

The honest summary is that the channel is unprotected but also unreachable from outside the host. The plaintext exposure window is therefore the loopback interface, where an attacker would already need local code execution — and any such attacker could read the process memory directly. This is containment by topology, and it evaporates the moment the bind literal changes.

#### 6.4.4.6 Compliance Controls

The repository names **no regulatory regime and declares no data-governance policy**. A scan of all three tracked files for 18 compliance terms — `gdpr`, `hipaa`, `pci`, `dss`, `sox`, `ccpa`, `pii`, `personal data`, `retention`, `consent`, `redact`, `anonym`, `threat`, `cve`, `owasp`, `license`, `privacy`, `codeowners` — returned **zero matches for every term** (**Audit result**). Audit group 8 confirms no governance artifact exists: no `SECURITY.md`, `security.txt`, `PRIVACY.md`, `COMPLIANCE.md`, `THREATMODEL.md`, `CODEOWNERS`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `LICENSE`, or `NOTICE` (**Audit result**).

| Regime or framework | Applicability to this system | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GDPR and UK GDPR | Not applicable | No personal data can be collected — the request is never read, no cookie is set, and nothing is stored (6.2.4.3). No data-subject right, consent record, lawful basis, or processing register has a subject |
| HIPAA | Not applicable | No protected health information enters or leaves; there is no data store or transmission of records |
| PCI DSS | Not applicable | No cardholder data, payment path, or account data exists; there is no data channel to segment |
| SOX | Not applicable | The system produces no financial record and participates in no reporting process |
| CCPA and CPRA | Not applicable | No consumer personal information is collected, sold, or shared |
| SOC 2 | Cannot be evidenced | The system implements no logical-access, change-management, or monitoring control that an examination could test; no policy artifact exists, and the commit that added `test.js` demonstrates that changes reach the branch head with no review or gate (6.4.3.5) |
| ISO/IEC 27001 | Cannot be evidenced | No ISMS artifact, risk register, or control statement exists in the repository |
| OWASP ASVS or similar verification standard | Not claimed | No verification artifact, test suite, or security requirement document exists — the root-level `test.js` contains no test and no assertion (6.6.1) |
| Software licensing and redistribution | Obligation unmet | No `LICENSE` file accompanies the artifact, so no redistribution or usage rights are granted to a recipient (2.4.4, feature F-005) |
| Cryptographic export controls | Not applicable | The system implements and ships no cryptography |
| Data retention and erasure obligations | Not applicable | Retention is effectively zero by construction — no request datum, derived datum, or log survives the process (6.2.4.1) |
| Cross-border transfer rules | Not applicable | No data leaves the host; there is no egress interface at all (5.1.3, 6.3.1) |

The disciplined reading is that these regimes are inapplicable because their **preconditions are absent**, not because controls satisfy them. Any change that introduces data collection, persistence, or network exposure would make several of them applicable immediately, and the repository contains no policy, artifact, or control on which such a change could build.

#### 6.4.4.7 Data Lifecycle Protection Status

Diagram 6.4-D shows the protection status of every stage a datum could pass through. The ingress stage is the only one with a real gap; the remaining stages are empty by construction.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Ingress["Ingress path - client to process"]
        direction TB
        Wire["HTTP/1.1 over plaintext TCP<br/>No TLS - handshake attempt fails<br/>Status: Absent"] --> Parsed["Runtime parses request line and headers<br/>Application never receives them"]
    end
    subgraph Processing["Processing inside the single process"]
        direction TB
        NoInput["No request attribute is read<br/>req dereference count is 0"] --> Constant["Response composed from a<br/>14-byte source literal at line 9"]
    end
    subgraph Egress["Egress path - process to client"]
        direction TB
        Body["14-byte public constant<br/>No version or environment detail"] --> Headers["One application header only<br/>No HSTS, CSP or CORS headers"]
    end
    subgraph Diagnostics["Diagnostic output"]
        direction TB
        Startup["One 41-byte readiness line on stdout<br/>Only the two bind constants"] --> FailTrace["Bind failure trace on stderr<br/>Address, port, errno, Node version<br/>No secret material"]
    end
    subgraph AtRest["Data at rest"]
        direction TB
        NoStore["Nothing is written at runtime<br/>No database, file, cache or queue"] --> Repo["Only durable artifacts are three tracked<br/>files in Git, unencrypted, holding no secret"]
    end
    Parsed -->|"request discarded unread"| NoInput
    Constant --> Body
    Constant -.->|"no per-request log record is emitted"| Startup
    Constant -.->|"no write path exists"| NoStore
```

**Diagram 6.4-D — Data lifecycle and protection status. Only the ingress channel carries an unprotected-transport gap; processing, egress, diagnostics, and storage are empty of protectable data by construction.**

#### 6.4.4.8 Data Protection Control Matrix

| Data protection control | Status | Provenance | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Encryption in transit | Absent | Host observation | HTTPS handshake to port 3000 fails; plaintext HTTP/1.1 only |
| Encryption at rest | Not applicable | Audit result | No data is written at runtime (6.2) |
| Key generation, storage, rotation | Not applicable | Audit result | 46 secret and PKI paths tested, 0 present |
| Secret injection and consumption | Not applicable | Source fact | `process.` = 0; no environment variable or argument is read |
| Data classification scheme | Not applicable | Source fact | The single payload is a public constant |
| Personal-data collection | Not applicable | Host observation | Request never read; a JSON body POST was verified ignored |

| CORS policy | Absent | Host observation | Preflight-shaped `OPTIONS` produced zero `Access-Control-*` headers |

| Artifact integrity verification | Present, unenforced | Audit result | Git content-addressed blobs `320a75a` for `server.js`, `5fb5231` for `README.md`, and `2c87c79` for `test.js`; commit signatures exist but no policy requires or verifies them |
| Retention and erasure | Not applicable | Audit result | Retention effectively zero; no policy artifact exists (6.2.4.1) |

#### 6.4.4.9 Standards to Apply If Data Is Introduced

The rows below are standard-practice requirements keyed to the change that would trigger them. They describe obligations, not current behaviour.

| Requirement | Triggering change | Rationale grounded in this system |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Terminate TLS 1.2 or higher with managed certificates, and add HSTS | Any change that widens the bind address beyond loopback | The channel is plaintext today and the process cannot terminate TLS at all — `https` and `tls` are not imported and no certificate material exists |
| Introduce a secret-consumption path deliberately, outside version control | The first credential, key, or connection string | `process.` = 0 means there is no configuration input today; a secret path must be designed rather than retrofitted, and no `.gitignore` currently protects against committing one |
| Classify data and document a retention period before first persistence | The first data store, cache, or file write | Retention is currently zero by construction; introducing storage creates retention, erasure, and integrity obligations where none exist |
| Add redaction rules at the same time as the first per-request log statement | The first access or security log | The current log line cannot leak because it interpolates only constants; per-request logging removes that guarantee immediately |
| Add key management with defined rotation and revocation | The first cryptographic key | No key exists and no rotation mechanism, escrow, or revocation path is present anywhere |
| Emit standard security response headers | Any change that returns content to a browser | The response sets exactly one header today, and `text/plain` with no `X-Content-Type-Options` becomes materially riskier once content is dynamic |
| Establish a licence and a security-contact artifact | Any distribution of the artifact outside its origin | No `LICENSE` grants usage rights and no `SECURITY.md` or `security.txt` provides a disclosure channel |

### 6.4.5 Security Zones and Trust Boundaries

The system's security posture reduces to a single question — *which zone is the caller in?* — and to a single enforcement mechanism that the repository does not own. This sub-section defines the zones, names each boundary and its enforcer, records the reachability measurements that prove where the one real boundary lies, and states the host assumptions the design silently depends on.

#### 6.4.5.1 Zone Model

Four zones are distinguishable. Only one boundary between them is enforced, and it is enforced by the host operating system.

| Zone | Contents | Trust level as designed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zone 0 — External network | Every off-host client, scanner, and adversary | Untrusted, and also **unreachable**: no listener exists on any non-loopback address |
| Zone 1 — Host-local | Every process on the same host, at any privilege level, plus whatever captures the process's stdout | Implicitly trusted; the design equates "same host" with "authorised" |
| Zone 2 — Process interior | The single Node.js process: the listening socket, the runtime's HTTP parser and event loop, and the handler with its two bind constants. Only `server.js` is loaded into it; `test.js` is never required and never enters this zone | Uniform — no internal privilege separation, sandbox, or sub-boundary exists |
| Zone 3 — Source-control lifecycle | The Git working tree, its three tracked files, and the `github.com` remote whose URL embeds an access token | Outside the runtime entirely; crossed only by developer actions, never by the running service |

Diagram 6.4-C shows the zones, what crosses each boundary, and which crossings were verified.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph ZoneExternal["Zone 0 - External network - untrusted and unreachable"]
        direction TB
        RemoteClient["Off-host client"]
        Scanner["Network scanner or remote adversary"]
    end
    subgraph ZoneHost["Zone 1 - Host-local - implicitly trusted by design"]
        direction TB
        LocalProcess["Any local process<br/>any OS user, any privilege level"]
        StdoutConsumer["Parent shell or supervisor<br/>capturing stdout"]
    end
    subgraph ZoneProcess["Zone 2 - Process interior - one Node.js process"]
        direction TB
        Listener["Listening socket 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>single IPv4 entry, no IPv6 listener"]
        RuntimeLayer["Node.js HTTP parser and event loop<br/>400 and 431 rejections, 16 KiB header cap"]
        AppHandler["Handler and bind constants<br/>server.js lines 3-4 and 6-10"]
        Listener --> RuntimeLayer
        RuntimeLayer --> AppHandler
    end
    subgraph ZoneSource["Zone 3 - Source-control lifecycle - not part of runtime"]
        direction TB
        WorkTree["Git working tree<br/>three tracked files, mode 100644<br/>only server.js is ever loaded"]
        GitRemote["github.com remote over HTTPS<br/>URL embeds an access token"]
        WorkTree --- GitRemote
    end
    RemoteClient -.->|"Boundary B1 ENFORCED - connect refused<br/>by the host TCP/IP stack"| Listener
    Scanner -.->|"no listener bound to any non-loopback address"| Listener
    LocalProcess -->|"Boundary B2 OPEN - unauthenticated<br/>plaintext HTTP, no rate limit"| Listener
    AppHandler -->|"one 41-byte readiness line"| StdoutConsumer
    WorkTree -->|"out-of-band launch: node server.js"| Listener
```

**Diagram 6.4-C — Security zones and trust boundaries. Boundary B1, between the external network and the host, is the only enforced boundary and is enforced outside the application by the host network stack. Boundary B2, between any local process and the service, is fully open. Zone 2 has no internal boundary at all.**

#### 6.4.5.2 Trust Boundary Analysis

| Boundary | Separates | Enforced by | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B1 — Host perimeter | Zone 0 from Zones 1 and 2 | Host TCP/IP stack, acting on the literal `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` at `server.js` line 3 | **Enforced** — verified by connection refusal (F-002-RQ-002) |
| B2 — Service ingress | Zone 1 from Zone 2 | Nothing | **Open** — unauthenticated, unauthorised, plaintext, unrate-limited, unlogged |
| B3 — Protocol conformance | Malformed traffic from the handler | Node.js HTTP parser | **Delegated** — `400` for malformed requests, `431` above 16,384 header bytes, both before the handler runs |
| B4 — Intra-process privilege | Nothing from nothing | No mechanism | **Absent** — no privilege drop, sandbox, seccomp filter, or capability restriction originates in the repository |
| B5 — Observability egress | Zone 2 from its stdout consumer in Zone 1 | Host process plumbing | **Delegated** — carries exactly one 41-byte line that interpolates only the two bind constants |
| B6 — Lifecycle | Zone 3 from Zone 2 | GitHub authentication on push and fetch, performed by a developer, never by the service | **Outside runtime** — the local remote URL is credential-sensitive and must not be published (3.4.4) |

Two properties of this boundary set deserve emphasis. First, **the only enforced boundary is topological and externally owned**: the repository contributes a string constant, and the host kernel does the enforcing. Second, **B2 carries the entire risk**: once a caller is in Zone 1, nothing between it and the constant response exists — a fact that the nine attack-shaped probes in 6.4.1.5 confirm from the outside and the zero-conditional source confirms from the inside.

#### 6.4.5.3 Reachability Verification

Every claim about zone reachability in this section was measured, not inferred.

| Probe | Result | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | `200`, 14-byte body | Zone 1 reaches the service without any credential |
| `GET http://<host's own non-loopback address>:3000/` | Connect failed, HTTP status `000` | The listener is not bound to any interface other than loopback — so even a caller on the same host using a different local address is refused, and Zone 0 is a fortiori unreachable |
| Entries for port 3000 in `/proc/net/tcp6` | 0 | No IPv6 listener; the exposure is a single IPv4 address family (corroborates 5.2.5) |
| `https://127.0.0.1:3000/` | TLS handshake failure, status `000` | No TLS-protected crossing of B2 is possible |
| Outbound connection attempts by the service | None — the single import is used only to *create* a server | There is no egress boundary crossing at all (6.3.1) |
| Repository tree after all probes | `git status --porcelain` = 0 tracked-file lines | No boundary crossing altered the artifact |

On Linux the loopback interface is scoped to a network namespace, so a process in a different network namespace — a separate container, for example — is in Zone 0 with respect to this service unless forwarding is deliberately configured. The repository contains no artifact that configures any such forwarding: audit groups 9 and 10 tested 36 isolation and perimeter paths, including `networkpolicy.yaml`, `compose.yaml`, `Dockerfile`, and `iptables.rules`, and found none present (**Audit result**).

#### 6.4.5.4 Process and Host Assumptions

The design depends on the following host properties. None is asserted or checked by the repository, which makes each one an assumption whose failure changes the security posture.

| Assumption | Basis and status | Consequence if it does not hold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The host's loopback interface is not forwarded or published | No repository artifact configures or prevents forwarding (**Audit result**) | Any operator-side port publication — a container port mapping, an SSH tunnel, or a relay — moves the endpoint into Zone 0 reach **without a single source change**, and B2 has nothing behind it. This is the concrete form of the "step function of one source token" risk recorded in 5.4.4 |
| Every process on the host is trustworthy | The design equates Zone 1 with authorised; no code distinguishes callers (**Source fact**) | Any local process, including an unprivileged one, has full access; there is no logging to attribute its requests afterwards |
| The service runs under a least-privilege account | `setuid`/`setgid` occurrences are 0, so the process inherits the invoking identity (**Source fact**). On the verification host it was measured at `Uid 0`, `Gid 0`, full effective capabilities, `NoNewPrivs 0`, `Seccomp 0` (**Host observation**). No `Dockerfile USER`, systemd `User=`, or Kubernetes `securityContext` exists (**Audit result**) | A defect elsewhere in the process would execute with whatever privilege the launcher held; port 3000 is unprivileged, so nothing about the design requires the elevated identity that was observed |
| The runtime is patched and supported | No version is pinned anywhere — no `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, or container image (**Audit result**). All verification used Node.js v22.23.1 | With zero third-party dependencies, the runtime is the *entire* vulnerability surface (5.4.4). External fact: the Node.js project directs production use to Active LTS or Maintenance LTS lines; the v22 line is in Maintenance LTS, receiving critical bug fixes and security updates only, while v24 is the Active LTS line. Patch currency is therefore an operator responsibility with no repository support |
| The source files are not writable by untrusted users | All three tracked files are mode `100644`, non-executable, with no shebang; ownership is host-managed (**Audit result**) | A writable `server.js` is equivalent to arbitrary code execution as the launching user at next start |
| Port 3000 is free at launch | A bind conflict raises an unhandled `'error'` event and exits with code 1 (F-002-RQ-004, 5.4.3) | Two consequences follow from verified facts: the legitimate service fails to start, and because clients have neither authentication nor TLS with which to verify the endpoint, a local process that binds `127.0.0.1:3000` first would be indistinguishable from the real service to any local caller |
| Only `server.js` is executed | The documented start procedure is `node server.js` (3.6.5); nothing requires `test.js`, and executing that file instead exits 1 with a `ReferenceError` (**Host observation**) | Invoking the wrong tracked file — or a runner that discovers it, such as `node --test` at the repository root — produces an immediate non-zero exit and no listener (6.6.1) |
| The single stdout line is captured | The application writes it once and never persists it (**Source fact**) | The only signal the system emits is lost; with no access log, an outage or an abuse episode produces no evidence at all (5.4.6, 6.4.3.5) |

#### 6.4.5.5 Zone and Boundary Control Matrix

| Zone or boundary | Control in force | Status | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zone 0 → service | Loopback bind, enforced by the host network stack | Delegated | Source fact and Host observation |
| Zone 1 → service | None | Absent | Source fact |
| Protocol conformance at ingress | Runtime parser rejections `400` and `431`; 16,384-byte header cap | Delegated | Runtime default |
| Connection resource limits | `keepAliveTimeout` 5,000 ms; `headersTimeout` 60,000 ms; `requestTimeout` 300,000 ms; `maxConnections` unset; `maxRequestsPerSocket` 0 | Delegated | Runtime default |
| Request volume limits | None — a 300-request burst returned 300 `200` responses | Absent | Host observation |
| Transport confidentiality across B2 | None — plaintext HTTP/1.1 | Absent | Host observation |
| Address-family exposure | Single IPv4 loopback listener; zero IPv6 entries | Delegated, favourable | Host observation |
| Intra-process isolation | None — no privilege drop, sandbox, or seccomp filter | Absent | Source fact and Audit result |
| Container or namespace isolation | None specified — 19 hardening and isolation paths tested, 0 present | Absent | Audit result |
| Host firewall or network policy | None specified — 17 perimeter paths tested, 0 present | Absent | Audit result |
| Boundary-crossing audit | None — stdout invariant at 41 bytes under attack traffic | Absent | Host observation |
| Lifecycle boundary (Zone 3) | GitHub authentication via a token-bearing remote URL, used by developers only | Outside runtime | Audit result |

#### 6.4.5.6 Attacker-Position Reachability

| Attacker position | Can reach `127.0.0.1:3000` | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remote internet or LAN host | No | No listener on any non-loopback address; connect attempt to the host's own routable address was refused |
| Process in a different network namespace or container on the same machine | No, absent deliberate forwarding | Loopback is namespace-scoped; no forwarding or network-policy artifact exists in the repository |
| Unprivileged local user in the same namespace | Yes, fully | Every probe — including credential-bearing, traversal, and injection-shaped requests — returned the identical `200` |
| Privileged local user | Yes, fully, plus the ability to read the process's memory and replace `server.js` | All tracked files are mode `100644`; no in-process isolation exists |
| Operator who publishes or forwards the port | Yes — the forwarding terminates outside the application, so B1 is bypassed without a code change | No repository artifact controls forwarding |
| Party who obtains the local `.git/config` | Repository access, not endpoint access | The embedded token grants repository access only and has no relationship to the running service (3.4.4) |
| Party able to push to the repository | No endpoint access, but unrestricted change access | Three commits have reached the branch head with no review, status check, or hook; the most recent added a file that fails on execution (6.4.3.5) |

### 6.4.6 Standard Security Practices and Compliance Controls

Since no security architecture exists to specify, this sub-section discharges the remaining obligation of the section prompt: it records precisely which standard security practices are in force, who owns each one, which are missing, and what compliance position follows. The practices are grouped by owner — the committed code, the platform, the operating environment, and the next change — because attributing them correctly is the difference between an accurate posture statement and a false assurance.

#### 6.4.6.1 Practices Satisfied by the Committed Codebase

| Standard practice | How the repository satisfies it | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimise dependencies and supply-chain exposure | Exactly one `require`, of a Node.js built-in; no manifest, lockfile, or `node_modules` exists, so there is no third-party or transitive package to compromise and nothing for a composition scan to flag | Source fact and Audit result |
| Keep secrets out of version control | 24 secret-management paths tested and absent; keyword scan for `secret`, `credential`, and `password` across all three tracked files returned zero matches; the source reads no environment variable (`process.` = 0), so no secret is consumed either | Audit result and Source fact |
| Bind to the narrowest interface by default | `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` at line 3; a connect attempt from the host's own non-loopback address was refused | Source fact and Host observation |
| Minimise functionality and attack surface | One handler, one response header, one status code, one constant body; zero occurrences of `eval(`, `child_process`, `fs.`, and `JSON.parse`, so there is no code-execution, command, filesystem, or deserialisation sink | Source fact |
| Avoid handling sensitive data | The request is never read and the response is a compile-time constant; nothing is persisted, cached, or reflected | Source fact and Host observation |
| Avoid version and banner disclosure | Neither `Server` nor `X-Powered-By` appears on any response; the header-name set was invariant across all probes | Runtime default |
| Ship non-executable, minimally permissioned artifacts | All three tracked files are mode `100644` with no shebang | Audit result |
| Make execution reproducible without a build or install step | The program runs exactly as committed (requirement F-005-RQ-002), so there is no build pipeline to compromise and no artifact substitution step | Source fact |

An honest qualification belongs here: most of these properties follow from the program's triviality rather than from deliberate hardening. They are nonetheless real and verifiable, and several — the dependency-free posture and the loopback default in particular — are the properties that keep the overall risk low despite the complete absence of security controls.

#### 6.4.6.2 Protections Delegated to the Platform

| Delegated protection | Value or behaviour in force | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Network admission control | Refusal of connections to any non-loopback address for the bound socket | Host TCP/IP stack |
| HTTP parser strictness | `400 Bad Request` with `Connection: close` for a malformed request line or an unrecognised method token; the handler is never entered | Node.js runtime |
| Header-size capping | `maxHeaderSize` 16,384 bytes; a 20,000-byte header field produced `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` | Node.js runtime |
| Idle connection reclamation | `keepAliveTimeout` 5,000 ms | Node.js runtime |
| Slow-request mitigation | `headersTimeout` 60,000 ms and `requestTimeout` 300,000 ms | Node.js runtime |
| Protocol correctness for interim and entity-less responses | Automatic `100 Continue` generation; entity suppression for `HEAD`; pipelined response ordering | Node.js runtime |
| Address-family scope | A single IPv4 loopback listener; no IPv6 listener exists | Node.js runtime and host stack |

Every value in this table is a **Runtime default** that `server.js` does not set, catalogued authoritatively in 5.2.6. Two consequences follow. First, these protections change silently if the runtime changes, and the repository pins no runtime version. Second, the delegated set has real holes: `maxConnections` is unset, `maxRequestsPerSocket` is 0, and `server.timeout` is 0, so there is **no connection ceiling, no per-connection request ceiling, and no socket inactivity timeout** — which is why the 300-request burst in 6.3.2.4 met no resistance whatsoever.

#### 6.4.6.3 Practices the Operating Environment Must Supply

| Practice | Repository position | Operator responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run a patched, supported runtime | No version is pinned anywhere — no `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, or container image | With zero dependencies, the runtime is the entire vulnerability surface (5.4.4). External fact: the Node.js project directs production use to Active LTS or Maintenance LTS lines; the v22 line used for all verification here is in Maintenance LTS, which receives critical bug fixes and security updates only, while v24 is the Active LTS line |
| Run under a least-privilege, non-root account | No privilege drop in source; measured `Uid 0` with full effective capabilities, `NoNewPrivs 0`, `Seccomp 0`; no `USER`, `User=`, or `securityContext` artifact exists | Port 3000 is unprivileged, so a dedicated unprivileged account is available at no functional cost |
| Filter network access and avoid port publication | 17 perimeter paths and 19 isolation paths tested, none present | Any port publication or tunnel moves the endpoint into external reach without a code change, and nothing sits behind that boundary |
| Supervise the process and manage restarts | No supervisor artifact; a bind conflict exits with code 1 and termination is immediate and undrained | Recovery is manual; failure detection is the weakest link because an outage emits no signal (5.4.6) |
| Capture and retain the process output | One 41-byte readiness line, never persisted by the application | Capturing stdout is the only observability available; note there is no access or security log to collect |
| Launch the correct file | The documented start command is `node server.js`; the tree also contains a non-application `test.js` that exits 1 with a `ReferenceError` if executed, and which `node --test` discovers and fails at the repository root (6.6.1) | Invoke `node server.js` explicitly; do not rely on a runner or wrapper to select the entry point, because no manifest declares one |
| Restrict write access to the source tree | All three files are mode `100644`; ownership is host-managed | A writable `server.js` is equivalent to code execution as the launching user at next start |
| Protect the repository credential | The local Git remote URL embeds an access token | Exclude `.git` from images and artefacts; never publish or paste the URL. The token grants repository access only and is unrelated to the running service |
| Monitor for vulnerabilities | No scanning, dependency-update, or advisory-tracking configuration exists among the 21 audited CI and scanning paths | With no dependencies, monitoring reduces to tracking runtime security advisories for the deployed Node.js line |

#### 6.4.6.4 Practices Mandatory Before Any Exposure or Feature Change

The determination in 6.4.1.1 is contingent on the code staying as it is. Each row below names a change and the controls that must land **in the same change**, not afterwards — the sequencing point made explicitly in 5.4.4.

| Change | Controls that must land in the same change | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Widening the bind address, or publishing or forwarding the port | Authentication boundary, TLS termination, a denial path, rate limiting, and per-request security logging | The loopback literal is the only control; removing it leaves nothing behind it (5.4.4, ADR-003) |
| Reading any request attribute | Input validation, size and encoding limits, and output encoding | `req.` = 0 today, which is what eliminates the injection, deserialisation, and mass-assignment classes entirely (2.4.4, 6.4.1.5) |
| Introducing a second response path | An authorization model with deny-by-default semantics and a `403` path | Zero conditionals and one status literal today mean there is no mechanism to refuse anything (6.4.3) |
| Introducing persistence or a data source | Data classification, at-rest protection, retention and erasure rules, access control, and a data-access audit trail | Retention is zero by construction today and no classification scheme exists (6.2.4, 6.4.4) |
| Introducing a secret, key, or certificate | A secret-consumption path outside version control, ignore rules to prevent commits, and defined rotation and revocation | `process.` = 0 and no `.gitignore` exists, so nothing currently prevents a secret from being committed (6.4.4.3) |
| Adding a third-party dependency | A lockfile, dependency scanning in a CI gate, and an SBOM or provenance attestation | Zero dependencies today means zero supply-chain surface and also zero supply-chain tooling (2.4.4 for F-005) |
| Returning content to a browser | Security response headers, including a content-security policy and `X-Content-Type-Options` | Exactly one header is set today, and `text/plain` with no nosniff protection becomes materially riskier once content is dynamic |
| Adding any per-request logging | Redaction rules for credentials and personal data | The current log line cannot leak because it interpolates only the two bind constants (F-004-RQ-002) |
| Introducing any of the above at all | A change gate that can refuse a commit — review, status check, or hook | Three commits have reached the branch head unreviewed and ungated, the most recent adding a file that fails on execution (6.4.3.5); without a gate, every control above can be removed as easily as it was added |

#### 6.4.6.5 Compliance Requirements

The repository names no regulatory regime, declares no data-governance policy, and contains no artifact that could evidence a control to an auditor. No compliance obligation is therefore satisfied *or* violated by the code, with one exception: the absence of a `LICENSE` file means no redistribution or usage rights are granted to any recipient of the artifact — an obligation that is unmet rather than inapplicable (2.4.4, feature F-005).

| Compliance requirement class | Current position | What would create the obligation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Privacy and personal-data protection | Not applicable — no personal data can be collected, stored, or transferred | Reading any request attribute, setting a cookie, or logging a client address |
| Payment, health, and financial-record regimes | Not applicable — no such data category exists in the system | Introducing a data path that carries cardholder, health, or financial-reporting data |
| Security certification programmes such as SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001 | Cannot be evidenced — no logical-access, change-management, or monitoring control exists to test | Bringing the service into a certified environment, which would require policies, access control, and audit logging to be introduced first |
| Vulnerability disclosure | Absent — no `SECURITY.md`, `security.txt`, or contact channel exists | Any external distribution or third-party use of the artifact |
| Software composition and provenance | Absent — no SBOM, signature bundle, or attestation exists; the dependency set is empty | Procurement or distribution requirements, or the addition of any dependency |
| Change management and segregation of duties | Present but unenforced — a three-commit signed history exists with full attribution, yet no `CODEOWNERS`, review policy, branch-protection descriptor, or enforcing hook stands in front of it. The most recent commit, `43ed37c`, demonstrates the gap concretely: it added `test.js`, a file that exits 1 with a `ReferenceError` when executed, and reached the branch head with no review and no gate of any kind (6.4.3.5) | Any environment that requires reviewed, attributable change control |
| Audit-log retention | Not applicable — no audit log is produced, and retention is effectively zero by construction | The first security-relevant event record |
| Licensing and redistribution | **Obligation unmet** — no `LICENSE` accompanies the artifact | Already applicable to anyone who receives or reuses the code |
| Cryptographic export controls | Not applicable — the system implements and ships no cryptography | Introducing any cryptographic capability |

Established the absence of `https`, `tls`, and `crypto` imports; of any `req` dereference; of any conditional construct; of any `process.*` access; and of any privilege-drop, filesystem, deserialisation, or code-execution call.

Examined byte by byte for this section and found to contain no credential, token, secret, key, URL, import, or security-relevant identifier of any kind — its content is two undefined bare identifiers. It is required by nothing, exports nothing, and is never loaded into the server process, so it contributes no attack surface and no control. Its security relevance is evidentiary only: it is the artifact that demonstrates the unenforced change-admission posture recorded in 6.4.3.5, since `node --check test.js` reports valid syntax and exits 0 while executing the file raises `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and exits 1.

## 6.5 Monitoring and Observability

### 6.5.1 Monitoring Applicability and Baseline Practices

#### 6.5.1.1 Determination

**Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The repository tracks exactly three files — `server.js` (14 lines, 342 bytes), `README.md` (27 bytes, a single heading line), and `test.js` (2 lines, 13 bytes), 382 bytes in total. `server.js` imports one Node.js built-in, binds one loopback listener, and answers every request with a constant. It contains **no metrics endpoint, no health or readiness route, no logging framework, no trace context, no exporter, no agent, no alert transport, and no dashboard definition** — and, because it also contains no timer and no configuration layer, it possesses neither the means to emit telemetry periodically nor the means to have telemetry switched on without editing source.

`test.js` adds no telemetry and no observability surface. Its 13 bytes are two undefined bare identifiers; it emits nothing, is required by nothing, and is never loaded into the server process, so it appears in none of the signal, emission, or observation paths described below.

The whole of the system's telemetry implementation is three lines:

```javascript
server.listen(port, hostname, () => {
  console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
});
```

That statement fires exactly once, at bind time. Measured across roughly 2,300 requests plus four deliberate protocol-error probes, the process's **stdout remained at exactly 41 bytes and its stderr at exactly 0 bytes** (*Host observation*) — traffic volume, latency, errors, and shutdown are all invisible in the system's own output.

This sub-section therefore does two things the prompt requires. It records the determination together with the evidence that establishes it (6.5.1.1 – 6.5.1.5), and it specifies the **basic monitoring practices that apply instead** (6.5.1.6), which are entirely external and synthetic. Sub-sections 6.5.2 through 6.5.4 then walk every mandated topic — metrics collection, log aggregation, distributed tracing, alert management, dashboard design, health checks, performance metrics, business metrics, SLA monitoring, capacity tracking, and the full incident-response set — recording for each a status, its evidence, and what an operator can actually determine. A documented gap is more useful to an operator than a silent one, and in a system whose only failure signal is the absence of a response, an undocumented gap is actively dangerous.

#### 6.5.1.2 Determination Criteria

A detailed monitoring architecture is warranted when at least one of the following preconditions holds. Each was tested against the committed source rather than assumed.

| Precondition for a monitoring architecture | Result | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The application emits a metric, counter, gauge, or histogram | **Not satisfied** — no metrics library, no `/metrics` route, and no self-introspection call (`process.memoryUsage`, `process.cpuUsage`, `perf_hooks`, `diagnostics_channel` all absent) | Audit result |
| The application emits more than one log record | **Not satisfied** — one `console.log` at line 13; stdout invariant at 41 bytes under all traffic and error probes | Source fact and Host observation |
| A dedicated health or readiness endpoint exists | **Not satisfied** — the request object is never dereferenced, so no route exists; every URI including `/healthz` and `/readyz` reaches the same handler | Source fact and Host observation |
| The service participates in a trace | **Not satisfied** — no trace context is read, generated, or propagated, and the service makes no outbound call to propagate to | Source fact |
| A declared SLA, SLO, error budget, or threshold exists | **Not satisfied** — no service-level or capacity artifact of any kind; 5.4.5 and 6.1.1.3 record the same finding | Audit result |
| An alerting, paging, or dashboard destination is configured | **Not satisfied** — no alert rule, receiver, webhook, or dashboard definition; no supervisor or orchestrator to act on a signal | Audit result |
| Telemetry can be enabled without editing source | **Not satisfied** — `process.env`, `dotenv`, and any configuration read are absent, so there is no toggle, endpoint, or sampling rate to set | Source fact |

Not one of seven preconditions is satisfied, and two of them — the absence of any timer and the absence of any configuration input — mean the gap cannot be closed operationally. That is the basis of the determination in 6.5.1.1.

#### 6.5.1.3 Telemetry Artifact Audit

An observability-specific existence audit was executed for this section over the complete tracked corpus (`README.md`, `server.js`, and `test.js` — the definitive file set, since `git ls-files` and `git ls-tree -r` return exactly these three at HEAD; the same commands on `main`, which still points at the earlier commit `06492d7`, return the first two). **104 telemetry keyword terms across twelve concern groups were tested individually. Total matches: zero.**

| Telemetry concern group | Terms tested | Matches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Metrics libraries and exposition endpoints (`prometheus`, `prom-client`, `statsd`, `dogstatsd`, `/metrics`, `micrometer`, `expvar`) | 7 | 0 |
| 2. OpenTelemetry and collector pipeline (`opentelemetry`, `@opentelemetry`, `otel`, `otlp`, `collector`) | 5 | 0 |
| 3. APM and monitoring SaaS (`datadog`, `newrelic`, `sentry`, `elastic-apm`, `dynatrace`, `appdynamics`, `honeycomb`, `lightstep`, `grafana`, `loki`, `tempo`, …) | 12 | 0 |
| 4. Logging frameworks and shippers (`winston`, `pino`, `bunyan`, `log4js`, `morgan`, `fluentd`, `fluent-bit`, `filebeat`, `logstash`, `syslog`, `splunk`, `cloudwatch`, `stackdriver`) | 13 | 0 |
| 5. Tracing and correlation (`traceparent`, `tracestate`, `span`, `jaeger`, `zipkin`, `b3`, `x-request-id`, `correlation`, `requestid`, `trace`) | 10 | 0 |
| 6. Health, readiness, and heartbeat routes (`health`, `healthz`, `readyz`, `livez`, `liveness`, `readiness`, `/status`, `/ping`, `heartbeat`) | 9 | 0 |
| 7. Alert transports and receivers (`alertmanager`, `pagerduty`, `opsgenie`, `victorops`, `webhook`, `slack`, `smtp`, `nodemailer`, `notify`, `alert`) | 10 | 0 |
| 8. Service levels, dashboards, runbooks, post-mortems (`slo`, `sla`, `error budget`, `apdex`, `percentile`, `p95`, `p99`, `dashboard`, `panel`, `runbook`, `oncall`, `postmortem`, …) | 14 | 0 |
| 9. Runtime self-introspection APIs (`process.memoryUsage`, `process.cpuUsage`, `process.hrtime`, `process.uptime`, `perf_hooks`, `diagnostics_channel`, `inspector`, `v8.`, `async_hooks`) | 9 | 0 |
| 10. Additional stream writes (`console.error`, `console.warn`, `console.info`, `console.debug`, `console.trace`, `stderr`, `process.stdout`, `process.stderr`) | 8 | 0 |
| 11. Periodic emission machinery (`setInterval`, `setTimeout`, `timer`, `cron`) | 4 | 0 |
| 12. Configuration layer that could enable telemetry (`process.env`, `dotenv`, `config`) | 3 | 0 |
| **Total** | **104** | **0** |

Four independent checks corroborate the keyword audit without overlapping it:

- **Descriptor audit.** Sixteen deployment and pipeline descriptor classes were searched across the entire worktree — `Dockerfile*`, `*compose*`, `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.json`, `*.service`, `*.conf`, `*.ini`, `*.toml`, `*.sh`, `*.env*`, `*.tf`, plus the `.github/`, `.circleci/`, `ci/` directories and `.gitlab-ci.yml` — and **none exists**. There is therefore no container `HEALTHCHECK`, no Compose `healthcheck`, no Kubernetes `livenessProbe` or `readinessProbe`, no systemd unit with `Restart=`, no scrape configuration, no alert rule file, and no Grafana dashboard JSON (*Audit result*).
- **History audit.** `git log --stat --all` shows three commits adding exactly `README.md` (1 insertion), `server.js` (14 insertions), and `test.js` (2 insertions). **No monitoring artifact has ever existed in this repository and later been removed** (*Audit result*).
- **Neighbouring audits reached the same result from different directions.** Section 6.1.1.2 tested 171 distributed-artifact paths including 28 resilience, health-probe, and runbook paths and 19 service-level and capacity paths — zero present. Section 6.4.1.3 tested 224 security-artifact paths including a 13-path audit-log-infrastructure group (`auditd.rules`, `rsyslog.conf`, `fluentd.conf`, `fluent-bit.conf`, `filebeat.yml`, `vector.toml`, `promtail.yaml`, `logs/`, and others) — zero present.
- **Deployment posture.** Section 3.6.5 records the operational shape independently: a foreground, non-daemonized, single-process service with **no PID file, no log file, no daemonization flag, no health endpoint, and no restart policy**, whose standard streams are whatever the launching shell provides.

#### 6.5.1.4 Evidence Conventions

This sub-section reuses the status vocabulary of 6.4.1.6 and the provenance labels of 6.1.1.3 so that a term means the same thing across chapter 6.

| Term | Meaning in section 6.5 |
| --- | --- |
| **Delegated** | A signal or protection exists and is exercised, but it is produced by the Node.js runtime or the host operating system rather than by repository code |
| **Absent** | The observability concern is meaningful for the interface that exists, but nothing implements it at any layer |
| **Not applicable** | The concern presupposes a structure the system does not have — a metric source, a business transaction, a second service, a declared service level |
| **Source fact** / **Audit result** | A property verifiable by reading a tracked file at a cited line / the outcome of an existence or content probe over the repository |
| **Runtime default** / **Host observation** | Behaviour supplied by Node.js because `server.js` configures nothing / a value measured by executing the unmodified source on one verification host |

**No number in section 6.5 may be read as a commitment.** The repository declares no SLA, SLO, error budget, availability target, latency target, or capacity assumption, so every threshold, target, or figure appearing here is either an inherited runtime default or a single-occasion measurement, explicitly labelled as such. All runtime evidence was produced against **HEAD `43ed37c`** on branch `2907_01` with a clean working tree, on one verification host running **Node.js v22.23.1** (16 vCPU, 124,784 MiB memory, file-descriptor ceiling 1,048,576), exercising the loopback interface only. `server.js` is byte-identical at HEAD and at its introducing commit `06492d7`, so the measurements apply to both revisions. All probe scripts were written outside the repository checkout and no tracked file was modified.

#### 6.5.1.5 The Signals the System Actually Emits

Section 5.4.1 identifies four passive signals. The table below restates them with the measurements taken for this section and separates a fifth, distinct client-visible signal: the protocol errors the runtime generates before the handler is entered.

| Signal | What it is, measured | What it establishes — and cannot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Startup readiness line | One 41-byte stdout record, `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, written once by the listen callback at line 13 | Proves the bind succeeded at the endpoint named in the line. Never repeated, so it says nothing about any later moment; it is a *transition* record, not a heartbeat |
| Constant HTTP response | `200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, 14-byte body, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5` | The only liveness evidence available: proves the listener accepted a connection and the event loop turned at least once. Carries no `Server`, version, build, or instance header, so it cannot identify *which* build or instance answered |
| Process and socket presence | `pgrep -fc "node server.js"`; the `/proc/net/tcp` entry `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A` (LISTEN) | Distinguishes "not running" from "running". Cannot distinguish a healthy event loop from a blocked one, because a LISTEN socket persists while the loop is stalled |
| Runtime-authored fatal trace | On a bind conflict: an unhandled `'error'` event trace on stderr naming `listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`, exit code 1, **zero stdout bytes** | Diagnoses one fatal startup condition precisely. Silent for every non-fatal condition; written by the runtime, not by the application, which registers zero `'error'` listeners |
| Runtime-generated protocol errors | `400 Bad Request` for a malformed request line (47 bytes on the wire), `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` above the 16,384-byte header cap (67 bytes), both with `Connection: close` | Visible to the *client* only. The handler is never entered and the application writes nothing, so these events are invisible to anyone watching the service's own output |

Three properties of this signal set determine everything in the rest of section 6.5. **The set is entirely passive** — no signal is pushed anywhere, and with `setInterval`/`setTimeout` absent the process cannot self-report on a schedule even in principle. **Termination is silent**: the server registers zero `'close'` listeners and the process registers zero `exit`, `beforeExit`, `SIGTERM`, and `SIGINT` listeners, so a stop — planned or not — produces no record at all; stdout was still exactly 41 bytes and stderr 0 bytes after `SIGTERM` (exit code 143) and after `SIGINT` (exit code 130). And **every signal must be read by an outside observer**, which makes the observation plane an operator responsibility rather than a system capability.

#### 6.5.1.6 Baseline Monitoring Practices Applied Instead

Because the system emits no telemetry, monitoring it consists of five external checks. Each row below is a practice grounded in a verified signal, with the verified interpretation of its outcome. Together they constitute the complete monitoring capability available for the code as committed.

| Baseline practice | Mechanism and verified behaviour | What a failure of the check means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synthetic endpoint probe with body assertion | Request any URI on `127.0.0.1:3000` and assert status `200`, `Content-Length: 14`, and the exact 14-byte body. The body was byte-identical across every probe in this section, and 6.4.1.5 records its SHA-256 prefix `c98c24b677ef` | A refused connection or absent process means the service is down. **Asserting the body — not merely the status — is the only correctness check available**, because a foreign process that seized port 3000 would also answer, and no header identifies the real service |
| Process and listener presence check | `pgrep -fc "node server.js"` returned 1 while serving and 0 after termination; the LISTEN entry for `0100007F:0BB8` disappears with the process | Separates "process gone" from "process present but not answering" — the only degradation-shaped distinction obtainable without instrumentation |
| Capture and retain stdout and stderr | The launching shell owns both streams (3.6.5). Presence of the 41-byte line proves a successful bind; a non-empty stderr means a fatal startup fault | Absence of the readiness line after a launch attempt means the bind failed. If the streams are not captured, the only signal the system emits is lost outright (6.4.5.4) |
| Inspect the process exit code | Measured: `1` on `EADDRINUSE`, `143` on `SIGTERM`, `130` on `SIGINT` | Distinguishes a startup failure from an operator-initiated stop after the fact — the closest thing to a post-incident event record the system produces |
| Pre-launch port-availability check | A second instance exits immediately with code 1 and no readiness line while the port is held | Port 3000 must be confirmed free before any recovery attempt; a bind conflict is *recovery-blocking*, as 6.1.4.2 records |

Two constraints bound all five practices, and both were measured. **The observer must be co-located on the host**: a request to the host's routable address `10.76.0.92:3000` failed to connect (`curl` exit 7, HTTP status `000`) while the loopback request returned `200`, so no off-host agent, external uptime service, or remote scraper can reach the endpoint as committed. And **a probe cannot hold a pooled connection between polls**: an idle keep-alive connection received a server-side close 6.01 s after its response, consistent with the 5,000 ms `keepAliveTimeout` default, so each poll should open its own connection.

A third, procedural constraint follows from the tracked inventory: **the probe must target the process started by `node server.js`**. No manifest declares an entry point, and the tree contains a second `.js` file, `test.js`, which is not the application — executing it exits 1 with a `ReferenceError` and starts no listener, and `node --test` at the repository root discovers it and fails (6.6.1). An operator or wrapper that selects the wrong file produces no readiness line and no listener at all.

Diagram 6.5-A shows the resulting monitoring architecture. Everything inside the system boundary is a passive signal source; everything in the observation plane must be supplied by the operator; every emission path in the middle group is verified absent.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SystemBoundary["System boundary — one Node.js process, all signals passive"]
        direction TB
        Listener["TCP listener 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>LISTEN entry 0100007F:0BB8 state 0A"]
        Handler["Handler, server.js lines 6-10<br/>constant 200, 14-byte body, no counters"]
        Readiness["Listen callback, line 13<br/>one 41-byte stdout record, once per lifetime"]
        RuntimeErr["Runtime fault path<br/>EADDRINUSE trace on stderr, exit code 1"]
        Listener --> Handler
        Listener --> Readiness
        Listener --> RuntimeErr
    end
    subgraph AbsentEmission["Telemetry emission paths — every class verified absent"]
        direction TB
        NoMetrics["Metrics endpoint or push exporter<br/>7 metrics terms, 5 OTel terms: 0 matches"]
        NoAgent["Sidecar agent or APM SDK<br/>12 vendor terms: 0 matches"]
        NoShipper["Log shipper or syslog transport<br/>13 logging terms: 0 matches"]
        NoTrace["Trace exporter or context propagation<br/>10 tracing terms: 0 matches"]

    end

        ProcCheck --> Human
        StreamCapture --> Human
        ExitWatch --> Human
    end
    Handler -->|"200 with 14-byte body — only liveness evidence"| Prober
    Listener -->|"LISTEN entry and process record"| ProcCheck
```
