```mermaid
    RuntimeErr -->|"stack trace, fatal faults only"| StreamCapture
    RuntimeErr -->|"process exit status"| ExitWatch
    Handler -.->|"no code path reaches any emission class"| NoMetrics
    Loopback["Reachability constraint: routable address 10.76.0.92:3000<br/>refused, curl exit 7 — off-host observers cannot poll"]
    Loopback -.-> Prober
```

**Diagram 6.5-A — Monitoring architecture as it exists. The system contributes four passive signal sources and no emission path; the entire observation plane is operator-supplied, co-located on the host by necessity, and correlated only by a human.**

#### 6.5.1.7 Change Conditions That Void This Determination

The determination in 6.5.1.1 is contingent on the code staying as it is. Each row names a change and the observability capability that must land **in the same change**, because in every case the change removes a property that currently makes the absence of monitoring tolerable.

| Change | Observability that must accompany it | Why, grounded in this system |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Widening the bind address beyond loopback, or publishing the port | Access logging and a request-rate signal | Today no request is recorded at all; once the endpoint is reachable off-host, abuse and outage would both be invisible (6.4.3.5) |
| Adding a second response path or any conditional | An error counter and per-request error logging | With one status literal and zero conditionals, there is currently no failure mode to miss; a branch creates one immediately |
| Adding any outbound dependency | Dependency latency and failure metrics, plus trace context propagation | The service opens no outbound socket today, which is the only reason the absence of tracing costs nothing |
| Introducing a second instance or any supervisor | A real health endpoint distinct from the service path | Every URI answers `200` identically, so no arbiter could distinguish a healthy instance from a listening-but-broken one (6.1.4.4) |
| Declaring any availability or latency target | A metric source capable of measuring it | No counter, histogram, or timer exists, so a target declared today would be unmeasurable — 6.1.3.5 records the same constraint for capacity |
| Running the service unattended or in the background | Stream capture with retention, plus supervision | The single readiness line is the only signal emitted, and it is lost if the streams are not captured (6.4.5.4, 6.4.6.3) |

### 6.5.2 Monitoring Infrastructure

There is no monitoring infrastructure in this system. This sub-section walks each mandated infrastructure topic — metrics collection, log aggregation, distributed tracing, alert management, and dashboard design — and records for each the status, the evidence, and precisely what an operator can build from the signals that do exist. The consistent finding is that **no component of a monitoring pipeline lives inside the system**: whatever monitoring exists must be constructed entirely in the observation plane of Diagram 6.5-A.

#### 6.5.2.1 Metrics Collection

**Status: Absent.** No metric is produced by the application, and no collection mechanism of any kind exists — no exposition endpoint for a scraper to pull, no push exporter, no agent, no StatsD socket, and no self-introspection call from which a value could be derived (groups 1, 2, 3, and 9 of the audit in 6.5.1.3: 33 terms, zero matches).

Two findings make the collection gap sharper than a simple absence:

- **A scrape of `/metrics` succeeds at the HTTP layer and fails at the parse layer.** Because the handler never dereferences the request, `/metrics` reaches the same code path as every other URI and returns the ordinary constant body:

```text
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/metrics
Hello, World!
```

  A Prometheus-style scraper therefore receives `200 OK` with `Content-Type: text/plain` and a 14-byte payload that is not valid exposition format — the failure mode is a **parse error rather than a clear `404`**, which is materially harder to diagnose (*Host observation*).

- **The process cannot push a metric even if one existed.** There is no `setInterval` or `setTimeout` anywhere in the source, so no periodic emission can occur; and the module opens no outbound socket at all (6.1.2.2), so there is no path to a collector. Combined with the absence of any configuration read, this means metrics collection cannot be enabled operationally — only by editing `server.js`.

Every quantity an operator can obtain is therefore produced *outside* the application, by a prober or by the host. The table below defines the complete obtainable set, all of which were measured for this section.

| Metric | Definition and unit | Source and provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Probe reachability | Boolean per poll: connection established and `200` received | External prober; `200` while serving, `curl` exit 7 / status `000` after termination (*Host observation*) |
| Response integrity | Boolean per poll: body equals the 14-byte constant and `Content-Length: 14` | External prober; byte-identical across every probe, SHA-256 prefix `c98c24b677ef` (6.4.1.5) |
| Probe round-trip latency | Seconds per poll, client-observed, including connection setup | External prober; 12 `curl` samples gave min 0.000181 s, median 0.000294 s, max 0.000735 s (*Host observation*) |
| Process presence | Count of matching processes | `pgrep -fc "node server.js"`; 1 while serving, 0 after termination (*Host observation*) |
| Listener presence | Boolean: LISTEN entry exists for the port | `/proc/net/tcp` entry `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A` (*Host observation*) |
| Resident memory | KiB of RSS | `ps` / `/proc`; 50,868 KiB idle rising to 59,212 KiB after a 300-request burst; the process's own report was 46.7 MiB at idle (*Host observation*) |
| Open file descriptors | Count, usable as a concurrent-connection proxy | `/proc/<pid>/fd`; 22 at idle, exactly one additional descriptor per connection per 6.1.3.3, returning to 22 after connections close (*Host observation*) |
| Thread count | Count of OS threads | `ps -o nlwp`; 7 before and after load, unchanged at every concurrency level tested in 6.1.3.1 (*Host observation*) |
| Process exit status | Integer, available only after termination | 1 on `EADDRINUSE`, 143 on `SIGTERM`, 130 on `SIGINT` (*Host observation*) |

Everything else that a monitored service would normally expose is unobtainable, and the reasons are structural rather than incidental.

| Metric that cannot be obtained | Reason it cannot be obtained |
| --- | --- |
| Request rate, total request count | No counter exists and no request is logged; stdout stayed at 41 bytes across roughly 2,300 requests (*Host observation*) |
| Server-side latency distribution, percentiles | No timing instrumentation; only client-observed round-trip time is available, and it includes client-side cost |
| Application error rate, status-code breakdown | One status literal (`200`) and zero conditionals; runtime-generated `400` and `431` are visible to the client but never recorded by the service |
| In-flight requests, queue depth, event-loop lag | No gauge, no `dropRequest` listener, and no event-loop observation; descriptor count is the only concurrency proxy |
| Per-route or per-method metrics | Every URI and every method reaches the identical handler, so no dimension exists to break down by |
| Build, version, or instance identity | No `Server` or version header is emitted (6.4.4.4), no tag or version field exists (3.6.6), and the log line carries no identifier |
| Saturation relative to capacity | 6.1.3.5 records the same limitation: with no request counter or latency histogram, there is no way to observe where the deployed system sits against the measured ceiling |

#### 6.5.2.2 Log Aggregation

**Status: Absent** for aggregation; the single emitted record is **Delegated** to whatever captures the process's streams.

The complete logging implementation is the `console.log` at line 13. Its output is one 41-byte free-text record for the entire process lifetime, and the process writes nothing else: after roughly 2,300 requests and four protocol-error probes, **stdout was still exactly 41 bytes and stderr exactly 0 bytes** (*Host observation*). Section 6.4.3.5 independently confirmed that the process opens no regular file for writing — its descriptors are only event-loop anonymous inodes, pipes, and `/dev/null` — so nothing is written to disk by the application under any circumstance.

| Log-aggregation dimension | Position in this system | Consequence for an aggregator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Destination | Inherited stdout descriptor; the launching shell owns both streams (3.6.5) | There is no log file to tail and no socket to receive; capture must wrap the launch command |
| Volume and cardinality | Exactly one record per process lifetime, independent of traffic | Log volume is a *constant*, so it can never indicate load, errors, or activity |
| Structure | Free text; no JSON, no key–value pairs | Not machine-parseable; an aggregator can only match the literal string |
| Severity | None — one call, at the default level | No level-based routing or filtering is possible |
| Timestamp | **None in the record** — the 41 bytes are the message only | Event time must be supplied by the capturing tool at ingest; the record itself cannot be ordered or correlated |
| Process identity | None — no PID, host, build, or instance field | Successive restarts produce byte-identical records, so restarts are distinguishable only by repetition, not by content |
| Request and error logging | None; the application logs neither | No access log and no error log exists — 6.4.3.5 states the resulting position as "the system is not auditable at runtime" |
| Rotation and retention | Not applicable — nothing is persisted by the system | Retention is whatever the capturing shell or supervisor provides; if streams are unattended, retention is zero (6.4.5.4) |
| Shipping transport | Absent — 13 logging and shipper terms, zero matches; no `rsyslog`, `fluentd`, `filebeat`, `vector`, or `promtail` artifact (6.4.1.3, group 11) | There is nothing to configure; a shipper would have to consume the captured stream out-of-band |

One further gap deserves explicit statement because it is easy to overlook: **there is no shutdown record**. The server registers zero `'close'` listeners and the process registers zero `exit`, `beforeExit`, `SIGTERM`, and `SIGINT` listeners, so a stop emits nothing — after `SIGTERM` the captured stdout was unchanged at 41 bytes with 0 bytes on stderr (*Host observation*). A log stream for this service therefore contains start transitions only, never stop transitions; an operator reconstructing a timeline must infer each stop from the *next* start or from the exit code observed at the time.

#### 6.5.2.3 Distributed Tracing

**Status: Not applicable — the system is neither traceable nor a trace participant.**

Section 5.4.2 states the posture; the measurements taken for this section confirm each of its three components independently.

| Tracing capability | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inbound context extraction | Absent | `traceparent`, `tracestate`, `b3`, and `x-request-id` all return zero matches (*Audit result*), and `req` is never dereferenced, so no header can be read (*Source fact*) |
| Span creation and export | Absent | No OpenTelemetry, OTLP, collector, Jaeger, or Zipkin artifact among the 15 tracing and OTel terms tested; no tracing SDK could be present, as no dependency manifest exists |
| Outbound context propagation | Not applicable | The service makes no outbound call of any kind (6.1.2.2), so there is no downstream hop to propagate to |
| Correlation identifier generation | Absent | No identifier is generated or emitted; the only log record carries no field of any kind |
| Sampling configuration | Not applicable | No sampler exists, and with no configuration read there is no rate to set |

The architectural consequence is precise: a distributed trace that arrives at this service **terminates at it with no span recorded**, and the caller's own span is the only evidence the hop occurred. There is also no instrumentable seam — no middleware chain, no framework hook, and no `diagnostics_channel` subscription — so tracing could not be added by wrapping the application; it would require editing the handler itself.

#### 6.5.2.4 Alert Management

**Status: Absent — there is no alert source, no rule evaluation, and no delivery path.**

Alerting requires a signal, a rule, and a receiver. All three are missing, and the first absence is the decisive one: with no metric and no log beyond the startup line, **there is nothing for a rule to evaluate**. Section 6.1.3.2 reaches the same conclusion from the scaling side, observing that an operator confronting overload "has no signal to observe it with".

| Alerting component | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Signal source | Absent | No metric, no counter, no error log, no access log; stdout invariant at 41 bytes under all traffic (*Host observation*) |
| Rule engine or evaluator | Absent | No alert rule file, recording rule, or evaluator configuration; the 16 descriptor classes searched in 6.5.1.3 include every YAML and JSON form and none exists |
| Notification transport | Absent | 10 alert-transport terms — `alertmanager`, `pagerduty`, `opsgenie`, `webhook`, `slack`, `smtp`, and others — returned zero matches; the process opens no outbound socket, so it cannot notify anything |
| Alert state and suppression | Not applicable | With no alert source there is no firing state to track, deduplicate, group, silence, or inhibit |
| Self-healing actuator | Absent | No supervisor, restart policy, or orchestrator exists (3.6.3, 3.6.5), so no alert could trigger an automated response |

Consequently **all alert generation must live in the operator's prober**, not in the system. The complete set of conditions that are detectable at all, and the signal each is detected from, is enumerated in the alert threshold matrix in 6.5.4.2; the routing model that follows from having a single human recipient is documented in 6.5.4.1.

#### 6.5.2.5 Dashboard Design

**Status: Absent** in the repository — no dashboard definition, panel specification, or visualisation artifact exists (14 terms in group 8 of the audit, zero matches; no Grafana JSON among the descriptor classes searched).

A dashboard is nonetheless constructible from the obtainable metrics of 6.5.2.1, and stating its shape is the most useful thing this sub-section can do, because it makes the boundary between the observable and the unobservable visible at a glance. Diagram 6.5-B lays out the minimum viable operator view: four panel groups whose every panel is backed by a measured signal, plus a fifth group listing the panels that **cannot** be built because no data source exists.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph AvailabilityRow["Panel group 1 — Availability, prober-derived"]
        direction LR
        A1["UP / DOWN single stat<br/>last probe returned 200<br/>DOWN evidence: curl exit 7, status 000"]
        A2["Probe success ratio over window<br/>the only availability figure obtainable"]
        A3["Body-integrity indicator<br/>body equals 14 bytes, SHA-256 c98c24b677ef<br/>guards against a foreign process on port 3000"]
    end
    subgraph LatencyRow["Panel group 2 — Response time, prober-derived"]
        direction LR
        B1["Probe round-trip time series<br/>observed 0.000181 to 0.000735 s over 12 samples<br/>includes client connection setup"]
        B2["Probe interval and poll count<br/>this is the PROBE rate, never the service request rate"]
        B3["Note panel: server-side latency unavailable<br/>no timing instrumentation exists"]
    end
    subgraph ProcessRow["Panel group 3 — Process and capacity, host-derived"]
        direction LR
        C1["Resident memory<br/>50,868 KiB idle to 59,212 KiB under burst"]
        C2["Open descriptors as connection proxy<br/>22 baseline, plus exactly 1 per connection"]
        C3["CPU time against the one-core ceiling<br/>6.1.3.1: one thread held 97.4% of process CPU"]
        C4["Thread count invariant at 7<br/>a change here would indicate a code change, not load"]
    end
    subgraph EventRow["Panel group 4 — Lifecycle events, stream and exit-code derived"]
        direction LR
        D1["Readiness-line occurrences<br/>one 41-byte record per successful bind"]
        D2["stderr byte count<br/>0 in steady state; non-zero means a fatal fault"]
        D3["Last exit code<br/>1 bind conflict, 143 TERM, 130 INT"]
        D4["Restart count and uptime<br/>derived from process start time"]
    end
    subgraph Unbuildable["Panels that cannot be built — no data source exists in the system"]
        direction LR
        E1["Request rate and total requests"]
        E2["Error rate and status-code breakdown"]
        E3["Server-side latency percentiles"]
        E4["Per-route, per-method, per-tenant breakdowns"]
        E5["Trace waterfall and dependency map"]
        E6["Business or conversion KPIs"]
    end
    AvailabilityRow --> LatencyRow
    LatencyRow --> ProcessRow
    ProcessRow --> EventRow
    EventRow -.->|"boundary of the observable"| Unbuildable
```

**Diagram 6.5-B — Dashboard layout for the observable signal set. Panel groups 1 to 4 are each backed by a measured signal; every panel in group 5 is unbuildable because the system produces no corresponding data. Note that group 1 is the only availability evidence, group 2 measures the prober rather than the service, and group 3 is host-level rather than application-level.**

Three design cautions follow directly from the evidence and should accompany any such dashboard. **A green availability panel is weak evidence**: it confirms only that something on `127.0.0.1:3000` answered with the expected bytes, which is why the body-integrity panel exists alongside it. **The latency panel measures the prober**, since client-observed round-trip time includes connection setup and client process cost — 6.1.3.1's in-process measurements at concurrency 1 are an order of magnitude lower than the `curl`-observed values recorded here, and neither figure is a service-level target. And **no panel on this dashboard can show degradation**: 6.1.4.5 establishes that overload manifests only as latency, and with no server-side latency signal a degraded system renders identically to a healthy one until it stops answering.

#### 6.5.2.6 Monitoring Infrastructure Status Matrix

| Infrastructure capability | Status | Where it would have to live |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metrics instrumentation | Absent | Inside `server.js` — no seam exists to wrap |
| Metrics exposition endpoint | Absent; `/metrics` returns the constant body and fails a scraper's parse | Inside `server.js` — requires reading the request URL, which the handler never does |
| Metrics collection and storage | Absent | Operator-supplied prober plus a time-series store, co-located on the host |
| Log emission beyond one record | Absent | Inside `server.js` — one `console.log` exists, at bind time only |
| Log capture and retention | Delegated to the launching shell | Operator-supplied stream capture; nothing is persisted by the system |
| Log aggregation and search | Absent | Operator-supplied, consuming the captured stream out-of-band |
| Trace context and span export | Not applicable | Inside `server.js`; no downstream hop exists to propagate to |
| Alert rule evaluation | Absent | Operator-supplied prober; no in-system signal exists to evaluate |
| Alert delivery and escalation | Absent | Operator-supplied; the process opens no outbound socket |
| Dashboard definition | Absent | Operator-supplied, from the nine obtainable metrics of 6.5.2.1 |
| Automated remediation | Absent | Operator-supplied supervisor; none exists in the repository (3.6.3) |

### 6.5.3 Observability Patterns

This sub-section addresses the five mandated observability patterns. One of them — health checking — is genuinely available in a degenerate form and is therefore documented in operational detail. The remaining four are absent or not applicable, and for each the useful content is what an operator can nonetheless determine from outside, and where the resulting blind spot lies.

#### 6.5.3.1 Health Checks

**Status: Delegated and degenerate.** No health-check code exists — the nine health-route terms tested in 6.5.1.3 return zero matches, and 3.6.5 records the same finding operationally ("no health endpoint"). What exists instead is a **side effect of path-insensitivity**: because the handler never dereferences the request, every URI is a health endpoint and none of them means anything more than the others.

This was measured exhaustively. Nine URIs — `/`, `/healthz`, `/health`, `/readyz`, `/livez`, `/metrics`, `/status`, `/does-not-exist`, and `/admin` — each returned `200` with the identical `Hello, World!` body, and six methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, `OPTIONS`) each returned `200` with a 14-byte body while `HEAD` returned `200` with a zero-length body, the runtime suppressing the entity (*Host observation*; 6.4.3.3 records the equivalent result over a different URI set). An `HTTP/1.0` request to `/healthz` was answered as `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `Connection: close`.

Two consequences must be stated plainly because they invert normal expectations:

- **A `200` from `/healthz` is not a health signal.** It proves that the listener accepted a connection, that the event loop turned at least once, and that a response was written. It proves nothing about correctness of any dependent behaviour, because the path is never examined and no dependency exists.
- **Liveness and readiness are indistinguishable.** Section 5.4.1 states this posture; the mechanism is that the process reaches its serving state atomically at bind time and has no warm-up, cache fill, or state rebuild (6.1.4.2 verified byte-identical responses across independent restarts). There is therefore no interval during which the process is alive but not ready, and no signal that could express one.

Because the endpoint is uniform, the discriminating power of a health check comes entirely from **what the prober asserts**. The table below records the assertion set that the measurements support.

| Assertion | Value to assert | What it adds over a weaker check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transport reachable | TCP connect to `127.0.0.1:3000` succeeds | Distinguishes "down" from every other state; after termination `curl` exits 7 with status `000` |
| Response received within a timeout | A response arrives before the prober's deadline | The **only** way to detect a stalled event loop: the LISTEN socket and the process entry both persist while the loop is blocked |
| Status and length | `200` with `Content-Length: 14` | Confirms a complete response rather than a truncated or chunked one |
| Body equality | Body is exactly `Hello, World!\n`, SHA-256 prefix `c98c24b677ef` | Guards against a foreign process holding port 3000 — no `Server`, version, or instance header exists to identify the real service (6.4.4.4, 3.6.6) |

Three operational parameters follow from measurements rather than convention. A probe must use **`GET`, not `HEAD`**, if it asserts the body, since `HEAD` legitimately returns zero bytes. A probe issued sooner than roughly **28 ms after launch** may observe a refused connection — the measured time to first accepted connection was 27.9 ms, and 6.1.4.2 measured 31.3–33.0 ms from launch to first `200` across four trials — so any startup grace period must exceed that window to avoid a false negative. And each poll should **open its own connection**, because an idle keep-alive connection was closed by the server 6.01 s after its response, consistent with the 5,000 ms `keepAliveTimeout` default (*Runtime default* plus *Host observation*).

Diagram 6.5-C shows the resulting evaluation flow. It is the complete diagnostic decision procedure available for this system, and it resolves to exactly five distinguishable states.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Poll(["Scheduled poll from a co-located prober"])
    Poll --> Connect{{"TCP connect to 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>succeeds?"}}
    Connect -->|"No — curl exit 7, status 000"| ProcCheck{{"Does a matching process exist?<br/>pgrep -fc node server.js"}}
    ProcCheck -->|"Count is 0"| StateDown["STATE: DOWN — process absent<br/>Recovery: relaunch after confirming port 3000 is free"]
    ProcCheck -->|"Count is 1"| StateBound["STATE: ANOMALOUS — process present, port not answering<br/>Check the LISTEN entry 0100007F:0BB8 in /proc/net/tcp"]
    Connect -->|"Yes"| Respond{{"Response received before<br/>the prober deadline?"}}
    Respond -->|"No"| StateStalled["STATE: STALLED — event loop blocked or saturated<br/>Only detectable by timeout; process and socket both look healthy"]
    Respond -->|"Yes"| Verify{{"Status 200, Content-Length 14,<br/>and body equals the 14-byte constant?"}}
    Verify -->|"No"| StateImpostor["STATE: UNVERIFIED — something else answers on port 3000<br/>No Server or version header exists to identify the service"]
    Verify -->|"Yes"| StateUp["STATE: UP — listener accepting and event loop turning<br/>Says nothing about latency margin or load"]
    StateUp --> NoDegrade["Blind spot: degradation is invisible here<br/>6.1.4.5 — overload manifests only as latency,<br/>and no server-side latency signal exists"]
```

**Diagram 6.5-C — Health-check evaluation flow. The five terminal states are the complete set of conditions this system's signals can distinguish. Note that STALLED is detectable only by a response timeout, and that no state on this diagram represents partial or degraded health.**

#### 6.5.3.2 Performance Metrics

**Status: Absent** in the application; performance is observable only from outside, and only as a client-side or host-level quantity. Section 5.4.5 establishes the two-category convention that governs every figure here, and it is applied strictly: nothing below is a target.

**Category 1 — inherited runtime budgets.** The application sets no timing or limit property, so the entire performance envelope consists of Node.js defaults, read directly from the live server object created by the unmodified `server.js`.

| Inherited budget | Value | Observability consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `keepAliveTimeout` | 5,000 ms | Idle connections are reclaimed silently; measured close at 6.01 s. A prober holding a connection between polls will be disconnected without any log record |
| `headersTimeout` | 60,000 ms | A client may spend a minute sending headers with nothing observable happening |
| `requestTimeout` | 300,000 ms | The single most consequential inherited value: a slow client can occupy a connection for five minutes, invisible to every available signal except a descriptor count |
| `server.timeout` | 0 (per-socket inactivity timeout disabled) | No socket is closed for inactivity by policy, so descriptor occupancy is bounded only by the values above |
| `maxRequestsPerSocket` | 0 (unlimited) | No socket is retired after a request quota, so per-connection volume is unmeasurable and uncapped |
| `maxConnections` | `undefined` (uncapped) | No admission ceiling exists, so overload cannot be signalled by rejection — only absorbed as latency |
| `http.maxHeaderSize` | 16,384 bytes | Exceeding it yields `431` with `Connection: close` — a client-visible event that the service never records |

**Category 2 — measured host characteristics.** These figures were obtained by executing the unmodified `server.js` on one verification host on one occasion. They describe that host on that occasion; they are not requirements, capacity guarantees, or service levels.

| Measured characteristic | Observed value | Interpretation and caveat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time to first accepted connection | 27.9 ms from process spawn | Startup is dominated by runtime initialisation; the application performs one `require` and no I/O. Sets the floor for any startup grace period |
| Client-observed request latency | min 0.000181 s, median 0.000294 s, max 0.000735 s over 12 `curl` samples | Includes connection setup and client process cost. 6.1.3.1's in-process measurements at concurrency 1 are an order of magnitude lower — the two are not comparable, and neither is a target |
| Burst behaviour | 300 requests at concurrency 30 completed in 0.062 s with a **single** distinct outcome, `(200, 14)`, 300 times | No error, truncation, or request loss at that level; also confirms that no rejection signal exists to observe |
| Throughput ceiling | Authoritative figures are in 6.1.3.1: a plateau of roughly 66,000–81,000 requests per second, peaking near concurrency 8 | A single-connection Python-client measurement taken for this section returned ~12,376 requests per second and is **client-bound**, illustrating how strongly measurement method affects any such figure |
| Memory footprint | 50,868 KiB resident at idle, 59,212 KiB after the 300-request burst; the process reported 46.7 MiB itself at idle | Baseline is dominated by the runtime, not the application, which allocates nothing per request |
| Thread and descriptor stability | 7 threads and 22 descriptors before and after load | Invariance is itself the signal: a change in thread count would indicate a code change, not load |

The observability conclusion is uncomfortable and worth stating directly: **the system's performance is measurable only by the party generating the load.** A prober measures its own round trip; the host measures memory and CPU. Nothing measures what real callers experience, and 6.1.4.5 records the consequence — a degraded system is externally indistinguishable from a healthy one until it stops answering.

#### 6.5.3.3 Business Metrics

**Status: Not applicable — the system performs no business transaction.**

Every candidate subject of a business metric is absent, and each absence is structural:

| Business-metric prerequisite | Position in this system |
| --- | --- |
| A distinguishable business operation | None — every URI and method produces the identical constant response, so no operation can be named or counted separately |
| A user or account identity | None — the request is never dereferenced, so no caller attribute is ever observed (6.4.2.1) |
| A state change to count | None — nothing is written, stored, cached, or queued (6.2), so no created, updated, or completed entity exists |
| A value, quantity, or outcome dimension | None — the response is a 14-byte compile-time constant with no variable content |
| A funnel, conversion, or session concept | None — no session is established and no cookie is set (6.4.2.3) |

The only countable event associated with the system is "a request was answered", and even that count exists **nowhere inside the system** — it can only be tallied by the client that made the requests. Section 1.2.3.1 records the corresponding finding at the specification level: the repository defines no success criteria of any kind.

#### 6.5.3.4 SLA Monitoring

**Status: Not applicable — no service level is declared anywhere in the repository, and none could currently be measured.**

This is a verified absence: the 14 service-level terms tested in 6.5.1.3 (`slo`, `sla`, `error budget`, `apdex`, `percentile`, `p95`, `p99`, and others) return zero matches; 6.1.1.2 tested 19 service-level and capacity artifact paths with zero present; and 5.4.5 records "no SLA, SLO, error budget, availability target, latency target, throughput target, capacity assumption, benchmark, or load-test artifact". The table below documents the position for each conventional SLA dimension, together with the measurement that would be available if a target were ever declared.

| SLA dimension | Declared in the repository | Measurement available today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Availability / uptime | **None declared** | Probe success ratio only. Its resolution equals the poll interval, and detection latency is unbounded between polls (5.4.6) |
| Response-time objective | **None declared** | Client-observed round-trip time only; no server-side timing exists, so any percentile would describe the prober |
| Error-rate objective / error budget | **None declared** | **Not computable** — there is no request counter and no error counter, so neither the numerator nor the denominator of an error rate exists |
| Throughput commitment | **None declared** | Only load-generator-side counts; the plateau in 6.1.3.1 is a host observation, not a commitment |
| Recovery time objective | **None declared** | The recovery *action* was measured at 31.3–33.0 ms (6.1.4.2), but total recovery time is dominated by unbounded detection latency |
| Recovery point objective | **Not applicable** | No data exists to lose; a restart returns the system to a byte-identical condition (5.4.6) |
| Maintenance and change windows | **None declared** | Termination is abrupt and undrained, so any restart is indistinguishable from a crash to a client |
| Dependency / counterparty SLAs | **Not applicable** | No outbound dependency exists; 5.1.4 records "none declared" for every counterparty |

Two structural obstacles must be cleared before *any* service level could be monitored for this system, and neither is a configuration matter. **The denominator is missing**: with no request count, availability can only be expressed as a ratio of synthetic probes, which measures the endpoint's response to the prober rather than to real traffic. And **the clock is missing**: the single log record carries no timestamp (6.5.2.2), so event times must be assigned at ingest by the capturing tool, which places a floor on the accuracy of any downtime accounting. The honest position is the one recorded in 5.4.5: the system offers no telemetry on which a service-level measurement could be based, so a target would have to be accompanied by the instrumentation to measure it.

#### 6.5.3.5 Capacity Tracking

**Status: Absent** in the application; partially observable from the host, with no saturation signal at any layer.

Section 6.1.3.5 establishes the capacity model and its coefficients, and this sub-section does not restate them beyond what is needed to identify each tracking signal. The point of interest here is which capacity dimensions can be *watched over time* and which cannot.

| Capacity dimension | Observable proxy | Limitation of the proxy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concurrent connections | Open descriptor count from `/proc/<pid>/fd`, above the 22-descriptor idle baseline; exactly one descriptor per connection, verified at 100, 250, and 500 held connections (6.1.3.3) | Counts connections, not requests; a keep-alive connection issuing thousands of requests looks identical to an idle one |
| Memory headroom | Resident set size; 50,868 KiB idle to 59,212 KiB under a 300-request burst, with roughly 1.63 kB per held idle connection (6.1.3.3) | Host-level only; there is no per-request or per-allocation attribution |
| CPU headroom against the real ceiling | Process CPU time compared with one core — 6.1.3.1 measured one thread holding 97.4% of process CPU and a ceiling of 102.5% of a single core, or 6.4% of the 16-core host | The ceiling cannot be raised by granting more cores, so a host-level CPU dashboard understates saturation by a factor of roughly sixteen |
| Event-loop saturation | **None** | No `dropRequest` listener, no loop-lag measurement, and no queue gauge; saturation appears only as growing latency that nothing records |
| Descriptor headroom | Ceiling of 1,048,576 on the verification host | Not the binding constraint; concurrency is limited by event-loop throughput and memory |
| Instances per host | Fixed at one while the port literal stands; a second instance exits with code 1 | There is no aggregation path, so per-host capacity equals per-instance capacity (6.1.3.1) |
| Growth trend and forecast | Only host-level memory and CPU series | With no traffic counter, demand cannot be trended at all — only the resources consumed by unknown demand |

The decisive limitation is the one 6.1.3.5 states for capacity planning generally: with no request counter, latency histogram, or saturation metric, **there is no way to observe where the deployed system sits relative to its measured ceiling**. Capacity tracking for this system therefore consists of watching host-level resource series that are dominated by the runtime baseline, against a throughput ceiling that can only be established by deliberately generating load — which is a benchmark exercise, not monitoring.

### 6.5.4 Incident Response

No incident-response mechanism exists in the repository: there is no alert rule, no notification transport, no on-call artifact, no runbook, and no post-mortem or improvement-tracking process — 6.1.1.2 tested 28 resilience, health, and runbook paths with zero present, and 6.4.1.3 found no monitoring, SIEM, or alerting artifact among 224 audited paths. What follows is therefore not a description of a configured process. It is a specification of the response capability the measured signals actually support, so that an operator confronting an outage of this service knows exactly what can be detected, what can be diagnosed, and what is unknowable.

#### 6.5.4.1 Alert Routing

**Status: Absent — no alert originates in the system, so all routing is external by necessity.**

Three verified facts fix the routing model. The process **cannot emit an alert**: it opens no outbound socket (6.1.2.2), holds no configuration through which a destination could be supplied, and has no timer with which to fire. There is **no automated recipient**: no supervisor, restart policy, or orchestrator exists (3.6.3, 3.6.5), so nothing could act on an alert if one arrived. And the endpoint is **loopback-only** — a request to the host's routable address `10.76.0.92:3000` failed to connect while the loopback request returned `200` — so even detection must occur on the host itself.

Diagram 6.5-D traces the resulting flow. Detection, classification, and delivery all live in the operator plane; the system contributes only passive signals, and the terminal recipient is a human.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Signals["Passive signals — the system's only contribution"]
        direction LR
        S1["Probe response<br/>200 with 14-byte body, or refusal"]
        S2["Process and LISTEN entry<br/>present or absent"]
        S3["stdout readiness line<br/>41 bytes, at bind time only"]
        S4["stderr trace and exit code<br/>fatal faults only, 1 / 143 / 130"]
    end
    subgraph Detection["Detection — operator-supplied, co-located on the host"]
        direction TB
        D1["Poll evaluator: connect, timeout, status,<br/>Content-Length, exact body"]
        D2["Presence evaluator: pgrep count<br/>and /proc/net/tcp entry 0100007F:0BB8"]
        D3["Stream evaluator: readiness line present,<br/>stderr byte count greater than 0"]
        D1 --> Classify
        D2 --> Classify
        D3 --> Classify
        Classify{{"Classify against the<br/>threshold matrix in 6.5.4.2"}}
    end
    subgraph Delivery["Delivery — single tier, no transport in the repository"]
        direction TB
        R1["Human operator with host access<br/>the only recipient and the only correlator"]
        R2["No pager, webhook, chat, or mail receiver<br/>10 alert-transport terms: 0 matches"]
        R3["No automated actuator<br/>no supervisor, no restart policy"]
    end
    Runbook["Manual response per 6.5.4.4<br/>verify port free, relaunch, assert 200 and 14 bytes"]
    S1 --> D1
    S2 --> D2
    S3 --> D3
    S4 --> D3
    Classify -->|"actionable condition"| R1
    Classify -.->|"no in-system emitter exists<br/>process opens no outbound socket"| R2
    Classify -.->|"no automated remediation path"| R3
    R1 --> Runbook
    Runbook -->|"re-probe to confirm recovery"| D1
    Silent["Undetectable by any route: client-visible 400 and 431,<br/>slow responses, and every stop event —<br/>termination emits no record at all"]
    Silent -.-> Classify
```

**Diagram 6.5-D — Alert flow. Every element outside the signal group must be supplied by the operator; the two dashed paths mark capabilities that do not exist, and the lower note records the conditions that no route can detect.**

#### 6.5.4.2 Alert Threshold Matrix

The matrix below is the complete set of conditions that the available signals can distinguish. **Provenance is stated for every threshold, and where a numeric value has no basis in the repository that is said explicitly** — the repository declares no threshold, target, or budget of any kind (6.5.3.4).

| Condition | Detecting signal | Threshold and provenance | Verified disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Endpoint unreachable | Probe connect result | Any single failed connect (*Host observation* — after termination every poll failed with `curl` exit 7 and status `000`; there is no partial-availability state to average away) | Service is down; nothing restarts it automatically |
| Process absent | `pgrep -fc "node server.js"` | Count `< 1` (*Host observation* — measured 1 while serving, 0 after termination) | Requires manual relaunch (6.5.4.4) |
| Listener absent while process present | `/proc/net/tcp` entry `0100007F:0BB8` state `0A` | Entry missing (*Host observation*) | Anomalous; not reproduced in any probe, since the socket's lifetime equals the process's |
| Response body mismatch | Body bytes and `Content-Length` | Any deviation from the 14-byte constant (*Host observation* — byte-identical on every probe, SHA-256 prefix `c98c24b677ef`) | Something other than this service is answering on port 3000; no header identifies the real service |
| No response before deadline | Prober timeout | **No repository basis for any value.** Observed client-side maximum was 0.000735 s over 12 samples; the inherited `requestTimeout` of 300,000 ms and `headersTimeout` of 60,000 ms bound the *client's* pace, not the server's | Sole detector of a stalled event loop; process and socket both continue to look healthy |
| Readiness line missing after launch | Captured stdout | Absent beyond the measured 27.9 ms to first accepted connection and the 31.3–33.0 ms to first `200` (*Host observation*, 6.1.4.2) | Bind failed; inspect stderr and the exit code |
| stderr non-empty | Captured stderr byte count | `> 0` bytes (*Host observation* — exactly 0 in steady state through roughly 2,300 requests and four protocol-error probes) | A fatal runtime fault occurred; the trace names it |
| Bind conflict on start | Exit code plus stderr trace | Exit code `1` with `listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` and **zero** stdout bytes (*Host observation*) | Recovery-blocking: the port must be freed before a relaunch can succeed (6.1.4.2) |
| Unexpected termination | Exit code | `143` for `SIGTERM`, `130` for `SIGINT` are operator-initiated; anything else is unexpected (*Host observation*) | Available only after the fact; no stop record is ever written |
| Wrong file launched | Exit code plus stderr trace | Exit code `1` with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and zero stdout bytes if `test.js` is executed instead of `server.js` (*Host observation*) | No listener is created at all; relaunch with `node server.js` (6.6.1) |
| Descriptor growth without traffic | `/proc/<pid>/fd` count | **No repository basis for any value.** Baseline 22, exactly one per connection, returning to 22 after connections close, with no leak observed (*Host observation*, 6.1.3.3) | Sustained growth with no offered load would indicate connection accumulation |
| Memory growth | Resident set size | **No repository basis for any value.** Observed 50,868 KiB idle, 59,212 KiB after a 300-request burst, and 77,388 KiB after 382,144 requests (6.1.3.3) | No leak was observed; the baseline is dominated by the runtime |
| Elevated protocol errors | **None available** | Not applicable — `400` and `431` are visible only to the client; the handler is never entered and the service records nothing (*Host observation*) | Detectable only from the caller's side |
| Latency degradation under load | **None available** | Not applicable — no server-side timing exists; 6.1.4.5 records that overload manifests only as latency | Undetectable until the service stops answering |

#### 6.5.4.3 Escalation Procedures

**Status: Absent — no escalation artifact exists, and the structure of the system collapses escalation to a single tier.**

There is no on-call rotation, no `CODEOWNERS`, no `SECURITY.md` or `security.txt` disclosure channel, no issue or pull-request template, and no branch-protection or review policy — 6.4.1.3 tested 18 governance paths with zero present, and 3.6.4 confirms no such metadata exists in-tree. Three properties of the system determine the escalation model that remains:

| Escalation property | Position, with basis |
| --- | --- |
| Who can detect an incident | Only a party with access to the host: the endpoint refuses non-loopback connections, and the readiness line goes to the launching shell's stdout |
| Who can resolve an incident | Only a party with host shell access, since recovery is a manual relaunch and there is no supervisor or remote control surface (3.6.5) |
| Who can fix a defect | Only a party who can commit to the repository; the history contains three commits by a single author of record with no review gate, and the most recent of them added a file that fails on execution (6.4.3.5, 3.6.4) |
| How severity is assigned | **It cannot be.** Availability is binary (6.1.4.5) and no signal expresses partial health, so every detectable incident carries the same severity: the service is not answering |
| Escalation trigger | None definable from telemetry — there is no error rate, latency percentile, or budget-burn signal to escalate on (6.5.3.4) |
| Time-based escalation | Not supportable — detection latency is unbounded between polls, so elapsed-time accounting begins at the first failed poll rather than at the failure |

The practical shape is a **one-hop path**: detection by whoever is watching the host, resolution by whoever holds a shell on it, and — only if the cause was a defect rather than an environment condition — a commit by whoever holds repository access. There is no second tier to escalate to, because there is no capability a second tier would possess that the first does not.

#### 6.5.4.4 Runbooks

**Status: Absent** in the repository; the procedures below are derived entirely from behaviour verified for this specification and are stated so that each step has an observable success criterion. Section 3.6.5 documents the launch procedure itself; these are the incident-response procedures that surround it.

The complete recovery sequence, with its verification, is three commands:

```bash
pgrep -fc "node server.js"        # 0 confirms the process is absent
node server.js                    # expect the 41-byte readiness line on stdout
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/    # expect exactly: Hello, World!
```

| Procedure | Verified steps and success criteria |
| --- | --- |
| **P1 — Confirm an outage** | Probe the endpoint: a refusal (`curl` exit 7, status `000`) plus `pgrep -fc "node server.js"` returning 0 is a confirmed outage. Both were observed together after termination. If the process is present but no response arrives before the deadline, treat it as a stall (P5), not an outage |
| **P2 — Recover from an outage** | Confirm port 3000 is free, then run `node server.js` — the entry point must be named explicitly, since no manifest declares one and the tree contains a second, non-application `.js` file. Success is the 41-byte readiness line followed by a `200` with the exact 14-byte body. Measured recovery action: 31.3–33.0 ms from launch to first `200` across four trials (6.1.4.2), with no warm-up or state rebuild |
| **P3 — Resolve a bind conflict** | Symptom: exit code 1, zero stdout bytes, and a stderr trace naming `EADDRINUSE ... 127.0.0.1:3000`. The port holder must be identified and stopped before any relaunch; **no fallback port is attempted and no retry occurs**, because the application registers zero `'error'` listeners. This condition blocks recovery entirely |
| **P4 — Perform a planned restart** | `SIGTERM` (exit 143) or `SIGINT` (exit 130) terminates immediately. **There is no draining**: in-flight requests are abandoned, open keep-alive connections are closed with no protocol-level notice, and **no shutdown record is written** — stdout remained at 41 bytes and stderr at 0. A planned restart is therefore indistinguishable from a crash from both the client's and the log's point of view |
| **P5 — Investigate a stalled process** | The process entry and the LISTEN socket both persist while the event loop is blocked, so presence checks cannot detect a stall. The only evidence is a probe that connects but receives no response before its deadline. There is no loop-lag metric, `dropRequest` hook, or queue gauge to consult, so diagnosis must proceed from host-level CPU and descriptor observation |
| **P6 — Investigate a body mismatch** | A `200` whose body is not the 14-byte constant means the responder is not this service; no `Server`, version, or instance header exists to confirm identity (6.4.4.4). Verify the process identity in the process table and the owner of the LISTEN socket before assuming a service defect |
| **P7 — Preserve evidence before recovery** | Capture the current stdout and stderr, the exit code, the process's resource counters, and the failing probe output **before relaunching**, because a restart produces byte-identical output and leaves no trace of the prior instance — the readiness line carries no timestamp, PID, or build identifier (6.5.2.2) |
| **P8 — Resolve a failed launch that is not a bind conflict** | Symptom: exit code 1, zero stdout bytes, and a stderr trace that names neither `EADDRINUSE` nor `server.js` — for example `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` at `test.js:1`. Cause: the wrong tracked file was executed, or a test runner selected it (`node --test` at the repository root discovers `test.js` and fails; 6.6.1). Re-run `node server.js` explicitly |

#### 6.5.4.5 Post-Mortem Processes

**Status: Absent** as a process; and severely constrained as an activity, because the forensic record is nearly empty. Section 6.4.3.5 states the underlying finding without qualification: the system is not auditable at runtime.

| Post-mortem question | Can it be answered? | Evidence and limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did the service stop? | Yes | Probe refusal plus absent process; both verified |
| When did it stop? | **Only bounded, never determined** | No stop record exists (zero `'close'`, `exit`, and `beforeExit` listeners), so the stop time is only known to lie between the last successful poll and the first failed one |
| Why did it fail to start? | Yes, for the one fatal class | The `EADDRINUSE` trace names the address, port, `errno`, and Node version (6.4.4.4); other fatal classes would likewise surface on stderr |
| Was it stopped deliberately? | Yes, if the exit code was captured | `143` and `130` indicate signals; `1` indicates a bind conflict or a failed launch |
| What requests were served? | **No** | No access log exists; stdout was invariant at 41 bytes across roughly 2,300 requests and nine attack-shaped probes (6.4.1.5) |
| What did callers experience? | **No** | No server-side status, latency, or error record; client-visible `400` and `431` responses leave no trace in the service |
| Which build was running? | **No** | No version field, tag, or `CHANGELOG` exists (3.6.6), and no response header or log field identifies a build |
| Was the failure preceded by degradation? | **No** | No latency or saturation signal exists; 6.1.4.5 records that a degraded system is indistinguishable from a healthy one |
| Was there abuse or misuse? | **No** | Attack-shaped traffic generates no security event record at all (6.4.1.5, 6.4.3.5) |

The consequence for post-mortem practice is specific: a review of an incident with this service can establish **that** it stopped, **roughly when** it was noticed, and — in the single case of a bind conflict — **why** it would not start, and nothing more. Any deeper finding must come from outside the system: from the client that made the requests, from host-level resource series if they were being collected, or from the operator's own recollection. Section 6.1.4.2 quantifies why this matters: the recovery action is roughly 32 milliseconds while detection latency is unbounded, so nearly all of an incident's duration is time during which the system emitted nothing at all.

#### 6.5.4.6 Improvement Tracking

**Status: Absent** as a process; **present but unenforced** for source change, in the minimal form Git provides.

There is no issue tracker artifact, no `TODO` or `CHANGELOG`, no tag, no CI gate, no test suite, and no `CODEOWNERS` — 3.6.4 records that all three commits landed without any automated verification and that change verification is entirely manual ("launch the server and probe it"), while 3.6.6 records that the commit SHA is the only version identity the artifact has. An improvement arising from an incident can therefore be *made* (as a commit) but cannot be *tracked* against an identifier, *verified* by an automated gate, or *correlated* with the incident that motivated it.

The one artifact that does support improvement tracking is the Git history itself: three commits — `241598b` adding `README.md`, `06492d7` adding `server.js`, and `43ed37c` adding the 13-byte `test.js` — all signed server-side but with no policy requiring or verifying the signature (6.4.3.5). Because no monitoring change has ever been made, the history contains no observability improvement to trace; and the one change that has been made since the application landed added no test, no assertion, and no signal, while itself passing through no gate.

What can be recorded concretely is the **gap register** below: each observability gap established in this section, and the specific incident-response capability it currently blocks. It is a statement of documented position, not a plan.

| Observability gap | Incident-response capability it blocks | Documented in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No request, error, or latency counter | Alert thresholds, error budgets, and any severity classification | 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.4 |
| No access or error log | Post-incident reconstruction of what was served and what callers experienced | 6.5.2.2, 6.5.4.5 |
| No timestamp in the only log record | Timeline construction and downtime accounting | 6.5.2.2, 6.5.3.4 |
| No stop or shutdown record | Determining when an outage began | 6.5.2.2, 6.5.4.5 |
| No build, version, or instance identifier | Attributing an incident to a deployed change | 6.5.2.1, 6.5.4.4 (P6) |
| No dedicated health route distinct from the service path | Distinguishing a healthy instance from one that merely listens | 6.5.3.1 |
| No supervisor, restart policy, or alert transport | Automated detection, notification, and remediation | 6.5.2.4, 6.5.4.1 |
| No off-host reachability for a poller | Detection by anyone without host access | 6.5.1.6, 6.5.4.3 |
| No configuration layer or timer | Enabling any of the above without editing `server.js` | 6.5.1.2, 6.5.2.1 |
| No automated verification of any change | Preventing a regression — or a non-functional file — from reaching the branch head | 3.6.4, 6.4.3.5, 6.6.1 |

#### 6.5.5.3 Runtime Probes and Host Interfaces Consulted

- **Stream-volume probes** — captured stdout and stderr across the process lifetime: 41 bytes and 0 bytes at startup, unchanged after roughly 2,300 requests (16 probe requests, 2,000 keep-alive requests, and a 300-request burst) and after four protocol-error probes, and unchanged again at `SIGTERM` shutdown. Basis for 6.5.1.1, 6.5.1.5, 6.5.2.2, and the log-volume rows of 6.5.4.2.
- **Response-contract probe** — `curl -D -` established `200 OK`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Date`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, `Content-Length: 14`, and the 14-byte body, and the absence of any `Server`, version, build, instance, or request-identifier header. Basis for 6.5.1.5 and 6.5.3.1.
- **Path- and method-insensitivity probes** — nine URIs (`/`, `/healthz`, `/health`, `/readyz`, `/livez`, `/metrics`, `/status`, `/does-not-exist`, `/admin`) and seven methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, `OPTIONS`, `HEAD`) all returned `200`, with `HEAD` returning a zero-length body. Basis for the health-check findings in 6.5.3.1 and the `/metrics` scrape finding in 6.5.2.1.
- **Live server-object introspection** — a preloaded wrapper around `http.createServer` read the actual object created by the unmodified `server.js`, establishing `keepAliveTimeout` 5,000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60,000 ms, `requestTimeout` 300,000 ms, `server.timeout` 0, `maxRequestsPerSocket` 0, `maxConnections` `undefined`, `maxHeadersCount` `null`, and `http.maxHeaderSize` 16,384 bytes; and listener counts of `error` 0, `clientError` 0, `timeout` 0, `close` 0, `request` 1, `connection` 1, `listening` 1, with process-level `SIGTERM`, `SIGINT`, `SIGHUP`, `uncaughtException`, `unhandledRejection`, `exit`, and `beforeExit` all 0. Basis for 6.5.3.2 and the silent-termination finding in 6.5.1.5 and 6.5.2.2.
- **Latency, burst, and throughput probes** — 12 `curl` round-trip samples (min 0.000181 s, median 0.000294 s, max 0.000735 s); a 300-request burst at concurrency 30 completing in 0.062 s with a single distinct `(200, 14)` outcome; and a 2,000-request single-connection Python measurement recorded explicitly as client-bound. Basis for 6.5.2.1 and 6.5.3.2.
- **Process and host counters** — `ps -o pid,rss,nlwp`, `/proc/<pid>/fd`, `pgrep -fc "node server.js"`, `/proc/net/tcp` (entry `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A`), `ulimit -n` (1,048,576), `nproc` (16), and `free -m` (124,784 MiB). Established the 7-thread / 22-descriptor / 50,868 KiB-idle footprint, the 59,212 KiB post-burst figure, and the listener and process presence signals. Basis for 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.5, and 6.5.4.2.
- **Failure, recovery, and reachability probes** — a second instance exiting with code 1, zero stdout bytes, and the `listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` trace; `SIGTERM` exit 143 and `SIGINT` exit 130; post-termination probe refusal (`curl` exit 7, status `000`) with a process count of 0; successful manual relaunch re-emitting the readiness line and restoring `200`; time to first accepted connection of 27.9 ms; an idle keep-alive connection closed by the server at 6.01 s; runtime-generated `400 Bad Request` (malformed request line, and TLS ClientHello bytes to the plaintext port), `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` (~20 KiB of headers), and an `HTTP/1.0` request answered as `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `Connection: close`; and a refused connection to the host's routable address `10.76.0.92:3000` while loopback succeeded. Basis for 6.5.1.5, 6.5.1.6, 6.5.3.1, 6.5.4.2, and 6.5.4.4.
- **Wrong-entry-point probe** — `node test.js` exited 1 with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and produced no listener and no stdout, while `node --check test.js` exited 0. Basis for the launch-selection constraint in 6.5.1.6 and procedure P8 in 6.5.4.4.

## 6.6 Testing Strategy

### 6.6.1 Testing Strategy Applicability Assessment

#### 6.6.1.1 Determination

**Detailed Testing Strategy is not applicable for this system.**

The repository at HEAD `43ed37c` (branch `2907_01`, clean working tree) contains exactly three tracked files totalling 382 bytes: `server.js` (342 bytes, 14 lines), `README.md` (27 bytes, 1 line), and `test.js` (13 bytes, 2 lines). `server.js` creates one HTTP server, binds it to the hard-coded loopback endpoint `127.0.0.1:3000`, answers every request with an unconditional `200` / `Content-Type: text/plain` / 14-byte `Hello, World!\n` body, and prints a single readiness line to stdout. There is no second module, no routing table, no configuration layer, no persistence, no authentication, no outbound dependency, and no user interface. The system is a single-file demonstration server, not a multi-component application, so the layered discipline a full testing strategy exists to coordinate — test pyramids across services, contract tests between components, fixture databases, browser matrices, environment promotion — has no subject matter here.

**`test.js` is a test in name only, and this distinction governs the whole of §6.6.** Its complete content is two bare identifier expression statements, `asdsa` and `asdasd`. It declares no test, registers no case with any runner, makes no assertion, imports no framework, requires nothing, and exports nothing. `node --check test.js` exits 0, so the file is syntactically valid JavaScript; executing it raises `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and exits 1 (**Host observation**). It therefore contributes **zero test coverage of `server.js`** and satisfies no acceptance criterion in §2.1. Its one operational consequence is documented in §6.6.1.3: because Node's default test-runner discovery pattern includes `**/test.?(c|m)js`, `node --test` at the repository root now finds this file and **fails**.

The absence of a testing capability is therefore not merely one of tooling — it survives the presence of a file whose name suggests otherwise. A repository-wide audit found **no functioning testing artifact of any kind**: no test that asserts anything, no test directory, no test runner or coverage configuration, no CI/CD pipeline, no quality gate, no linter, no dependency manifest, and no test environment descriptor (§6.6.1.3). Git history confirms nothing was removed: across all three commits on all branches the only files ever added are `README.md`, `server.js`, and `test.js`.

What this section therefore documents is the **basic unit testing approach appropriate to a system of this size**, together with the integration- and end-to-end-level checks that the observable contract admits. To keep the recommendation honest rather than aspirational, the proposed baseline was executed against the unmodified committed file on the verification host before being written down: a 14-test suite built exclusively on the Node.js built-in test runner reached **100.00% line, branch, and function coverage of `server.js`** in approximately 0.094 s wall time with **zero packages installed**. The harness lived entirely outside the repository checkout — which is also why it is unaffected by the root-level `test.js` — and `git status --porcelain` returned zero tracked-file lines before and after all experimentation.

#### 6.6.1.2 Determination Criteria

| Criterion | Observed state | Effect on determination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number of deployable components | One process, one module (`server.js`) | No inter-component contract to test; integration testing collapses to a single-process HTTP probe |
| Branching / decision points in application logic | Zero conditionals in the handler (`server.js` L6–L10) | One request achieves total coverage; no equivalence classes, boundary values, or error paths to partition |
| Request inputs consumed | None — method, path, query, headers, and body are never read | No input-validation, injection, or parsing test surface |
| Persistent state | None — no database, cache, file, or in-memory store | No fixture loading, no migration testing, no teardown of data |
| External integrations | None — one `require('http')` of a Node.js core module | Nothing to stub, mock, record, or replay |
| User interface | None — response is `text/plain`, not HTML | UI automation and cross-browser testing have no subject |
| Committed test infrastructure | Absent in every category audited (§6.6.1.3). One path, `test.js`, matches a test-file name pattern but contains no test, no assertion, and no framework reference | The non-applicability clause is triggered on evidence, not on judgement; the name of a file is not a capability |
| Declared quality thresholds | None anywhere in the repository | No coverage target, success-rate requirement, or performance budget can be reported as existing |

Consistency with previously documented sections: §1.3 already places "Automated testing and coverage enforcement" and "CI/CD pipelines and quality gates" out of scope, and lists "Unit or integration testing within a test harness" as an unsupported use case — findings that remain correct, because the file added since then contains no test, no assertion, and no framework; §2.2 records "Requirements covered by automated tests | 0" and "Requirements with a declared performance target | 0"; §3.6.4 records that all three commits landed without any automated verification and that change verification is entirely manual — launch the server and probe it. This section does not contradict those findings — it quantifies them and defines the minimal, right-sized approach that would change them.

#### 6.6.1.3 Testing Artifact Audit

Each group below was probed by direct filesystem existence tests, a repository-wide content grep, git-history inspection, and semantic search. Every probe returned an absence of testing *capability*; one probe returned a matching *path*, and that distinction is recorded explicitly rather than averaged away.

| Artifact group | Representative paths / patterns probed | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Test code and directories | `*test*`, `*spec*`, `__tests__/`, `test/`, `tests/`, `spec/`, `e2e/`, `cypress*`, `playwright*` | **One matching path** — the root-level `test.js` (13 bytes) added by commit `43ed37c`. It contains no test case, no assertion, and no runner import; it is a placeholder, not a test. No test directory exists in any form |
| Dependency and task manifests | `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `yarn.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `npm-shrinkwrap.json`, `node_modules/`, `Makefile`, `Taskfile.yml`, `justfile` | Absent — no `npm test` script, no devDependencies, no task runner |
| Test runner configuration | `jest.config.{js,ts,mjs,json}`, `vitest.config.{js,ts}`, `.mocharc.{json,yml,js}`, `karma.conf.js`, `ava.config.js`, `tap.yml`, `.taprc` | Absent |
| Coverage and quality configuration | `.nycrc`, `.c8rc.json`, `.coveragerc`, `codecov.yml`, `sonar-project.properties`, `coverage/` | Absent — no thresholds, no report output |
| CI/CD pipelines | `.github/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, `.travis.yml`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`, `.drone.yml`, `appveyor.yml` | Absent — no automated trigger of any kind |

| Test environment definition | `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.{yml,yaml}`, `.env`, `.env.example`, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.tool-versions`, `tsconfig.json` | Absent — no pinned runtime, no containerised environment |
| Assertion / runner tokens in source | grep for `describe(`, `it(`, `test(`, `assert`, `expect(`, `jest`, `mocha`, `vitest`, `supertest`, `nyc`, `coverage`, `npm test`, `node --test` | Absent — **zero matches across all three tracked files**, including `test.js`, whose 13 bytes contain no token from this set |
| Historical test assets | `git log --all --diff-filter=A --name-only` across `241598b`, `06492d7`, and `43ed37c` | Only `README.md`, `server.js`, and `test.js` were ever added, so **no test asset ever existed and was removed**; the one path whose name resembles a test was added, not deleted, and asserts nothing |
| Built-in runner behaviour at the repository root | `node --test` (Node.js v22.23.1) | **Fails.** Discovery matches `test.js` against the default pattern; the file throws on evaluation, producing `not ok 1 - test.js` with `failureType: 'testCodeFailure'` and `code: 'ERR_TEST_FAILURE'`, totals of `# tests 1`, `# pass 0`, `# fail 1`, and **exit code 1** |
| Semantic index corroboration | four natural-language searches for test suites, CI pipelines, test directories, and package manifests | All returned empty result sets |

The runner result deserves to be stated plainly because it inverts the naive expectation. Before commit `43ed37c` the built-in runner was inert at the repository root — there was nothing for it to discover. It is now the opposite of inert and no more useful: **the repository's only runner-visible artifact is a non-test file that makes the built-in runner fail**, so a `node --test` gate introduced today would block every change until the file is fixed or removed, while still asserting nothing whatsoever about `server.js`. The coverage finding is unchanged and unaffected: `test.js` exercises no line of `server.js`, so committed test coverage of the application remains **0%** (§6.6.4.1).

This audit is consistent with, and narrower than, the 224-path / 11-group security artifact audit recorded in §6.4, whose "Security scanning and CI gates" and "Supply chain" groups also returned zero present paths.

#### 6.6.1.4 Testability Constraints Imposed by the Source

Four properties of `server.js` dictate the shape of every test discussed in §6.6.2 onward. They are structural facts about the committed code, not preferences.

| Constraint | Source evidence | Consequence for testing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The module exports nothing | No `module.exports` / `exports.` / `export` anywhere; `Object.keys(exports)` is empty (F-005-RQ-003) | The handler and the server instance cannot be imported by name; a unit test must create its own seam |
| Binding is a module-load side effect | `server.listen(port, hostname, cb)` executes at top level on `require` (L12) | A naive `require()` inside a test binds TCP `127.0.0.1:3000`, or fails with `EADDRINUSE` if the port is held |
| Endpoint constants are hard-coded | `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` (L3), `port = 3000` (L4); no `process.env`, no argv parsing (F-002-RQ-003) | Per-worker port allocation is impossible without a source edit, which caps parallel execution at one live instance |
| The handler has zero branches | L7–L9 set status, one header, and one literal body unconditionally | Total statement, branch, and function coverage is reachable with a single invocation; coverage ceases to be a meaningful progress signal |

A fifth constraint is contributed not by `server.js` but by the tracked inventory around it: **the file name `test.js` is already taken by a non-test file that throws on evaluation.** Any suite added at the repository root must therefore either repair or replace that file, or select a discovery pattern that excludes it — otherwise the runner's default glob will pick it up and fail the run before any real assertion executes.

Two testing seams follow directly from the first two constraints, and both were exercised successfully: intercepting `http.createServer` to capture the handler **without** binding a socket (in-process, §6.6.2.1), and spawning the file as a child process and probing it over loopback (out-of-process, §6.6.2.2 and §6.6.2.3). §3.6.1's observation that any future unit test would need the code refactored to separate construction from binding describes the alternative — a source change — and remains the cleaner long-term option; the interception seam is what is available without modifying the artifact.

#### 6.6.1.5 Evidence Conventions and Status Vocabulary

This section reuses the vocabulary established in §6.1, §6.4, and §6.5 so that statuses read identically across Chapter 6.

| Term | Meaning in this section |
| --- | --- |
| Delegated | The behaviour exists but is provided by the Node.js runtime, not by application or test code |
| Absent | The capability is not present in the repository at HEAD `43ed37c` |
| Not applicable | The capability has no subject matter in this system, so its absence is correct rather than a gap |

Every factual claim carries one of four provenance labels.

| Label | Basis |
| --- | --- |
| Source fact | Read directly from `server.js`, `README.md`, or `test.js` at HEAD `43ed37c` |
| Audit result | Produced by an existence probe, content grep, git query, or tool exit code |
| Runtime default | A Node.js-supplied value or behaviour that the application does not set |
| Host observation | Measured on the single verification host by executing the unmodified file |

Because the repository contains no test harness, this section additionally labels certain statements **Harness result**: measurements produced by an illustrative suite written to a scratch directory outside the checkout (`/tmp/ts66`, 8,128 bytes) and executed against the unmodified committed file. Harness results demonstrate feasibility and cost; they are not repository contents. All runtime and harness evidence was produced on one host with Node.js v22.23.1, npm 11.18.0, and Git 2.43.0, against HEAD `43ed37c` with a clean tree; `server.js` is byte-identical at HEAD and at its introducing commit `06492d7` (blob `320a75a`), so the coverage and timing figures apply to both revisions. **No number, threshold, or duration in this section may be read as a commitment, an SLA, or an existing requirement** — the repository declares none, and §2.2 records zero requirements with a declared performance target.

#### 6.6.1.6 Scope of the Baseline Documented in This Section

The remainder of §6.6 documents, in order: the three-level testing approach the observable contract admits (§6.6.2), the automation that would carry it (§6.6.3), the quality metrics and gates that would govern it (§6.6.4), the environment and resource footprint it requires (§6.6.5), and the security testing that is meaningful for a component with no inputs and no dependencies (§6.6.6). Throughout, **Observed** state at HEAD `43ed37c` — in every case either nothing at all, or, for the single runner-visible path, a file that asserts nothing and fails on execution — is kept strictly separate from the **Verified baseline** (what was proven achievable against the unmodified artifact).

The verified baseline at a glance:

| Dimension | Measured result (Harness result) |
| --- | --- |
| Packages installed | 0 — `node:test` and `node:assert` ship with the runtime |
| Suite size | 14 tests across 2 files: 6 unit, 8 black-box contract |
| Outcome | 14 pass / 0 fail / 0 skipped / 0 todo |
| Coverage of `server.js` | 100.00% line, 100.00% branch, 100.00% function |
| Wall time, three consecutive runs | 0.100 s, 0.094 s, 0.093 s |
| Exit-code gating | pass gives 0; failing assertion gives 1; coverage threshold breach gives 1 |
| Repository impact | None — `git status --porcelain` empty for tracked files; harness confined to `/tmp` |

For contrast, the **committed** state measured with the same runner on the same host: `node --test` at the repository root yields 1 test, 0 pass, 1 fail, exit code 1, and 0% coverage of `server.js` (§6.6.1.3). The 14-test baseline above was executed from `/tmp/ts66`, outside the checkout, so its result is independent of the root-level `test.js`.

Diagram index for this section:

| Diagram | Subject | Location |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6.6-A | Test execution flow across the three levels, including the binding decision | §6.6.2.4 |
| 6.6-B | Test environment architecture and the port-contention boundary | §6.6.5.1 |
