### 6.6.2 Testing Approach

Three testing levels are documented below. For each, the **Observed** state at HEAD `43ed37c` is stated first — in every case it is *Absent*, since the tree's one test-named path contains no test and no assertion (§6.6.1.3) — followed by the **Verified baseline**, meaning a concrete approach that was executed successfully against the unmodified committed file from a scratch directory outside the checkout. Topics that have no subject matter in this system are marked *Not applicable* with the evidence that makes them so, rather than being padded with generic advice.

#### 6.6.2.1 Unit Testing

##### 6.6.2.1.1 Testing Frameworks and Tools

**Observed:** Absent. There is no test framework, no dependency manifest that could declare one, and no `node_modules/` directory. `npm` 11.18.0 is installed on the host but idle, since there is nothing for it to resolve.

**Verified baseline:** the Node.js **built-in test runner** (`node:test`) with `node:assert/strict`. Both modules loaded successfully on the verification host with **zero packages installed**, and the complete flag surface needed for organisation, filtering, coverage, sharding, and reporting was present in `node --help`. Externally, the built-in runner shipped as experimental in Node.js 18 and has been stable since Node.js 20, so it is available wherever a currently supported runtime is available; code coverage is still gated behind `--experimental-test-coverage`, and the coverage *threshold* flags used in §6.6.4 were introduced in Node.js 22.8.0.

This choice is not stylistic. The repository has no manifest and no lockfile (§3.3), and `npm audit` is structurally inoperable here — it exits 1 with `ENOLOCK`, "This command requires an existing lockfile". Adopting Jest, Vitest, or Mocha would introduce a `package.json`, a lockfile, and a transitive dependency tree — and therefore a supply-chain surface and a scanning obligation — into a 382-byte repository that currently has none. The built-in runner preserves the zero-dependency posture that §3.3 and §6.4 document.

| Tool | Role in the baseline | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `node:test` | Test declaration, discovery, execution, concurrency | Delegated to the runtime — ships with Node.js |
| `node:assert/strict` | Assertions, including deep and byte-exact comparisons | Delegated to the runtime |
| `--experimental-test-coverage` | V8-based line, branch, and function coverage | Delegated to the runtime — flag is experimental |
| `--test-reporter` (`spec`, `tap`, `dot`) | Human and machine-readable result output | Verified working on the host |
| `node --check server.js` | Syntax pre-flight; exit 0 observed | Only in-repo verification that exists today (§3.6.2) |
| `npm audit` | Dependency vulnerability scanning | Not applicable — inoperable without a lockfile |

One operational detail worth recording, because it cost a run during verification: passing a directory to the runner (`node --test --test-reporter=spec unit/`) failed with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on Node.js v22.23.1. Auto-discovery from the working directory (`node --test`) worked and found every test file. Scripts should rely on discovery or on explicit file paths, not on directory arguments.

A second discovery detail is specific to this repository and must be handled before the runner is used inside the checkout: auto-discovery from the repository root matches the existing root-level `test.js`, which declares no test and throws on evaluation, so the run fails with exit code 1 before any assertion executes (§6.6.1.3).

##### 6.6.2.1.2 Test Organization Structure

**Observed:** Absent — no `test/`, `tests/`, `__tests__/`, or `spec/` directory has ever existed in this repository's history. The only test-named path is the root-level `test.js` file added by commit `43ed37c`, which contains no test case and no assertion (§6.6.1.3).

**Verified baseline:** a four-directory layout that the runner discovers without any configuration file, because the default discovery patterns already match files under `test/`, files named `test.js`, and files ending in `.test.js`:

```text
repository-root/
  server.js                      <- the artifact under test, never modified by tests
  test.js                        <- exists today; not a test, throws on load - repair,
                                    remove, or exclude it from discovery first
  test/unit/handler.test.js      <- Level 1, no socket bound
  test/integration/contract.test.js  <- Level 2, probes a live listener
  test/e2e/lifecycle.test.js     <- Level 3, spawns and terminates a child
  test/fixture/server.port-3100.js   <- port-shifted copy for isolated Level 3 runs
```

The runner executes **each matching file in its own child process**, so file boundaries are also isolation boundaries. This matters more here than in a typical project: the Level 1 file must never bind a socket, while the Level 3 file deliberately does. Keeping them in separate files means a stray listener in one cannot leak into the other, and a crash in one does not mask results in the other. The verified harness used exactly this separation — six unit tests in one file, eight contract tests in another — and reported 14 tests, 14 pass, 0 fail, 0 skipped, 0 todo.

The same per-file isolation is what makes the existing `test.js` a blocking rather than a cosmetic problem: it would be discovered as a peer of the real test files and would contribute one failing "test" to every run, so the layout above is only adoptable once that file is dealt with.

##### 6.6.2.1.3 Mocking Strategy

The mocking strategy is dictated entirely by the constraint in §6.6.1.4: `server.js` exports nothing, and `require`-ing it binds `127.0.0.1:3000` as a load-time side effect. There is no function to import and no injection point to supply.

**Verified baseline:** create the seam at the module boundary by replacing `http.createServer` before loading the file, capturing the handler that the application passes in, and returning a stub whose `listen` merely invokes its callback. No socket is ever created, so the unit level is immune to port contention.

```javascript
const real = http.createServer;
http.createServer = (h) => { captured = h; return { listen: (p, host, cb) => (cb && cb(), {}) }; };
delete require.cache[require.resolve(TARGET)]; require(TARGET); http.createServer = real;
```

Two details are load-bearing. First, `delete require.cache[...]` is mandatory: without it the second and subsequent loads are no-ops and the handler is never re-captured. Second, restoring `http.createServer` in a `finally` block is mandatory, because a leaked patch would silently disable the integration and end-to-end levels running later in the same process. The response object is a hand-rolled double recording `statusCode`, `setHeader` calls, and the `end` payload — a plain object is sufficient because the handler touches only those three members.

One observed side effect: because the stub's `listen` invokes the application's callback, the readiness line is printed once per module load — six times in the verified six-test run. Tests must tolerate that output, or capture stdout deliberately; a test asserting "no output" in the same file would fail for the wrong reason.

| Candidate mock target | Present in this system? | Approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `http.createServer` | Yes — the only seam (`server.js` L6) | Module-property interception, restored in `finally` |
| Database client / ORM | No driver, no connection string (§6.2) | Not applicable |
| Outbound HTTP client | Zero outbound sockets; no `fetch`/`axios` | Not applicable |
| Message broker / queue | Zero of the messaging paths audited in §6.1 | Not applicable |
| Filesystem, clock, timers | No `fs`, no `setTimeout`, no `Date` usage in source | Not applicable |
| Environment variables | No `process.env` reference anywhere | Not applicable |

`node:test` also exposes a built-in `mock` object for spies and method replacement; it is available should the seam ever be widened, but the verified baseline needs only direct property assignment, which keeps the pattern legible in three lines.

##### 6.6.2.1.4 Code Coverage Requirements

**Observed:** Absent. No `.nycrc`, `.c8rc.json`, `codecov.yml`, `sonar-project.properties`, or `coverage/` output directory exists, and no threshold is declared anywhere in the repository. Measured coverage of `server.js` by committed code is **0%** — nothing in the tree exercises it (§6.6.1.3).

**Verified baseline:** running the six unit tests under `--experimental-test-coverage` reported **`server.js` at 100.00% line, 100.00% branch, and 100.00% function coverage** with no uncovered line ranges; the aggregate across all files was also 100.00/100.00/100.00.

The important caveat is interpretive. Because the handler contains zero conditionals, coverage here is effectively a **binary liveness check on the test suite itself**: either the module was loaded and the handler invoked, giving 100%, or it was not. A drop below 100% would not mean "new untested logic appeared" — it would mean a test stopped executing. That is still worth gating on, precisely because the ceiling is trivially reachable; §6.6.4 therefore sets the threshold at 100 rather than at a conventional 80. Coverage must not be mistaken for the real quality signal in this system, which is the byte-exactness of the response contract assertions.

##### 6.6.2.1.5 Test Naming Conventions

**Observed:** Absent — there are no test names to have a convention.

**Verified baseline:** each test name states the observable behaviour and terminates with the governing requirement identifier from §2.2, so that a failure message alone identifies the violated requirement.

```javascript
test('handler sets Content-Type text/plain (F-003-RQ-002)', () => { /* assertions */ });
```

| Convention | Rule | Practical benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File names | `<subject>.test.js` under `test/<level>/` | Matched by default discovery — no config file needed |
| Test names | `<behaviour in the present tense> (<F-ID>)` | Failure output names the requirement, not just the file |
| Selection | `--test-name-pattern="F-003"` | Runs the whole response-contract group in isolation |
| Exclusion | `--test-skip-pattern` | Skips socket-binding levels when a port is unavailable |

The pattern-selection flags were observed on the verification host, so requirement-scoped subsets are executable without restructuring files.

##### 6.6.2.1.6 Test Data Management

**Observed and structurally determined:** Not applicable in the conventional sense. `server.js` never reads the request method, path, query string, headers, or body, and the response body is a hard-coded literal. There are no input fixtures to manage, no factories or builders to write, no seed files, and no anonymisation concern — there is no data. The tracked tree contains no fixture or seed artifact either: `test.js` holds 13 bytes of placeholder text with no schema and no data content.

The only "test data" that exists is the **expected-value set**, five constants read directly from the source and confirmed on the wire:

| Expected value | Verified value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status code | `200` | `server.js` L7 (F-003-RQ-001) |
| Content type | `text/plain` | `server.js` L8 (F-003-RQ-002) |
| Body | `Hello, World!\n`, 14 bytes | `server.js` L9 (F-003-RQ-003) |
| Body digest | SHA-256 `c98c24b677eff44860afea6f493bbaec5bb1c4cbb209c6fc2bbb47f66ff2ad31` | Host observation, matches §6.3 and §6.4 |
| Readiness line | `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`, 41 bytes | `server.js` L13 (F-004-RQ-001) |

These should be declared once in a shared module and imported by all three levels. Asserting the digest in addition to the literal is cheap insurance against an invisible whitespace change — a stray trailing space would keep the string looking correct in a diff while changing `Content-Length` from 14, which is itself asserted.

#### 6.6.2.2 Integration Testing

##### 6.6.2.2.1 Service Integration Test Approach

**Observed:** Absent. §6.1 documents a service inventory of exactly one and an empty inter-service edge set — zero outbound sockets, zero messaging paths, zero database drivers, zero service-mesh or proxy descriptors. There is no second service with which to integrate.

Integration testing therefore has a different, narrower, and genuinely useful subject in this system: the **boundary between application code and the Node.js runtime**. `server.js` sets only `statusCode` and one header; the response line framing, `Content-Length`, `Date`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` headers, the HTTP parser, and the `400`/`431` protocol rejections are all runtime-supplied (F-003-RQ-004). A black-box HTTP test is the only mechanism that can assert *which side of that boundary each observable behaviour comes from*, and it is the reason this level is worth running at all despite there being a single process.

**Verified baseline:** eight black-box tests issuing `node:http` requests against a live listener, wrapped in a small promise helper. Result: 8 pass, 0 fail. No HTTP assertion library is required — adding `supertest` would demand a manifest and an exported app object, neither of which exists.

```javascript
const res = await get({ method: 'HEAD', path: '/' });
assert.equal(res.status, 200);
assert.equal(res.body.length, 0);              // HEAD body is empty, F-003-RQ-005
```

##### 6.6.2.2.2 API Testing Strategy

The API surface is one endpoint that answers every method and path identically, so the test strategy is not "cover the routes" but "pin the invariants and prove the delegation boundary". All eight cases below were executed and passed.

| Case | Assertion | Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Canonical response | `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, body exactly 14 bytes | F-003-RQ-001/002/003 |
| Header provenance | Emitted key set is exactly `connection`, `content-length`, `content-type`, `date`, `keep-alive`; `keep-alive` is `timeout=5` | F-003-RQ-004 |
| No version disclosure | `server` and `x-powered-by` headers are undefined | §6.4 hardening posture |
| `HEAD` semantics | `200` with a zero-byte body | F-003-RQ-005 |
| Request-shape invariance | `GET /`, `POST /admin`, `DELETE /x`, `TRACE /`, `GET /healthz` all return the identical body | F-001-RQ-002 |
| Input inertness | XSS-encoded query, `?secret=CANARY123` canary, forged `Cookie`, invalid `Bearer` — none reflected, body byte-identical | §6.6.6 |
| Malformed frame | Raw socket writing `BADREQUEST\r\n\r\n` yields `400`, handler never invoked | Runtime default |
| Oversized header | A 20,000-byte header field yields `431`, handler never invoked | Runtime default, `maxHeaderSize` 16384 |

The last case carries a trap worth documenting: `431` arrives as a **normal HTTP response**, not as a socket error. An initial version of this test used `assert.rejects` and was the single failure in the first harness run; asserting `status === 431` corrected it. The same applies to `400`. Tests must treat runtime protocol rejections as responses, because that is what a client observes.

##### 6.6.2.2.3 Database Integration Testing

**Not applicable.** There is no database, cache, or file-backed store of any kind: no driver dependency, no connection string, no ORM, no schema, no migration mechanism — as documented in §6.2. There is consequently nothing to provision, seed, truncate, snapshot, or roll back, and no transactional test isolation problem to solve. Test-container tooling has no image to start.

##### 6.6.2.2.4 External Service Mocking

**Not applicable.** The application makes zero outbound network calls. Its only dependency is one `require('http')` of a Node.js core module (F-005-RQ-001), and §6.1 records zero outbound sockets under sustained load. Request interception libraries, service virtualisation, contract-test brokers, and record/replay proxies all lack a subject. The single mock in the entire baseline is the `http.createServer` seam of §6.6.2.1.3, which mocks the *runtime*, not an external service.

##### 6.6.2.2.5 Test Environment Management

**Observed:** Absent. There is no `Dockerfile`, no `docker-compose.yml`, no `.env` or `.env.example`, and no runtime pin (`.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.tool-versions`, and `package.json` `engines` are all absent). The environment contract is therefore undocumented in the repository and must be stated externally.

The environment a test needs is minimal — a Node.js runtime and one free loopback TCP port — but the second half of that is the whole difficulty, and it was demonstrated from both directions during verification:

| Environment concern | Verified behaviour | Consequence for the suite |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Port already held | Launching a second instance on the same port exits **code 1** with `EADDRINUSE`, 0 bytes stdout, 626 bytes stderr | The suite cannot blindly start the committed file |
| Foreign process holding 3000 | A pre-existing `node server.js` on the host produced exactly the same failure for the harness | Port 3000 must be treated as shared, not owned |
| No port override | `port = 3000` is a constant with no environment or argv path (F-002-RQ-003) | Isolation requires a port-shifted fixture copy |
| Loopback-only bind | Probing the host's routable address is refused (§6.4) | The test client must be co-located with the server |
| No runtime pin | Verified on Node.js v22.23.1; runner stable since Node.js 20 | CI must pin the version itself |
| Two `.js` files in the tree | Only `server.js` starts a listener; `test.js` exits 1 with a `ReferenceError` | The entry point must be named explicitly, never inferred |

Two management patterns follow, and both are legitimate. **Attach mode** treats an already-listening `127.0.0.1:3000` as a precondition, probes it, and fails fast with a clear message if nothing is listening — this is what the verified eight-test suite did, and it never risks disturbing a running instance. **Own mode** spawns a port-shifted fixture whose only difference from the committed file is line 4 (verified by `diff`: `port = 3000` becomes `port = 3100`), giving the suite exclusive control of a port it allocated. Own mode is required for the end-to-end level and for any parallel execution.

#### 6.6.2.3 End-to-End Testing

##### 6.6.2.3.1 E2E Test Scenarios

For this system, "end to end" means the **process lifecycle**: launch, readiness, service, and termination — the same workflow §1.3 identifies as the single user workflow and §3.6.4 describes as today's entirely manual verification. Six scenarios cover it; all constituent behaviours have been observed on the verification host.

| Scenario | Steps | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S1 Cold start to first success | Spawn the fixture, wait for the readiness line, issue `GET /` | `200` with a 14-byte body; readiness observed at 29.1 ms |
| S2 Readiness signal contract | Capture stdout from launch through many probes | Exactly one 41-byte line and no per-request output (F-004-RQ-001/003) |
| S3 Termination behaviour | Send `SIGTERM` while a keep-alive connection is open | Immediate undrained exit (F-002-RQ-005); teardown measured at 1.9 ms |
| S4 Port contention | Start a second instance on the same port | Second process exits 1 with an `EADDRINUSE` stderr trace (F-002-RQ-004) |
| S5 Restart determinism | Terminate, relaunch, probe again | Byte-identical body across restarts — no warm-up or state rebuild |
| S6 Loopback confinement | Probe the host's routable address | Connection refused (F-002-RQ-002) |

S4 and S6 are the only genuinely negative end-to-end scenarios this system offers, which is itself a finding: there are no error responses, no validation failures, and no dependency outages to simulate.

##### 6.6.2.3.2 UI Automation Approach

**Not applicable.** The response is `Content-Type: text/plain` carrying 14 bytes; there is no HTML document, no script or stylesheet asset, no DOM, and no client-side state. Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and WebDriver have nothing to drive. Introducing any of them would add a browser download and a dependency manifest to a repository whose entire tracked content is 382 bytes — a cost with no corresponding assertion it could make that a three-line HTTP probe cannot.

##### 6.6.2.3.3 Test Data Setup and Teardown

Setup is a process spawn; teardown is a signal. There is no data to create or destroy at any level.

```javascript
const child = spawn(process.execPath, [FIXTURE], { stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'] });
await once(child.stdout, 'data');                     // 41-byte readiness line gates the probe
try { await probe(); } finally { child.kill('SIGTERM'); }
```

Two rules are non-negotiable, and both are grounded in measurement rather than preference:

- **Gate on the readiness line, never on a fixed sleep.** Across eight spawns of the fixture, readiness latency was 27.2, 27.2, 27.7, 29.1, 29.2, 29.6, 30.2, and 30.8 ms — median 29.2 ms. Any fixed delay below roughly 31 ms is intrinsically flaky on this host, and any value above it wastes time on every run. Because the application emits exactly one readiness line (F-004-RQ-001), the first stdout chunk is an exact, deterministic signal.
- **Terminate unconditionally in a `finally` or `after` hook.** A surviving child keeps the port bound and poisons every subsequent run — precisely the condition the verification host was in, where a leftover process from another session held port 3000 and caused an `EADDRINUSE` failure. `SIGTERM` was measured at 1.9 ms to exit, so unconditional teardown is essentially free. If a test ever leaves its own server handle open, the runner exposes `--test-force-exit` as an escape hatch.

##### 6.6.2.3.4 Performance Testing Requirements

**Observed:** Absent, and deliberately so. §2.2 records "Requirements with a declared performance target | 0"; there is no benchmark script, no load-test harness, no performance budget, no SLO, no latency ceiling, and no timeout the application itself sets. Every timeout in effect is a runtime default (`requestTimeout` 300000 ms, `headersTimeout` 60000 ms, `keepAliveTimeout` 5000 ms).

Load characterisation already exists and should not be re-derived here: §6.1.3 is authoritative, recording a throughput plateau of roughly 66,000–81,000 requests per second, median latency growing about 32× between concurrency 1 and 64, and 97.4% of process CPU confined to a single thread. Those are host observations on one machine, not thresholds.

If a performance check were ever added, the only defensible form is a **regression tripwire, not a target**: re-measure on identical hardware, compare against a recorded baseline, and alert on a wide relative deviation. Two candidate tripwires already have measured baselines — startup-to-readiness (median 29.2 ms) and full-suite wall time (0.093–0.100 s). Both are host-bound and neither may be published as a commitment.

##### 6.6.2.3.5 Cross-Browser Testing Strategy

**Not applicable** — no browser participates in any interaction. The meaningful analogue of a browser matrix for a `text/plain` HTTP endpoint is **client and protocol variance**, and that axis has been exercised:

| Browser-matrix analogue | Variance exercised | Verified result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP method | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, `HEAD` | Identical `200`/14-byte body; `HEAD` returns 0 bytes |
| Request target | `/`, `/api/v1/hello`, `/a/b`, `/x`, `/y`, `/healthz`, `/admin` | Byte-identical responses, identical SHA-256 |
| Malformed client behaviour | Raw socket frames, 20,000-byte header | Runtime returns `400` and `431` respectively |
| Transport | HTTPS attempt against port 3000 | Fails at TLS handshake — plaintext only (§6.4) |

#### 6.6.2.4 Test Execution Flow and Level Strategy Matrix

Diagram 6.6-A traces one invocation of the runner through all three levels, including the decision that separates the socket-free unit level from the two levels that require a listener.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Dev(["Developer or CI runner"])
    Cmd["Invoke the built-in runner<br/>node --test from a directory scoped to the suite"]
    Disc["Runner auto-discovers files matching<br/>the default test-name patterns<br/>one child process per file"]

    Dev --> Cmd
    Cmd --> Disc

    subgraph UnitLevel["Level 1 - Unit, in process, no socket"]
        U1["Patch http.createServer<br/>capture the handler argument"]
        U2["Clear require cache<br/>then require the unmodified server.js"]
        U3["Stub listen invokes its callback<br/>without binding any TCP port"]
        U4["Assert statusCode, Content-Type,<br/>exact 14-byte body, empty exports"]
        U5["Restore http.createServer in a finally block"]
        U1 --> U2 --> U3 --> U4 --> U5
    end

    subgraph ContractLevel["Level 2 - Integration, black box over loopback"]
        I0{"Is 127.0.0.1 port 3000<br/>already in LISTEN state?"}
        I1["Issue http.request probes<br/>methods, paths, HEAD, malformed frames"]
        I2["Assert response line, header key set,<br/>body bytes, runtime rejections 400 and 431"]
        I3["Fail fast - no listener to probe<br/>suite does not auto-start the committed file"]
        I0 -- Yes --> I1
        I1 --> I2
        I0 -- No --> I3
    end

    subgraph LifecycleLevel["Level 3 - End to end, spawn and teardown"]
        E1["Spawn a port-shifted copy of server.js<br/>as a child process"]
        E2{"Readiness line of 41 bytes<br/>observed on child stdout?"}
        E3["Probe the child over loopback<br/>then read RSS from proc"]
        E4["Send SIGTERM<br/>confirm undrained immediate exit"]
        E5["Abort on timeout<br/>report startup failure"]
        E1 --> E2
        E2 -- Yes --> E3
        E3 --> E4
        E2 -- No --> E5
    end

    Disc --> U1
    Disc --> I0
    Disc --> E1

    U5 --> Agg
    I2 --> Agg
    I3 --> Agg
    E4 --> Agg
    E5 --> Agg

    Agg["Runner aggregates results<br/>and V8 coverage per file"]
    Gate{"All tests passed and<br/>coverage thresholds met?"}
    Pass["Process exit code 0<br/>change is verified"]
    Fail["Process exit code 1<br/>reporter prints failing assertions"]

    Agg --> Gate
    Gate -- Yes --> Pass
    Gate -- No --> Fail
```

*Diagram 6.6-A — Test execution flow. The three levels are independent child processes; only Levels 2 and 3 touch a socket, which is why port availability is a gate for them and irrelevant for Level 1. Invoking the runner from the repository root instead of a scoped directory adds the non-test `test.js` to discovery and drives the run straight to the failure branch (§6.6.1.3).*

Level strategy matrix:

| Level | Seam used | Binds a socket | Verified outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `http.createServer` interception plus require-cache reset | No | 6 tests, 6 pass, 54.7 ms, 100% coverage |
| Integration | `node:http` client against a live listener | Yes — connects only | 8 tests, 8 pass, 59.8 ms |
| End-to-end | `child_process.spawn` of a port-shifted fixture | Yes — binds a new port | Readiness 29.1 ms, `SIGTERM` exit 1.9 ms |
| Combined | Runner auto-discovery, `--test-concurrency=2` | Levels 2 and 3 only | 14 tests, 14 pass, 64.1 ms |

| Requirement | Level that covers it | Representative assertion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| F-001-RQ-001 | Unit | Exactly one handler is registered and it is a function |
| F-001-RQ-002 | Unit and Integration | Identical response across request shapes |
| F-001-RQ-003 | Integration | Repeated probes return one unique body, no per-request state |
| F-002-RQ-001 | Unit | Loading the module triggers `listen` — observed via the stub |
| F-002-RQ-002 | End-to-end | Routable-address probe refused, loopback probe succeeds |
| F-002-RQ-003 | Unit | Stub records host `127.0.0.1` and port `3000` from the constants |
| F-002-RQ-004 | End-to-end | Second instance exits 1 with `EADDRINUSE` on stderr |
| F-002-RQ-005 | End-to-end | `SIGTERM` closes an open keep-alive connection without draining |

| F-003-RQ-005 | Integration | `HEAD` returns 200 with a zero-byte body |

### 6.6.3 Test Automation

#### 6.6.3.1 CI/CD Integration

**Observed:** Absent. `.github/` does not exist, and neither does `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `.circleci/`, `.travis.yml`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`, `.drone.yml`, or `appveyor.yml`. §3.6.4 records the same finding from the deployment perspective and states that all three commits landed without any automated verification, with change verification performed entirely by hand — launch the server and probe it. There is no `package.json`, so there is also no `npm test` entry point for a pipeline to call.

**Verified baseline:** a single job with no service containers, no build step, and no package installation. Every command below was executed on the verification host against the unmodified file, and each one's exit code was confirmed.

| Step | Command | Verified result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-flight | `node --check server.js` | Exit 0 — parses as CommonJS (§3.6.2) |
| Unit level | `node --test` with the unit file discovered | 6 pass, 54.7 ms |
| Full suite | `node --test` from the harness working directory, outside the checkout | 14 pass, 0 fail, 67.0 ms |
| Coverage gate | `node --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-lines=100 …` | 100% reported; a deliberate breach exits 1 |
| Whole job | Aggregate process exit code | 0 on success, 1 on any failure |

The working directory in the third row is not incidental. A job that ran `node --test` **inside the checkout** would fail on the current tree, because default discovery matches the root-level `test.js`, which throws on evaluation and produces exit code 1 with no assertion executed (§6.6.1.3). Any adoption of this baseline must therefore either place its test files somewhere the runner is scoped to, or repair or remove that file first.

Two integration properties make this trivial to wire into any CI system. First, the entire pipeline is expressible in shell with no third-party action or plugin, because the runner and the coverage collector are part of the runtime. Second, gating requires no wrapper script: the runner already exits 1 on a failing assertion and on an unmet coverage threshold, so the job's own exit status is the gate.

One obligation the repository does not discharge: **the pipeline must pin the runtime itself.** There is no `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.tool-versions`, or `engines` field, so nothing in the repository states which Node.js version is expected. The baseline was verified on v22.23.1; the built-in runner has been stable since Node.js 20, and the coverage-threshold flags relied on in §6.6.4 require Node.js 22.8.0 or later. A pipeline that does not pin a version is therefore capable of failing for reasons unrelated to any change in the tracked files.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Triggers["Trigger sources - none configured at HEAD 43ed37c"]
        T1(["Push to a branch"])
        T2(["Pull request opened or updated"])
        T3(["Manual dispatch by an operator"])
        T4(["Scheduled runtime-matrix run"])
    end

    subgraph Pipeline["Single job - would-be pipeline"]
        P1["Checkout the three tracked files<br/>382 bytes, only server.js is the application"]
        P2["Pin the Node.js runtime<br/>no version is declared in the repository"]
        P3["Pre-flight - node --check server.js"]
        P4["Level 1 unit run<br/>no socket, safe to parallelise"]
        P5["Allocate a free loopback port<br/>and write the port-shifted fixture"]
        P6["Level 2 and Level 3 runs<br/>serialised on the allocated port"]
        P7["Collect V8 coverage<br/>and emit spec plus TAP output"]
        P8["Unconditional teardown<br/>SIGTERM every spawned child"]
        P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P6 --> P7 --> P8
    end

    subgraph Gates["Quality gates - evaluated by process exit code"]
        G1{"Syntax pre-flight exit 0?"}
        G2{"All 14 tests passed?"}
        G3{"Coverage at 100 percent<br/>lines, branches, functions?"}
        G4{"No child process<br/>left holding a port?"}
        G1 -- No --> Block
        G2 -- No --> Block
        G3 -- No --> Block
        G4 -- No --> Block
        G1 -- Yes --> G2
        G2 -- Yes --> G3
        G3 -- Yes --> G4
    end

    T1 --> P1
    T2 --> P1
    T3 --> P1
    T4 --> P1

    P3 -.-> G1
    P7 -.-> G2
    P7 -.-> G3
    P8 -.-> G4

    G4 -- Yes --> Allow

    Allow["Exit code 0<br/>change carries evidence of verification"]
    Block["Exit code 1<br/>publish reporter output and coverage summary<br/>no retry, triage the reported cause"]
```

*Diagram 6.6-D — Automated trigger and quality-gate flow. Solid edges are execution order; dotted edges show which step feeds which gate. Every trigger and every gate shown is a recommendation — none exists in the repository at HEAD `43ed37c`.*

#### 6.6.3.2 Automated Test Triggers

**Observed:** Absent. No trigger of any kind exists — no workflow file, no `.husky/` directory, no `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, and no server-side hook configuration in the repository.

| Trigger | Applicability to this system | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push to any branch | Recommended primary trigger | The suite runs in under 0.1 s with no install, so per-push cost is negligible |
| Pull request | Recommended gate | The only mechanism that could block an unverified change; branches `main` (at `06492d7`) and `2907_01` (at `43ed37c`) both exist and have diverged |
| Manual dispatch | Useful for environment checks | Lets an operator confirm a runner's Node.js version before relying on it |
| Scheduled run | Narrowly useful | Zero dependencies means no drift to detect; the one real use is a runtime matrix across Node.js LTS lines |
| Tag or release | Not applicable | §3.6.6 records no tags, no `CHANGELOG`, and no version field — there is no release event to hook |
| Pre-commit hook | Optional | Would duplicate the push trigger; at 0.1 s it is affordable, but nothing in the repository installs hooks |

The pull-request row is the one with demonstrated value rather than theoretical value: commit `43ed37c` reached the branch head with no review and no status check, carrying a file that fails on execution (§6.4.3.5). A pull-request trigger running even the syntax and test gates of §6.6.4.4 is the smallest change that would have surfaced it.

Because the repository has no dependency manifest, the trigger class that dominates most Node.js projects — dependency-update pipelines from Dependabot or Renovate — has no subject here. Both configuration files were probed and are absent, and `npm audit` cannot run at all (§6.6.6).

#### 6.6.3.3 Parallel Test Execution

**Observed:** Not applicable — there are no tests to parallelise.

**Verified baseline:** the runner already provides process-level parallelism, executing each discovered test file in its own child process. Running the two-file suite with `--test-concurrency=2` completed in 64.1 ms against 67.0 ms for the default configuration — a difference within run-to-run noise at this scale, since three consecutive full-suite runs measured 0.100 s, 0.094 s, and 0.093 s wall time. At this size the cost is dominated by process startup, not by test execution, so parallelism is a correctness concern rather than a performance lever.

The correctness concern is hard and was proved empirically:

| Parallelism axis | Constraint | Verified evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit-level files | None — no socket is bound | 6 unit tests ran with the `createServer` stub, never touching TCP |
| Two listeners on one port | Forbidden — second process dies | Second instance exited **code 1** with `EADDRINUSE`, 0 bytes stdout, 626 bytes stderr |
| Per-worker port allocation | Blocked by the source | `port = 3000` is a constant with no override path (F-002-RQ-003); a fixture copy per port is required |
| Sharding across machines | Available but pointless | `--test-shard` exists on the host; a 0.094 s suite has nothing to distribute |

The practical rule: **Level 1 may run at any concurrency; Levels 2 and 3 must be serialised unless each worker owns a distinct port**, and because the committed constant cannot be overridden, owning a distinct port means generating a fixture file per port. The verified fixture differed from `server.js` by exactly one line (`diff` confirmed only line 4 changed), which makes generation safe and auditable, but it is a generated artifact and must never be committed in place of the original.

#### 6.6.3.4 Test Reporting Requirements

**Observed:** Absent — no reporter, no artifact directory, no coverage upload configuration (`codecov.yml`, `sonar-project.properties`, and `coverage/` are all absent).

**Verified baseline:** three of the runner's bundled reporters were exercised directly; one did not produce usable output in this configuration and is called out because a pipeline that assumed otherwise would publish an empty report.

| Reporter | Verified output | Recommended role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spec` | Default; per-test lines plus `# pass`/`# fail`/`# duration_ms` summary | Console output for humans |
| `tap` | `TAP version 13`, `1..8`, `# pass 8`, `# fail 0` | Machine-readable artifact of record |
| `dot` | Compact `........` progress output | Noise-free logs on frequent triggers |
| `junit` | **Emitted only an empty `<testsuites></testsuites>` pair** | Do not rely on it without first validating output in the target pipeline |
| `lcov` | Not exercised here; documented as coverage-only output | Candidate for coverage upload if a service is ever added |

Coverage reporting needs no extra tool: the `spec` and `tap` reporters print the coverage summary inline when `--experimental-test-coverage` is active, which is how the 100.00/100.00/100.00 figure for `server.js` was obtained.

Two cautions apply to anything that parses this output. The Node.js documentation states that reporter output may change between versions and should not be relied on programmatically, directing programmatic consumers to the runner's event stream instead. And the empty-`junit` result above is a concrete instance of exactly that fragility. **Gate on the process exit code, and treat reporter text as evidence for humans, not as a contract.**

#### 6.6.3.5 Failed Test Handling

Exit-code semantics were verified explicitly, because they are the whole of the enforcement mechanism:

| Condition | Verified exit code | Effect in a pipeline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All tests pass | 0 | Job succeeds |
| One failing assertion | 1 | Job fails; reporter prints the failing test name and diff |
| Coverage below threshold | 1 | Job fails even though every test passed |
| Server fails to bind during a test | 1 from the child, with `EADDRINUSE` on stderr | Job fails; the stderr trace names the address and port |
| A discovered file throws before declaring any test | 1, reported as `testCodeFailure` | Job fails with 0 pass and 1 fail — the current outcome of `node --test` at the repository root (§6.6.1.3) |

The following triage table lists the failure modes that were actually encountered while building and running the baseline, which makes it a record of real diagnostics rather than a generic checklist.

| Symptom | Cause established during verification | First action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EADDRINUSE` and a 626-byte stderr trace | Another process — possibly not this suite — already holds the port | Identify the holder; switch to an own-mode fixture on an allocated port |
| `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` from the runner | A directory was passed to `node --test` | Use auto-discovery or explicit file paths |
| `not ok 1 - test.js` with `testCodeFailure` and 0 tests declared | The runner discovered the repository's non-test `test.js`, which throws `ReferenceError` on evaluation | Scope discovery away from it, or repair or remove the file |
| A `431` or `400` case fails as "did not reject" | Runtime protocol rejections arrive as normal responses | Assert on `status`, not with `assert.rejects` |
| Unit test reports no captured handler | `require.cache` was not cleared before re-requiring | Delete the cache entry before each load |
| Suite does not exit | An open server handle keeps the loop alive | Close the handle, or apply `--test-force-exit` |
| Coverage drops below 100% | A test file stopped executing | Investigate the load failure — not missing tests for new logic |

**No automatic retry policy is recommended.** The application is deterministic — the response body is byte-identical across requests, methods, paths, and process restarts — so a repeatable assertion failure is a genuine defect in the code or in the expected-value set. The single environmental failure mode that *could* motivate a retry, port contention, is precisely the one that must be surfaced rather than hidden, because a leaked listener will otherwise corrupt every subsequent run on that machine. Retrying would convert a visible, fixable environment fault into intermittent noise.

#### 6.6.3.6 Flaky Test Management

Every source of nondeterminism identified during verification is environmental or harness-induced. None originates in the application code, which has no timers, no randomness, no clock dependency, no state, and no external calls.

| Flake source | Verified mechanism | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared fixed port | Two instances on one port — second exits 1 with `EADDRINUSE` | Own-mode fixture on an allocated port; never assume 3000 is free |
| Fixed-sleep readiness waits | Readiness spanned 27.2–30.8 ms across 8 spawns, median 29.2 ms | Gate on the single 41-byte readiness line, which is an exact signal |
| Leaked child processes | A surviving child keeps the port bound and breaks later runs | `SIGTERM` in an unconditional `finally`/`after` hook — measured 1.9 ms |
| Leaked `http.createServer` patch | A non-restored patch silently disables later levels | Restore in `finally` within the same helper that patches |
| Unintended discovery of a non-test file | The repository root already holds a `test.js` that matches the default pattern and throws | Run from a scoped directory or pass explicit file paths; this is deterministic, not flaky, but it presents as an unexplained failure |
| Parsing reporter text | `junit` produced an empty document in this configuration | Assert on exit codes; treat reporter output as human evidence |

Determinism evidence supporting a strict, zero-tolerance stance on flakes: three consecutive full-suite runs each reported 14 pass / 0 fail; the eight readiness samples fell within a 3.6 ms band; and repeated probes across nine different method-and-path combinations returned byte-identical bodies with identical SHA-256 digests.

Given a 14-test suite that completes in under a tenth of a second, **quarantine lists, retry budgets, and flake-tracking dashboards are disproportionate overhead**. The appropriate policy is that any flake is fixed in the same change that observes it, using the mitigations above. The one legitimate use of exclusion is capability-based rather than reliability-based: `--test-skip-pattern` can omit the socket-binding levels on a machine where no loopback port can be allocated, and that omission should be reported as reduced coverage of scope, not as a passing run.

### 6.6.4 Quality Metrics

Every metric in this sub-section is reported twice: as **Observed** at HEAD `43ed37c`, where without exception the value is *none declared*, and as a **Verified baseline** or **Recommended** figure. No value here is a commitment; §2.2 records zero requirements with a declared performance target, and the repository contains no threshold of any kind.

#### 6.6.4.1 Code Coverage Targets

**Observed:** no target. There is no coverage configuration file, no threshold declaration, and no coverage output directory. Committed coverage of `server.js` is **0%**: the only runner-visible file in the tree, `test.js`, exercises no line of the application and asserts nothing (§6.6.1.3).

**Verified baseline:** the six unit tests of §6.6.2.1 produced 100.00% line, 100.00% branch, and 100.00% function coverage of `server.js`, with no uncovered line ranges reported.

| Coverage dimension | Observed target | Baseline for this system | Enforcement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Line | None declared | 100% — verified reachable | `--test-coverage-lines=100` |
| Branch | None declared | 100% — the handler has no branches | `--test-coverage-branches=100` |
| Function | None declared | 100% — one function exists | `--test-coverage-functions=100` |
| Aggregate across files | None declared | 100% — verified 100.00 for all files | Same flags; runner exits 1 when unmet |

Enforcement was proved rather than assumed: setting an impossible line threshold (`--test-coverage-lines=101`) caused the runner to exit **1** while every test still passed, confirming that coverage gating is available without any third-party tool. The threshold flags require Node.js 22.8.0 or later, which the verification host satisfies at v22.23.1.

Setting the bar at 100% rather than a conventional 80% is a consequence of §6.6.2.1.4: with zero conditionals in the application, 100% is the trivial result of loading the module and invoking the handler once. A figure below 100% would therefore not indicate untested new logic — it would indicate that a test file failed to execute. The threshold is valuable as a **suite-liveness alarm**, and it should be read as nothing more than that.

#### 6.6.4.2 Test Success Rate Requirements

**Observed:** no requirement — §2.2 records "Requirements covered by automated tests | 0". The measured pass rate of the committed tree is worse than undefined: `node --test` at the repository root reports 1 test, 0 pass, 1 fail and exits 1, because discovery matches a file that throws (§6.6.1.3).

**Verified baseline:** 14 tests, 14 pass, 0 fail, 0 skipped, 0 todo, reproduced on three consecutive runs.

| Metric | Baseline requirement | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pass rate per run | 100% — any failure blocks | 14/14 observed on three consecutive runs |
| Tolerated skips | 0, except capability-based exclusion of socket levels | `--test-skip-pattern` is the only sanctioned mechanism |
| Tolerated flakes | 0 — see §6.6.3.6 | Application is deterministic; flakes are environmental and fixable |
| Retry allowance | None | A repeatable failure is a real failure |

A zero-tolerance rate is defensible here because the system under test is deterministic in a directly measured sense: nine different method-and-path combinations returned byte-identical bodies with identical SHA-256 digests, and the body is unchanged across process restarts. There is no timing-sensitive logic, no shared state, and no dependency whose availability could vary.

#### 6.6.4.3 Performance Test Thresholds

**Observed:** none. There is no benchmark, no load harness, no performance budget, no SLO, and no application-set timeout — every timeout in effect is a Node.js default. §2.2 records zero requirements with a declared performance target, and §5.4.5 records the absence of any SLA, error budget, availability target, latency target, throughput target, or capacity assumption.

The figures below are the only performance numbers this section can offer. Each is a single-host measurement, and each is a **candidate tripwire**, not a threshold.

| Dimension | Measured baseline | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Startup to readiness line | median 29.2 ms, range 27.2–30.8 ms over 8 spawns | Host observation |
| Full-suite wall time | 0.093 s, 0.094 s, 0.100 s over 3 runs | Harness result |
| Suite internal duration | 66.97 ms default, 64.10 ms at concurrency 2 | Harness result |
| `SIGTERM` to exit | 1.9 ms | Host observation |
| Request throughput | plateau of roughly 66,000–81,000 requests per second | Host observation — §6.1.3 is authoritative |
| Latency under concurrency | median grows about 32× from concurrency 1 to 64 | Host observation — §6.1.3 is authoritative |

Three constraints govern any use of these numbers. They are **hardware-bound**, so a comparison is meaningful only between runs on identical machines. They are **not derived from any requirement**, so exceeding them indicates change, not violation. And the throughput and latency figures belong to §6.1.3 and must not be re-derived or restated as targets here. If a performance gate is ever introduced, the appropriate form is a wide-tolerance regression alarm on startup latency and suite duration — the two dimensions a test pipeline can measure cheaply and repeatably.

#### 6.6.4.4 Quality Gates

**Observed:** Absent. No gate exists in the repository, and no commit-time or push-time enforcement is configured. Branch-protection rules are a hosting-platform setting rather than repository content, so their state cannot be established from the checkout and is not asserted here.

The five gates below are the complete set that is both meaningful for this system and implementable with runtime-only tooling. Each has a verified enforcement mechanism.

| Gate | Condition to pass | Mechanism | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| G1 Syntax | `node --check server.js` exits 0 | Runtime parser; verified exit 0 today | Absent — recommended |
| G2 Test outcome | Every discovered test passes | Runner exits 1 on any failing assertion | Absent — recommended |
| G3 Coverage | 100% line, branch, and function | Coverage threshold flags; verified exit 1 on breach | Absent — recommended |
| G4 Environment hygiene | No spawned listener survives the job | Post-run port check plus unconditional `SIGTERM` | Absent — recommended |
| G5 Dependency introduction | No manifest, lockfile, or `node_modules/` appears without review | Shell existence check — cheap because none exists today | Absent — recommended |

G2 carries an immediate practical consequence that did not exist before commit `43ed37c`: a gate implemented as `node --test` at the repository root **would fail on the current tree**, because discovery matches `test.js` and that file throws on evaluation (§6.6.1.3). Adopting G2 therefore requires first repairing or removing that file, or scoping discovery to exclude it — and the fact that it reached the branch head at all is the clearest available demonstration of why G1 and G2 are worth having (§6.4.3.5).

G5 deserves emphasis because it protects a property this repository currently has for free. The system depends on exactly one Node.js core module and therefore has no lockfile to scan, no transitive tree to audit, and no supply-chain surface — a posture §6.4 documents and §6.6.6 quantifies. Introducing a test framework would silently destroy that property; a two-line existence check makes the loss a reviewable event rather than an accident.

G1 through G3 are enforced entirely by process exit codes, so no gate requires a parser, a plugin, or a service. G4 cannot be expressed as an exit code and needs an explicit check, which is why §6.6.3.6 treats a leaked listener as the highest-priority flake source.

#### 6.6.4.5 Documentation Requirements

**Observed:** `README.md` contains one line — the repository name as a level-1 heading — with no prerequisites, no run instructions, no test instructions, and no port information. There is no `CONTRIBUTING.md`, no `docs/` directory, and no `CHANGELOG.md`. §3.6.5 records that even the launch command is not encoded anywhere in the repository and survives only as an operator convention.

Because there is no `package.json`, there is also no `scripts.test` entry that could serve as self-documenting invocation. Consequently, if the baseline suite is ever adopted, the following items must be written down or the suite becomes unrunnable by anyone who did not write it.

| Documentation item | Why it is mandatory here | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exact invocation command | No `npm test` exists; directory arguments fail with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` | Absent |
| Which tracked file to run | The tree holds two `.js` files and only `server.js` is the application; `test.js` exits 1 if executed | Absent |
| Required Node.js version | No `.nvmrc`/`engines`; runner needs ≥ 20, threshold flags need ≥ 22.8.0 | Absent |
| Port precondition and mode | Attach mode needs 3000 listening; own mode needs a free allocated port | Absent |
| Expected-value set and its source lines | Five constants define every assertion (§6.6.2.1.6) | Absent |
| Reporter and artifact conventions | `junit` produced an empty document; TAP is the verified artifact | Absent |
| Provenance disclaimer | All timings are single-host observations, not commitments | Absent |

One structural benefit of the naming convention in §6.6.2.1.5 is that it makes the suite partly self-documenting: each test name terminates in the requirement identifier it verifies, so the test list *is* a traceability report. Adopting the baseline would also invalidate two counters currently recorded in §2.2 — "Requirements covered by automated tests | 0" and the accompanying statement that every acceptance criterion is an externally executable check rather than an assertion in a committed suite — and those counters would need to be updated in the same change.

#### 6.6.4.6 Consolidated Quality Metrics Matrix

| Metric | Observed at HEAD `43ed37c` | Verified or recommended baseline |
| --- | --- | --- |

| Runner outcome on the committed tree | `node --test` exits 1: 1 test, 0 pass, 1 fail | 14/14 pass, exit 0 — verified |
| Line / branch / function coverage | 0% / 0% / 0% — no tooling and no test | 100% / 100% / 100% — verified |
| Coverage enforcement | None | Threshold flags; breach exits 1 — verified |
| Pass-rate requirement | None | 100%; zero skips, zero retries |
| Suite duration | Not applicable | 0.093–0.100 s wall — verified |
| Startup latency baseline | Not declared | median 29.2 ms — host observation |
