| Dependencies to audit | 0 — one core module | Keep at 0; G5 guards it |
| Test documentation | None | Seven mandatory items enumerated above |

### 6.6.5 Test Environment Architecture and Resource Requirements

#### 6.6.5.1 Test Environment Architecture

**Observed:** Absent. The repository defines no test environment. `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.dockerignore`, `.env`, `.env.example`, and every runtime-version pin were probed and are absent, so nothing in the repository describes where or how tests would run.

**Verified baseline:** the environment is a **single host** running one Node.js installation. Every participant — runner, test client, and service under test — is co-located, and that co-location is mandatory rather than convenient: the service binds `127.0.0.1` (`server.js` L3), so a probe from the host's routable address is refused. There is no environment to promote between, no staging tier, and no service to provision.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Ext(["Off-host client on the routable address"])

    subgraph Runner["Test runner process tree - one host, no containers"]
        R0["node --test parent process<br/>discovery, aggregation, coverage rollup"]
        R1["Child process - unit file<br/>http.createServer stubbed, no socket"]
        R2["Child process - contract file<br/>node http request client"]
        R3["Child process - lifecycle file<br/>spawns and signals a fixture"]
        R0 --> R1
        R0 --> R2
        R0 --> R3
    end

    subgraph Loopback["Loopback interface 127.0.0.1 - the only reachable path"]
        L1["Port 3000 - the committed constant<br/>shared resource, attach mode target"]
        L2["Port 3100 or another allocated port<br/>exclusive, own mode target"]
    end

    subgraph SUT["Service under test - one process per port"]
        S1["node server.js<br/>342 bytes, one require, zero exports"]
        S2["Generated fixture copy<br/>identical except the port constant"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentTier["Test infrastructure that does not exist"]
        A1["No database, cache, or message broker"]
        A2["No browser engine or UI driver"]
        A3["No container image, compose file, or service stub"]
        A4["No environment variables and no config file"]
        A5["No package registry access - zero installs"]
    end

    R2 --> L1
    R3 --> L2
    L1 --> S1
    L2 --> S2

    S1 --> Std
    S2 --> Std
    R0 --> Art

    Ext -. "connection refused - loopback bind" .-> L1
    R1 -. "requires none of these" .-> A1

    Std["Host stdout - one 41-byte readiness line per instance"]
    Art["Job workspace - reporter output and coverage summary"]
```

*Diagram 6.6-B — Test environment architecture. The unit child never touches the loopback interface; the contract child attaches to a shared port; the lifecycle child owns an allocated port. The dashed edge from the off-host client records a verified refusal, not a supported path.*

| Environment component | Role | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node.js runtime | Supplies the runner, the assertion library, the HTTP client, and the server | Delegated — verified v22.23.1, runner needs ≥ 20 |
| Loopback interface | The only network path that works | Source fact — `hostname = '127.0.0.1'` |
| Port 3000 | Attach-mode target; a shared, contended resource | Source fact — `port = 3000`, no override |
| Allocated port plus fixture | Own-mode target for isolated and parallel runs | Generated artifact, never committed |
| Host stdout | Carries the readiness signal the lifecycle level gates on | Source fact — one 41-byte line |
| Job workspace | Holds reporter output; no coverage directory is created | Audit result — verified no new files appear |
| Database, broker, browser, container, registry | Not required by any level | Not applicable |

#### 6.6.5.2 Test Data Flow

The data flow is unusual and worth stating plainly: **no data flows into the application at any level.** `server.js` never reads the request object, so a test cannot influence the response by varying its input. The only way a test can change what it observes is by changing *which* observable it inspects — status, header set, body bytes, stdout, exit code — not by supplying different data.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["Test inputs - synthesised in code, none loaded from storage"]
        I1["Expected-value set<br/>status 200, text/plain, 14-byte body,<br/>SHA-256 digest, 41-byte readiness line"]
        I2["Request shapes<br/>methods, paths, HEAD, malformed frames"]
    end

    subgraph Exec["Execution path - no data enters the application"]
        X0["Fixture spawn for the lifecycle level"]
        X1["Test issues a request<br/>or invokes the captured handler"]
        X2["Handler ignores the request object<br/>no parse, no validation, no lookup"]
        X3["Response composed from a literal<br/>plus runtime framing headers"]
        X1 --> X2
        X2 --> X3
    end

    subgraph Artifacts["Artifacts produced by a run"]
        O1["Assertion results to the reporter<br/>spec for humans, TAP as the artifact"]
        O2["V8 coverage summary<br/>100 percent lines, branches, functions"]
        O3["Child stdout - readiness line only"]
        O4["Teardown - SIGTERM, no data cleanup needed"]
    end

    subgraph NoStore["Data stores that never participate"]
        N1["No fixture files, factories, or seed data"]
        N2["No database, migration, or truncation step"]
        N3["No recorded cassettes or golden files"]
        N4["No state persisted between tests or runs"]
    end

    I1 --> X1
    I2 --> X1
    X0 --> O3
    X3 --> O1
    X2 -.-> O2
    X0 --> O4

    X2 -. "never read or written" .-> N1
    X2 -. "never read or written" .-> N2
    X3 -. "never compared against" .-> N3
    O4 -. "nothing to reset" .-> N4
```

*Diagram 6.6-C — Test data flow. Inputs are literals declared in the test files; the request path carries nothing into the application; the only outputs are assertion results, a coverage summary, the readiness line, and a signal.*

| Flow element | Content | Persistence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inbound test data | Five expected-value constants and a set of request shapes | Declared in code; nothing loaded from disk |
| Application input | None consumed — request object is ignored | Not applicable |
| Application output | 14-byte literal plus runtime framing headers | Not persisted anywhere |
| Run artifacts | Reporter text, inline coverage summary | Job-scoped; no `coverage/` directory is created |
| Cleanup obligation | Terminate spawned children | No data cleanup exists to perform |

#### 6.6.5.3 Environment Provisioning and Isolation

Provisioning is limited to four preconditions, three of which the repository cannot state because it declares nothing about its environment.

| Precondition | Requirement | How it is satisfied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime present | Node.js ≥ 20 for the runner; ≥ 22.8.0 for coverage thresholds | Must be pinned by the pipeline — no in-repo pin exists |
| Network installs | None required | Verified: zero packages installed, so the job needs no registry |
| Port availability | One free loopback port per live instance | Must be checked; port 3000 is shared and may be held |
| Writable working directory | Only for reporter artifacts | Coverage needs none — verified no files created |

Isolation follows from the two modes defined in §6.6.2.2.5. **Attach mode** provides no isolation and must not mutate or terminate the instance it probes — during verification, port 3000 was held by a process belonging to another session, and the correct behaviour was to probe it read-only and leave it running rather than reclaim the port. **Own mode** provides full isolation by generating a fixture that differs from `server.js` only in the port constant, spawning it, and terminating it unconditionally. Because the committed constant cannot be overridden at runtime, own mode is the only route to isolation, and the generated fixture must be treated as a build artifact — it is a copy of the artifact under test, and any divergence beyond line 4 would silently invalidate the level.

Two isolation properties are worth recording because they are free here and expensive in most systems: there is **no shared database or cache** to reset between tests, and there is **no environment-variable surface** to leak configuration between runs, since `server.js` never reads `process.env`.

A third isolation property is now a hazard rather than a convenience: the repository root already contains a file named `test.js` that matches the built-in runner's default discovery pattern and throws on evaluation (§6.6.1.3). A harness executed from inside the checkout inherits that discovery result and fails before its own assertions run, which is why the verified baseline was executed from a scratch directory outside the checkout.

#### 6.6.5.4 Resource Requirements for Test Execution

All figures below were measured on the verification host — 16 vCPU, 124,784 MiB total memory, Node.js v22.23.1 — against the unmodified committed file. They characterise the cost of the baseline suite; they are not minimum system requirements, and they will differ on other hardware.

| Resource | Measured requirement | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU | ~0.12 s user plus ~0.03 s system per full run | One core is sufficient; cost is process startup, not computation |
| Peak memory, whole run | 154,804–154,976 KB across three runs, 3 processes | Runner parent plus one child per test file |
| Memory, bare runtime | 43,560 KB for a Node.js process doing nothing | Runtime overhead dominates; test code adds little |
| Memory, spawned service | 47,916 KB per `server.js` instance | Add one instance's worth per own-mode worker |
| Wall-clock time | 0.093–0.100 s for 14 tests | Plus ~29 ms per spawned instance and ~2 ms per teardown |
| Disk, repository | 382 bytes across three tracked files, of which only `server.js` (342 bytes) is under test | No `node_modules/`, no build output |
| Disk, test harness | 8,128 bytes for the entire verified harness | Coverage creates no directory unless `NODE_V8_COVERAGE` is set |
| Network | Loopback only; zero egress; no DNS; no registry | The job can run with external networking disabled |
| TCP ports | One per live instance; 3000 by default | The binding constraint on parallelism (§6.6.3.3) |

Three planning consequences follow. First, memory scales per **process**, not per test: a run with three test files and one spawned fixture should be budgeted at roughly four Node.js processes, and at ~43–48 MB each that is on the order of 175–200 MB — an estimate derived from the measured per-process figures rather than a measurement of that exact configuration. Second, because nothing is installed, the test job requires **no network access at all**, which removes registry availability, proxy configuration, and install-time supply-chain exposure from the list of things that can make a run fail. Third, the scarce resource is neither CPU nor memory but **loopback ports**, which is why §6.6.3.3 caps parallelism on port ownership rather than on core count.

### 6.6.6 Security Testing Requirements

#### 6.6.6.1 Observed Security Testing Posture

**Observed:** Absent in every category. §6.4 records a security artifact audit spanning 224 paths across 11 groups with zero present, and two of those groups are directly relevant here: "Security scanning and CI gates" (21 paths including `.snyk`, `.semgrep.yml`, CodeQL workflows, `sonar-project.properties`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `audit-ci.json`, `renovate.json`) and "Supply chain" (15 paths including `package.json`, four lockfile variants, `node_modules/`, and SBOM, provenance, and attestation files). There is no static analysis, no dependency scanning, no secret scanning, no container scanning, and no dynamic scanning configured.

One finding from this section's own verification quantifies the supply-chain position precisely: **`npm audit` cannot run at all.** It exits 1 with `npm error code ENOLOCK` and the message "This command requires an existing lockfile", the underlying error being that resolution requires a shrinkwrap file. That is not a gap to be closed — it is the correct outcome for a system whose only dependency is `require('http')`, a Node.js core module (F-005-RQ-001). Dependency vulnerability scanning has no subject here, and §6.6.4.4's G5 gate exists to make sure that stays true.

The one change made to the repository since the application landed does not alter this posture. Commit `43ed37c` added a 13-byte `test.js` containing no credential, token, URL, or import (§6.4.1), so it introduces no secret-scanning subject and no new attack surface; what it does illustrate is the change-admission finding recorded in §6.4.3.5 — a file was admitted to the branch head with no scan, review, or gate of any kind.

#### 6.6.6.2 Applicable Security Test Cases

Security testing in this system is **posture pinning**, not vulnerability hunting. There is no authentication logic to bypass, no query to inject into, and no dependency to exploit; what exists instead is a small set of deliberate configuration choices whose accidental reversal would be materially significant. A test that asserts a protection is *absent* may look strange, but it serves two concrete purposes: it makes adding that protection a visible, reviewed change, and it catches a regression in the opposite direction.

All eight cases below assert behaviour that has already been observed. Cases marked as drawn from §6.4 reuse evidence recorded there rather than re-deriving it.

| Security test case | Assertion | Verified basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ST-1 Bind-address confinement | The service is reachable on `127.0.0.1` and refused on the host's routable address | Loopback probe succeeds; routable probe refused (§6.4) |
| ST-2 Plaintext-only transport | An HTTPS request to the port fails at the TLS handshake | Handshake failure observed (§6.4) |
| ST-3 No version disclosure | Neither `server` nor `x-powered-by` appears in any response | Verified — emitted header set is exactly five keys |
| ST-4 Input inertness | Injection-shaped and canary inputs are never reflected; the body stays byte-identical | Canary `?secret=CANARY123` not reflected; nine attack-shaped probes byte-identical (§6.4) |
| ST-5 Credentials are ignored | HTTP Basic and `Bearer` credentials neither authenticate nor appear in the response; no `WWW-Authenticate` or `Set-Cookie` is emitted | Verified in the contract suite; corroborated by §6.4 |
| ST-6 Parser limits are runtime-enforced | An oversized header yields `431` and a malformed request line yields `400`, both without invoking the handler | Verified — `maxHeaderSize` 16384 is a runtime default |
| ST-7 No throttling exists | A burst produces no `429` and no connection rejection | 300 requests at 50-way parallelism returned 300 × `200` (§6.4) |
| ST-8 Attack traffic is not recorded | stdout remains exactly 41 bytes and stderr 0 bytes after hostile probes | Verified across all probe campaigns (§6.4, §6.5) |

**ST-1 is the single most valuable security test in this system.** The loopback bind is what keeps an unauthenticated, unencrypted, unthrottled endpoint from being an exposure; a one-character edit to `server.js` L3 — `'127.0.0.1'` to `'0.0.0.0'` — would silently remove that protection while leaving every functional test passing. ST-1 is the only assertion in the entire baseline that would fail on that change.

ST-8 records a finding rather than a protection, and it should be read as such: because the application writes nothing after its startup line, a test can prove that hostile traffic leaves no audit trail. That is precisely the deficiency §6.5 documents, and pinning it in a test means any future logging work has a failing assertion to update.

#### 6.6.6.3 Static and Dependency Analysis Applicability

| Technique | Applicability | Evidence and consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syntax pre-flight | Available today | `node --check server.js` exits 0; validates form, not behaviour (§3.6.2). The tree now contains a direct demonstration of that limitation: `node --check test.js` also exits 0, yet executing the same file throws `ReferenceError` and exits 1 |
| Linting and SAST | Applicable, not configured | No `eslint` config of any variant; 14 lines give a linter little to flag, but it would catch a future regression — and a linter run over the tracked tree today would flag `test.js`'s two undefined identifiers |
| Dependency vulnerability scanning | Not applicable — inoperable | `npm audit` exits 1 with `ENOLOCK`; zero third-party dependencies to scan |
| SBOM generation | Not applicable | No manifest and no lockfile; §6.4 records zero supply-chain artifacts |
| Secret scanning | Applicable, empty subject | No `.env`, no `process.env` reference, and zero `crypto` usage — there is nowhere for a secret to live, and none of the three tracked files contains a credential-shaped token |
| Container image scanning | Not applicable | No `Dockerfile`, `Containerfile`, or compose file exists |
| Dynamic scanning | Partially performed manually | Nine attack-shaped probes plus raw-socket frames constitute a minimal DAST pass; every path returns an identical `200` |
| License compliance scanning | Not applicable | No dependencies to reconcile; the absence of a `LICENSE` file is a governance gap, not a scanning finding |

The applicability column changes the moment a dependency manifest appears. Adding any test framework would create a lockfile, a transitive tree, an `npm audit` obligation, and an SBOM subject — converting four "Not applicable" rows into live requirements. This is the practical reason §6.6.2.1.1 selects the runtime's built-in runner and §6.6.4.4 defines G5.

#### 6.6.6.4 Security Test Requirements Matrix

Every requirement below is **proposed**; none exists at HEAD `43ed37c`.

| ID | Level that would execute it | Blocking? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ST-1 Bind-address confinement | End-to-end — requires a live listener and two client addresses | Yes — protects the primary control |
| ST-2 Plaintext-only transport | End-to-end | Yes — a silent TLS change must be reviewed |
| ST-3 No version disclosure | Integration | Yes — cheap, and header sets drift with runtime upgrades |
| ST-4 Input inertness | Unit and Integration | Yes |
| ST-5 Credentials are ignored | Integration | Yes |
| ST-6 Parser limits enforced | Integration | No — asserts a runtime default that may change between versions |
| ST-7 No throttling exists | Integration | No — documents posture; slow relative to the rest of the suite |
| ST-8 Attack traffic not recorded | End-to-end — needs stdout capture | No — expected to be replaced when logging is added |

ST-6 is deliberately non-blocking because it asserts a Node.js default (`maxHeaderSize` 16384) rather than repository behaviour; a runtime upgrade that changed the limit would fail the test without any change to the tracked source. That distinction — application contract versus runtime default — is the same one §6.6.2.2.1 identifies as the real purpose of the integration level.

#### 6.6.6.5 Boundaries of Security Testing for This System

The following vulnerability classes have **no sink** in this codebase, so tests for them would assert nothing. The zero-occurrence content probes recorded in §6.4 are the evidence.

| Vulnerability class | Why no test is possible | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQL / NoSQL injection | No query is ever constructed | Zero database drivers; no connection string (§6.2) |
| Command injection | No process is ever spawned by the app | `child_process` occurrences: 0 |
| Path traversal | No filesystem access | `fs.` occurrences: 0 |
| Code injection | No dynamic evaluation | `eval(` occurrences: 0 |
| Deserialisation attacks | No parsing of request payloads | `JSON.parse` occurrences: 0; `req.` occurrences: 0 |
| SSRF | No outbound request is ever made | Zero outbound sockets (§6.1) |
| Session and CSRF | No cookies, no state, no state-changing operation | `Set-Cookie` occurrences: 0; every method returns the same body |
| Cryptographic weakness | No cryptography is used | `crypto`, `https`, `tls` occurrences: 0 |
| Privilege escalation | No privilege manipulation | `setuid`/`setgid` occurrences: 0; no `process.` usage at all |

The conclusion is narrow and firm: for this system, meaningful security testing consists of **configuration and posture assertions** — where it binds, whether it encrypts, what it discloses, what it ignores, and what it fails to record. There is no application logic in which a vulnerability could hide, and consequently no penetration-testing scope beyond the nine probes already executed and documented in §6.4.

### 6.6.7 References

#### 6.6.7.1 Repository Files and Folders Examined

- `server.js` — the sole artifact under test. Established the complete testable surface: the single `require('http')` at L1, the hard-coded `hostname`/`port` constants at L3–L4, the branch-free handler at L6–L10 that ignores the request object and emits `200` / `text/plain` / `Hello, World!\n`, and the load-time `server.listen` with its readiness log at L12–L14. Also established, by absence, that the module exports nothing — the constraint that shapes every test level.
- `README.md` — established that no build, run, or test instruction exists anywhere in the repository, which is why §6.6.4.5 treats invocation documentation as a mandatory deliverable.
- `test.js` — examined byte by byte (13 bytes, 2 newline-terminated lines, mode `100644`, added by commit `43ed37c`). Established that despite its name it contains **no test, no assertion, no runner import, and no framework reference** — only two bare identifier expression statements, `asdsa` and `asdasd`. It therefore covers no line of `server.js` and satisfies no acceptance criterion. Its behavioural significance is that it matches the built-in runner's default discovery pattern, so `node --test` at the repository root discovers it and fails (§6.6.1.3).
- `./` (repository root) — established that the repository contains exactly three tracked files, no subdirectories, and no hidden configuration files other than `.git/`; 382 bytes in total excluding Git metadata.

#### 6.6.7.2 Static Audits and Content Probes Used as Evidence

- Existence probes across roughly eighty conventional paths — test directories, test-runner configurations, coverage and quality configurations, CI/CD descriptors, linter and hook configurations, container and environment descriptors — every one returned absent, with the single exception of the root-level `test.js`, which matches the `*test*` name pattern while containing no test. Basis for §6.6.1.3 and for the "Observed: Absent" statement opening each sub-section.
- Repository-wide case-insensitive grep for `describe(`, `it(`, `test(`, `assert`, `expect(`, `jest`, `mocha`, `vitest`, `supertest`, `nyc`, `coverage`, `npm test`, and `node --test` — **zero matches across all three tracked files**. Extending the scan surface from two files to three changed no result.
- `git ls-files` — authoritative three-file inventory (`README.md`, `server.js`, `test.js`). `git log --all --diff-filter=A --name-only` across all three commits on all branches — confirmed that only `README.md` (`241598b`), `server.js` (`06492d7`), and `test.js` (`43ed37c`) were ever added, so no test asset ever existed and was removed; the only path resembling a test was added, not deleted, and asserts nothing.
- `git status --porcelain` and `git rev-parse` — confirmed a clean working tree at HEAD `43ed37c` on branch `2907_01` both before and after all experimentation, establishing that no evidence in this section came from a modified artifact; also confirmed that `server.js` is byte-identical at HEAD and at its introducing commit `06492d7` (blob `320a75a`), so every coverage and timing figure applies to both revisions.
- Four natural-language searches of the repository index for test suites, CI pipelines, test directories, and dependency manifests — all returned empty result sets, corroborating the filesystem probes.
- `node --check server.js` — exit 0; the only verification the repository supports today. `node --check test.js` — also exit 0, establishing that the syntax pre-flight validates form and not behaviour (§6.6.6.3).
- `npm audit --json` — exit 1 with `ENOLOCK`; established that dependency scanning is structurally inoperable without a lockfile (§6.6.6.1).
- `du -sb --exclude=.git` and `wc -c` — established the 382-byte repository footprint used in §6.6.5.4, of which `server.js` accounts for 342 bytes.

#### 6.6.7.3 Runtime and Harness Probes Executed

All runtime evidence was produced on a single verification host (16 vCPU, 124,784 MiB memory, Node.js v22.23.1, npm 11.18.0, Git 2.43.0) against the unmodified committed file. The illustrative harness was written to a scratch directory outside the repository checkout and was **never committed**; the working tree remained clean throughout.

- `node --test` executed at the repository root against the committed tree — established the section's single most consequential behavioural fact: discovery matches `test.js`, the file throws on evaluation, and the run **fails** with `not ok 1 - test.js`, `failureType: 'testCodeFailure'`, `code: 'ERR_TEST_FAILURE'`, totals of `# tests 1` / `# suites 0` / `# pass 0` / `# fail 1`, and **exit code 1** (§6.6.1.3).
- `node test.js` — exit 1 with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` thrown at `test.js:1`; establishes that the file is inert as documentation and non-functional as code, and that only `node server.js` starts the application.
- Live-listener probes over loopback — established the observable contract: `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, `Connection: keep-alive`, `Keep-Alive: timeout=5`, body `Hello, World!\n` with SHA-256 `c98c24b677eff…`, invariance across nine method-and-path combinations, and `HEAD` returning a zero-byte body.
- Raw-socket probes — established the runtime-owned rejections `400` (malformed request line) and `431` (20,000-byte header field), and that both arrive as ordinary responses rather than socket errors.
- `unit/handler.test.js` (out-of-repo harness) — the `http.createServer` interception pattern of §6.6.2.1.3; 6 tests, 6 pass, 54.7 ms.
- `integration/contract.test.js` (out-of-repo harness) — the black-box contract pattern of §6.6.2.2.2; 8 tests, 8 pass after correcting the `431` assertion, 59.8 ms.
- `fixture/server_p3100.js` (out-of-repo harness) — a port-shifted copy whose `diff` against `server.js` shows exactly one changed line, supporting the own-mode isolation pattern.
- `e2e_lifecycle.js` (out-of-repo harness) — spawn, readiness-gate, probe, `SIGTERM`; established readiness at 29.1 ms, child RSS 47,916 KB, and 1.9 ms teardown.
- Readiness-variance sampler, eight spawns — established the 27.2–30.8 ms spread and 29.2 ms median that justify readiness-line gating over fixed sleeps (§6.6.3.6).
- Resident-memory sampler across three full runs — established peak process-tree RSS of 154,804–154,976 KB at three processes, and a 43,560 KB baseline for a bare Node.js process (§6.6.5.4).
- Coverage runs with `--experimental-test-coverage` — established 100.00% line, branch, and function coverage of `server.js`, that no coverage directory is created, and that an unmet threshold exits 1.
- Reporter and concurrency runs — established `spec`, `tap`, and `dot` output; the empty `<testsuites></testsuites>` document produced by `junit` in this configuration; 14/14 pass at `--test-concurrency=2`; and the `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` failure when a directory is passed to `node --test`.
- Port-contention trials — established `EADDRINUSE` with exit code 1 from both directions: a second instance of the fixture, and the harness's own launch against a port held by a pre-existing process.

- §6.5 Monitoring and Observability — confirmed that no per-request or per-error telemetry exists, the basis for security test case ST-8.

# 7. User Interface Design

## 7.1 User Interface Assessment

This section records the outcome of a user-interface-specific audit of the repository at HEAD `43ed37c`. The audit was run because the section is mandated for every specification of this kind, not because a candidate interface was found; the finding is stated first, and the evidence that establishes it follows.

Status labels reuse the vocabulary established in section 6.3.1.3 — **Delegated** (a mechanism exists but is owned by the runtime, the host, or the calling client rather than by repository code), **Absent** (the concern is meaningful but nothing implements it at any layer), and **Not applicable** (the concern presupposes a structure the system does not have).

### 7.1.1 Determination

> **No user interface required.**

The repository contains exactly three tracked files — `server.js` (14 lines, 342 bytes), `README.md` (27 bytes, a single heading line), and `test.js` (13 bytes, two lines) — totalling 382 bytes across zero source subdirectories. None of the three defines, renders, serves, or documents a user interface of any kind. The application's entire authored output to a caller is three statements that set an HTTP status, set a plain-text content type, and write a fixed 14-byte body:

```javascript
res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');  // the only header the application sets
res.end('Hello, World!\n');                   // 14 bytes, containing zero markup tags
```

`test.js`, added by the most recent commit, holds two bare identifier expression statements (`asdsa` and `asdasd`) and contains no markup, stylesheet reference, template, asset path, or framework token. It is imported by nothing, is never loaded into the server process, and exits 1 with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` if executed directly (section 6.6.1). Extending the audit surface from two tracked files to three therefore changed no result recorded below.

Because the content type is `text/plain` and the body contains no markup, there is nothing for a browser or any other client to render as an interface. Every interface class was tested individually and every one is absent.

| Interface Class | Status | Decisive Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server-rendered web UI (HTML documents) | Absent | `Content-Type: text/plain` is set unconditionally on line 8; a markup-tag scan of the response body returns 0 |
| Single-page or client-side application | Absent | No `.jsx`, `.tsx`, `.vue`, `.svelte`, or `.astro` file exists; no bundler or framework config exists; no dependency manifest exists through which one could be installed (section 3.2.1) |
| Static asset delivery (styles, scripts, images, fonts) | Absent | No `public/`, `static/`, `assets/`, `dist/`, or `build/` directory; the source performs no filesystem read, and requests for `/styles.css`, `/app.js`, and `/favicon.ico` each return the same 14-byte plaintext body |
| Server-side template or view layer | Absent | No template file or view directory exists; section 1.3.2.1 records that "the response body is a source-code literal; no template engine or content negotiation exists" |
| Command-line or terminal UI | Absent | No `process.argv`, `process.stdin`, `readline`, or prompt usage in `server.js`; the only write to standard output is the startup readiness line on line 13 |
| Desktop or mobile client | Not applicable | No Electron, Tauri, React Native, or Flutter reference or manifest exists; the artifact is a single Node.js process with one TCP listener |
| API-documentation or developer-portal UI (Swagger UI, Redoc, GraphQL Playground, Storybook) | Absent | No specification descriptor and no UI route exist; section 6.3.2.6 records that every URI, "including discovery-style paths, returns the same 14-byte plaintext body" |

Consequently the remaining topics mandated for this section — core UI technologies, UI use cases, UI/backend interaction boundaries, UI schemas, screens, user interactions, and visual design considerations — have no subject matter in this repository. Sub-section 7.1.4 resolves each one explicitly rather than omitting it, so that coverage can be confirmed without inferring silence.

| --- | --- | --- |

The only extensions present anywhere in the tree are `.js` (`server.js` and `test.js`) and `.md` (`README.md`) |
| Directory existence test | 34 conventional UI directories: `public`, `static`, `assets`, `www`, `web`, `client`, `frontend`, `ui`, `src`, `app`, `views`, `templates`, `layouts`, `partials`, `components`, `pages`, `screens`, `styles`, `css`, `img`, `images`, `fonts`, `icons`, `dist`, `build`, `.next`, `.nuxt`, `.storybook`, `design`, `mockups`, `wireframes`, `docs` and others | **None present.** The repository has one directory — the root itself |

#### 7.1.2.1 Browser-Perspective Verification

Because the absence of markup in source does not by itself prove how a browser would experience the endpoint, the running server was probed with browser-shaped requests. Probes were issued against a verbatim copy of `server.js` placed outside the repository checkout with only the port literal changed (port 3000 was already held on the verification host); no tracked file was modified, and the copy was deleted afterwards. Values below are host observations.

| Probe | Request | Observed Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser-shaped document request | `GET /` with `Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml` and a Chrome `User-Agent` | `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Content-Length: 14`, body `Hello, World!` — content negotiation is ignored, and no HTML is produced for a browser any more than for `curl` |
| Markup inspection of the body | Tag scan of the returned payload | 0 markup tags — there is no element, attribute, or entity a rendering engine could lay out |
| Sub-resource requests a browser would make | `GET /favicon.ico`, `/index.html`, `/styles.css`, `/app.js`, `/manifest.json` | Each returned `200`, `text/plain`, 14 bytes, `Hello, World!` — no asset pipeline exists, and no `404` distinguishes a missing asset from the single response |
| Startup advertisement | Process start | One newline-terminated line naming the bound endpoint, matching the template literal on line 13; section 6.3.5.5 records this as exactly 41 bytes for the committed endpoint |

The third row is the architecturally significant one: a browser pointed at this endpoint receives the identical plain-text string for the document and for every sub-resource it subsequently requests. There is no document to parse, therefore no sub-resource graph, therefore no interface.

### 7.1.3 Human-Observable Surfaces That Do Exist

Two surfaces are observable by a person, and neither is a user interface: presentation is entirely the consumer's responsibility in both cases. Section 6.3.5.5 catalogues the same surfaces as integration points; they are restated here in presentation terms.

| Surface | Consumer | Rendering Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP response body — `200`, `text/plain`, 14 bytes | Any same-host HTTP client: `curl`, a script, or a browser | **Delegated to the client.** The application contributes one status, one header, and one literal; how those bytes are displayed is determined wholly by whatever issued the request |
| Standard-output readiness line, emitted once at startup | The operator or supervisor that launched the process | **Delegated to the host.** Whatever captures the stream — shell, supervisor, or log driver — is unconfigured by the repository (section 6.3.4.5) |

Neither surface is interactive. The response is invariant, so nothing a person types, clicks, or sends can change it: section 6.3.2.1 records that method, URI, query string, headers, and body are all discarded, and that eight structurally different URIs returned byte-identical responses. The readiness line is written once and never again — sections 6.3.1.3 and 6.3.3.5 record that standard output remained at exactly 41 bytes and standard error at zero bytes across every probe, including deliberate error probes — so there is no progress indicator, status display, or feedback channel of any kind.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Operator(["Operator at a terminal<br/>starts and stops the process"])
    Caller(["Any same-host HTTP client<br/>curl, a script, or a browser"])
    subgraph AbsentTiers["Presentation tiers a user interface requires — every one verified absent"]
        direction TB
        U1["Screens, pages, routes, layouts<br/>0 of 34 conventional UI directories present"]
        U2["Markup and styling assets<br/>0 files across 50+ tested extensions"]
        U3["Template or view engine<br/>no engine artifact; the body is a source literal"]
        U4["Client framework and bundler<br/>no manifest exists, so none is installable"]
        U5["Design system, tokens, typography, imagery<br/>no stylesheet, theme, font, or image file"]
        U1 --> U2
        U2 --> U3
        U3 --> U4
        U4 --> U5
    end
    subgraph Process["node server.js — the entire system, 14 lines"]
        direction TB
        H["Request handler, lines 7 to 9<br/>status 200, Content-Type text/plain, 14-byte body"]
        L["Listener and readiness log, lines 12 to 14<br/>one line to standard output at startup only"]
    end
    Operator -->|"node server.js"| L
    L -->|"one readiness line naming the endpoint"| Operator
    Caller -->|"any method, any URI, plaintext over loopback"| H
    H -->|"200, text plain, fixed 14-byte body"| Caller
    Caller -.->|"no presentation code is shipped to the consumer"| U1
    H -.->|"nothing is rendered, negotiated, or templated"| U3
```

**Diagram 7.1-A — Presentation-tier map: the two surfaces that exist and the UI tiers verified absent.** Solid edges carry the only traffic the system produces. Dotted edges mark the presentation concerns a consumer might expect to find behind those surfaces and that this repository does not implement at any layer.

### 7.1.5 Source Facts That Gate Any Interface Work

The determination above traces to a small number of source facts. The mapping below is a change-impact reference recording what each fact currently precludes; it is **not** a recommendation, requirement, or plan. Section 1.3.2.2 records that the repository declares no future phases, so every entry describes a present-state absence rather than approved scope.

| Source Fact | Location | What It Currently Precludes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')` is unconditional | `server.js` line 8 | Any browser-rendered document, styled output, image, or downloadable asset; content negotiation is impossible because the header is never varied |
| The response body is a single literal written in one `res.end` call | `server.js` line 9 | Templated or data-driven pages, error pages, partial updates, streamed or paginated views, and any payload a client could bind to a view model |
| `req` is never dereferenced | `server.js` line 6 | Route-to-screen resolution, form and query handling, file upload, session or cookie state, per-user or per-locale rendering, and any request-driven navigation |
| No filesystem access occurs anywhere in the source | `server.js`, whole file | Serving a stylesheet, script bundle, font, icon, or image from disk; there is no static-file path to add assets to |
| `hostname` is the loopback literal | `server.js` line 3 | Reaching the endpoint from a browser on any other device or host; section 6.3.4.3 records that the routable-address probe failed at connect while loopback returned `200` |
| No `package.json`, lockfile, or `node_modules/` exists | Repository root | Installing a UI framework, component library, CSS toolchain, bundler, or design system without simultaneously introducing the dependency and build workflow the project does not have (section 3.2.4) |
| The repository holds no asset, schema, or documentation file | Repository root — three-file inventory (`server.js`, `README.md`, `test.js`; 382 bytes) | Any wireframe, mockup, screen inventory, design token set, or style guide that a specification could reference or that a reviewer could compare an implementation against. The second `.js` file in the tree is a 13-byte placeholder, not an asset or a schema |

# 8. Infrastructure

## 8.1 Deployment Environment

**Applicability determination: Detailed Infrastructure Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The repository consists of exactly three tracked files — `server.js` (342 bytes, 14 newline-terminated lines), `README.md` (27 bytes, one heading line), and `test.js` (13 bytes, two lines) — for a total working tree of **382 bytes across 3 files and zero subdirectories**. `server.js` is a standalone CommonJS script that requires only the Node.js core `http` module, binds a listener to the hard-coded literals `127.0.0.1` and `3000`, and answers every request with an unconditional `200` / `text/plain` / `Hello, World!\n`. `test.js` ships with every checkout but is **never executed by the documented deployment procedure**: the procedure in §3.6.5 runs `node server.js` and nothing else, `test.js` is required by no module, and executing it directly exits 1 with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` (§6.6.1). There is no build system, no dependency manifest, no container image definition, no infrastructure-provisioning descriptor, no orchestration manifest, no pipeline definition, and no cloud binding of any kind. The system is a standalone script executed directly by a Node.js interpreter on a single host; the phrase "the committed file is the deployed artifact" established in §3.6 is literally true.

Four structural facts, each independently verified, make a conventional infrastructure architecture inapplicable rather than merely undocumented:

1. **There is nothing to build.** No `package.json`, lockfile, `node_modules`, or compiler configuration exists, so there is no dependency-resolution step, no compilation step, and no packaging step between the source and the running process.
2. **There is nothing to provision declaratively.** Every conventional infrastructure descriptor class was probed by path and found absent (see the audit table below), so no environment can be reconstructed from the repository.
3. **The service cannot be fronted by an infrastructure tier.** The bind address is the compile-time literal `127.0.0.1`. A probe against the host's own routable address (`10.76.0.92:3000`) is refused (`curl` exit 7), confirming that no load balancer, ingress controller, reverse proxy, published container port, or Kubernetes Service can reach the listener without a source change (requirement **F-002-RQ-002**, and the "containerization hazard" noted in §3.6.3).
4. **There is exactly one deployable unit and one instance of it.** A second process on the same host and port terminates with an unhandled `EADDRINUSE` error event and exit code 1 (**F-002-RQ-004**), so the deployment topology has no replica dimension.

What follows therefore documents, for each infrastructure area in this section's scope: the **minimal build and distribution requirements the repository actually imposes**, the **as-built single-host execution environment** measured directly against the tracked source, and an **explicit determination with its evidence** where a capability is not present. Every quantitative statement carries a provenance label consistent with §6.1.1.3 and §6.5 — **Source fact** (read from the tracked source), **Audit result** (produced by an existence or content audit of the repository), **Runtime default** (inherited from Node.js and catalogued in §5.2.6), or **Host observation** (measured on the verification host). Status values follow the vocabulary fixed in §6.3.1.3: **Delegated** (the mechanism exists but is owned by the runtime or host, not the repository), **Absent** (the concern is meaningful here but nothing implements it), and **Not applicable** (the concern presupposes a structure this system does not have). No figure in this section is a service-level commitment: the repository declares no SLA, SLO, error budget, capacity model, or performance target (§2.4.2, §6.1.1).

### 8.1.1 Target Environment Assessment

#### 8.1.1.1 Environment Type and Classification

The repository does not declare an environment type. It contains no cloud provider binding, no on-premises inventory, no hybrid connectivity descriptor, and no multi-cloud abstraction — consistent with §3.4, which finds no third-party service, API, SDK, or cloud service of any kind. The **as-built environment type is therefore "single operator-provisioned host, unspecified"**: any machine that supplies a Node.js interpreter, a free TCP port 3000, and an available loopback interface satisfies every technical requirement enumerated in §1.3.1. Whether that machine is a developer workstation, a virtual machine, or a cloud instance is an operator decision that the repository neither records nor constrains.

Because the listener is bound to loopback, the choice of host is also the choice of client population: only processes on the same host can reach the service. The environment is consequently **self-contained and non-distributed** — one process, one host, one network namespace, no external dependency at run time and no egress requirement (§3.4).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph SourceChannel["Source distribution channel - no runtime coupling"]
        GitRemote[("GitHub origin repository<br/>3 commits, 0 tags<br/>pack payload 4.12 KiB")]
    end

    subgraph HostBoundary["Single operator-provisioned host - no IaC descriptor in repository"]
        Checkout["Working tree<br/>server.js 342 B + README.md 27 B + test.js 13 B<br/>382 B, 3 files"]
        NodeRuntime["Node.js runtime binary<br/>~119 MiB on host, version unpinned"]
        Process["OS process: node server.js<br/>1 process / 7 threads / 22 fds<br/>RSS ~47 MiB idle"]
        Socket(["TCP listener 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>plaintext HTTP/1.1"])
        Stdout["stdout: 41-byte readiness line<br/>stderr: 0 bytes"]
        Client["Co-located HTTP client"]
    end

    GitRemote -->|"git clone - manual, 7 ms"| Checkout
    Checkout -->|"node server.js - operator convention"| Process
    NodeRuntime -->|"interprets source at launch"| Process
    Process --> Socket
    Process --> Stdout
    Client -->|"GET / - 59 B request"| Socket
    Socket -->|"200 text/plain - 135 B response"| Client
```

**Diagram 8-A — As-built infrastructure architecture.** Every element inside the host boundary is provisioned by operator action; the repository contributes only the 382-byte working tree, of which the single 342-byte `server.js` is the only file the launch step reads. The Git remote is a source-distribution channel with no run-time coupling to the process (§3.4, §1.2.1.3). There is no tier above the listener and no tier below the host.

#### 8.1.1.2 Geographic Distribution Requirements

**None. The system has no geographic dimension.** §1.3.1 records that the repository contains no internationalisation, locale, or timezone handling, and no region, availability-zone, CDN, edge, or data-residency configuration; the infrastructure and compliance keyword audits for `region`, `residency`, `sovereignty`, and `cdn` returned zero matches. The response payload is a fixed 14-byte English string with no locale variation (§2.4).

Because the listener accepts only loopback connections, **distance between client and server is architecturally fixed at zero network hops**: the client must execute on the same host. Multi-region deployment, geo-routing, latency-based DNS, and anycast are all not applicable — not because they were considered and rejected, but because the reachability model admits exactly one client location.

#### 8.1.1.3 Resource Requirements

The repository declares no resource requirement: there is no container resource block, no orchestration request/limit pair, no cgroup configuration, and no capacity document (§6.1.1.2 found all 19 SLA/SLO/capacity/benchmark paths absent). The figures below are therefore **measurements of the as-built process**, not requirements the repository states. The sizing guidance in the fourth column is derived from those measurements for operator convenience and is explicitly an inference of this specification, not a repository artifact.

| Resource dimension | Observed value | Provenance | Derived sizing guidance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CPU — parallelism | 1 JavaScript event-loop thread; 7 OS threads, invariant at every concurrency level tested | Host observation (§6.5) | One core is sufficient and is also the ceiling; extra cores cannot be used |
| CPU — measured ceiling | One thread at 97.4% of process CPU; 102.5% of a single core, i.e. 6.41% of the 16-vCPU verification host | Host observation (§6.1.3.1) | Allocate 1 vCPU; the process cannot saturate more |
| Memory — resident set | 46.8 MiB idle → 57.7 MiB after 500 sequential requests → 75.6 MiB after 382,144 requests (0.06% of the 124,784 MiB host) | Host observation | Allocate at least 128 MiB to accommodate the observed ~29 MiB growth plus headroom |
| Memory — virtual reservation | `VmSize` 750,236 KiB / `VmPeak` 751,224 KiB (typical V8 address-space reservation, not committed memory) | Host observation | Do not size from virtual figures; no overcommit tuning is required |
| Storage — application | 382 bytes working tree across 3 tracked files, of which only `server.js` (342 bytes) is executed; 32.3 KiB complete checkout including `.git` | Audit result | Negligible; any filesystem suffices |
| Storage — runtime prerequisite | Node.js binary 124,835,376 bytes (119.1 MiB) on the verification host, plus a 19 MiB bundled npm tree that this repository never uses | Host observation | The interpreter dominates the disk requirement by a ratio of roughly 327,000 : 1 against the tracked tree |
| Storage — persistent data | None. No database, cache, file write, or log file (§3.5, §6.2) | Source fact | No volume, no backup target, no growth model |
| File descriptors | 22 at idle; exactly +1 per held connection; host ceiling 1,048,576 | Host observation (§6.5) | Default `ulimit -n` is ample; ~1.63 kB per held idle connection |
| Network — interfaces | One IPv4 loopback LISTEN socket (`/proc/net/tcp` entry `0100007F:0BB8`, state `0A`); no IPv6 listener | Source fact / Host observation | No NIC configuration, no firewall rule, and no egress allowance are required |
| Network — per request | 59-byte request in, 135-byte response out (121 header bytes + 14 body bytes) | Host observation | Wire cost is constant per request; payload size is invariant |
| Network — derived bandwidth | About 10.98 MB/s (87.9 Mbit/s) of response bytes at the measured 81,361 req/s plateau; about 5.06 MB/s at 37,455 req/s | Derived host observation | All of it traverses `lo`; physical NIC bandwidth consumed is zero |
| Privileges | Port 3000 is above 1024, so no `root` and no `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` are needed | Source fact | Run as an unprivileged user |

The only hard prerequisites the repository imposes are those enumerated in §1.3.1: a Node.js runtime whose core `http` module and CommonJS resolution are available, a free TCP port 3000, an available loopback interface, and a client on the same host. **No runtime version floor is declared** — there is no `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, or container base image — so runtime selection is unconstrained and unverified (§2.4.1, §2.4.5). As an external reference point, the Node.js project advises that production applications run only an Active LTS or Maintenance LTS line, with LTS lines receiving critical fixes for approximately 30 months; as of mid-2026 Node.js 24 is the Active LTS line, Node.js 22 is in Maintenance LTS, and Node.js 26 (released 5 May 2026) is Current and scheduled for LTS promotion in October 2026. All verification reported in this specification, including the measurements above, ran on **Node.js v22.23.1** — a line that receives security fixes only. This is an observation about patch currency, not a repository requirement and not a version recommendation.

### 8.1.2 Environment Management

#### 8.1.2.1 Infrastructure as Code Approach

**There is no Infrastructure as Code approach.** No provisioning, configuration-management, or supervision descriptor exists, which means the runtime environment cannot be reconstructed from the repository and is not version-controlled in any form.

| Environment-management concern | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Infrastructure provisioning descriptor | Absent | `terraform/`, `main.tf`, `Pulumi.yaml`, `cdk.json`, `cloudformation.yaml`, `template.yaml`, `serverless.yml` all absent |
| Host configuration management | Absent | `ansible/`, `playbook.yml` absent; no Chef, Puppet, or Salt artifact |
| Container and orchestration descriptors | Absent | `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `k8s/`, `kubernetes/`, `helm/`, `Chart.yaml`, `manifests/` all absent |
| Platform-as-a-service descriptor | Absent | `Procfile`, `app.yaml`, `fly.toml`, `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `render.yaml`, `railway.json`, `.ebextensions/`, `.platform/` all absent |
| Process supervision and restart policy | Absent | No `systemd` unit, `ecosystem.config.js`, `pm2.json`, `supervisord.conf`, or `nodemon.json` (§3.6.3) |
| Environment variable schema | Absent | No `.env`, `.env.example`, or `config/`; `server.js` performs zero `process.env`, `process.argv`, or `dotenv` reads |
| Runtime version pin | Absent | No `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, or `.tool-versions` pin |
| Launch command declaration | Absent | No `npm start` script, `Procfile`, or service unit; `node server.js` is operator convention recorded as assumption **A-04** (§3.6.5) |

The practical consequence is that **the deployment procedure lives outside the repository**. Two engineers given only this checkout have no artifact telling them which interpreter version to install, which of the two `.js` files is the application, how to start the process, how to keep it running, or how to stop it cleanly. §3.6.5 documents the five-step manual procedure that convention supplies.

#### 8.1.2.2 Configuration Management Strategy

The configuration strategy is **immutable configuration by source literal**. Every operational parameter is a constant in `server.js`; there is no configuration file, no environment-variable override, no command-line flag, and no defaults-plus-overrides layering. A complete distinct-token inventory of `server.js` confirms the total surface — the file mentions no configuration mechanism at all.

```javascript
const hostname = '127.0.0.1';   // line 3 - bind address, compile-time literal
const port = 3000;              // line 4 - listen port, compile-time literal
```

| Configuration parameter | Effective value | Change procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bind address | `127.0.0.1` (`server.js` line 3) | Edit the literal, commit, redistribute, restart the process |
| Listen port | `3000` (line 4) | Edit the literal, commit, redistribute, restart the process |
| Response status code | `200` (line 7) | Edit the literal, commit, redistribute, restart the process |
| Response content type | `text/plain` (line 8) | Edit the literal, commit, redistribute, restart the process |
| Response body | `Hello, World!` plus newline, 14 bytes (line 9) | Edit the literal, commit, redistribute, restart the process |
| Connection and header timeouts, header size limits, backlog | Node.js defaults, catalogued in §5.2.6 | Not settable without adding code; no repository artifact influences them |

Because configuration and code are the same artifact, **there is no environment-specific configuration and no configuration drift**: the process either runs the committed constants or it runs modified source. This eliminates an entire class of misconfiguration incidents and simultaneously eliminates any ability to retarget a deployment without a code change (**F-002-RQ-003**).

#### 8.1.2.3 Environment Promotion Strategy

**No environment promotion strategy exists, because only one environment is defined and it is not named.** §1.3.2 places environment-specific operation (development, staging, production) explicitly out of scope, and the audit confirms that nothing in the repository distinguishes one execution context from another.

| Environment | Defined by a repository artifact? | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local / development | No named definition; direct execution only | No manifest script, `Procfile`, or dev-server config; launch is operator convention (**A-04**) |
| Staging | Absent | No environment descriptor, overlay, or profile of any kind |
| Production | Absent | No environment descriptor; loopback bind would make a production deployment unreachable by design |
| Ephemeral / preview | Absent | No `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `render.yaml`, or `railway.json` |

    subgraph DefinedScope["Defined by repository artifacts"]
        Commit["Commit 43ed37c, head of branch 2907_01<br/>no tags, no version field"]
        LocalRun["Direct execution on one host<br/>node server.js"]
