**Diagram 8-D — Environment promotion flow.** Only the solid edges exist. The repository's promotion model is a single hop from a commit to a running process on whichever host the operator chose; the dashed elements are drawn to record precisely which promotion machinery is absent. Note that an environment-specific configuration overlay could not participate even if it existed, because the bind address and port are compile-time literals. `server.js` is byte-identical at `43ed37c` and at its parent `06492d7` (blob `320a75a`), so the head commit and the commit that introduced the application promote the same application bytes.

Should promotion ever be required, the minimum change set is structural rather than additive: the bind address and port would have to become externally supplied (removing the sole security control, §6.4), a launch declaration and supervision policy would have to be introduced, and a versioned artifact identity beyond the commit SHA would have to be established (§8.5).

#### 8.1.2.4 Backup and Disaster Recovery

The recovery posture is simple because there is almost nothing at risk. **No application data exists to lose**: the request object is never read, nothing is written to disk, and no database, cache, queue, or file store is used (§3.5, §6.2). The only durable artifact is the source itself.

| Recovery dimension | As-built posture | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data at risk | None — the process holds no state across requests | Source fact |
| Recovery point objective | Not applicable — there is no state to recover to a point in time | Source fact |
| Recovery time objective | Not declared. Measured relaunch: 40 ms from process spawn to first HTTP 200 | Host observation |
| Artifact backup | The Git remote is the only durable copy; the entire history is a 4.12 KiB pack of 9 objects | Audit result |
| Configuration backup | Implicit in the source artifact; nothing separate to back up | Source fact |
| Automated recovery | Absent — no supervisor, no restart policy, no health check to trigger one | Audit result |
| Failure detection | Absent — an outage produces no signal; §6.1.4.5 notes that "degraded is indistinguishable from healthy" | Audit result (§5.4.1) |
| Redundancy | None — one process, one host, one port; every element is a single point of failure | Source fact (§5.4.6) |
| Restore procedure | `git clone` (measured 7 ms locally, delivering 3 files and 382 bytes) followed by `node server.js` | Host observation |

Two operational hazards deserve explicit statement, both verified empirically:

- **Bind conflict is recovery-blocking.** If a stale process still holds `127.0.0.1:3000`, the replacement instance dies immediately with an unhandled `EADDRINUSE` error and exit code 1. Recovery therefore requires the operator to confirm the port is free before relaunching; nothing in the repository does this.
- **Shutdown is never graceful.** `SIGTERM` terminates the process in 2 ms with exit code 143 and the socket is refused immediately afterwards; no handler drains in-flight connections, because none is registered (**F-002-RQ-005**).

A third hazard is specific to the current tree: the restored checkout contains two `.js` files and only `server.js` starts a listener. Launching `test.js` by mistake produces no listener at all — the process exits 1 with `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` (§6.6.1) — so the restore step must name `server.js` explicitly.

A recovery plan for this system is consequently a two-line runbook — restore the source from the Git remote, confirm the port is free, and relaunch `server.js` — and that runbook is not present in the repository (§6.1.1.2 found all 28 resilience, health, and runbook paths absent). The Git remote configured as `origin` in the local `.git/config` is a standard GitHub HTTPS URL, but the local configuration embeds an access token; that credential must never be copied into images, logs, or documentation (§3.4.4).

## 8.2 Cloud Services

**The system uses no cloud services. This sub-section records that determination and its evidence, then documents the dependencies and costs the system does have.**

The repository contains no cloud provider binding of any kind. A case-insensitive audit of the complete tracked corpus for `aws`, `azure`, `gcp`, `cloud`, `s3`, `ec2`, `lambda`, `cdn`, and `registry` returned **zero matches** (Audit result), and §3.4 independently establishes that the system integrates with no third-party service, API, or SDK whatsoever. Two run-time properties make the absence structural rather than incidental: `server.js` **opens no outbound socket and performs no DNS lookup**, so there is no client-side path to any cloud endpoint, and the process reads **no environment variable, credential file, or configuration source** from which a cloud endpoint or key could be supplied. §3.4 summarises the consequence precisely — the service "requires no egress allowance in any network policy".

| Cloud concern | Determination | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider selection | Not applicable — no provider is selected or referenced | 9-term cloud keyword audit, zero matches; no provider SDK imported (the single `require` is core `http`) |
| Cloud credentials | Absent | `.aws/`, `.docker/`, `serviceAccount.json`, `credentials`, `.env*` all absent (§6.4.1.3, group 3) |
| Managed compute (VM, container service, function) | Absent | No `template.yaml`, `serverless.yml`, `samconfig.toml`, `app.yaml`, `cloudbuild.yaml`, `fly.toml`, `render.yaml`, or `railway.json` |
| Managed data services | Not applicable | No database, cache, queue, or object store is used or referenced (§3.5, §6.2) |
| Managed networking (DNS, CDN, load balancer, gateway) | Not applicable | Listener is loopback-only, so no managed network service could reach it (**F-002-RQ-002**) |
| Identity and access management | Absent | No IAM policy, role, or federation artifact; the only control is topological (§6.4) |
| Cloud monitoring and logging services | Absent | No agent, exporter, or collector configuration (§6.5) |

Because there is no cloud footprint, the questions this sub-section would normally answer — provider justification, service versions, multi-availability-zone design, reserved-capacity strategy, and shared-responsibility boundaries — have no subject. The remainder of the sub-section therefore documents what the system genuinely depends on and what it genuinely costs, so that an operator can plan a deployment without inferring cloud machinery that does not exist.

### 8.2.1 External Dependencies

The system's complete dependency set is four local interfaces plus one distribution channel. §3.4 enumerates the four interfaces — the inbound `127.0.0.1:3000` listener, the core `http` request/response API, the standard-output stream, and the process lifecycle — all provided by the Node.js runtime and the host operating system. **There are zero third-party packages**: no `package.json`, lockfile, or `node_modules` exists, and `server.js` contains exactly one `require` call, for a built-in module. The third tracked file, `test.js`, contains no `require`, `import`, or package reference of any kind, so it adds nothing to this set (§3.3.1).

| Dependency | Provider | Coupling | Impact if unavailable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Node.js runtime (core `http`, CommonJS resolution) | Node.js project; installed on the host by the operator | Run-time, mandatory, version unpinned | The process cannot start at all |
| Host TCP/IP stack and loopback interface | Host operating system | Run-time, mandatory | `listen` fails; the process exits |
| TCP port 3000 on the loopback address | Host operating system | Run-time, mandatory and exclusive | `EADDRINUSE`, unhandled error event, exit code 1 |
| Standard output stream | Host process environment | Run-time, diagnostic only | The 41-byte readiness line is lost; serving is unaffected |
| Git client (2.43.0 observed, §3.6) | Operator workstation | Distribution-time only | No way to obtain, update, or restore the source |
| GitHub `origin` remote repository | GitHub, software as a service | Distribution-time only; no run-time coupling (§1.2.1.3) | New checkouts and source restores are blocked; a running process is unaffected |
| Third-party libraries and frameworks | None | None | Not applicable — zero dependencies means zero transitive supply-chain surface (§2.4.4) |

The **minimum distribution requirement** is therefore a Git client with read access to the remote, or any other means of copying the 382-byte tracked tree onto the target host — of which only `server.js`'s 342 bytes are needed to run the service; the **minimum execution requirement** is a Node.js interpreter and a free loopback port. Nothing else is required, and nothing else is provided.

### 8.2.2 High Availability Design

**Not applicable.** High availability presupposes redundancy, and the repository defines a single process bound to a single port on a single host with no supervisor and no failover target. §8.1.2.4 records the full recovery posture; §6.1 establishes that the unit of deployment, the unit of failure, and the unit of capacity are the same OS process. The two structural blockers are the fixed port literal, which prevents a second instance on the same host, and the loopback bind, which prevents any instance from being reached across hosts — so neither an active-active nor an active-passive arrangement can be assembled from the committed artifact without a source change.

### 8.2.3 Cost Profile

The repository declares no paid infrastructure, so **the recurring infrastructure cost attributable to the repository is zero**. The table below states each cost element with its basis; figures are determinations about the repository, not price quotations, and no external pricing is assumed.

| Cost element | Cost attributable to the repository | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloud compute, storage, and managed services | 0 | No cloud resource is declared or provisioned by any artifact |
| Container registry storage and transfer | 0 | No image is defined, built, or pushed (§8.3) |
| CI/CD compute minutes | 0 | No pipeline definition exists; all three commits landed with no automated verification (§3.6.4) |
| Data services (database, cache, queue, object store) | 0 | None used or referenced (§3.5) |
| Network egress | 0 | No outbound socket and no DNS lookup; all traffic traverses the loopback interface |
| Third-party licences, subscriptions, and API quotas | 0 | Zero dependencies and no third-party service (§3.4) |
| Source hosting | 0 on a free public-repository tier | Entire history is a 4.12 KiB pack of 9 objects across 3 commits |
| Observability and monitoring services | 0 | No agent, exporter, or collector (§6.5) |
| Operator-provided host | Not determinable from the repository | The host is outside the repository; measured footprint is 1 vCPU, under 128 MiB resident memory, and about 120 MiB of disk dominated by the interpreter — an operator can multiply that footprint by their own rate |

The only meaningful cost-optimization observation is structural: because the process cannot use more than one core (measured ceiling 102.5% of a single core, §6.1.3.1) and cannot be replicated in its committed form, **over-provisioning is the dominant cost risk**. A host sized beyond one vCPU and a few hundred mebibytes of memory cannot be exploited by this workload. There is no cost-monitoring, budget, or tagging artifact in the repository — the `cost`, `budget`, and `billing` keyword audit returned zero matches — so no cost attribution is possible from the repository side (§8.6.3).

### 8.2.4 Security and Compliance Considerations

With no cloud footprint there is no shared-responsibility boundary to document, no cloud IAM surface to review, and no provider compliance attestation to inherit. Three repository-side facts remain relevant to any future cloud deployment and are recorded here so they are not lost:

- **The sole access control is topological and would be voided by cloud exposure.** The loopback bind is the only security control in the repository (§2.4.4, §6.4). Any change that makes the service reachable from a cloud network removes that control entirely and must add authentication and TLS in the same change (§5.4.4).
- **There is no transport security.** The listener is plaintext HTTP/1.1; `https`, `tls`, and `crypto` are never required. A cloud deployment would require TLS termination that the repository does not provide.
- **The distribution channel carries a credential.** The `origin` remote in the local `.git/config` is a GitHub HTTPS URL whose local configuration embeds an access token. That credential governs repository access only and has no relationship to the running service, but it must never be copied into an image layer, a build log, an environment variable, or this document (§3.4.4, §6.3.4.4).

Compliance determinations are enumerated once, in §8.1.1.4, and are not repeated here.

## 8.3 Containerization

**The system is not containerized, and in its committed form it cannot be containerized usefully without a source change. This sub-section records the determination, the evidence, and the single structural blocker.**

Every container-related descriptor was probed by path and found absent: `Dockerfile`, `dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.dev`, `Containerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `docker-compose.yaml`, `compose.yml`, `.dockerignore`, `devcontainer.json`, and `.devcontainer/` — **0 of 9 probed paths present** (Audit result). The wider audits agree: §6.1.1.2 found all 25 multi-service orchestration paths absent, and §6.4.1.3 found all 19 runtime-hardening and isolation paths absent, including `seccomp.json`, `apparmor.profile`, and `securitycontext.yaml`. The `docker`, `container`, and `registry` keyword scans over the tracked corpus returned zero matches. §3.6.3 reaches the same conclusion from the toolchain side and adds the operative caution: "Containerizing this service would be trivial but is not defined."

### 8.3.1 The Loopback Bind Is a Containerization Blocker

The reason containerization is not merely undocumented but structurally obstructed is the bind address literal on line 3 of `server.js`. A container receives its own network namespace. A process that binds `127.0.0.1` inside that namespace is reachable only from **inside the container**, so publishing the port (`-p 3000:3000`) or exposing it through a Kubernetes Service would produce a port mapping that forwards to nothing. This was verified in the equivalent host case: a request to the machine's own routable address (`10.76.0.92:3000`) is refused with `curl` exit code 7, while the loopback request succeeds (**F-002-RQ-002**). §3.6.3 names this exactly — "the hard-coded loopback bind is a containerization hazard" — and §5.2.2 records that the same literal is what makes the bind component the binding constraint on horizontal scaling.

Consequently, the first change any containerization effort would require is not a `Dockerfile` but a source change: the bind address would have to accept `0.0.0.0` or an externally supplied value, and that change removes the only security control the repository has (§6.4, §8.2.4).

### 8.3.2 Topic-by-Topic Determinations

| Containerization topic | Determination | Evidence and consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container platform selection | Not applicable — no platform is selected | No Docker, Podman, or Buildah artifact; no registry reference anywhere in the corpus |
| Base image strategy | Absent — no base image is named | No `Dockerfile` exists; the effective "base" today is whatever Node.js binary the operator installed, which the repository does not pin (§8.1.1.3) |
| Image versioning approach | Not applicable — nothing is versioned as an image | The repository has 0 tags and no version field; the abbreviated commit SHA `43ed37c` at the branch head is the only version identity (§3.6.6) |
| Build optimization | Not applicable — there is no build | 382 bytes of source across three files, zero dependencies, no compile step; a hypothetical image would be dominated entirely by the runtime layer, measured at 119.1 MiB against a 382-byte application tree (a ratio of roughly 327,000 : 1) |
| Layer caching and `.dockerignore` hygiene | Not applicable | With three small files and no dependency install step there is no layer to cache and nothing to exclude — though the one file worth excluding, the non-application `test.js`, has no exclusion mechanism to be listed in |
| Image security scanning | Absent | No `.trivyignore`, `trivy.yaml`, `.snyk`, or scanning workflow (§6.4.1.3, group 6); no image exists to scan, and with zero third-party packages there is no dependency CVE surface — the interpreter is the entire vulnerability surface (§5.4.4) |
| Runtime hardening (non-root user, read-only filesystem, capability drop, seccomp) | Absent | No hardening descriptor exists; the process writes nothing to disk and needs no privileged port, so it could run unprivileged and read-only, but nothing in the repository asserts that |
| Reproducible development container | Absent | No `.devcontainer/` or `devcontainer.json`; the development environment is unpinned and undocumented (§3.6.1 notes `README.md` supplies no prerequisite, install step, or run command) |

### 8.3.3 What Containerization Would Require

Recorded as a constraint set derived from the observed evidence, not as a recommendation: an image definition would need to (a) select and pin a runtime, since the repository pins none; (b) alter the bind literal so the listener is reachable through the namespace boundary, accepting the loss of the topological control; (c) supply the launch command, which exists nowhere in the repository and is currently pure operator convention (assumption **A-04**, §3.6.5); (d) add a health probe target, since no health endpoint exists and a `/metrics` or `/healthz` request returns the same constant 14-byte body rather than a distinguishable response (§6.5); and (e) add signal handling, because `SIGTERM` currently terminates the process in 2 ms with no connection draining, which conflicts with the graceful-termination grace period every container runtime assumes.

## 8.4 Orchestration

**The system does not require orchestration and cannot be orchestrated in its committed form. This sub-section records the determination and the evidence.**

Orchestration coordinates multiple replicas or multiple services across a scheduler-managed pool of hosts. This system has **one service, one process, and one possible instance**, so there is nothing to schedule, place, replicate, or reconcile. The absence is confirmed by audit: no `k8s/`, `kubernetes/`, `manifests/`, `helm/`, `Chart.yaml`, `kustomization.yaml`, `skaffold.yaml`, `Tiltfile`, `nomad.hcl`, `swarm.yml`, `ecs-task-definition.json`, or `task-definition.json` exists (§6.1.1.2, group 1 — 0 of 25 present), and no autoscaling or IaC descriptor exists (§6.1.1.2, group 8 — 0 of 26 present, including `hpa.yaml`, `vpa.yaml`, `keda.yaml`, `autoscaling.yaml`, and `asg.json`). The `kubernetes`, `helm`, `scale`, and `replica` keyword scans over the tracked corpus returned zero matches.

| Orchestration capability | Status | Blocking evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Orchestration platform selection | Not applicable | No manifest, chart, or task definition of any kind exists |
| Cluster architecture (control plane, node pools, namespaces) | Not applicable | Nothing to schedule; the deployment target is a single operator-chosen host (§8.1.1.1) |
| Service deployment strategy (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet) | Not applicable | One process, no workload descriptor, no launch declaration in the repository (**A-04**) |
| Service discovery and internal networking | Not applicable | The endpoint is two hard-coded literals; nothing publishes, resolves, or registers an address (§6.1) |
| Readiness and liveness probes | Absent | No health endpoint; a probe of any path returns the same constant 14-byte body, so a probe could not distinguish healthy from degraded (§6.1.4.5, §6.5) |
| Auto-scaling configuration | Absent | No trigger, no metric source, no policy, and no metric endpoint to scale on (§6.5) |
| Resource allocation policy (requests, limits, quotas) | Absent | No container or orchestration resource block; on the verification host `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max` and `memory.max` are absent, so the process ceiling is architectural rather than administrative (§6.1.3) |
| Rolling update and disruption budget | Not applicable | No replica set to roll; restart is a manual stop-then-start with no draining (§8.1.2.4) |
| Config and secret injection | Not applicable | Zero `process.env` reads; configuration is compile-time literals (§8.1.2.2) |

### 8.4.1 Why Scaling Cannot Be Delegated to a Scheduler

Even if an orchestration manifest were written, the committed source would defeat it. §6.1.3 analyses the scaling dimensions in full; the summary relevant to infrastructure planning is:

| Scaling dimension | Available today | Blocking evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Within the process (multi-core) | No | Only `http` is required — no `cluster`, `worker_threads`, or `child_process`; one JavaScript thread carries 97.4% of process CPU and the measured ceiling is 102.5% of a single core |
| Within one host (multiple instances) | No | The port is a fixed literal; a second instance dies with unhandled `EADDRINUSE` and exit code 1 (**F-002-RQ-004**) |
| Across hosts (replicas behind a load balancer) | No | The loopback bind makes every instance unreachable from off-host, so no Service, ingress, or load balancer could route to it (**F-002-RQ-002**) |
| Vertically (a larger host) | No practical benefit | Thread count is invariant at 7 and throughput plateaus near concurrency 8 at roughly 66,000–81,000 req/s; the process consumed 6.41% of the 16-vCPU verification host at its ceiling |

The consequence for capacity planning is that **the process is both the unit of capacity and the unit of failure** (§2.4.3, §6.1): an operator cannot add capacity by adding replicas, and cannot recover from a process loss by having a scheduler restart it, because no supervisor, restart policy, or scheduler participation exists. Introducing orchestration would require the same structural changes listed in §8.3.3 — an externally supplied bind address and port, a launch declaration, a distinguishable health endpoint, and signal handling — before any manifest could be meaningful.

## 8.5 CI/CD Pipeline

**No CI/CD pipeline exists in this repository.** The `.github/` directory does not exist at all, and every alternative pipeline descriptor was probed and found absent: `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.circleci/`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`, `.travis.yml`, `.drone.yml`, `appveyor.yml`, `.buildkite/`, `Makefile`, `Taskfile.yml`, `scripts/`, `build.sh`, `deploy.sh`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `.releaserc`, `release.config.js`, and `.changeset/` — **0 of 16 probed paths present** in this section's audit, corroborated by the independent audit in §3.6.4. §1.3.2 places CI/CD pipelines explicitly out of scope.

This sub-section therefore documents the manual process that stands in for a pipeline, measured end to end against the tracked source, and states for each pipeline concern whether it is Absent (meaningful but unimplemented) or Not applicable (presupposes a structure this system lacks). The purpose is to make the real path from commit to running process auditable, and to make the missing gates explicit rather than implied.

### 8.5.1 Build Pipeline

#### 8.5.1.1 Source Control Triggers

Source control is Git, with a GitHub `origin` remote that serves as a source-distribution channel only and has no run-time coupling to the process (§3.4, §1.2.1.3). **Nothing in the repository reacts to a source-control event.**

| Trigger surface | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push, pull-request, or merge trigger | Absent | `.github/workflows/` does not exist; no alternative CI descriptor exists |
| Scheduled or cron-driven build | Absent | No workflow file and no `cron` reference anywhere in the corpus |
| Tag-driven release trigger | Not applicable | `git tag` returns 0 tags, so no tag event can occur |
| Branch protection and required review | Absent | No in-tree branch-protection, review, or `CODEOWNERS` metadata (§3.6.4) |
| Local pre-commit or pre-push hook | Absent | `.git/hooks/` contains only the default `*.sample` files (§6.4) |
| Commit provenance | Delegated | All three commits carry a signature applied server-side by the GitHub web flow (committer `GitHub <noreply@github.com>`); the signature is unverifiable in a local checkout and no in-repository policy requires it (§6.4) |

The commit history makes the consequence concrete: the repository contains exactly **three commits** — `241598b` "Initial commit" adding `README.md`, then `06492d7` "Add files via upload" adding `server.js`, then `43ed37c` "Create test.js" adding `test.js` — and **all three landed with no automated verification of any kind** (§3.6.4). Two branches exist, `main` and `2907_01`, and they have **diverged**: `main` is at `06492d7` (two files) while `2907_01`, the checked-out branch, is one commit ahead at `43ed37c` (three files).

The third commit is the clearest available demonstration of what the missing triggers cost. It reached a branch head with no review, no status check, and no gate, and the file it added throws `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and exits 1 when executed (§6.6.1). No trigger surface in the table above would have observed that, because none of them exists.

There is no artifact-generation step; **the committed source is the artifact** (§3.6). Nothing is compiled, minified, bundled, archived, versioned as a package, or published to a registry.

One gate is worth calling out because it is both the most obvious candidate and currently unsatisfiable: **a gate implemented as `node --test` at the repository root would fail on the tree as it stands.** Node's default test-file discovery matches files named `test.js`, so the runner finds the repository's non-test `test.js`, evaluates it, and reports `not ok 1 - test.js` with `failureType: 'testCodeFailure'`, totals of 1 test / 0 pass / 1 fail, and exit code 1 (§6.6.1.3). Adopting such a gate therefore requires first repairing or removing that file, or scoping discovery to exclude it.

§3.6.4 states the practical position exactly: "Change verification is entirely manual: launch the server and probe it."

#### 8.5.1.6 Minimal Build and Distribution Requirements

For a standalone script with no infrastructure, this is the complete and authoritative requirement set:

- **Build:** none. There is no compilation, bundling, packaging, or install step. The only pre-flight verification available is `node --check server.js` (22 ms, exit 0).
- **Distribution:** obtain the 4.12 KiB Git pack via `git clone` or `git pull` (measured at 7 ms for a local clone, delivering 3 files and 382 bytes), or copy those 382 bytes by any other means — 342 of which are the application. No registry, artifact repository, or release channel is involved.
- **Runtime provisioning:** install a Node.js interpreter on the target host. The repository imposes no version floor; the interpreter accounts for essentially the whole disk requirement (119.1 MiB observed).
- **Execution:** run `node server.js` from the checkout root with `127.0.0.1:3000` free. This command appears nowhere in the repository and is operator convention recorded as assumption **A-04**; the checkout contains a second `.js` file that is not the application and exits 1 if launched instead (§6.6.1).
- **Not required:** signing, packaging, publication, dependency installation, environment-variable provisioning, migration, or warm-up.

| Pipeline step | Measured wall time | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `git clone` (local, distribution stand-in) | 7 ms | 3 files, 382 bytes, HEAD `43ed37c`, branch `2907_01` |
| `node --check server.js` | 22 ms | Exit 0, no stdout or stderr |
| Launch to first HTTP 200 | 40 ms | 41 bytes on stdout, 0 bytes on stderr |
| Complete cycle | About 69 ms of machine time | A serving listener on `127.0.0.1:3000` |

*Host observation. Every step is operator-initiated; none is encoded in the repository. Elapsed wall time in practice is therefore dominated by human latency, not by the software.*

### 8.5.2 Deployment Pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start(["Operator decides to deploy"]) --> Clone["git clone or git pull<br/>7 ms, 382 B, 3 files"]
    Clone --> Check{"node --check server.js<br/>22 ms"}
    Check -->|"exit 0"| Launch["node server.js<br/>foreground, non-daemonized"]
    Check -->|"non-zero exit"| FixSource["Correct source and retry<br/>no pipeline exists"]
    FixSource --> Check
    Launch --> Bind{"127.0.0.1:3000<br/>available?"}
    Bind -->|"no - EADDRINUSE"| FailFast["Unhandled error event<br/>exit code 1, no retry, no supervisor"]
    Bind -->|"yes"| Ready["41-byte readiness line on stdout<br/>launch to first 200: 40 ms"]
    Ready --> Validate{"curl 127.0.0.1:3000<br/>status 200 and 14-byte body?"}
    Validate -->|"yes"| Serving["Serving - no health endpoint,<br/>no restart policy"]
    Validate -->|"no"| ManualDiag["Manual diagnosis<br/>only signal is process presence"]
    Serving --> Stop["SIGTERM: exit 143 in 2 ms<br/>no connection draining"]
```

**Diagram 8-C — Deployment workflow as practised.** Every node is an operator action or an inherited runtime behaviour; no node is automated by a repository artifact. The two decision points that can end the deployment are the syntax check, which the operator must choose to run, and the bind, which fails fatally and without retry when the port is occupied (**F-002-RQ-004**). Timings are host observations from the measured cycle in §8.5.1.6. The launch step names `server.js` explicitly because the checkout contains a second `.js` file that is not the application (§6.6.1).

#### 8.5.2.1 Deployment Strategy

| Strategy | Applicability | Blocking evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blue-green | Not applicable | Requires two instances running concurrently; the fixed port literal permits exactly one, the second exiting with code 1 |
| Canary | Not applicable | Requires traffic splitting at a proxy or load balancer; the loopback bind prevents any such component from being placed in front (§5.2.2) |
| Rolling update | Not applicable | Requires two or more replicas and a scheduler to sequence them; neither exists (§8.4) |
| Feature-flagged or dark launch | Not applicable | `server.js` contains zero conditionals and reads no configuration source, so no behaviour can be toggled |
| Recreate (stop, then start) | **This is the de-facto strategy** | The only sequence the artifact supports; measured stop 2 ms (exit 143) and start 40 ms to first HTTP 200 |

The recreate strategy implies an unavailability window on every change. Its **software-imposed floor is about 42 ms** (2 ms to terminate plus 40 ms to become ready again); in practice the window is bounded by operator reaction time, because no automation closes it. Zero-downtime restart is explicitly out of scope (§1.3.2) and is unreachable without a second instance, which the port literal forbids.

#### 8.5.2.2 Environment Promotion Workflow

The promotion workflow is a single hop from a commit to a running process, illustrated in **Diagram 8-D** (§8.1.2.3). There is no staging environment, no promotion gate, no approval step, and no environment-specific configuration to carry across a boundary. Promotion in the conventional sense — the same artifact advancing through progressively production-like environments — has no second environment to advance into.

#### 8.5.2.3 Rollback Procedures

The only rollback mechanism available is `git checkout` of an earlier commit, measured at **2 ms**. Its usefulness is determined by the shape of the commit graph, which was verified directly inside a disposable clone:

| Rollback target | Working-tree content at that commit | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `43ed37c` (HEAD, branch `2907_01`) | `server.js` + `README.md` + `test.js` | The current state. `test.js` is not the application and is never executed by the launch procedure (§6.6.1) |
| `06492d7` (parent; also the head of `main`) | `server.js` + `README.md` | **A working state.** `server.js` carries the identical blob `320a75a` here, so the service runs and answers exactly as it does at HEAD; only the non-application `test.js` is absent |
| `241598b` (grandparent, "Initial commit") | `README.md` only — **`server.js` does not exist** (verified by file-existence test at that commit) | Rolling back this far removes the application entirely; there is nothing left to run |
| Any tag | No tag exists (`git tag` returns 0) | There is no semantic or named rollback target |

**The deployment finding, graded against the current three-commit graph: the most recent commit is revertible, but there is still no previous version of the application to roll back to.** Two backward steps now exist where earlier revisions of this specification recorded one, and the first of them is genuinely useful: a checkout of `06492d7` yields a tree that serves the same `200` / `text/plain` / 14-byte response, because `server.js` is byte-identical at both commits. That makes a defect introduced by `43ed37c` — such as the file that exits 1 on execution — trivially reversible.

What the graph still does not provide is an earlier *revision of the application*. Exactly one commit has ever touched `server.js`, so there is one and only one version of the application in the entire history; the second backward step deletes it. Recovery from a bad change to `server.js` is therefore necessarily *roll-forward* — re-checkout `06492d7` or `43ed37c`, or commit a corrected version — and never *roll-back*. Because the deployed artifact is the source, the rollback action and the redeploy action are the same two commands (`git checkout <sha>` then `node server.js`), and the same bind-conflict hazard applies: the previous process must have fully exited or the replacement dies with `EADDRINUSE`.

#### 8.5.2.4 Post-Deployment Validation

No automated post-deployment validation exists — there is no health endpoint, smoke test, or synthetic check in the repository. The following manual checks are what the artifact makes possible, and all of them were exercised during verification. Every check must run **on the deployment host**, because the listener refuses connections from any other address (§3.4, §6.5).

| Validation check | Method | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Process readiness | Read the process's standard output | Exactly 41 bytes: the single line `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/` |
| Endpoint liveness | `curl` the root path and inspect the status code | `200` |
| Payload correctness | Compare the response body | `Hello, World!` plus a newline — 14 bytes, `Content-Length: 14`, SHA-256 prefix `c98c24b677ef` (§6.5) |
| Listener presence | Inspect `/proc/net/tcp` | Exactly one entry `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A`, and no IPv6 listener |
| Error stream cleanliness | Read standard error | 0 bytes (the stream remained empty across every probe, **F-004-RQ-003**) |
| Isolation confirmation | Request the host's routable address | Connection refused, confirming the loopback boundary is intact (**F-002-RQ-002**) |

A caveat worth recording: because every path returns the same constant body, a validation probe of a conventional health path such as `/healthz` or `/metrics` succeeds with the greeting rather than failing distinguishably (§6.5). Validation must therefore assert the exact 14-byte payload, not merely a 2xx status.

#### 8.5.2.5 Release Management Process

| Release attribute | Value | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Version identity | The abbreviated commit SHA; `git describe --always --tags` returns `43ed37c` | Audit result |
| Tags and named releases | 0 | Audit result |
| Semantic version field | None — no `package.json` version, no `VERSION` file | Audit result |
| Changelog or release notes | Absent | Audit result |
| Release approval or sign-off | Absent — no review requirement, `CODEOWNERS`, or branch protection in-tree | Audit result |
| Release cadence | 3 commits: two authored on 2026-07-29 about eleven seconds apart, the third on 2026-07-30; all by the same author | Audit result |
| Branch topology | `main` at `06492d7` and `2907_01` at `43ed37c` — the two branches have diverged by one commit; the checked-out branch is `2907_01` | Audit result |
| Artifact retention | Indefinite, by virtue of Git history; no separate retention policy exists | Audit result |

Release management therefore consists of "the commit SHA that is currently checked out on the host". §3.6.6 states the same conclusion from the toolchain perspective: the commit SHA is the only version identity, and distribution is by Git clone alone. A consequence of the divergence recorded above is that "the current release" is branch-dependent: a clone that follows `origin/HEAD` lands on `main` at `06492d7`, which contains the same application but not `test.js`.

## 8.6 Infrastructure Monitoring

**The repository contains no monitoring infrastructure, and it emits nothing that a monitoring system could consume beyond a single 41-byte startup line.** §6.5 reaches the formal determination for the observability domain — "Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system" — on the strength of a 104-term telemetry audit across 12 groups returning zero matches. This section's independent audit agrees: `prometheus.yml`, `grafana/`, `otel-collector-config.yaml`, `newrelic.js`, and `datadog.yaml` are all absent, as are the 13 audit-log-infrastructure paths tested in §6.4.1.3 (`auditd.rules`, `logrotate.conf`, `rsyslog.conf`, `fluentd.conf`, `fluent-bit.conf`, `filebeat.yml`, `vector.toml`, `promtail.yaml`, and others).

The consequence for infrastructure monitoring is specific: **all monitoring of this system must be external to it, host-side, and co-located.** External because the process exposes no metric, health, or management interface; host-side because the only observable facts are operating-system facts about the process; and co-located because a probe from any non-loopback address is refused (§6.5 records `curl` exit 7 and status `000` against the routable address). This sub-section documents what an operator can actually observe, what they cannot, and the maintenance procedures those limits imply.

### 8.6.1 Resource Monitoring Approach

Resource monitoring is entirely delegated to host tooling reading the standard process interfaces. The baselines below are measurements of the as-built process and are the reference values an operator would alert against; none of them is a threshold the repository declares.

| Resource signal | How an operator obtains it | Observed baseline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Process liveness | Process table lookup (`pgrep -fc "node server.js"`) | 1 while serving, 0 after exit (§6.5) |
| Resident memory | `/proc/<pid>/status` `VmRSS` | 46.8 MiB idle, 57.7 MiB after 500 requests, 75.6 MiB after 382,144 requests |
| Virtual reservation | `/proc/<pid>/status` `VmSize` / `VmPeak` | 750,236 KiB / 751,224 KiB — V8 address-space reservation, not committed memory |
| Thread count | `/proc/<pid>/status` `Threads` | 7, invariant at every concurrency level tested |
| Open file descriptors | `/proc/<pid>/fd` | 22 at idle, exactly +1 per held connection, about 1.63 kB each (§6.5) |
| CPU utilisation | Per-thread CPU sampling | One thread carries 97.4% of process CPU; measured ceiling 102.5% of a single core (§6.1.3.1) |
| Listener presence | `/proc/net/tcp` | Exactly one entry `0100007F:0BB8` in state `0A`; no IPv6 listener |
| Termination cause | Shell exit status of the process | 1 for `EADDRINUSE`, 143 for `SIGTERM`, 130 for `SIGINT` (§6.5) |

Because the process is not cgroup-limited on the verification host (`/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max` and `memory.max` absent, §6.1.3), there are no container-level utilisation ratios to monitor — the numerator is the process and the denominator is the whole host. An operator sizing alert thresholds should note that memory growth is bounded and modest (about 29 MiB from idle across 382,144 requests) and that thread and descriptor counts are structurally stable, so the only volatile dimension is descriptor count under held keep-alive connections.

### 8.6.2 Performance Metrics Collection

**No performance metric is collected or exposed.** The system emits exactly one line of output in its lifetime, at startup, and nothing per request.

| Metric class | Availability | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request rate, latency, error rate | Not available from the system | No per-request logging and no counters; these can only be inferred by an external synthetic prober that measures its own calls (**F-004-RQ-003**) |
| Saturation indicators (queue depth, event-loop lag) | Not available | Nothing instruments the event loop; saturation is only visible as rising client-observed latency |
| Metric scrape endpoint | Absent | A request to `/metrics` returns the same constant 14-byte greeting, so a scraper receives a **parse error rather than a clean 404** (§6.5) |
| Health and readiness endpoints | Absent | Every path returns `200`, so a probe cannot distinguish healthy from degraded — §6.1.4.5 puts it as "degraded is indistinguishable from healthy" |
| Distributed tracing | Not applicable | The system is neither traceable nor a trace participant; no context is propagated (§5.4.2) |
| Log-derived metrics | Not available | Standard output remained invariant at 41 bytes and standard error at 0 bytes across roughly 2,300 requests and four protocol-error probes (§6.5) |
| Runtime budget visibility | Delegated | The effective timeouts and limits are Node.js defaults catalogued in §5.2.6; nothing reports them at run time |

For reference, the throughput and latency envelope an operator would be monitoring against was measured externally in §6.5 and §6.1.3.1 — a plateau of roughly 66,000 to 81,000 requests per second peaking near concurrency 8, with the single event-loop thread as the serialisation point. **These are host observations, not commitments**: §2.4.2 records that the repository declares no performance requirement for any feature, and §6.1.3.5 notes there is no way to observe where a deployed instance sits against its measured ceiling.

### 8.6.3 Cost Monitoring and Optimization

**No cost monitoring is possible from the repository side, and there is nothing to attribute.** The `cost`, `budget`, and `billing` keyword audit over the tracked corpus returned zero matches, and §8.2.3 establishes that every declarable infrastructure cost element is zero.

| Cost-monitoring capability | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resource tagging and cost allocation | Not applicable | No cloud or IaC resource exists to tag (§8.1.2.1, §8.2) |
| Budget definition or spend alerting | Absent | No budget artifact; zero keyword matches |
| Utilisation telemetry for right-sizing | Absent from the repository; available only via host tooling | The measured one-core ceiling and sub-128 MiB resident set are the only right-sizing inputs (§8.1.1.3) |
| Idle-cost detection and scale-to-zero | Not applicable | The process holds about 47 MiB whether idle or serving, and no mechanism exists to stop or start it on demand |
| Per-request cost attribution | Not applicable | No request is recorded, so no unit-cost denominator exists |

The single actionable optimisation observation, repeated from §8.2.3 because it is the only one grounded in measurement: **over-provisioning is the dominant cost risk.** The process cannot use more than one core or a few hundred mebibytes of memory, and it cannot be replicated in its committed form, so any host provisioned beyond that footprint is paid for and unusable by this workload.

### 8.6.4 Security Monitoring

**Security monitoring is not possible with the artifact as committed.** The system produces no security-relevant event of any kind.

| Security signal | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access log | Absent | No per-request logging exists; the only output is the startup line (§6.4) |
| Authentication and authorization events | Not applicable | No authentication or authorization exists; every caller is anonymous and indistinguishable (§5.4.4, §6.3.2.2) |
| Attack visibility | Absent | Standard output remained exactly 41 bytes across nine attack-shaped probes, so **an attack is indistinguishable from normal operation** (§6.4.1.5) |
| Intrusion detection or anomaly detection | Absent | No IDS or anomaly artifact, and no event stream to feed one |
| Perimeter monitoring | Delegated | The loopback bind is the entire perimeter; only host-level tooling could observe connection attempts against it (§6.4) |
| Rate-limit and abuse signals | Absent | No rate limiting; a 300-request burst returned 300 identical `200` responses with no signal emitted (§6.3.2.4) |
| Secret exposure monitoring | Absent | No secret scanning is configured, and the credential embedded in the local `origin` remote is therefore unmonitored (§3.4.4) |
| File integrity monitoring | Absent | No FIM tooling; `git status --porcelain` against the 382-byte, three-file tree is the only integrity check available, and it is manual |
| Version and banner disclosure | Delegated (favourable) | No `Server` header and no runtime version are returned, so responses disclose nothing about the host (§6.4.4.4) |

### 8.6.5 Compliance Auditing

**The system is not auditable at run time.** §6.4.3.5 states this directly, and the evidence is simply that nothing is recorded: no request, no response, no error, no configuration read, and no lifecycle event other than the startup line.

| Audit requirement | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run-time activity audit trail | Absent | No access, error, or lifecycle logging; nothing to retain or review |
| Change audit trail | Delegated to Git | 3 commits with server-side signatures that cannot be verified in a local checkout; no in-repository review, approval, or ownership policy (§6.4) |
| Configuration baseline evidence | Delegated to Git | Configuration is the source, so `git status --porcelain` returning zero lines is a complete drift attestation for the 382-byte, three-file tree |
| Access review and entitlement reporting | Not applicable | No accounts, roles, credentials, or permissions exist anywhere in the system |
| Evidence retention policy | Absent | There are no logs to retain, and no retention artifact exists |
| Control attestation (SBOM, signature, provenance) | Absent | Zero third-party code makes the input set trivially enumerable, yet nothing attests to it (§2.4.4) |
| Infrastructure configuration audit | Not applicable | No infrastructure is declared, so there is no infrastructure state to audit against a baseline (§8.1.2.1) |

An external auditor examining this deployment would find that the only auditable surface is the Git history of three commits and the byte-for-byte identity of a 382-byte working tree. That is genuinely strong evidence of *what is deployed*, and no evidence at all of *what the deployment did*. The history is also evidence of what the change process does not do: the most recent of those three commits added a file that fails on execution and was admitted with no review and no gate (§6.4.3.5, §8.5.1.1).

### 8.6.6 Monitoring Gaps and Maintenance Procedures

The gap summary below is the operational bottom line of this section. It is a gap list, not a defect list: for a three-file demonstration server whose application is a single 342-byte script these absences are consistent with the system's scope (§1.3.2), but they must be understood before the artifact is placed anywhere it matters.

| Monitoring capability | Status | Operational consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Availability detection | Absent | An outage produces no signal; loss of service is discovered only by a client failing or by an operator checking the process table (§5.4.1) |
| Failure diagnosis | Minimal | The only diagnostic artefacts are the exit code (1, 143, or 130) and, for a bind conflict, a stack trace disclosing address, port, errno, and Node version |
| Automated recovery | Absent | No supervisor, restart policy, or scheduler; recovery is a manual relaunch (§8.1.2.4) |
| Capacity and saturation visibility | Absent | No way to observe where a running instance sits against its measured ceiling (§6.1.3.5) |
| Security event visibility | Absent | Attack traffic and legitimate traffic produce identical, empty telemetry (§8.6.4) |
| Change and configuration visibility | Delegated | Complete, but only through Git; nothing reports at run time which commit is executing, and the two branches have diverged, so the commit that is checked out determines whether the tree carries two files or three (§8.5.2.5) |

The maintenance procedures that follow are the complete set the artifact supports. Every one is manual; none is encoded in the repository, and none is automated by any artifact.

| Maintenance procedure | Trigger | Steps and observed evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start or restart the service | Process exit, host reboot, or any source change | Confirm `127.0.0.1:3000` is free, run `node server.js` — naming that file explicitly, since the checkout holds a second `.js` file that is not the application — then verify the 41-byte readiness line and a `200` with a 14-byte body — about 40 ms from launch to first response |
| Reclaim an occupied port | Launch fails with `EADDRINUSE` and exit code 1 | Identify and terminate the process holding the port, then relaunch; nothing in the repository performs this check (**F-002-RQ-004**) |
| Stop the service | Planned shutdown or host maintenance | Send `SIGTERM`; the process exits in 2 ms with code 143 and the socket is refused immediately — in-flight connections are not drained (**F-002-RQ-005**) |
| Upgrade the runtime | An external Node.js security or LTS release | Replace the interpreter, re-run `node --check server.js`, relaunch, and revalidate; nothing pins, records, or verifies the version, so the upgrade is unconstrained and unverified (§2.4.5) |
| Restore or redeploy the source | Host loss, corrupted checkout, or a bad change | `git clone` (7 ms, 3 files, 382 bytes) or `git checkout 43ed37c` / `git checkout 06492d7` (2 ms), then relaunch; either commit yields a byte-identical `server.js`, but **never roll back to `241598b`, which contains no `server.js`** (§8.5.2.3) |
| Verify a change | Any edit to `server.js` | `node --check server.js` (22 ms) followed by a manual probe; there is no test suite, linter, or pipeline to run, and `node --test` at the repository root exits 1 on the current tree without executing any assertion (§8.5.1.5, §6.6.1.3) |
| Rotate the distribution credential | Token expiry or suspected exposure | Update the `origin` credential in the local Git configuration; this affects source access only and has no relationship to the running service (§3.4.4) |

| --- | --- | --- |
| `server.js` | 342 bytes, 14 newline-terminated lines, index mode `100644` | blob `320a75a7649db30756f011001f299d20df1c44b3` |
| `README.md` | 27 bytes, 1 line with no terminator, index mode `100644` | blob `5fb52319aec99b5e66d84b4fb4dbe5eb51e66e68` |
| `test.js` | 13 bytes, 2 newline-terminated lines, index mode `100644` | blob `2c87c7907121bc5707a819591c3fe67031594aa0` |
| Root tree at `HEAD` | Three entries, no sub-tree | tree `7ffc72101b0c297135d7935c6e4580ded610bade` |
| Root tree at the parent commit | Two entries (`README.md` and `server.js`) | tree `61565d2ff1a950fc862fc6dfacad1d2493629339` |
| Root tree at the grandparent commit | One entry (`README.md` only) | tree `5e69e57cdbf60ad4d202f7cdd65e0bff0688a26a` |

The three commits that constitute the entire history resolve as follows: `HEAD` is commit `43ed37cd9876a62a2b9c3cb82f4d64863109fde9` ("Create test.js", adding `test.js`), its parent is commit `06492d749258f61267008249401ba09bbcb580d3` ("Add files via upload", adding `server.js`), and its grandparent is commit `241598b99b955a94755a55810999bdcab7c0db91` ("Initial commit", adding `README.md`). These object identities are the mechanical basis of the rollback grading recorded in chapter 8. The parent tree carries the **same `server.js` blob as `HEAD`**, so one backward step preserves the application byte for byte and removes only the non-application `test.js`; it is the grandparent tree, holding `README.md` alone, that has no application in it at all. Branch `main` points at the parent commit, so it references the two-entry tree.

A census of the object store confirms that these nine objects are the whole of it.

| Object-store measure | Value | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose objects | 0, occupying 0 bytes | Nothing is unpacked or half-written |
| Objects in pack | 9 in a single pack, 4.12 KiB | Exactly 3 commits, 3 trees and 3 blobs — the complete history with no unreferenced object |
| Prune-packable, garbage | 0 and 0 (0 bytes of garbage) | No redundant or corrupt object exists |

On disk all three files carry permissions `0644` (`-rw-r--r--`), matching the `100644` index mode, so none is executable and none can be launched directly — a property already noted from the security angle in 6.4.1.5 and confirmed independently here. Chapter 8 owns the derived distribution figures (the 4.12 KiB clone payload, the 33,107-byte checkout, and the runtime-to-application size ratio); this sub-section supplies only the identity of the objects those figures describe.

### 9.1.3 Text Encoding and Source Formatting Conventions

No section of this specification records the lexical form of the tracked files, yet those properties determine how the artifact behaves in a text pipeline, a diff, and a checksum. All values below are *Audit results* obtained by byte-level inspection.

| Characteristic | `server.js` | `README.md` | `test.js` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Character encoding | 7-bit US-ASCII — highest byte value 125 (`}`), no byte ≥ 128, no byte-order mark | 7-bit US-ASCII — highest byte value 121 (`y`), no byte-order mark | 7-bit US-ASCII — highest byte value 115 (`s`), no byte-order mark |
| Line terminator | LF only — zero carriage-return bytes | No terminator present (single line) | LF only — zero carriage-return bytes |
| Final byte | `0x0A` — the file is newline-terminated, so there is no partial final line | `o` — the file is **not** newline-terminated | `0x0A` — newline-terminated |
| Line count | 14 newline-terminated lines, of which 4 are blank (2, 5, 11 and the blank between 9 and 12 is line 11) | 1 | 2, neither blank |
| Indentation | Two spaces on lines 7, 8, 9 and 13 — the only indented lines; zero tab characters in the file | Not applicable | None — no leading whitespace and zero tab characters |
| String and statement style | Single-quoted string literals only (no double-quoted literal appears); 9 lines terminated with a semicolon | Not applicable | No string literal and **zero semicolons** — two bare identifier expression statements |
| Executable bit and shebang | Neither — the first two bytes are `co` from `const` | Neither | Neither — the first two bytes are `as` |
| Syntax validation | `node --check server.js` completes with no output | Not applicable (Markdown) | `node --check test.js` also completes with no output and exits 0 — yet *executing* the file raises `ReferenceError: asdsa is not defined` and exits 1 (6.6.1) |

Two consequences deserve statement. First, because the corpus is pure US-ASCII with LF terminators and no BOM, the files are byte-stable across platforms that do not rewrite line endings, and every byte count in this specification is also a character count. Second, **none of these conventions is enforced**: `.gitattributes`, `.editorconfig`, `.prettierrc`, `.eslintrc`, `eslint.config.js` and `.gitignore` were each tested for existence and none is present, so the formatting is de facto rather than declared, and nothing prevents a future edit from introducing CRLF terminators, tabs, or non-ASCII content. The language-level feature baseline implied by the source — `const` declarations, arrow functions and a template literal executed under CommonJS — is owned by chapter 3 and is not restated here.

A third consequence is specific to the last column: the `test.js` row is the document's clearest demonstration that **lexical validity is not evidence of executability**. Every encoding and formatting property of that file is unremarkable, and its syntax check passes, yet the file cannot run. This is why the specification classifies it as a placeholder artifact rather than as source (3.1.1, 6.6.1).

### 9.1.4 Line-Level Construct Index for `server.js`

Section 6.4.1.4 indexes the file by security consequence. The index below is navigational: it maps every line of the only executable artifact to the construct it contains and to the chapter that documents that construct's behaviour, so that any statement in this specification can be traced back to a line number in fourteen lines of source.

| Line | Source construct | What the line establishes | Documented in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `const http = require('http')` | The single dependency edge, to a Node.js built-in module; the entire supply chain of the system | 3.2, 3.3, 6.4.6.1 |
| 2 | *blank* | — | — |
| 3 | `const hostname = '127.0.0.1'` | The bind-address literal; the only access control in force, and the whole of the system's network exposure posture | 5.3.4 (ADR-003), 6.4.5.2 (boundary B1) |
| 4 | `const port = 3000` | The TCP port literal; unprivileged, so no elevated identity is needed to bind | 6.4.1.4, F-002-RQ-004 |
| 5 | *blank* | — | — |
| 6 | `http.createServer((req, res) => {` | One inline handler for every request; `req` is never dereferenced anywhere below it | 5.2, F-001-RQ-002 |
| 7 | `res.statusCode = 200` | The only status-code assignment in the repository; the response is unconditional | 4.1, 6.4.3.4 |
| 8 | `res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain')` | The only application-set response header; the remaining four observed headers are runtime-generated | 1.2.2.1, 3.2.2, 6.3.2.1 |
| 9 | `res.end('Hello, World!\n')` | The 14-byte constant body, and the call that completes the response | 1.1.1, 6.4.4.1 |
| 10 | `});` | Closes the handler — the complete request path is lines 6 to 10 | 4.1 |
| 11 | *blank* | — | — |
| 12 | `server.listen(port, hostname, () => {` | Binds the listener at module load; called without a backlog argument, so the runtime default applies | 5.2.5, 5.2.6 |
| 13 | `console.log(...)` with a template literal over `hostname` and `port` | The sole telemetry statement in the system: one 41-byte stdout record, once per process lifetime | F-004-RQ-002, 6.5.1.5 |
| 14 | `});` | Closes the listen callback; the file ends here, newline-terminated | 6.5.2.2 |

Four declarations exist in total (`http`, `hostname`, `port`, `server`), two of them functions passed inline, and no line contains a conditional construct. The index also makes the file's shape explicit: lines 1 to 4 are declarations, 6 to 10 are the request path, 12 to 14 are the startup path, and there is no other code — no export, no error handler, no signal handler, and no timer (6.5.1.5). No comparable index exists for the repository's other `.js` file because `test.js` contains no construct to index: its two lines are bare identifiers.

### 9.1.5 Effective Configuration Surface and Verified Environment-Variable Inertness

The effective configuration surface of this system is **two string and numeric literals in tracked source** — `hostname` at line 3 and `port` at line 4. Chapters 3, 5 and 6 establish the static basis for that claim: occurrences of `process.` in `server.js` are zero, so no environment variable, command-line argument, or configuration file is read (6.4.1.4), and requirement F-002-RQ-003 records that no runtime override path exists. This sub-section adds the positive experiment that was not previously performed: the unmodified tracked source was launched with the conventional override variables set, and its behaviour was observed.

```bash
PORT=8080 HOST=0.0.0.0 NODE_ENV=production HOSTNAME=example.com node server.js
```

| Observation | Measured value | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Endpoint actually attempted | The stderr trace named `EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` | The process targeted the line 3 and line 4 literals, not the values supplied in `HOST` and `PORT` |
| Listener on the requested port | A probe to `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` returned status `000` (no connection) | `PORT=8080` had no effect whatsoever; nothing was bound there |
| Process outcome | 0 bytes on stdout, 626 bytes on stderr, exit code 1 | The launch failed for the ordinary bind-conflict reason (F-002-RQ-004), not because of a configuration error — the variables were simply never consulted |

The port on the verification host happened to be held by another process at the time, which is what made the attempted address visible in the error text. The result is therefore stronger than a static count: it shows that the process reaches for `127.0.0.1:3000` **even when explicitly told otherwise**, and that `NODE_ENV` and `HOSTNAME` likewise change nothing. The only mechanism that can change the endpoint is editing a tracked literal and committing the change, which is precisely the property that makes exposure a step function of one source token (5.4.4).

Diagram 9-A summarises the closed surface and the experiment that confirms it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["Candidate configuration inputs tested at launch"]
        direction TB
        Env["Environment variables<br/>PORT, HOST, HOSTNAME, NODE_ENV"]
        Args["Command-line arguments<br/>process.argv"]
        Files["Config file or dotenv loader"]
        Manifest["Manifest, engines field or version pin"]
    end
    Gate{{"Does server.js read process.env, process.argv,<br/>a config file, or a manifest?"}}
    Env --> Gate
    Args --> Gate
    Files --> Gate
    Manifest --> Gate
    Gate -->|"No - process. occurrences in server.js are 0"| Literals
    subgraph Effective["Effective configuration surface - two source literals"]
        direction TB
        Literals["hostname = 127.0.0.1 at line 3<br/>port = 3000 at line 4"]
        Bind["Bind target fixed at 127.0.0.1:3000"]
        Literals --> Bind
    end
    Bind --> Proof["Measured with PORT=8080 and HOST=0.0.0.0 set:<br/>stderr named EADDRINUSE 127.0.0.1:3000, exit code 1,<br/>probe to 127.0.0.1:8080 returned status 000"]
    Proof --> Only["Only mechanism that changes the endpoint:<br/>editing a tracked literal and committing"]
```

**Diagram 9-A — Effective configuration surface. Every conventional input channel is closed at the source level, and the measured launch confirms that supplied overrides are inert.**

### 9.1.8 Verification Environment and Reachability Baseline

Every runtime figure in this specification is a *Host observation* taken in one environment. Its characteristics are recorded here so that a reader can judge which figures would travel to a different host and which would not.

| Property | Observed value | Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime | Node.js v22.23.1 for all verification | The repository pins no version — no `engines` field, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, or image — so every inherited default in 5.2.6 is specific to this runtime |
| Package client | npm 11.18.0 available on the host | Present but with nothing to act on: there is no manifest, lockfile, or `node_modules`, so no install, build, test, or audit command has a target |
| Host class | 16 vCPU (Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C); memory and file-descriptor ceiling as recorded in 6.5.1.4 | 6.1.3.1 establishes that the ceiling is one event-loop thread, so the additional cores cannot raise throughput |
| Loopback reachability | `http://127.0.0.1:3000/` returned `200` with the 14-byte body | The service's only reachable address |
| Name resolution | `http://localhost:3000/` also returned `200` | The name `localhost` resolves to the loopback interface in this environment, so the endpoint is reachable by name as well as by literal address — a host property, not an application one |
| Off-host reachability | The host's routable address `10.76.0.92:3000` failed to connect, status `000` | Confirms the line 3 literal confines the listener; recorded independently in 6.4.5.3 and 6.5.1.6 |
| Tooling constraint | `nc`, `ss`, `netstat`, `file` and `xxd` are not installed in the verification container | All wire-level and socket evidence was therefore gathered with `curl`, `ps`, `pgrep` and `/proc`, and byte-level evidence with `od` and scripted reads, which is why those interfaces appear throughout chapters 6 and 9 |
| Port-occupancy caveat | Port 3000 was intermittently held by an unrelated long-running `node server.js` process during measurement | Signal and exit-code measurements were taken against an out-of-repository copy differing only in the line 4 port literal, verified by `diff`; the checkout itself was never modified |

### 9.1.9 Operator Command Quick Reference

The commands below are the complete verified operational vocabulary for this repository. Each row states the observation that confirms success, because the system emits no other confirmation; the underlying behaviours are documented in 3.6.5, 6.5.1.6 and 6.5.4.4.

| Purpose | Command | Verified expected observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start the service | `node server.js` | One 41-byte line on stdout: `Server running at http://127.0.0.1:3000/`; the process stays in the foreground indefinitely. The file must be named explicitly — the checkout holds a second `.js` file that is not the application |
| Verify correct operation | `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/` | Exactly `Hello, World!` followed by a newline — 14 bytes, `Content-Length: 14`; asserting the body is the only correctness check available |
| Check presence | `pgrep -fc "node server.js"` | `1` while serving, `0` after termination |
| Stop the service | `kill -TERM <pid>`, or `Ctrl-C` in the foreground | Immediate exit with code 143 (`SIGTERM`) or 130 (`SIGINT`), no draining and no shutdown record |
| Diagnose a failed start | Inspect stderr and the exit code | Exit code 1 with an `EADDRINUSE ... 127.0.0.1:3000` trace and zero stdout bytes means the port is already held; the port must be freed before a relaunch can succeed |
| Validate the source without running it | `node --check server.js` | No output — the file parses as valid CommonJS |
| Confirm the tracked inventory | `git ls-files` | Exactly three paths: `README.md`, `server.js` and `test.js` |
| Confirm artifact identity | `git ls-files -s` | Mode `100644` and the full blob names recorded in 9.1.2 |
| Run the built-in test runner | `node --test` | **Exits 1.** Default discovery matches the root-level `test.js`, which declares no test and throws on evaluation, producing `not ok 1 - test.js` with `failureType: 'testCodeFailure'` and totals of 1 test, 0 pass, 1 fail (6.6.1.3). No command in the repository produces a passing test run |
| Install, build, or lint | *No command exists* | There is no manifest, script, or linter configuration in the repository, so none of these operations has a target (3.6.4, 6.6) |
